title: bd-gh-sync divergence guard never runs — ARG_MAX overflow fails open into an unguarded --prefer-github pull
description:
`.githooks/bd-gh-sync` builds a divergence guard that is supposed to abort the
pull when a bead description has diverged from its GH issue body — because
`bd github sync --pull-only --prefer-github` makes the GH body authoritative
and silently reverts local bd amendments.

That guard is dead. Observed at session start on 2026-07-30:

    .githooks/bd-gh-sync: line 78: /usr/bin/python3: Argument list too long

## Mechanism

The guard passes its inputs through the environment:

    _bd_beads=$(bd list --status all --limit 0 --json ...)
    _gh_bodies=$(gh issue list --state all --limit 1000 --json number,body ...)
    _diverged=$(BD_BEADS="$_bd_beads" GH_BODIES="$_gh_bodies" python3 - <<'PYEOF'

`execve` counts the environment block toward `ARG_MAX`. With 232 beads carrying
multi-KB descriptions plus up to 1000 GH issue bodies, the combined env exceeds
the limit and `python3` is never executed.

## Why it fails open

The script has no `set -e` and its header states the design intent: "Never
fails: exits 0 on any error so the git/session operation continues." So the
failed command substitution yields an empty `_diverged`, `[ -n "$_diverged" ]`
is false, and control falls straight through to:

    GITHUB_TOKEN="$_token" bd github sync --pull-only --prefer-github || true

The unguarded pull runs. The guard produces no signal on the path where it
matters, which is the shape recorded in memory `pr-blocking-two-halves`: a
detector that exits 0 is not a gate.

## Fix direction

Pass the payloads on stdin or via temp files rather than the environment, and
distinguish "guard found no divergence" from "guard did not run". The second
half matters more than the first — any future breakage of the guard must fail
loud rather than silently re-enabling the overwrite path.

## Acceptance

- The guard executes with the current bead/issue volume.
- A deliberately diverged bead is detected and the pull is skipped.
- A forced failure of the guard itself blocks the pull instead of falling
  through to it.

## Amendment 2026-07-31: the guard is also over-broad, not just dead

Fixing the ARG_MAX fault ALONE will wedge the repo. Moving the payload off the
environment turns a permanent no-op into a gate that blocks every pull, on
every session start, until someone hand-reconciles the corpus.

Measured against the live corpus (234 beads, 250 GH issues) by running the
guard's own logic with the payloads in temp files: exactly one divergence,
`gqlc-23e` / GH#171. Inspecting it shows why "block on any difference" is the
wrong predicate -- the two texts are COMPLEMENTARY, not one stale copy:

- bd description = the 2026-07-18 tagpr + GoReleaser DESIGN (scope, why not
  release-please, acceptance criteria).
- GH#171 body    = the 2026-07-19 DEFERRED status (GH013 attempts, what
  failed, revisit-when).

Neither is a superset of the other. `--prefer-github` loses the design
rationale; the guard's own prescribed remedy (mirror bd -> GH) loses the
deferral record. Both directions destroy information.

So the fix has three parts, and shipping only the first is worse than
shipping nothing:

1. Move both payloads off the environment (stdin or temp files), and
   distinguish "python did not run" from "python ran and found nothing" --
   the current code cannot tell those apart, which is the whole defect.
2. Replace the equality predicate. "GH ahead of bd" is the normal case that
   `--prefer-github` exists to serve and must not block. The data-loss shape
   is specifically "bd holds content GH lacks". A length or equality test
   cannot separate them.
3. Reconcile gqlc-23e / GH#171 into a merged body first, or the gate fails
   closed on its first real run. Fix the corpus in the same change.

The remedy text printed to the developer should offer a merge, not a
one-directional mirror.

See memory `bd-gh-divergence-guard-is-overbroad` for the reproduction.
notes:
=== LIVE REPRO 2026-08-01, and it is wider than the description says ===

Observed while sequencing epic gqlc-35yu. Sequence:

  1. bd update gqlc-35yu.4 --claim   -> IN_PROGRESS  (confirmed via bd show)
  2. bd update gqlc-35yu.6 --claim   -> IN_PROGRESS  (confirmed via bd show)
  3. export committed with both in_progress, merged as PR #643
  4. gh pr merge + git checkout master (post-merge/post-checkout bd hooks fire)
  5. bd show both beads -> OPEN, with started_at still set to 2026-08-01

The passive export then showed in_progress -> open for both, i.e. the
unguarded --prefer-github pull took the GH mirrors' OPEN state (issues
#629 / #627 — GitHub has no in_progress, so every claimed bead's mirror
reads OPEN) and clobbered the local status.

WIDER THAN RECORDED: this bead's description scopes the damage to "local
bd amendments" to DESCRIPTIONS. It also silently reverts STATUS. That is
worse in one specific way — GitHub cannot represent in_progress at all,
so the GH body is not merely stale for status, it is structurally
incapable of holding the local value. Every claimed bead is guaranteed to
be reverted by any pull, not just ones that happen to have diverged. A
divergence guard that compares descriptions would not have caught this
even if it ran.

started_at survives while status does not, so the DB ends in a state no
bd command produces: OPEN with a started_at. That inconsistency is a
cheap detector — a post-pull assertion that (started_at != null AND
closed_at == null) implies in_progress would flag it without needing the
ARG_MAX-heavy body diff at all.

Interacts with gqlc-jwuw, which reports the re-derivation running the
OTHER way (started_at -> in_progress, reverting a deliberate 'open'). Both
cannot be right; whichever fix lands must pick a direction and state it,
because today the two beads describe mutually contradictory behaviour and
at least one of them is a stale observation.

Workaround in use: re-issue `bd update <id> --status in_progress` after
any merge/checkout, and check `bd show` rather than trusting the export.
=== THIRD REPRO, 2026-08-01, with a sharper mechanism than 'statuses revert' ===
Trigger: agent claimed gqlc-3eyw (open -> in_progress in the local Dolt DB)
AFTER I had run 'bd export -o .beads/issues.jsonl' for PR #649 but BEFORE
'git pull' brought #649's merge commit back down. Post-pull, gqlc-3eyw was
'open' again.

The mechanism is JSONL-import-on-pull clobbering NEWER local Dolt state with
the committed snapshot. Verified by reading the merged commit directly:
  git show c6381cc:.beads/issues.jsonl
    gqlc-3eyw     -> open        | started_at: None
    gqlc-35yu.6   -> in_progress | started_at: 2026-08-01T03:22:47Z
gqlc-35yu.6 was in_progress in the committed export and SURVIVED the pull.
gqlc-3eyw was open in it and was reverted. So the import is not preferring
GitHub and is not merging by recency — it simply replays the file over the DB.

THE PART THAT MATTERS MOST: the clobber is PARTIAL and produces a state that
existed in NEITHER source. The committed record had status=open AND
started_at=None. After the import the bead reads:
  status:  open        (taken from the file)
  Started: 2026-08-01  (kept from the DB)
So 'status' was overwritten from the file while 'started_at' was not cleared
to match. This is neither record-level replace nor field-level merge — it can
synthesize an impossible bead: unstarted-by-status, started-by-timestamp.
Any consumer trusting started_at to imply in_progress (or the inverse) is
reading a state no writer ever wrote.

That impossible-state synthesis is the bug worth chasing; the visible
'my claim disappeared' symptom is downstream of it. Whether this shares a root
cause with the ARG_MAX divergence-guard failure this bead was filed for is
NOT established — the guard never running would explain why nobody is warned,
but not why the import merges fields inconsistently. Treat as possibly two
bugs until someone reads the import path.

Practical mitigation until fixed: re-assert claims with 'bd update <id>
--status in_progress' after every pull that carries a bd export commit.
=== FIX 2026-08-01 (branch fix/bd-gh-sync-state-fidelity) ===

MECHANISM CORRECTION, measured. The description blames ARG_MAX ("the combined
env exceeds the limit"). That is wrong. Measured on this box: ARG_MAX is
4194304; the two payloads combined are 1599151 bytes, comfortably under it.
What fires is MAX_ARG_STRLEN, the per-string cap execve applies to any single
argument or environment variable, empirically bracketed here between 130000
(ok) and 200000 (E2BIG) -> 131072. BD_BEADS alone is 1089638 bytes, 8x over.

This matters for the fix: the limit is per-variable, not aggregate, so no
ulimit raises it and shrinking the corpus 8x would not have helped. It would
have started failing at roughly 30 beads, not 232.

BLAST RADIUS, measured. `bd github sync --pull-only --prefer-github --dry-run`
unscoped proposes exactly four updates: GH #671, #650, #623, #667 = gqlc-kph4,
gqlc-rohp, gqlc-35yu.10, gqlc-h4ug -- precisely the beads that were claimed,
and nothing else. Zero creates. So the status reversion is not a side effect
of the pull, it is currently the ONLY effect. The amendment is right that a
description-comparing guard would never have caught it.

DESIGN FORK: gate the pull, or scope it. Rejected gating. `bd github sync`
1.0.4 exposes no field-level control (--dry-run, --pull-only, --push-only,
--prefer-github/local/newer, --issues, --parent), so status cannot be excluded
from a pull. --prefer-local would keep the claim but discard the GH close that
is the whole point of pulling. A gate can therefore only choose between
"revert claims" and "never pull".

Chose scope. --issues is the one lever that expresses per-bead intent
(`bd github pull [refs]` is documented as `sync --pull-only --issues <refs>`).
The guard became an allowlist: a bead is eligible only when GitHub is CAPABLE
of holding its value and is not BEHIND it --
  * status in {open, closed}: GitHub state is a two-value domain, so
    in_progress/blocked/deferred have no representable counterpart;
  * not (closed locally AND open on GH): pulling would reopen it;
  * no description line present in bd and absent from GH (the amendment part 2
    predicate -- "GH ahead of bd" stays eligible, which equality cannot say);
  * not already identical (see churn note below).

FAILS CLOSED. The selector emits a DONE sentinel as its last line; the caller
requires rc==0 AND that sentinel, so "ran and chose nothing" is distinguishable
from "did not run". Either failure yields an empty allowlist, and an empty
allowlist skips the bd invocation entirely rather than passing an empty
--issues (which would widen the pull back to everything). Payloads travel in
temp files, never argv or env. python3 absence is now an explicit skip rather
than a silent empty result.

AMENDMENT PART 3 IS MOOT. It required reconciling gqlc-23e/GH#171 before the
gate could run, or the gate would wedge on its first pass. Per-bead holds mean
one divergent bead excludes only itself, so no corpus reconciliation is needed.
gqlc-23e is in fact held on status grounds (blocked) before the body check.

CHURN, found by measurement and nearly shipped as a regression. Naming a bead
in --issues syncs it regardless of GitHubs update watermark, so the first
scoped dry-run proposed 129 updates where the unscoped one proposed 4. The
allowlist now also drops beads already identical to their mirror. Against the
live corpus the allowlist is 0: nine held, two orphan issues left alone, no
sync invoked -- i.e. nothing legitimate is pending, and the only thing the old
pull would have done was revert the six claims.

CORRECTION to the started_at detector proposed in these notes. "(started_at
!= null AND closed_at == null) implies in_progress" would false-positive:
`bd update <id> --status open` on a previously-claimed bead yields open with
started_at retained, verified in an isolated scratch DB, and four live beads
sit in that shape (gqlc-do1 open since 2026-07-12, gqlc-h9n.33, gqlc-h9n.1,
gqlc-23e). It is a reachable state, not a torn one. Replaced with a
postcondition that is actually invariant: a bead held out of the pull must
come back unchanged, checked by re-reading bd list after the sync and warning
per bead with the command to re-assert it.
HANDOFF 2026-08-01. Adversarial review of 0e05690 returned FAIL. Refix was dispatched but DIED ON SESSION QUOTA before making any change — branch is clean at 0e05690, nothing started. Blockers, all reproduced by the reviewer against a read-only snapshot of the live corpus (273 beads / 289 GH issues) with stubbed bd/gh on PATH:

B1 (gqlc-jwuw undelivered): .githooks/bd-gh-sync:163-166 exits before the postcondition at :176-215. ALLOW=0 is the STEADY STATE on the live corpus (270 mirrored, 261 dropped as in-sync, 9 HOLD, ALLOW=0), so every merge takes that exit and the revert detector never runs. Measured with a jwuw-shaped revert injected: bd list invocations 1 (2 would mean the postcondition ran), 0 WARNING lines. Both jwuw tests hard-code an eligible bead beside the claimed one (tests :282-287, :294) so CLAIMED is never tested alone — the fixtures are shaped so the bug cannot appear, which is the very thing the commit header indicts. FIX: hoist the postcondition above the eligibility bail, and add the CLAIMED-alone case.

B2 (eligibility rule does not implement its stated property): :119-124 is a subset test over .strip()ed line SETS, so four GH-is-behind-bd shapes are handed to --prefer-github anyway — deletion (local subset of remote), indent change (per-line strip), reordering (sets are order-blind), de-dup (sets collapse duplicates). Deletion is the ordinary way a description gets edited. MY RULING: adopt the append-only rule — ALLOW only when gh_body.startswith(desc); everything else HOLDs and warns. One test per row.

PROMOTED BY ME TO BLOCKING: (3) the summary line at :215 reports intent not outcome — :172-173 ends || true, so with a failing bd the run prints 'pulled 2 bead(s)' and the SessionStart consumer (.claude/settings.json:29, 'bd-gh-sync pull 2>&1 | tail -1') shows ONLY that line; same fail-open-in-reporting class the commit exists to end. (4) postcondition WARNINGs print at :183-211, before the summary at :215, so tail-1 always drops them — a detector nobody can see. (5) HOLD notices are structurally unconditional: 9 per git pull on the live corpus, 7 of them status-unrepresentable on beads whose GH body is BYTE-IDENTICAL, and they can never be silenced by the in-sync drop at :130 because status==gh_state is false by construction for any status GitHub cannot represent. Signal 2:9 forever is how 2>/dev/null gets re-added.

Filed as separate beads, NOT to be fixed here: gqlc-fc1v (no circuit breaker on the ALLOW count), gqlc-mdhr (--prefer-github write-back fidelity unverified; needs a scratch repo, never the real corpus).

VERIFIED GOOD, leave alone: fail-closed held under every probe (malformed JSON either side, gh/bd returning [], empty and hostile bead ids); MAX_ARG_STRLEN is structurally closed (_batch=100 constant bounds --issues; 1249 bytes at 5000 synthetic beads vs a 131072 limit); gqlc-w318 and gqlc-onji fixed as filed; the '14 of 20' re-derivation is exact and swapping the binary changed results; post-merge letting stderr survive is right; no CRLF in the current corpus; no title drift (270/270).
REFIX LANDED d25d947 (2026-08-01). All five blockers addressed; suite 20 -> 31 tests, all 9 new assertions red against 0e05690 first.

MANAGER VERIFICATION of the two structural claims (read the script myself, not the report): B1 is genuinely fixed — the eligibility bail at the old :163-166 is gone, replaced by an else-branch at :198-200 that prints 'no pull issued' WITHOUT exiting, so the postcondition at :202+ now runs on every path. The remaining 'exit 0' at :171 is the fail-closed bail for when the selection Python itself fails, which is correct and must stay. B2 is implemented at :142-143 as 'if not gh_body.startswith(desc): HOLD <id> <n> bd-description-not-a-prefix-of-gh-body'. Commit scope clean: 2 files, zero .beads/ churn.

DISAGREEMENT RULED IN THE IMPLEMENTER'S FAVOUR. I ruled for append-only; they implemented it verbatim and then pushed back that row 1 of my table (bd 'line one' / GH 'line one\nline two DELETED IN BD') is still admitted, because startswith is true and the shape is byte-identical to the legitimate GH-append case the b-ahead fixture requires to pull. They are right: no function of the two bodies separates an addition on one side from a deletion on the other. They pinned the residual with a passing test and a comment naming the collision rather than assert a HOLD they would have to weaken later. Split out as gqlc-6mx3 (add a timestamp discriminator — updated_at is already present in bd list --json).

Measured effect on the live corpus: HOLD notices 9 -> 2, both actionable (gqlc-3eyw, gqlc-23e); the gh_state == 'open' term is what preserves gqlc-23e, which is blocked/GH-closed. ALLOW remains 0 under both the old and new rule, and no bead is newly held, so the narrowing costs nothing today. Cost noted: the hoist adds a second 'bd list' per pull/session start (~0.84s).

STILL NEEDS A FRESH ADVERSARIAL REVIEW before merge.

title: codegen: unused dbtype/time import in querier.go when multi-param method has a temporal param
description:
## Summary

`renderQuerier` in `internal/codegen/render_querier.go` emits an unused import in `querier.go` whenever a query has 2+ parameters and at least one of them is a temporal type (`dbtype.X` or `time.Time`).

## Root cause

`querierImports` scans every entry in `p.ParamFields` for `dbtype.`/`time.Time`:

```go
for _, param := range p.ParamFields {
    scan(param.GoType)
}
```

But `writeMethodSignature` only surfaces the raw Go type in the signature when there is **exactly one parameter**. With 2+ parameters it emits `arg MethodNameParams` — a struct name with no import requirement. So the import is declared needed but never referenced in the interface body.

## Observed failure

User-generated `querier.go` contained:

```go
import (
    "context"
    "github.com/neo4j/neo4j-go-driver/v6/neo4j/dbtype"
)
```

where `dbtype` appeared in no method signature — Go rejected the file as invalid.

## Fix

In `querierImports`, mirror the same guard that exists for `RowFields` (single-column only):

```go
if len(p.ParamFields) == 1 {
    scan(p.ParamFields[0].GoType)
}
```

## TDD plan

1. Add `TestGoldenBuild` to `internal/codegen/codegen_test.go` — runs `go build ./...` on the nested `test/data/codegen` module; makes compile errors visible under `just test` (not just `test-codegen-fence`).
2. Add a golden fixture `write_exec_two_date_params` — a query with two `DATE`-typed parameters triggering a `Params` struct (and, before the fix, a spurious `dbtype` import).
3. Confirm RED: `TestGoldenBuild` fails because the generated `querier.go` has an unused import.
4. Fix `querierImports`.
5. Regenerate golden with `-update`.
6. Confirm GREEN.

## Acceptance criteria

- `go test ./internal/codegen/...` catches any future golden-package compile error (via `TestGoldenBuild`).
- `write_exec_two_date_params` golden `querier.go` imports only `"context"` (no `dbtype`, no `time`).
- All existing golden tests pass.
- `just test` and `just test-codegen-fence` both green.
close_reason: Closed

title: schema/gql: SIGNED/UNSIGNED INTEGER(w) silently drops its declared width and resolves to the machine word
description:
`SIGNED INTEGER(8)` resolves to graph.TypeInt — a machine word — instead of
TypeInt8. Same for every width, in both signednesses:

    SIGNED INTEGER(8|16|32|64|128|256)    -> TypeInt    (want TypeInt8 … TypeInt256)
    UNSIGNED INTEGER(8|16|32|64|128|256)  -> TypeUint   (want TypeUint8 … TypeUint256)

Twelve spellings. Not a rejection — the schema parses, and codegen emits a 64-bit
field where the author declared eight bits. Silent wrong output for valid ISO GQL.

Every neighbouring spelling is correct, which is what kept it hidden:

    INT(8)             -> TypeInt8    ok    explicit typeSpellings row
    INTEGER(8)         -> TypeInt8    ok    explicit row
    UINT(8)            -> TypeUint8   ok    explicit row
    SIGNED INTEGER8    -> TypeInt8    ok    alias row
    UNSIGNED INTEGER8  -> TypeUint8   ok    alias row
    SIGNED INTEGER(8)  -> TypeInt     BUG   no row; falls back to "SIGNED INTEGER"

GRAMMAR. verboseBinaryExactNumericType admits `INTEGER (LEFT_PAREN precision
RIGHT_PAREN)?` (GQL.g4:1827), and both signedBinaryExactNumericType
(`SIGNED? verboseBinaryExactNumericType`, :1803) and unsignedBinaryExactNumericType
(`UNSIGNED verboseBinaryExactNumericType`, :1816) wrap it. So the prefix and the
parenthetical compose, and all twelve spellings are well-formed. Confirmed by
probe: they parse, and land on the wrong constant.

`SIGNED INT(8)` is NOT grammatical — `SIGNED?` guards only the verbose rule, and
`INT (…)` is a sibling alternative — so the gap is exactly these twelve and no
more.

WHY THE GAP. typeSpellings' own doc states both rules. The parenthesised widths
"appear as explicit rows because their bit-width identifies a model constant",
and the SIGNED/UNSIGNED prefixes are "one alias row per bare verbose spelling".
Each rule was applied across its whole range. Their COMPOSITION was not, and
nothing in the file or its tests ranges over the product.

The same hole is in the test tables, which is why the suite was green:

    widthSpellingEquivalences        every row has a suffix width, none a prefix
    verboseSignednessEquivalences    every row has a prefix, none a parenthetical

Two properties, each pinned across all six widths, whose conjunction was pinned
nowhere. The completeness gate could not see it either: TestTypeSpellingsEveryRowPinned
checks that every EXISTING row is grounded, and these rows did not exist.

FIX. Twelve typeSpellings rows plus twelve verboseSignednessEquivalences pairs,
which is the shape the file already argues for ("alias rows over a pre-lookup
normalisation ... alternative-additions to the grammar are grep-visible here").
No ADR: ADR 0017 already decided that a width WITH an exact model counterpart
gets a row and only widths without one take the lossy fallback. INT(7) and
SIGNED INTEGER(7) still land on TypeInt, unchanged and correct.

VERIFIED 1:1 IN BOTH DIRECTIONS.
  - Pairs added without the rows: exactly 12 subtests fail, one per spelling.
  - Each row deleted in turn: exactly 1 subtest fails, and it names that spelling.
  - Rows kept, pairs removed: TestTypeSpellingsEveryRowPinned reports exactly the
    12 as ungrounded, so the pins are what grounds them and not something else.

FOUND BY the 36-case mutation sweep of propertytype.go (2026-07-28), 33 caught.
The bug was not a survivor — it surfaced from probing the three survivors, which
needed a matrix of real spellings to decide whether they were reachable.

The three survivors are all inert, and are recorded in bd memory rather than
filed. Instrumenting each branch and running the whole suite gave zero hits:

  :289  `end < 0` (unmatched paren) — parens in the grammar are balanced and a
        parse error aborts before property() runs, so a `(` with no `)` cannot
        reach here. Without the guard it panics on a slice bound.
  :297  the `s[end+1:]` tail — reachable in principle (`LIST<INT(8)>` has a `>`
        after the paren) but not observable: truncateParenthetical keeps only
        what precedes `(`, and no typeSpellings row has text after a
        parenthetical, so both spellings miss and land identically.
  :302  truncateParenthetical's TrimRight — redundant given collapseParenthetical
        already trimmed the space before the same `(`. It is reachable only via
        the `end < 0` early return above, so it is dead exactly while that is.
close_reason: Closed

title: schema/gql: a repeated property name silently keeps the last declaration and discards the first
description:
`{ id :: INT NOT NULL, id :: STRING }` parses, resolves, and produces a node type with ONE property: `{Name:id Type:STRING Nullable:true}`. The first declaration is gone -- its type and its NOT NULL with it -- and nothing anywhere says so.

Measured at 61a6cd1 with a probe against New().Parse:

    CREATE PROPERTY GRAPH TYPE T AS {
        (:Person { id :: INT NOT NULL, id :: STRING })
    }
    err=<nil>
    node Person props=1
      id -> {Name:id Type:STRING Nullable:true}

The mechanism is one line: listener.properties builds `out := make(map[string]schema.Property)` and writes `out[p.Name] = p` for every element of propertyTypeList, so a repeat overwrites in walk order (listener.go:498-516).

This is the class-2 shape -- a schema that says one thing resolving to a model that says another, with no diagnostic -- and it is the one duplicate gqlc does NOT reject. resolve() rejects a duplicate node type (ErrDuplicateNodeType) and a duplicate edge type (ErrDuplicateEdgeType) on exactly the reasoning that a map keyed by identity cannot hold two things with one key. A property map is keyed by name and has the same problem.

Downstream this is not cosmetic: codegen emits a struct field per property, so the generated Go silently carries the last spelling. An author who edits a property type and leaves the old line behind gets no error from the tool whose job is to catch that.

DECIDING IT NEEDS AN ADR, WHICH IS WHY THIS BEAD DOES NOT SHIP A FIX.

The ISO BNF admits the syntax: <property type list> ::= <property type> [{ <comma> <property type> }...] with no uniqueness constraint stated in the grammar. Whether a repeat is an error is Syntax Rules prose, which lives in the paid PDF gqlc-lir declined to buy. So this is the same bind as ErrEdgeKindArcMismatch and ErrImpliedLabelIsKeyLabel: two defensible readings, and choosing one silently is picking a dialect. The options are

  (a) reject with a new sentinel, consistent with ErrDuplicateNodeType and ErrDuplicateEdgeType and with the no-dialect principle -- rejecting rather than silently choosing is the move ADR 0015 and ADR 0016 both make; or
  (b) define last-wins (or first-wins) precedence explicitly and pin it with a corpus semantic case, which is the honest form of the status quo.

Note (b) is not free either: the status quo is last-wins by accident of map assignment, not by decision, and nothing pins it, so it can flip to first-wins under a refactor with no test going red.

REGARDLESS OF WHICH IS CHOSEN, the current behaviour is unrepresented in the tree today: no corpus entry, no semantic case, no invalid fixture. That is the part this bead measures.

Found by mutation sweep of internal/schema/gql while auditing the harness for fail-open defects (see gqlc-q5z, gqlc-fon, gqlc-d9b).
notes:
This loop (h9n-loop, 2026-07-28) cannot proceed with this bead. The description says the choice between (a) reject with a new sentinel or (b) define last-wins precedence needs an ADR before any change. The delegated ADR set for this loop is only h9n.6, h9n.9, h9n.12, h9n.25 — gqlc-4np is not in it. Additionally, even the 'measurement' deliverable (adding a corpus entry or semantic case) requires choosing an outcome, which is the same decision. Releasing the claim so an owner decision can unblock it.

--- 2026-08-22, agent-e — blocked on gqlc-oowt, deliberately, so it stops being offered ---

I was routed nothing and went looking for author work. This bead read READY,
and it is the only P1 in the uncongested part of the tree (internal/schema/ is
touched by none of the 20 open PRs). So I reached for it — and hit the same wall
the NOTES above record a previous loop hitting on 2026-07-28: the fix requires
choosing (a) a new sentinel or (b) a decided precedence, and an author may not
pick a dialect.

That is twice now that this bead has spent an agent's wake to send them back,
and nothing about the board said it would. It has been READY for 25 days, so it
was free to do it again to whoever came next.

Filed gqlc-oowt (P1, class:designer) carrying the decision, and made it BLOCK
this bead. This is no longer routable to an author, and unblocks the moment the
ADR lands. Nothing about the analysis here is superseded — gqlc-oowt cites it
rather than restating it, including PR #540's semanticCase, which pins today's
last-wins without prejudging the choice.

One thing in the NOTES above IS superseded, and it is why this could be
unstuck at all: "it needs the user's call". Under the agent fleet a dialect
question is settled by a designer writing an ADR — agents decide and amend
their own protocol, and humans do not block. Nothing here is waiting on
agent-n, and has not been for some time.
close_reason:
FIXED and merged: PR #1307, squashed to master 2026-08-23. Verified on master by content, not by commit count: git cat-file -e origin/master:docs/adr/0030-repeated-property-name-is-rejected.md succeeds, and origin/master:internal/schema/gql/errors.go carries ErrDuplicatePropertyName.

WHAT CHANGED. listener.properties now returns ErrDuplicatePropertyName, wrapped with the offending name, the first time a property name recurs within one <property type list>. Previously it wrote every element into a name-keyed map in walk order, so { id :: INT NOT NULL, id :: STRING } resolved to one property carrying only the second declaration -- the first, and its NOT NULL, gone with no diagnostic.

THE GUARD IS IN THE LISTENER, not in resolve() where the node and edge duplicate checks live, because listener.properties is the only place the LIST is still visible. The map is the thing that loses the collision, so a guard downstream of it has nothing left to compare. Worth knowing before anyone tries to consolidate the three duplicate checks.

THE DECISION is gqlc-oowt, now closed: ADR 0030 rejects rather than deciding a precedence, and does so as an interim posture -- the free ISO BNF settles only that the construct parses, and whether a repeat is an error is Syntax Rules prose gqlc has not bought. The full argument and the refetched SHA-256 are on gqlc-oowt close reason. gqlc-tlbo revisits it if the clause is ever bought.

TEST-FIRST, and what the RED actually showed. TestRepeatedPropertyNameIsRejected was written before the guard and failed on all three rows with Expected error ... but got nil -- the silent swallow itself, not a compile error. Rows: node type, edge type, and a non-adjacent repeat (id, name, id). Node and edge matter separately because nodeContent and edgeContent reach properties through separate hand-written paths -- the grammar gives node and edge fillers distinct generated types -- so a guard in one only would have left half the surface undiagnosed with the corpus green.

TWO GUARDS ON THE TEST ITSELF. (1) TestDistinctPropertyNamesStillResolve is the ALLOW half: without it a guard that rejected every multi-property block would pass every REJECT row. (2) The diagnostic must NAME the property, since that is the entire point of the rejection; mutating the fmt.Errorf wrap back to a bare sentinel was KILLED, all three rows red. Restored and green.

CORPUS BOOKKEEPING. 18.2-node-type/property_name_repeated.gql moved from a resolves entry to an unsupported one carrying the sentinel; the file stayed, only its declared outcome moved. semanticAreaB is empty again -- a rejected construct is not a model known to be wrong -- which is the once-per-case legitimate drop wantSemanticCases exists to make an author account for, the same passage kind_undirected_arc_directed made under gqlc-h9n.3. wantCorpusResolving 68 to 67, wantSemanticCases 18 to 17. The fixture header was rewritten; it had described the last-wins behaviour as current.

MEASURED COUNTS: go test ./... green, 24 packages ok and 0 fail, including internal/codegen and internal/codegen/conformance (so no generated-code fixture relied on a repeated name). just lint 0 issues, just fmt-check clean. CI on #1307: test, lint, tidy, codegen-fence, actionlint, govulncheck, live-smoke all pass; live-smoke-age skipping.

NOT VERIFIED: whether any user schema outside the repo now fails that previously compiled. It would, by design -- the model it compiled to had already discarded a declaration the author wrote -- but no external corpus was run.

BEHAVIOUR CHANGE NOTE for anyone reading the NOTES above: the it needs the user call line, and the this bead does not ship a fix line, are both superseded. The decision was made from the normative text under gqlc-oowt and the fix shipped with it.

comments.author: areqag
comments.text:
Partially addressed by PR #540 (bead gqlc-v1t, now closed): the corpus now carries 18.2-node-type/property_name_repeated.gql as an area-B semanticCase, so the last-wins behaviour is pinned and can no longer flip to first-wins silently. title: schema/gql: two invariants resolve.go states in prose have no witness in the corpus
description:
resolve.go argues for two design choices in comments, and neither claim is pinned by anything. A mutation sweep of the resolver (13 semantically meaningful mutations, run against `go test ./...` at 61a6cd1) caught 11 and left these two SURVIVED:

1. ORDER-INDEPENDENCE OF THE INHERITANCE CHECK. resolve.go:80-82 says the rejectInheritance call is "Deferred past the loop because a collision is order-independent: a later declaration's key label can collide with an earlier one's implied label." Moving the check inside the node loop -- so each declaration is only checked against the key labels seen so far -- passes the whole suite.

   The corpus has one file for this rule, 18.2-node-type/implied_key_label.gql, and it is written in the order that does not discriminate: `(:Person ...)` is declared FIRST and `(:Engineer => :Person ...)` second, so the key label is already in the set by the time the implying declaration is read. The deferral is load-bearing only in the other order, and no file uses it.

2. NODE AND EDGE LABELS ARE SEPARATE NAMESPACES. resolve.go:166-167 says "Node and edge labels are checked against their own kind only -- they are separate namespaces, keying separate maps, and an edge type labelled KNOWS says nothing about a node type's Person." Merging nodeKeyLabels into edgeKeyLabels before the edge-side rejectInheritance call passes the whole suite.

   Every GG21 file today keeps the two vocabularies disjoint by accident rather than by design: corpus 18.3-edge-type/key_label_set.gql implies WROTE over nodes keyed Person and Post; valid/key_label_set.gql implies Author over nodes keyed Engineer, Manager&Staff and Article. No file has an edge imply a label some node type holds as a key label, which is the only shape that can tell one namespace from two.

Both are the same failure as gqlc-q5z and gqlc-d9b: a claim stated in prose, believed on review, and unrepresented in the tree. ADR 0015 is the decision behind both -- the inheritance decline is the one part of GG21 gqlc refuses, and how far the refusal reaches is exactly what these two claims say.

FIX: two corpus files, one per claim.

  18.2-node-type: `(:Engineer => :Person { level :: INT }), (:Person { name :: STRING })` -- the implying declaration first. Rejects with ErrImpliedLabelIsKeyLabel under the deferral and resolves without it.

  18.3-edge-type: an edge whose implied label is spelled the same as a declared node type's key label. Resolves under separate namespaces and is rejected under one. The spelling looks odd on purpose: reusing a name across the two vocabularies IS the invariant.
close_reason: Closed

title: schema/gql: both carrier gates go green if the file-to-area partition collapses
description:
TestCorpusAreaParseCarriers and tier 2 of TestCorpusResolvingCarriers exist to answer one question -- does the area that OWNS a grammar name carry a file for it, rather than some unrelated area reaching it in passing. Both take that ownership from a file-to-area partition, and neither partition has a positive control. Break either one so that every area holds every file and the whole suite stays green.

Measured against origin/master at 9ddf10a, two independent mutations, both SURVIVED:

  corpusFilesByArea (corpus_carriers_test.go:492) rewritten to append every corpus file to every area -- go test ./internal/schema/gql/ ok
  resolvingFilesByArea (corpus_resolving_test.go:88) rewritten the same way -- ok

The mechanism is that both gates are silent registers: they assert an empty orphan list, and today that list is empty. Over-generous carriage can only remove orphans, so a partition that credits every area with every file reads exactly like a corpus with no gaps. TestUnmetGroups pins the orphan LOGIC with synthetic input, and nothing pins the input it is given.

This is the failure the two files were written to prevent, undetectable in the instrument that prevents it. The parse gate's own header cites PR #392 (localdatetimeType#2 carried only by five 18.3-edge-type files spelling TIMESTAMP incidentally) and says "no test stopped it from being reverted"; the resolving gate's header cites 7217b180 (no resolving path exercised an explicit node synonym). Both of those defects are area-attribution defects, and both gates would report clean under either mutation above.

A synthetic witness is not needed and would be weaker than what the tree already supports. The two partitions are independently derived: corpusFilesByArea reads directory prefixes off disk, resolvingFilesByArea reads corpusAreas[name].entries out of the manifest, and requireOwnedByArea (corpus_test.go:288) already pins each manifest entry's file to its declaring area's prefixes. So restricted to resolving entries the two must agree exactly, and a probe confirms they do over all 108 files today. Cross-checking them is a real invariant rather than a mock, and it kills both mutations: each rewrite makes one derivation disagree with the other.

Worth adding alongside it that the prefix partition is a function -- each file in exactly one area -- which TestCorpusAreasAreDisjoint asserts of the prefixes but nothing asserts of the mapping they produce.
close_reason: Closed

title: schema/gql: optionality coverage credits a branch inside an optional the file never entered
description:
forceOptional (corpus_branch_test.go:108) pins the nth optional node to one branch and leaves every other optional alone -- including the ones enclosing it. So for an optionality point nested inside another optional, both withElement and withoutElement still admit parses in which the enclosing group is absent, and any corpus shape that elides the whole group matches both. The point is credited on both branches by a file that never reached it.

This is the mistake the withElement/withoutElement design was written to avoid, one level up. The doc comment already argues that "x? x puts the same symbol on both branches, and a substring test would call it exercised" -- the same is true of a point under an elided parent, and matching a whole child sequence does not catch it because the sequence really does match.

8 of the 137 points are nested (depth 1, all of them), spread over 6 classes: 18.2::TYPE, 18.3::TYPE, 18.3::edgeKind, 18.9::COMMA scale, 18.9::minLength COMMA, 18.9::notNull.

Five of the six are covered legitimately by a sibling non-nested point in the same class, so the mis-credit changes nothing there. One is live today:

  18.3 :: edgeKind -- shallow{present,absent} vs correct{present only}

edgeTypePattern is `(edgeKind? edgeSynonym TYPE? edgeTypeName)? (edgeTypePatternDirected | edgeTypePatternUndirected)` and the corpus has exactly three shapes for it:

  edgeKind edgeSynonym edgeTypeName edgeTypePatternDirected
  edgeTypePatternDirected
  edgeTypePatternUndirected

The second and third elide the whole naming group, and are what currently satisfy "a file elides edgeKind". Nothing writes the pattern form that names the edge type without saying DIRECTED. That is not a cosmetic gap: an absent edgeKind is the input to the kind-vs-arc reconciliation that ErrEdgeKindArcMismatch and ErrUndirectedEdge guard, and gqlc-h9n.26 already found a real defect in the neighbouring nodeTypeFiller position under this clause.

Measured against origin/master at 941b746, with a probe that reimplements forceOptional forcing the optional ancestors on the path to the target present. Under that forcing exactly one class flips, and it flips to one-sided.

Fix has two halves. Force the enclosing optionals present so a point is only credited on a parse that reached it. Then discharge 18.3::edgeKind -- preferably with a corpus file spelling the pattern form with a named edge type and no kind, since a file is writable here and owedOptionality is for classes that are owed one, not for ones nobody got round to.
close_reason: Closed

title: schema/gql: allSentinels is hand-maintained and one sentinel already escaped it
description:
TestSentinelReachability calls itself the bidirectional sweep over Parse's sentinels, and allSentinels calls itself the single source of truth. Neither is checked against the errors the package actually declares, and the drift has already happened: ErrEndpointFillerHasProperties (errors.go:17) is a leaf sentinel returned by fillerLabels (edgetype.go:108) and is absent from allSentinels.

So the sweep never demanded a file for it. Adding it to allSentinels and re-running proves that: 'sentinel ... has no negative fixture or unsupported corpus entry'. The behaviour is covered by TestEndpointFillerRejectsProperties, but that is a direct unit test the sweep does not count, so the registry's own promise -- a declared sentinel with no file is an orphan -- is false for this one. Deleting that unit test today would be silent.

It is the only one missing: 21 leaves are declared, allSentinels lists 20, and ErrUnsupportedSource is the documented class-not-leaf omission.

Fix has two halves. Pin the escaped sentinel with a file. Then close the mechanism, so that a sentinel added to errors.go and forgotten here cannot pass again -- the doc comment already states the rule ('A new sentinel must be added here'), and a rule with no mechanism is what just failed.
close_reason: Shipped in PR #493 (merged): TestSentinelRegistryIsComplete parses errors.go and requires every declared Err* to be pinned by allSentinels or excused in sentinelsWithoutAFile; ErrEndpointFillerHasProperties pinned by test/data/schema/gql/invalid/endpoint_filler_properties.gql. 9/9 mutations caught.

title: tooling: bd-gh-sync pull silently reverts bead description amendments
description:
`.claude/settings.json` (SessionStart, including on compaction) and
`.githooks/post-merge` (every `git pull`) both run `.githooks/bd-gh-sync pull`,
which is:

```
bd github sync --pull-only --prefer-github
```

`--prefer-github` makes the **GitHub issue body authoritative for the bead
description**. A `bd update --body-file` that is not also mirrored to the GH
issue is overwritten the next time either trigger fires — in practice the very
next session. No warning, no diff, no record in `bd comments`.

## Cost so far

Four occurrences on 2026-07-26 during the gqlc-h9n.4 close-out, two
misdiagnoses (first a teammate accused of fabricating an amendment, then the
`.beads/hooks/post-checkout` JSONL import blamed), and one regression shipped to
master: PR #442 (`26d0879`) put `gqlc-h9n.21` on master at 3923 chars instead of
7659. Restored by PR #443.

## Why it is hard to see

1. The revert is **selective**. Status, labels and dependency edges survive,
   because none of them has a GH-body representation. A partial revert reads as
   a partial edit, i.e. as an agent lying, not as a store event.
2. The passive export is written **asynchronously**, so a revert followed by a
   re-export silently rewrites `.beads/issues.jsonl` with the older text. A `cp`
   of that file into a worktree then captures the reverted revision.
3. A **diffstat cannot catch it**: the amended and the reverted record are both
   one JSONL line, so `2 insertions, 2 deletions` is identical either way.

## Current manual workaround

Edit GitHub first, then bd, then prove it:

```bash
gh issue edit <N> --body-file /tmp/new.md   # N from `bd show <id>` -> External
bd update <id> --body-file /tmp/new.md
.githooks/bd-gh-sync pull                   # description must survive
BD_GIT_HOOK=1 bd hooks run pre-commit       # deterministic export flush
```

That is a workaround, not a fix — it depends on every agent remembering it, and
the failure is silent when they do not.

## Candidate fixes

- **Detect and refuse.** Before the pull overwrites a description, compare it
  with the local one; on divergence, print the bead id and both lengths and skip
  that field rather than clobbering it. Preserves `--prefer-github` for the
  create/close/comment mirroring that it is actually there for.
- **Push descriptions the other way.** If bd is to be authoritative for prose,
  the pull should not touch `description` at all, and the push side should
  mirror bd -> GH.
- **Guard at commit time.** A pre-commit check that every bead whose description
  changed in the staged export matches its GH issue body; fail with the `gh
  issue edit` command to run.

The first is the smallest change and closes the silent-loss path; the third
catches the case where someone edits bd without the sync running at all.

## Acceptance

A test or scripted repro that: amends a bead description via bd only, runs
`.githooks/bd-gh-sync pull`, and asserts the amendment survives (or that the
sync failed loudly naming the bead). Today that repro reverts silently.
close_reason: Shipped in PR #454. Pre-flight divergence check + bulk gh issue list + 11-case test suite. Linus 2-round review.

title: decision (RESOLVED: no buy): ISO/IEC 39075 CHF 227 — semantic beads held indefinitely
description:
**This is a spending decision for the repo owner, not an engineering task. No
agent should resolve it autonomously.**

## The situation

"Consult the standard" is two acts, and only one of them is free.

- **Syntactic half — free and normative.** ISO publishes the COMPLETE BNF (814
  productions) and the full Annex D feature list (228 codes) at
  https://standards.iso.org/iso-iec/39075/ed-1/en/ under the ISO Customer
  Licence. Does this production exist, what does it produce, is this feature
  code real, what is it called — all answerable today, at no cost, citably.
  This has already unblocked real work (gqlc-cfj, gqlc-h9n.3, gqlc-h9n.30).
- **Semantic half — CHF 227.** What the standard says a production *means*.
  The General Rules and Syntax Rules exist only in the paid PDF
  (https://www.iso.org/standard/76120.html).

## What is actually blocked on the paid half

- **gqlc-h9n.28** — does `FLOAT(p)` precision count bits or decimal digits?
  The BNF *proves the ambiguity is real and proves it is unresolvable
  syntactically*: `FLOAT [ (precision [, scale]) ]` (bnf.txt:1423) sits as a
  sibling of `FLOAT16..FLOAT256` while carrying the *decimal* type's
  scale-bearing shape. Nothing in the grammar decides it.
- **gqlc-h9n.29** — retire or confirm `ErrEndpointFillerHasProperties` against
  ISO 18.3. Same shape: `<source node type reference>` (bnf.txt:1250) does not
  distinguish declaration from reference in the grammar.
- **Parts of gqlc-0ri** — a deviation table cannot honestly record "we deviate
  from X" without knowing what X requires.

## Why these must NOT be resolved by inference

A deviation record is honest when *we decided something*. It is not honest when
the standard is the only possible arbiter and we skipped it — that launders a
coin-flip into documentation. A web-search paraphrase of what SQL's `FLOAT(p)`
means is inference dressed as evidence and must not be promoted to a citation.
Vendor conformance tables (Neo4j, Ultipa) match iso.org byte-for-byte on the
free artefacts, which makes them useful corroboration but never the citation.

So the honest states are: **buy it**, or **hold the beads at "blocked on ISO
purchase"**. Not "decide by inference and write it down confidently".

## Cost/benefit

- **Cost:** CHF 227, one-off. Single-user licence.
- **Buys:** unblocks h9n.28, h9n.29 and the semantic half of 0ri; and every
  future question of this shape, of which there will be more — the epic is
  explicitly aiming at full graph-schema DDL conformance, and each remaining
  type-system and cardinality question has the same free-syntax/paid-semantics
  split.
- **Cost of not buying:** those beads stay open indefinitely. It does NOT block
  the epic's bulk — coverage, corpus, grammar and rejection work all proceed on
  the free BNF. Two named beads and one section of a third are the whole
  exposure today.

## Also unresolved, and cheaper to settle

Whether the ISO Customer Licence permits *vendoring* the free files into a
public repo. The grant is "use in their original format without any
modifications for the purposes specified in their respective ISO standard(s)",
which is plausibly a use grant rather than a redistribution grant. Current
working ruling (team-lead, applied on gqlc-cfj): vendor **bare identifier
codes only, never ISO's descriptions** — bare alphanumeric identifiers are
facts rather than expression. That shipped and is defensible, but it is a
judgement call, not an answer. See gqlc-4jm.

## Recommendation

Buy it. The epic's stated goal is conformance with a specific published
standard; owning that standard is a normal cost of that goal, and the
alternative is a permanent floor of un-answerable questions that will keep
recurring. But it is the owner's money and the owner's call — this bead exists
to make the decision explicit rather than let it be made by default.
## Resolved 2026-07-27: NOT buying. Closed.

Repo owner's call, unambiguous: the CHF 227 is not being spent, now or later.
This is the "hold" branch of the decision, taken deliberately rather than by
default — which is what this bead existed to force.

**Consequences, stated plainly so nobody re-litigates them by inference:**

- `gqlc-h9n.28` (does `FLOAT(p)` count bits or decimal digits?) and
  `gqlc-h9n.29` (retire or confirm `ErrEndpointFillerHasProperties` against ISO
  18.3) are now **permanently blocked on an arbiter we will not have**. They
  stay open as honest unknowns. They are not "hard"; they are unanswerable from
  the free artefacts, and the BNF positively proves that — see the citations
  above.
- The semantic half of `gqlc-0ri`'s deviation table cannot be written. A
  deviation record needs to know what is being deviated from.

**The rule that survives this close, and matters more than the bead did:** a
web-search paraphrase, a vendor conformance table, or an analogy to SQL is
**not** a citation and must never be promoted to one. Closing this bead removes
the option to buy the answer; it does not license inventing it. Anything
resolved by inference gets recorded as a gqlc decision with gqlc's name on it,
never as "ISO says".

The free half is unaffected and remains the workhorse: the complete BNF (814
productions) and Annex D (228 codes) at
https://standards.iso.org/iso-iec/39075/ed-1/en/ are normative, citable, and
already carry the epic's coverage, corpus, grammar and rejection work. Nothing
about the epic's bulk depended on the purchase.

The separate, cheaper licence question — whether the ISO Customer Licence
permits vendoring the free files — is untouched by this and stays with
`gqlc-4jm`. The working ruling (bare identifier codes only, never ISO's
descriptive prose) still stands.
close_reason: Repo owner decided against the CHF 227 purchase. h9n.28, h9n.29 and the semantic half of 0ri stay open as permanently-blocked honest unknowns; they must not be resolved by inference.

title: githooks: reject commits authored by a test-fixture identity
description:
On 2026-07-26 a real feature commit landed on a real branch and was pushed to
origin authored as a test fixture:

    875fa4e schema/gql: reject edge kind that contradicts arc direction (gqlc-h9n.3)
    author=test <test@example.invalid>
    committer=test <test@example.invalid>

Nothing caught it. The commit succeeded, the hooks ran and passed, the test
suite was green, and it pushed cleanly. It was found only because a reviewer
read `git log --format=%ae` by hand while investigating an unrelated symptom.

## Cause

`internal/tools/bdguard`'s tests (gqlc-v2p, in flight) chdir'd into a
`t.TempDir()` fixture repo and ran `git config user.email test@example.invalid`
without pinning the command's directory. Process cwd is global to the test
binary, not per-test, so `t.TempDir()` cannot isolate it. During the window
where cwd was the real worktree, the config write landed on the real
repository.

`.git/config` is shared by every linked worktree — it is not per-worktree
state. The write therefore hit all seven worktrees at once, and any agent
committing during that window inherited the fixture identity. The same runs
also set `core.bare = true`, which broke `git rev-parse --show-toplevel` in the
main checkout, which is where bd writes its passive export. It recurred three
times before containment.

The cwd bug itself is fixed on gqlc-v2p (`cmd.Dir` on the fixture command
helper, plus `t.Chdir` for the run under test). This bead is the *other* half.
Fixing the one test removes the one known source; it does not make the failure
detectable, and the class is broader than this test — any fixture, script, or
mistyped `git config` produces the same silent result. The defect is not that a
bad identity was written. It is that a commit with a bogus author passed every
gate we have.

Commit time is also the only cheap point of repair. Once pushed, the fix is
`--amend --reset-author` plus a force-push, and if a PR is open the rewrite
churns the review.

## What to build

Extend `.githooks` to reject a commit whose author or committer email is
implausible. `.githooks/commit-msg` already rejects `Co-Authored-By` values
mentioning claude/@anthropic.com — this is the same shape of check on a
different field, so extend the existing hook rather than adding a new one.

Decisions to settle in the PR:

- **Denylist vs allowlist.** A denylist of known fixture spellings
  (`test@example.invalid`, `@example.com`, `@example.org`, `root@localhost`,
  empty) is low-friction and catches this incident. An allowlist is stronger
  but needs maintenance and misfires on new contributors. Recommend denylist,
  plus a shape check that the address contains `@` and a dot in the domain.
- **Author AND committer.** Check both. This incident set both, but rebase and
  cherry-pick can split them.
- **Which hook fires.** `commit-msg` receives the message, not the identity, so
  read the identity via `git var GIT_AUTHOR_IDENT` rather than a hook argument.
  Confirm the chosen hook fires for `--amend` and `cherry-pick`, since those
  are exactly the paths a repair takes.

## Acceptance — the gate must be shown to FAIL

Per the standing rule that a detector exiting 0 is not a gate: showing the hook
runs is not enough. Demonstrate that
`git -c user.email=test@example.invalid commit` is **rejected**, with exit
status and message, and that a normal commit still succeeds. Then mutation-test
the guard — change the denylist entry, confirm the rejection stops — so we know
the rejection is caused by the rule and not by something incidental.

## Related

- gqlc-v2p — the cwd fix that removes this instance's source.
- gqlc-5fm — `core.hooksPath` drift in this same shared `.git/config` silently
  killed the hooks in every worktree at once. Same file, same shared-state
  property, same invisibility. Confirm this hook cannot itself be disabled
  without notice.
close_reason: Shipped in PR #449. Extended commit-msg hook with _check_identity() denylist+shape guard for author and committer.

title: test(schema): measure grammar coverage against ISO's own BNF production list, not GQL.g4
description:
Our grammar-coverage gate measures coverage against `internal/grammar/gql/GQL.g4`.
That denominator is wrong for this epic's stated goal.

A gate built on our own grammar can only report **alternatives we implemented and
did not exercise**. It is structurally incapable of reporting a production that
exists in ISO/IEC 39075 and that we never implemented at all — such a production
is not in the denominator, so 100% coverage is reachable while arbitrarily much
of the standard is missing. "Have we covered our grammar" is not the question;
"have we covered the standard" is.

## This is now measurable, for free

Verified 2026-07-26 (team-lead, by fetch, not by report):

    https://standards.iso.org/iso-iec/39075/ed-1/en/           -> HTTP 200
    ISO_IEC_39075(en).bnf.txt                                   3502 lines
    productions matching ^<...> ::=                              814
    ISO_IEC_39075(en)-features.xml                               228 <feature> elements

Published by ISO themselves under the ISO Customer Licence, labelled as
containing the grammar specified by ISO/IEC 39075. This is a **normative,
machine-readable, complete** list of every production in the standard. It is
not a draft, not a vendor rendering, and not the community ANTLR adaptation
that `gqlc-h9n.11` exists to correct the provenance of.

## What to build

1. Derive the **graph-schema-relevant subset** of the 814 productions: the
   transitive closure from `<graph type specification>` / `<nested graph type
   specification>`. Derive it mechanically from the BNF file, do not hand-pick
   — the whole point is that a human-chosen denominator reintroduces the bias
   this bead exists to remove.
2. For each production in that subset, record one of: implemented and
   exercised by the corpus / implemented and unexercised / **not implemented**.
   The third bucket is the one no current gate can produce.
3. Gate on the third bucket not growing. Whether it must be empty is a
   separate decision — see the sequencing note.

## Sequencing note, and the reason this is P1 rather than P0

The third bucket is almost certainly large today, so this cannot start life as
"must be empty" without blocking every PR. Land it first as a **recorded
inventory with a ratchet** (the count may not increase), then drive the count
down bead by bead. Landing it as a hard zero-gate on day one would force either
a mass of stub implementations or an exemption list long enough to be
meaningless — both of which destroy the measurement.

Note the ratchet must gate on the count of *unimplemented productions*, not on
a percentage: a percentage moves when the denominator moves, so adding corpus
files could show improvement while nothing was implemented.

## Relationship to the existing coverage gate

This does not replace the g4-derived gate. That one answers "is our grammar
exercised", which is still worth knowing and catches a different defect
(dead alternatives). The two denominators measure different things and both
should exist. Do not fold them together.

Also relevant: `bd memories antlr-alt-order-unreachable-alternatives` — ANTLR
alternative ordering makes some GQL.g4 alternatives unreachable, so any
obligation set over grammar alternatives needs an exemption mechanism. That
applies to this gate too, and the exemption design in `gqlc-h9n.2` amendment
A9 should be reused rather than reinvented.

## What this does NOT do

The BNF is syntax only. It cannot resolve any question of the form "what does
the standard say this production *means*" — that prose is in the paid PDF.
`gqlc-h9n.28` and `gqlc-h9n.29` are both blocked on exactly that and are
**not** unblocked by this bead. Do not let a green coverage number be read as
a conformance claim; coverage of the production list is a necessary condition
for conformance, not a sufficient one, and the ADR should say so in those
words.
close_reason: Closed

comments.author: areqag
comments.text:
Denominator derived (iso-access, 2026-07-26). Artefacts preserved at
/tmp/lead/iso/ — iso-schema-productions.md, extract_productions.py,
iso39075.bnf.txt. **Commit the script with the implementation**; /tmp is
volatile and the closure must be reproducible, not a number someone once got.

Roots used: <create graph type statement> (247), <drop graph type statement>
(262), <graph type source> (253), <nested graph type specification> (1144),
<graph type reference> (1112), <catalog graph type parent and name> (1116).

Two closures:
- **DDL-only: 200 productions** (25% of the standard's 814), treating
  <graph expression> as an opaque leaf.
- Full/unpruned: 738 (91%).

The 538 difference is entirely the query-language subtree reachable through
<graph type like graph> (line 238) and the <copy of graph type> form. Those are
DDL *references* into a query-language value, not DDL structure. Taking
DDL-only, per iso-access's recommendation, which I agree with: the compliance
question at that frontier is "do we accept the reference", not "do we implement
the entire query grammar beneath it".

## Refinement the extraction does not yet make — do this before the gate lands

**Split the 200 into structural vs lexical before reporting any coverage
number.** Roughly 70 of the 200 are lexical terminals and identifier machinery:
<comma> (3422), <left paren> (3452), <digit> (3353), <hex digit> (3338),
<underscore> (3494), the whole 3413-3497 punctuation block, and the 2334-2725
name/identifier/quoted-sequence block.

Those are satisfied for free by any lexer. Counting them in the denominator
means the inventory opens at a high number that reflects having a tokeniser,
not having implemented graph-type DDL, and it will barely move as real features
land. The signal we want lives in the ~130 structural productions — the
1144-1573 graph-type-body range plus the 178-262 statement forms.

This does not change the ratchet design, which already gates on the **count of
unimplemented productions** rather than a percentage precisely so a moving
denominator cannot fake progress. It changes what a human reads off the
inventory. Report both buckets separately; let the ratchet run on structural.

## Unchanged from the original scope

Land as recorded inventory + ratchet, not as a hard zero-gate — the
not-implemented bucket is certainly large today and a day-one zero-gate forces
either stub implementations or an exemption list long enough to be meaningless.
Reuse the exemption mechanism from gqlc-h9n.2 amendment A9 rather than
reinventing it; ANTLR alternative ordering makes some alternatives unreachable
(see `bd memories antlr-alt-order-unreachable-alternatives`) and that applies
here too.

And the standing caveat, which the ADR must state in these words: coverage of
the production list is a **necessary** condition for conformance, not a
sufficient one. The BNF is syntax only. A green number must not be read as a
conformance claim — the prose that would justify that claim is in the paid PDF.

title: ci: codegen-fence runs on every PR but is not a required status check
description:
`codegen-fence` runs on every PR and cannot block a single one.

Found 2026-07-26 while checking why PR #421's CI had been computed against a
stale base. `gh api repos/areqag/gqlc/branches/master/protection` returns:

    required_status_checks.contexts:
      ["lint", "test", "tidy", "actionlint", "govulncheck", "live-smoke"]

Six. But `gh pr checks 421` and `gh pr checks 422` each list **seven**:
`actionlint`, `codegen-fence`, `govulncheck`, `lint`, `live-smoke`, `test`,
`tidy`. `codegen-fence` is defined at `.github/workflows/ci.yml:63`, triggers
on pull_request like every sibling job, runs, reports — and is absent from the
contexts list, so a red `codegen-fence` leaves the merge button green.

This is the `workflow-pr-blocking-two-halves` class exactly: `on: pull_request`
makes a workflow **run**; `required_status_checks.contexts` is what makes it
**block**. Someone landed the YAML half and never landed the protection half.
Every PR since has been merging with this gate advisory.

## What is actually unguarded

`just test-codegen-fence` is not a nicety. It is the only thing standing
between us and shipping generated code that does not compile:

    cd test/data/codegen && go build ./... && go vet ./...
    cd test/data/codegen && go mod tidy -diff
    cd test/data/codegen && golangci-lint run

`test/data/codegen` is a **separate Go module** — it is not reached by the
root `just test`, so no other required check compiles it. A codegen change that
emits uncompilable Go, leaves the fixture module's `go.mod` untidy, or trips a
linter currently produces a red advisory check and merges anyway.

The reason nobody has noticed is that it has never actually failed on a PR we
wanted to merge. That is luck, not evidence. Same shape as `gqlc-5fm`: ask
"does the check FAIL and does the failure stop anything?", never "is there a
check?".

## Fix

    gh api -X PATCH repos/areqag/gqlc/branches/master/protection/required_status_checks \
      -f 'contexts[]=lint' -f 'contexts[]=test' -f 'contexts[]=tidy' \
      -f 'contexts[]=actionlint' -f 'contexts[]=govulncheck' \
      -f 'contexts[]=live-smoke' -f 'contexts[]=codegen-fence'

**This is a shared-infrastructure change and needs the repo owner to make it or
explicitly authorise it.** It is deliberately not applied by the autonomous
loop: merge authority was delegated, branch-protection authority was not.

**Verify the fix the same way the defect was found** — re-read the protection
API and confirm seven contexts, then open a throwaway PR that deliberately
breaks the fixture module (e.g. a syntax error in a generated file) and confirm
the merge button is actually blocked. A protection change that has only been
verified by reading the API response is the same mistake one level up.

## Second, separate question: `strict` is false

The same response shows `required_status_checks.strict: false` — "require
branches to be up to date before merging" is OFF. That is why #421's green CI
was computed against a base that no longer existed once #422 landed, and both
PRs touch `internal/schema/gql`. I checked the combined tree by hand (clean
merge, 12 packages green) and it was fine, but nothing forced that check.

Do **not** bundle this with the fix above. Turning `strict` on serialises every
merge behind a rebase and a full CI re-run, which cuts directly against the
standing CI-wall-time priority, and this epic merges several PRs into one
package per session. The cheaper mitigation is a merge-time habit — test-merge
onto current master and run the affected package — which costs seconds and only
when the file sets actually overlap. Price both before choosing; if `strict`
stays off, record *that* as the decision so the next person does not rediscover
it as a bug.
close_reason:
Applied 2026-07-27 with owner's explicit authorisation (branch-protection authority delegated for this one change).

required_status_checks.contexts is now 7, was 6: lint, test, tidy, actionlint, govulncheck, live-smoke, codegen-fence. strict deliberately left false per this bead's 'do not bundle' instruction; filed separately.

VERIFIED THE WAY THE DEFECT WAS FOUND, not by reading the API response. Throwaway PR #451 added a syntax error in test/data/codegen/broken_probe.go, isolated to the separate fixture module so the root suite could not see it:
  - codegen-fence  FAIL
  - test           PASS  (confirms the break is invisible to the root suite)
  - merge state    BLOCKED
PR #451 closed unmerged, branch deleted.

CORRECTION TO THIS BEAD'S PREMISE, found by that test: the claim 'test/data/codegen is not reached by the root just test, so no other required check compiles it' is FALSE. live-smoke also failed, because 'just test-codegen-live' runs go test inside test/data/codegen and therefore compiles it — and live-smoke was already a required context. So the compile half was already guarded.

What codegen-fence uniquely adds is go vet, go mod tidy -diff and golangci-lint run over the fixture module, none of which live-smoke performs, plus it does not depend on the docker-gated job that GQLC_SKIP_LIVE=1 can short-circuit. The gate was still worth making required, for narrower reasons than the bead argued.

comments.author: areqag
comments.text:
Re-verified 2026-07-26 17:5x UTC, still true. Read-only check:

    $ gh api repos/areqag/gqlc/branches/master/protection \
        --jq '{contexts: .required_status_checks.contexts, strict: .required_status_checks.strict}'
    {"contexts":["lint","test","tidy","actionlint","govulncheck","live-smoke"],"strict":false}

Six contexts; `codegen-fence` still absent. Every PR merged since the YAML
landed — including four merged today — had this gate advisory.

## Second half, same object: `strict: false`

The `strict` flag is off. That is "require branches to be up to date before
merging" disabled, and it is why #421's CI had been computed against a base
that no longer existed. Two distinct holes in one API object:

- **`contexts`** decides which checks can block. `codegen-fence` cannot.
- **`strict`** decides whether a green check is even *about* the merge result.
  With it false, "CI passed" can mean "CI passed against a tree that is not
  what will land".

Fixing only the first leaves a required `codegen-fence` that can still go green
on a stale base. Decide both together.

## This needs the repo owner — not an agent

Changing branch protection is repo-admin configuration. Merge authority was
delegated to the agent team; repo configuration was not. **No agent should run
this PATCH.** Filed for the owner, deliberately not executed.

The fix, for whoever has admin:

    gh api -X PATCH repos/areqag/gqlc/branches/master/protection/required_status_checks \
      -f 'contexts[]=lint' -f 'contexts[]=test' -f 'contexts[]=tidy' \
      -f 'contexts[]=actionlint' -f 'contexts[]=govulncheck' \
      -f 'contexts[]=live-smoke' -f 'contexts[]=codegen-fence'

Add `-F strict=true` if the stale-base half is taken at the same time. Note
`strict=true` has a real cost — it forces a rebase whenever master moves during
review, which on a repo with several agents landing PRs in parallel means
frequent re-pushes. That is a genuine trade-off, not an oversight to correct
reflexively; the parallel-agent workflow here is exactly the case where it
bites hardest. Weigh it rather than defaulting.

## Verify it actually blocks

Per the standing rule that a detector exiting 0 is not a gate: after the PATCH,
confirm the contexts list contains all seven, then confirm a PR with a
deliberately red `codegen-fence` shows a blocked merge button. A required check
that is misspelled relative to the job name silently never matches and is
indistinguishable from not being required at all — so read the name back from
`gh pr checks` rather than trusting the string that was sent.

title: ci: nothing detects a PR that reverts the beads passive export
description:
Found 2026-07-26 on PR #422, caught by hand during a routine rebase check. Had
the lead not been checking that branch for an unrelated squash-duplicate
problem, it would have merged green and silently reverted master.

## What happened

`.beads/issues.jsonl` is a passive export: bd rewrites it as a side effect of
ordinary commands. A teammate worktree therefore accumulates a copy reflecting
whatever bd state existed when that worktree last ran a bd command. Staged with
a blanket `git add -A` and committed, it travels with an unrelated code PR.

PR #422 (h9n.18, endpoint fillers) carried an export snapshot taken before PR
#423 landed. Content comparison:

    branch:  gqlc-h9n.19 open     gqlc-h9n.17 open     gqlc-h9n.28 absent
    master:  gqlc-h9n.19 closed   gqlc-h9n.17 closed   gqlc-h9n.28 open

Merging it would have reopened two beads closed that morning and deleted a bead
from the export outright.

## Why nothing caught it

- **CI cannot.** A stale export is still syntactically valid JSONL. Every
  existing gate — lint, test, tidy, actionlint, govulncheck, codegen-fence,
  live-smoke — passes on it. There is no gate that looks at this file at all.
- **`git diff --stat` actively misleads.** It renders as
  `.beads/issues.jsonl | 34 ++++----` sitting among the real files, which reads
  as incidental churn. The revert is only visible by diffing *content* —
  parsing both copies and comparing per-issue status.
- **Review would not catch it either.** A reviewer told to focus on
  edgetype.go/listener.go has no reason to parse a 166-line JSONL, and the
  line-level diff is mostly reordering noise.

So this is a class with zero detectors, not a weak one. It is the inverse of
gqlc-5fm: there the detector existed and exited 0; here nothing looks.

## Proposed gate

A CI job that fails when a PR's `.beads/issues.jsonl` regresses against the
merge base. Cheapest sound form:

1. Parse `.beads/issues.jsonl` at the PR head and at `origin/master`.
2. FAIL if any issue id present on master is absent at head.
3. FAIL if any issue closed on master is open at head.
4. Additions and new closures are fine — that is what a sync PR does.

That is monotonicity, deliberately one-directional so `chore(bd)` sync PRs pass
unmodified and no exemption mechanism is needed. Reopening a bead legitimately
would trip it; that is rare enough to warrant a label escape hatch, and it is
better that it be loud.

Cheaper alternative worth pricing first: make the export path lead-only by
convention and add a pre-commit hook rejecting `.beads/issues.jsonl` in the
index unless the commit subject starts `chore(bd)`. Catches it earlier and
locally. But it is a local hook, and gqlc-5fm is the standing proof that local
hooks die silently and repo-wide — so the hook is a nicety and the CI job is
the gate. Do not ship only the hook.

## Notes for whoever takes this

- Mutation-test it against the real artefact: replay PR #422's `eb4e7f0` export
  against the master of that moment and confirm the gate FAILS naming both
  reopened beads and the dropped one. A gate for this class that has never been
  run against the incident that motivated it is not evidence of anything.
- Check `ci.yml` before adding a `just` recipe that exits non-zero — `just test`
  runs in CI, and gqlc-5fm is the incident where a fatal recipe would have
  failed every run. If the check belongs in `just`, guard it on `$CI` semantics
  deliberately rather than by reflex.
- Watch the cost: parsing two JSONL files is milliseconds, but a whole extra
  job has fixed runner overhead. Prefer folding it into an existing job unless
  it needs the merge base checked out.
close_reason: PR #429 merged as e067cb1; GH #424 auto-closed. bdguard monotonicity gate wired into required tidy job.

title: just: check-hooks warns and exits 0, so dead git hooks read as a green doctor
description:
Found 2026-07-26. Two agents independently hit this within an hour; the second
report is what made the scope clear.

## What was wrong

`core.hooksPath` was set in `.git/config` to the absolute path
`/home/antranig/Developer/gqlc/gqlc/.git/hooks`. That directory contains **only
`.sample` files**, which git ignores. So `commit-msg`, `pre-commit`, `pre-push`
and `post-merge` were all inactive — repo-wide, in every worktree, since
`.git/config` is shared by all of them.

Among the casualties: `.githooks/commit-msg`, which CLAUDE.md names as the
enforcement mechanism for the no-AI-attribution rule. CLAUDE.md's claim that the
rule is "enforced at commit time" was simply false for the duration.

Repaired by running `just init` (the project's own recipe:
`git config core.hooksPath .githooks`). Audited the last 40 commits for
`Co-Authored-By:` naming claude/anthropic and for the "Generated with Claude
Code" footer: **zero violations**. Discipline held where the gate did not, but
that is luck, not a control.

## The actual defect — the gate does not gate

`justfile:19` `check-hooks` detects the drift correctly and then does this:

```
echo "warning: core.hooksPath is '${got:-<unset>}', expected '.githooks' — local hooks are inactive. Run 'just init' to fix." >&2
```

It warns and exits 0. Consequences:

- `just doctor` runs `check-hooks` and then prints `ok`. It printed `ok` the
  entire time hooks were dead.
- `check-hooks` is wired into `just test`, where a single stderr line is buried
  in test output nobody reads line-by-line, and the recipe stays green.

So the detector is present, correct, and inert. This is the same shape as
`gqlc-h9n.15` (inert measurement guards) and the CI bead about a workflow that
runs but is not in `required_status_checks` — the mechanism executes and
influences nothing.

The comment above the recipe (justfile:15-17) makes it sharper: it says drift is
"the only way local pre-commit/pre-push gates can silently die (CI cannot see
local git config)". The author identified the exact silent-death mode and then
made the only detector for it non-fatal.

## Fix

Make `check-hooks` exit non-zero on drift. It is already wired into `just test`,
so this converts a buried warning into a hard stop with an actionable message
that already names the remedy (`just init`).

Points to weigh while doing it:

- **`just test` must still be runnable in a fresh clone.** A new contributor who
  has not run `just init` will now hit a hard failure. That is the intent, but
  the message must be unmissable and must lead with the fix. Confirm the failure
  text renders well when `just test` fails on it.
- **Does anything in CI run `check-hooks`?** CI has no local hooks and does not
  need them. If `just test` is invoked in CI, a hard failure there would be a
  self-inflicted outage. Check `ci.yml` before changing the exit status, and if
  CI does call it, make the check conditional on not-CI rather than weakening it.
  This is the load-bearing question — get it wrong and the fix breaks the build.
- **Mutation-test the fix**: unset `core.hooksPath`, set it to a wrong path, and
  set it to a path of `.sample`-only files. The third is the case that actually
  occurred and the one a naive "is it set?" check would miss. The current
  string-equality check against `.githooks` happens to catch it; do not
  regress that into an existence test.

## Follow-up worth considering, not required here

`check-hooks` compares the config value to the literal string `.githooks`. That
is right, but it does not verify the hooks are executable or that the directory
is non-empty. A `core.hooksPath = .githooks` pointing at a directory whose files
lost their executable bit would pass. Cheap to add while in there; do not let it
expand the change.
close_reason: Landed in PR #417. check-hooks now exits 1 on core.hooksPath drift, skipped under CI (ci.yml:51 runs 'just test' in a fresh clone where the value is unset, so a naive fatal check would have broken every CI run). Kept the value comparison rather than a directory-existence test — .git/hooks exists and holds only .sample files, so an existence test cannot see this failure; a justfile comment records that.
