title: ci: every live recipe selects tests by a hardcoded -run allowlist, so a new live test never runs
description:
Every live recipe selects tests by a hardcoded `-run` allowlist naming the
two top-level tests that existed when it was written:

    justfile:216  test-codegen-live:
      go test ... -run 'TestLiveSmoke|TestAGESessionInit' ./...
    justfile:221  test-codegen-live-neo4j:
      go test ... -run TestLiveSmoke -skip 'TestLiveSmoke/apache-age' ./...
    justfile:229  test-codegen-live-age:
      go test ... -run 'TestLiveSmoke|TestAGESessionInit' -skip 'TestLiveSmoke/neo4j' ./...

`go test -run` matches **top-level** test names, so a new top-level live
test is excluded from all three. It does not fail, it does not skip
visibly, it does not appear in the log at all — the package still reports
`ok` and the job still goes green.

On master the allowlist happens to be exhaustive:

    grep -rhoE "^func Test[A-Za-z0-9_]+\(t \*testing\.T\)" test/data/codegen/*.go

returns exactly `TestAGESessionInit` and `TestLiveSmoke`. **Nothing
enforces that.** The property the recipes depend on is maintained by
whoever happens to remember, and the failure mode when they do not is a
live battery that is green because it never ran.

## This is already live

`feat/age-edge-union-live` adds `TestAGERefusesRelationshipTypeAlternation`
as a top-level test in `test/data/codegen/live_age_dialect_test.go`, and
does not touch the recipes. That branch's central claim — that AGE 1.7.0
rejects relationship-type alternation, verified against a live container —
therefore has no execution path anywhere: not in PR CI, not in the
nightly, not under `just`.

It compounds with the AGE arm's gating. `live-smoke-age` is
`if: github.event_name != 'pull_request'` (`.github/workflows/codegen-live.yml:54`),
so the AGE half only runs on the nightly cron. A new top-level AGE live
test is thus excluded from the one job that would ever have run it.

## The nightly itself is real

Worth recording, because the sibling bead `gqlc-0oau` raises the adjacent
worry and this narrows it. `codegen-live.yml` fires on `schedule`
(cron `17 4 * * *`). Run `30794774319` on 2026-08-03 executed

    go test -count=1 -tags codegen_live \
      -run 'TestLiveSmoke|TestAGESessionInit' -skip 'TestLiveSmoke/neo4j' ./...

and reported `ok github.com/areqag/gqlc/test/data/codegen 12.677s`. The
container starts and the tests run. The defect is the selection, not the
schedule.

## Fix

Select structurally rather than by name. The recipes already have a
structural axis — the `codegen_live` build tag — and the arm split
(neo4j versus AGE) is what the `-run`/`-skip` pair is really encoding. A
recipe that names no test cannot go stale.

If a name-based split is genuinely needed for the arm separation, then
the exhaustiveness the recipes silently assume has to be **asserted**:
a test in the root module that parses `test/data/codegen/*.go` for
top-level `Test*` declarations and requires that set to equal the set the
recipes name. Set equality, not a count — it self-updates, and it catches
the declared-but-unselected case that a count cannot.

Note `-skip 'TestLiveSmoke/apache-age'` operates on **subtest** paths,
which is a different axis from the top-level `-run` and is not affected.

## Acceptance

Add a throwaway top-level live test that fails unconditionally. Confirm
it currently passes CI — that establishes the gate is watching nothing.
Then confirm the fix makes CI red naming it. Then remove it and confirm
green.

Found while auditing whether the nightly AGE battery had ever actually
executed, during the review round for gqlc-35yu.14. Pre-existing repo
condition; gqlc-35yu.14 is the first branch to trip it.

title: codegen: resolver.ResolvedType is not the closed sum prepare.go's switches assume
description:
`prepare.go`'s two catch-all arms — tagged `//gqlc:unreachable column-unknown-variant` and `//gqlc:unreachable list-elem-unknown-variant` — end their switch over `resolver.ResolvedType` by wrapping `ErrOutOfC6Scope` with `t.String()`.

`ResolvedType` is a sealed interface, but a nil interface value is not a member of any arm and reaches the default. Calling `String()` on it panics with a nil-pointer dereference before the `fmt.Errorf` that names the sentinel is ever evaluated.

Measured with an out-of-package caller assembling `codegen.Input` with `resolver.Column{Name: "x", Type: nil}` and calling `neo4j.New().Generate`: panic, not `ErrOutOfC6Scope`.

That is why both sites remain in §3 of `docs/specs/codegen-sentinel-taxonomy.md` after gqlc-h4ug moved the reachable ones to §2: they are unreachable only because the guard that would report them crashes first. A branch that cannot return its sentinel because it faults is not a branch nothing reaches.

Fix: guard the nil case (either at the arm, or once at the top of the column/list-element walk) so the refusal is a wrapped `ErrOutOfC6Scope` naming the offending position. Then the two sites move to §2 with their own assembled-Input cases and their tags come off.
acceptance_criteria:
- A nil `resolver.ResolvedType` in a `Column` and in a `ResolvedList` element returns a wrapped `ErrOutOfC6Scope` naming the query and the position, not a panic.
- `column-unknown-variant` and `list-elem-unknown-variant` move from §3 to §2 of `docs/specs/codegen-sentinel-taxonomy.md`, with assembled-Input cases in `internal/codegen/conformance/assembled_input_test.go` asserting the sentinel and the exact message.
- Their `//gqlc:unreachable` tags are removed and `TestSentinelTaxonomy` stays green.
notes:
# gqlc-edze — widened description (proposed; tracker owner to apply)

Current title still fits, but is narrower than the defect:

> codegen: the unknown-ResolvedType arms panic before they can return their sentinel

Suggested title:

> codegen: resolver.ResolvedType is not the closed sum prepare.go's switches assume

---

## Why the current description is incomplete

The bead says the two catch-all arms are unreachable because the guard
that would report them crashes first, and that they move from §3 to §2
once the nil case is guarded.

Both halves are now false, and `gqlc-h4ug` has landed the correction:

- **The arms are already reachable, and already return their sentinel
  cleanly.** `resolver.ResolvedType`'s unexported `isResolvedType()`
  marker seals the interface against *new implementations*. It does not
  seal it against the **pointer forms of the existing eight**: every
  variant declares both `isResolvedType()` and `String()` with **value
  receivers** (`internal/resolver/validated.go:97-364`), and a pointer's
  method set contains its value methods, so `*resolver.ResolvedNode`
  satisfies `ResolvedType` while `case resolver.ResolvedNode:` does not
  match it. The sum an out-of-package caller can inhabit has **sixteen**
  forms plus the nil; each of the three switches names **eight**.
  `t.String()` on a non-nil pointer dispatches to the value method, so
  the refusal completes as written.
- **The §3→§2 move is done.** `column-unknown-variant` and
  `list-elem-unknown-variant` are §2 rows in
  `docs/specs/codegen-sentinel-taxonomy.md`, paid by assembled-`Input`
  cases using `&resolver.ResolvedNode{}`, and both `//gqlc:unreachable`
  tags are off. Those three acceptance criteria are satisfied and should
  be struck.

The nil panic is real and unfixed — but guarding nil alone leaves the
eight pointer inhabitants, which is the part the current criteria cannot
see.

## What is actually broken

**Two distinct defects at the same arms.**

1. **Nil panics at three reachable sites, not two.** The bead names the
   column arm and the list-element arm. The parameter assertion is a
   third: `prepare.go:626` calls `p.Type.String()` on the value that just
   failed the `ResolvedProperty` assertion. Confirmed by an
   out-of-package caller — a nil column, a nil list element and a nil
   param each panic with a nil-pointer dereference rather than refusing.
   Two further sites carry the same call behind a shadow
   (`prepare.go:705`, `prepare.go:879`); they are §3 today and would
   inherit the panic if their shadow ever moved.

2. **The sum is not closed.** Go offers no way to seal an interface
   against the pointer forms of its own value-receiver implementations,
   so "the switch names every variant, therefore the default is dead" is
   not an argument this codebase can make about `ResolvedType` — which
   is why §5.1 step 5 now tells a classifier to count *inhabitants*, not
   declarations. Decide the posture deliberately: either normalise
   pointer forms away at `Prepare`'s boundary so the switches see value
   forms only, or keep refusing them and treat the default arm as a
   permanent §2 branch. What is not acceptable is a default arm whose
   behaviour nobody chose.

## Corrected acceptance criteria

- A nil `resolver.ResolvedType` in a `Column`, in a `ResolvedList`
  element, and in a `ResolvedParameter` returns a wrapped
  `ErrOutOfC6Scope` naming the query and the position — not a panic.
  Three assembled-`Input` cases, one per site, each asserting the
  sentinel and the exact message.
- No `%s`/`String()` on a `ResolvedType` that has not been proven
  non-nil, at all five sites (`prepare.go:620`, `:626`, `:705`, `:879`,
  `:1050`).
- The posture on the eight pointer inhabitants is chosen and recorded:
  either they are normalised to their value forms before the switches
  run (and the existing `column-unknown-variant` /
  `list-elem-unknown-variant` §2 cases are re-pointed at the nil input,
  which then becomes what reaches those arms), or they stay refused and
  the §2 rows stand as written. Whichever is chosen, no row anywhere in
  the taxonomy argues that a `ResolvedType` switch is total because the
  interface is sealed.
- `docs/specs/codegen-sentinel-taxonomy.md` §3's `param-type-invariant`
  and `column-type-invariant` rows drop their `(gqlc-edze)`
  parentheticals, since the nil panic they cite is gone. Their
  *conclusions* are unaffected — Phase A still shadows both — so the
  rows stay in §3.
- `TestSentinelTaxonomy`, `TestReachableBranchesAreReached` and
  `just test-codegen-fence` stay green, and every §2 case still names a
  distinct `prepare.go` line under mutation.

## Note on sequencing

This still lands after `gqlc-h4ug`. It edits the same `prepare.go` arms
and the same taxonomy rows, and it now also edits §2 cases `h4ug`
created.
MEASURED (2026-08-03, gqlc-h4ug round-6 review). Two facts that sharpen this bead's posture question.

1. All EIGHT typed-nil pointer forms fault, not only the nil interface. Go emits an explicit nil check for a value method reached through a nil pointer, so even the zero-sized (*resolver.ResolvedUnknown)(nil) panics: 'value method ...ResolvedUnknown.String called using nil *ResolvedUnknown pointer'. This closes, in the harsher direction, the open question of whether a typed nil panics or not depending on whether the method body dereferences. It always panics.

2. resolver.ResolvedList{Element: nil} also faults, at prepare.go:1050, with 'invalid memory address or nil pointer dereference'. That is a third carrier of the same defect beyond the five call sites this bead already names.

3. The premise is wider still: the marker seals ResolvedType against NOTHING. Go promotes an embedded type's unexported methods, so 'type embedNode struct{ resolver.ResolvedNode }' satisfies ResolvedType from any package and reaches prepare.go:620, :1050 and the parameter assertion cleanly, no panic. So the 'normalise pointer forms away at Prepare's boundary' option in this bead's description does NOT close the sum — an embedded form is neither a value form nor a pointer form. If the posture chosen is normalisation, it must be normalisation to the eight KNOWN value forms with an explicit refusal for everything else, not a pointer-to-value deref. See [[gqlc-856f]].
Round 3 (head 02f4161c): round 2's own justification for calling the witness list open was itself a false universal -- 'a struct embedding an embedder faults here too' -- carried in resolvedTypeName's doc comment, taxonomy §2:138, the test file's doc comment and the PR body. Measured with go test -overlay (nothing dropped in the tree): struct{ embeddedNode }{} ANSWERS 'node', because an embedder holding a variant by value gives the promoted String() a receiver to reach; the branch already witnesses that one level down as the value-embedder case. Corrected in all three gated carriers plus the PR body. The openness argument no longer rests on composition: faulting is a property of the String() a value dispatches, and ResolvedType is satisfiable by types codegen never sees. One measured composing shape that does fault is named instead -- (*embeddedNode)(nil), which declares no String() of its own. That qualifier is not decoration: (*T)(nil) where T embeds a variant by value AND declares its own pointer-receiver String() ANSWERS, measured, so the unqualified form would have repeated the defect a round later. Four witnessed shapes stands (nil interface, eight typed-nil pointer forms, nil embedded pointer, embedded ResolvedType); five resolvedTypeName call sites stands (grep -cE 'resolvedTypeName\(' = 6, five calls plus the declaration).

title: codegen/age: the offset-sidecar collision gate keys on the time.Time carrier, so admitting zoned TIME silently drops its coverage
description:
`rejectOffsetSidecarCollisions` (internal/codegen/age/errors.go) refuses
a schema that declares the property name the AGE backend derives for a
TIMESTAMP property's zone. It decides which properties derive a sidecar
by testing `f.GoType != goInstant`, i.e. by the Go carrier text
`time.Time`.

That test is right today only because TIMESTAMP is the sole admitted
width that derives a sidecar. The owner-approved encoding table on
gqlc-35yu.11 gives the same flat `<f>Offset` sidecar to an
offset-bearing TIME. TIME's carrier is not `time.Time` — it is
`dbtype.Time` on the neo4j targets, and whatever backend-invariant
temporal carrier eventually unblocks it here. So the day TIME is
admitted, the gate keeps compiling, keeps passing its own tests, and
silently stops covering the width that was just added. The schema that
declares both `startedAt :: TIME` and `startedAtOffset :: INT64` would
then generate a decoder that reads one key twice and re-zones the value
by the author's own property, which is the exact defect this gate was
built to refuse.

WHAT TO DO: key the gate on "this field derives a sidecar" rather than
on the carrier text. The cleanest spelling is a single predicate beside
`offsetProperty` that both the gate and `writeEntityFieldDecode`
consult, so a width that gains zoning gains collision-refusal in the
same edit and cannot gain one without the other.

The negative fixture
test/data/codegen/invalid/property_field_collision_offset_sidecar/ and
the `TestRejectsAnAuthorOwnedOffsetSidecar` sweep in
internal/codegen/age/age_test.go both pin the TIMESTAMP case and should
grow a row per zoned width as each is admitted.
notes: Round 2 (PR #848, head 45ae5930): the sweep's width walk was itself fail-open at 'const TypeFoo = PropertyType("FOO")' and 'var TypeFoo PropertyType = "FOO"' — this bead's own fail-open survived against either spelling. declaresAWidth now admits a PropertyType conversion and the walk reads var blocks; rows C/D kill by name. The sweep's carried figure is pinned by membership (require.ElementsMatch) rather than require.NotZero. Leave in_progress; close on merge — the coordinator holds the merge.

title: codegen/age: agtypeZone accepts any int64 as a UTC offset, so a foreign graph decodes into a fictional zone
description:
The emitted `agtypeZone` helper reads the `<f>Offset` sidecar with
`agtypeInt64` and hands whatever integer it finds straight to
`time.FixedZone("", int(offset))`. Any int64 is accepted. `1000000000`
seconds is a zone 31 years east of UTC, and the decoder returns it
without complaint; the caller gets a `time.Time` whose `Zone()` reports
a fictional offset and whose wall clock is decades off the instant it
was stored beside.

This is not a theoretical hole. The sidecar exists precisely because
gqlc does not write it — it is the interop affordance for a graph some
other tool populated (see the read-without-write note on gqlc-35yu.11).
So every value that ever reaches this helper comes from outside gqlc,
which is exactly the input a decoder should not trust. The one class of
malformed sidecar the helper does reject is a non-integer agtype, and
that rejection is incidental: it comes from `agtypeInt64`, not from any
decision about what an offset is.

The instant itself has the same shape of gap one level down —
`agtypeInstant` accepts any int64 micros, so a sidecar-free property
holding `9e18` decodes to a year in the 290-thousands rather than
failing — but that one is far less reachable, since gqlc does write the
instant.

WHAT TO DO: range-check the offset in the emitted helper and return an
error naming the property when it falls outside. The bound worth
picking is the one Go's own zone handling and ISO 8601 agree on:
strictly within +/- 24 hours, i.e. (-86400, 86400). Tightening further
to ISO 8601's actual range (-64800, 57600) is defensible but rules out
offsets no real zone uses, so it buys nothing and could refuse a graph
a future zone database would accept.

The test belongs in `internal/codegen/age/testdata/corpus_test.go.txt`,
beside `TestAgtypeZoneReadsAnOffsetInSeconds`, which already exercises
the malformed-agtype arm and runs the emitted helper for real rather
than reading its source.
notes:
Round 2 (PR #848, head 45ae5930): independent adversarial review returned REVISE on one blocker + 4 nits; all addressed. Blocker was in the round-1 B1 fix, not in this bead's bound. Bound itself measured clean both edges both directions by the reviewer. Leave in_progress; close on merge — the coordinator holds the merge.
CORRECTION (PR #848 round 3) to this bead's DESCRIPTION. Two claims in it are withdrawn; the defect, the bound and WHAT TO DO's first sentence all stand.

1. WITHDRAWN, false: 'The sidecar exists precisely because gqlc does not write it -- it is the interop affordance for a graph some other tool populated ... So every value that ever reaches this helper comes from outside gqlc.' gqlc derives no sidecar PARAMETER of its own, but the key is an ordinary property, and a query whose own text names it binds it through the emitted agtypeArgs. Measured with gqlc built at this branch head: a schema declaring (:Event {occurredAt :: TIMESTAMP}) beside (:Note {occurredAtOffset :: INT64}) generates rc=0, and in that ONE emitted package models.go:40 reads agtypeZone(props, "occurredAtOffset", value1) while queries.cypher.go:51 binds the same key through agtypeArgs -- both helpers declared in models.go. Across two packages on one label, one gqlc package writes the key and the other zone-reads it, which closes vertex identity. So a value reaching this helper may well be one a gqlc encoding produced. The bound is still correct, on the narrower ground that nothing here constrains the integer's origin -- not on the ground that the input is necessarily foreign.

2. WITHDRAWN, unsourced: 'Tightening further to ISO 8601's actual range (-64800, 57600) is defensible.' No source for that range was produced by the author or by two independent reviewers. The ranges implementations actually cite are +/-14:00 (XSD) and +/-18:00 (Java ZoneOffset), neither asymmetric. The shipped bound is (-86400, 86400) exclusive, which is what WHAT TO DO's first sentence already specified.

GH #735 mirrors this description; it was deliberately NOT hand-edited, so the correction lives here.

Still in_progress. Close on merge -- the coordinator holds the merge.

title: ci: shellcheck is not wired into CI, so the hooks' disable directives are comments
description:
`.githooks/bd-gh-sync:510` carries a load-bearing directive:

    # shellcheck disable=SC2086 # deliberate split
    bd github push $1

The unquoted expansion is **wanted** — the ids must become separate argv words —
and `gqlc-w4q9` added the id gate that makes it safe. Adversarial review
confirmed the split is load-bearing: quoting `$1` reddens the batching case and
the assertion "each bead id is its own argv word", which reports
`argv was: github|push|b-a1 b-a2|`.

So the directive documents a genuine, deliberate exception. But **nothing
enforces it**, because `shellcheck` is not installed on the development machine
and is not wired into CI. `just check-hooks` only verifies that `core.hooksPath`
points at `.githooks`; it does not lint anything.

The consequence is that every other SC-class defect in the hooks — the ones the
directive is carving an exception *out of* — is also unchecked. This repo has
already been bitten by three of exactly that class: a pipeline reporting only
its last command's status, `if cmd | tail -2; then` being unconditionally true,
and `${_l##*FAILED*}` matching both "contains" and "is empty".

A disable directive in a tree with no linter is a comment.

## Fix

Add `shellcheck` to CI over `.githooks/`. It must be a job that already exists
or, if a new one is genuinely needed, note that **GitHub derives required status
contexts from job ids** — adding a job means the branch-protection contexts need
updating in the same change, and renaming or splitting an existing job breaks
every open PR.

Folding it into the existing `lint` job is the lower-risk option and needs no
branch-protection change.

## Acceptance

Introduce a real SC2086 violation elsewhere in `.githooks/` and confirm CI goes
red naming the file and line. Then confirm the deliberate `disable` at `:510`
does **not** redden — that is the whole point of the directive, and a linter
that fails on the sanctioned exception is one nobody will keep.

Verify the violation currently passes CI first, so the gate is known to be
watching something.

Found during the adversarial review of `gqlc-w4q9`. Pre-existing repo
condition, not that branch's doing.

title: bd-gh-sync: the GH listing is a count over a set the script never witnessed
description:
`gqlc-w4q9` established the rule that **a count reaches the summary only if the
script enumerated the set behind it**, and applied it to both bead snapshots.
It was not applied to the GitHub listing.

`gh issue list --state open` answering a valid `[]` yields `stale=[]`, which
walks to `closed 0 of 0 stale GH mirror(s)` and exit 0 — a count over a set the
script never witnessed, which is the class the rule exists to close.

This is genuinely weaker than the bead case, which is why it was returned
non-blocking rather than promoted: an empty open-issue list is a legitimate
answer, so emptiness alone is not decidable as failure.

## But a witness exists

After a run that pushed **N > 0** new beads, `bd github push` has just minted N
open issues. An empty open listing in the same run is therefore a lost one, not
a true empty. That is a decision procedure for the case that matters, and it
costs one comparison.

## The same bead covers listing truncation

`--limit 500` and `--limit 1000` (both pre-existing on master) silently cut a
listing at the cap. A run that hits the cap produces `closed C of S stale` over
a **truncated** set — the identical defect, arriving by a different route, and
one that gets more likely as the repo grows. A listing that returns exactly the
cap is indistinguishable from one that was cut, unless the script asks.

## Fix

Two guards, one rule:
- If the run pushed N > 0 and the subsequent open listing is empty, the count is
  unwitnessed. Say so and do not exit 0 claiming success.
- If a listing returns exactly its `--limit`, treat it as truncated rather than
  complete — either paginate or refuse to count over it.

reports the unwitnessed count rather than `closed 0 of 0` at exit 0. Mutate it
to return exactly `--limit` records and confirm the run refuses to count.
Verify both currently pass silently first, so the tests are known to be watching
something.

title: codegen/neo4j: the query-column path emits elem.(any), which is false for the null it exists to carry
description:
The neo4j emitter's **query-column** path emits `elem.(any)` when narrowing a
list whose element width is `ANY VALUE`. That assertion is false for exactly the
value the width exists to carry: `x.(any)` is **false when the interface value
is nil**. Demonstrated — `[]any{1, nil, "x"}` type-asserted element-wise to
`any` gives `ok=true, ok=false, ok=true`.

So a list containing a null decodes as a decode error rather than as a nil
element. AGE's `agtypeListOfAny` decodes the same value to `nil`, so the two
backends disagree at runtime on a value both are supposed to carry — which
`TestBackendInvariantSurface` cannot see, because it compares **declarations
only**.

## Reproduction

Add `RETURN b.bag, b.piles` to
`test/data/codegen/valid/schema_list_any_property/queries.cypher`. The emitted
`queries.cypher.go` contains `elem.(any)` and `elem4.(any)`.

## Why it is not caught today

No fixture routes an `ANY`-width list through a query column — the entity-property
path is covered, the query-column path is not. `gqlc-35yu.13`'s driver-carrier
census **does** catch this the moment a fixture reaches it, so the fix is a
fixture plus the narrowing correction, not new guard machinery.

## Fix

Narrow through the same driver-carrier rule the entity path uses: an `ANY`-width
element rides `[]any` and its elements need no assertion at all, because they are
already `any`. Emit the element directly rather than asserting it.

## Acceptance

Add the query columns above as a fixture. Verify the census names `elem.(any)`
as an offender **before** the fix, so the test is known to be watching
something, then fix the narrowing and confirm the emitted decoder returns a nil
element rather than an error for a list containing a null — asserted as a
**value** in `internal/codegen/neo4j/corpus_test.go`, which runs the emitted
bytes, not in a golden.

## Provenance

Pre-existing on master: `internal/codegen/neo4j/types.go` already recursed lists
and mapped `ANY VALUE` to `any`, and `internal/codegen/neo4j/render_queries.go`
is untouched by `gqlc-35yu.13`.

Commit `eeab7ff` on that branch says this "is filed rather than baked into a
golden here". It was not filed — an adversarial review searched `bd list`, every
record in `.beads/issues.jsonl`, and everything created since 2026-08-02, and
found no such bead. This bead makes that claim true.

title: codegen/age: decodeFunc's default arm decodes an unknown carrier as text, with no diagnostic
description:
`decodeFunc` (`internal/codegen/age/render_queries.go:547-559`) maps a carrier
type to the name of the `models.go` helper that decodes it. It names `bool`,
`int64` and `float64` explicitly and then has:

    default:
        return "agtypeString"

That `default` is a fail-open. It does not mean "everything else is a string";
it means "anything I was not taught about is a string". A carrier the AGE
backend gains later — a new numeric width, a byte slice, a composite — reaches
this arm and is silently decoded as text. There is no diagnostic, and the
emitted package still compiles, because `agtypeString` returns a `string` and
the field it is assigned to was typed from the same carrier table that
`decodeFunc` disagrees with. The failure surfaces at runtime, on real data, as
a wrong value or a decode error attributed to the wrong place.

Contrast `agtypeCarrier`, whose job is to *decide* the carrier. Here the
decision has already been made upstream, so `decodeFunc` is a total function
over a closed set — and a closed set is exactly the case where `default` should
be a refusal rather than a guess.

## Why this is not caught today

Every carrier currently reachable is one of the four named. So the `default`
arm is unreachable, which means no test exercises it and no test *can* fail
when it becomes reachable. This is the same shape as the other guards this
epic has been closing: green because it is looking at nothing.

## Fix

Make the switch exhaustive against the carrier set and refuse the unknown case
at generate time rather than emitting a guess — either a `codegen` sentinel
error returned up the emission path, or, if the emission path genuinely cannot
fail here, a panic naming the carrier, since an unnamed carrier at that point
is a generator bug and not a user error.

Then pin it: a test that adds a carrier to the carrier table and does not add
it to `decodeFunc` must go red. A test that merely asserts the four known
carriers map correctly does not close this — that is satisfiable by the table
it copies.

## Acceptance

Add a fifth carrier to whatever `agtypeCarrier` can return without touching
`decodeFunc`. Generation must fail, naming the carrier. Verify it does *not*
fail today first, so the test is known to be watching something.

Found during the adversarial review of `gqlc-35yu.13` and confirmed
pre-existing on master.

title: codegen: the edge-union sum type name is half author-chosen, so the emitted package scope is not closed
description:
Phase B builds an edge-union sum type as `interfaceName := q.Name + field`
where `field = rowFieldName(col.Name)` (internal/codegen/prepare.go, both
the ColumnEdgeUnion and the list-leaf arm). A query named ListActions
returning `r` therefore emits the package-level interface `ListActionsR`
and a marker method `isListActionsR`, and both halves of that name are
outside the generator's control: the method name comes from the query
file and the suffix comes from the author's RETURN clause.

That makes the emitted package's TOP-LEVEL scope not the closed
generator-owned set the method scope became on
fix/neo4j-param-name-capture. Two queries whose name-plus-column mangle
coincides collide:

    // name: ListActions
    MATCH (:Person)-[r]->(:Post) RETURN r
    // name: ListAction
    MATCH (:Person)-[sr]->(:Post) RETURN sr

both derive `ListActionsR`, so `gqlc generate` exits 0 and `go build`
reports "redeclared in this block". Not silent -- unlike the parameter
capture this is a compile error, which is why it was left out of that
branch -- but it is a generation that succeeds and produces a package
that cannot build, and the diagnostic names neither query.

Measured, not unmeasured. Two censuses on that branch bound it:

- internal/codegen/conformance/scope_test.go TestColumnNamesBindNothing
  holds all three targets to renaming every column moving no name the
  emission BINDS (arguments, receivers, results, body locals).
- internal/codegen/age/capture_test.go
  TestOnlyPackageLevelNamesFollowAColumnName holds the AGE corpus to the
  same thing, plus equality of what each method RESOLVES modulo the
  package-level declarations that moved. Its substitution is read off
  the two emissions' own declaration lists, so this residue is exactly
  the set of names it admits.

Closing it means either putting the sum-type name on the same collision
sweep the query-text const wants (see gqlc-dfcb's neighbourhood), or
making the suffix positional -- `<Method>Col0` -- which is a rename of a
generated PUBLIC type and so an API change with a golden-corpus-wide
diff. The census stays either way; only what it admits changes.
acceptance_criteria: Two queries whose `<Method> + rowFieldName(<column>)` mangle coincides either generate a compiling package or are refused at generate time with a message naming both queries and both columns; a fixture holds the colliding pair; and the guard goes red if the disambiguation is removed. The two censuses that bound the residue — TestColumnNamesBindNothing in internal/codegen/conformance/scope_test.go and TestOnlyPackageLevelNamesFollowAColumnName in internal/codegen/age/capture_test.go — stay, and the AGE one's declRenaming substitution narrows to admit nothing once the suffix stops being author-chosen.
notes:
Promoted from a code comment by the adversarial review of gqlc-lhs3 (2026-08-03): both censuses carried a comment saying the residue 'is an API change and not this branch's', which is deferred work living only in a comment. Those comments now cite this bead.

title: resolver: describeColumnType panics on a nil type that resolvedTypeEqual guards against
description:
`describeColumnType` panics on a nil `ResolvedType`, while `resolvedTypeEqual`
— the function it exists to explain — explicitly guards nil. Both are called on
the same value, `Column.Type`, from the same two lines of
`compareBranchColumns` (`internal/resolver/resolve.go`). One of the two is
wrong about what it can be handed.

Executed:

    describeColumnType(nil)                     -> panic (nil interface, t.String())
    describeColumnType(ResolvedList{Element: nil}) -> panic (recurses to the same)

    resolvedTypeEqual(a, b) opens with:
        if a == nil || b == nil { return a == nil && b == nil }

`describeColumnType`'s `default` arm and its `ResolvedList` recursion both call
`.String()` on the interface without a nil check.

**Pre-existing, not a regression.** The message this arm was built from
(pre-`gqlc-nkjt`) called `.String()` on the same value and panicked identically.
`gqlc-nkjt` moved the call into a helper and added a variant switch; it did not
introduce the reachability, and it did not remove it.

Raised as an unverified suspicion by the `gqlc-nkjt` round-4 adversarial
reviewer, who could execute the panic but could not settle whether anything can
produce the input.

## The question this bead exists to answer

**Is a nil `Column.Type` constructible from user input?**

`Column.Type` is written at exactly one place — `scope.go:548`,
`Column{Name: item.Name, Type: colType}` — from `projectionType`'s return. So
the question reduces to: does any arm of `projectionType`, or of the
`resolveType` / `unify` / edge- and node-projection helpers it delegates to,
return `(nil, nil)`? The nested case is the same question one level down: can a
`ResolvedList` be built with a nil `Element`? There are three construction sites
(`resolve.go:1058`, `resolve.go:1135`, `scope.go:731`), and each takes its
element from a call that also returns an error or an ok flag.

Two branches, and exactly one of them is true:

**If yes** — some arm returns a nil type with a nil error — this is a **live
panic on user input**. A `UNION` whose branches disagree on a column reaching
that arm crashes the compiler instead of refusing the query. Fix:
`describeColumnType` renders nil as something honest, and a fixture reaches it.

**If no** — nothing can produce a nil `Column.Type` — then `resolvedTypeEqual`'s
nil guard is **dead code claiming a reachability that does not exist**, which is
worse than absent: the next reader takes it as evidence that nil is expected
here and writes more nil handling around it. Fix: delete the guard and say in a
comment why nil is not constructible, or make the impossibility structural.

Do not resolve this by adding a nil check to `describeColumnType` and moving on.
That satisfies both branches without deciding either, and leaves the same
contradiction one function over.

## Acceptance

The answer is stated with the evidence that settles it, and one of the two arms
is removed:

- **Live-panic branch:** an invalid-corpus fixture reaches the type arm with a
  nil (or nil-element) column type and refuses with a message rather than
  panicking. Mutation: deleting the new nil handling in `describeColumnType`
  reddens that fixture — a panic, not a wrong string.
- **Dead-guard branch:** `resolvedTypeEqual`'s nil guard is gone. Mutation:
  reinstating it as `if a == nil || b == nil { return true }` — a compile-valid
  change that inverts what the guard said — reddens nothing, which is the proof
  that nothing reached it. Record that negative in the commit message alongside
  the reachability argument, because a "reddens nothing" result is only evidence
  when the sweep that produced it is named.

Either way, `describeColumnType` and `resolvedTypeEqual` must agree about
whether nil is a value they can be handed, and say so in one place.

## The premise moved before I got here. Read this before the answer.

This bead's title says describeColumnType PANICS on a nil. It does not, as of
PR #2087 (bd gqlc-t802), merged 2026-09-01T22:52Z — about nine minutes before I
claimed this. That PR added `if t == nil { return "<nil>" }` at the top of
describeColumnType and pinned it with two tests.

That is the fix this bead forbids in as many words: "Do not resolve this by
adding a nil check to describeColumnType and moving on." I want to be exact
rather than scoring a point — #2087 did not move on. It argued the posture
(a render called while BUILDING a refusal must total, or the refusal becomes a
crash), matched internal/codegen's resolvedTypeName from PR #937, and said
plainly in its body that no query originates the value and the fault is latent.
What it did not do is settle the reachability question, which is this bead.

## The answer: NO. A nil Column.Type is not constructible from user input.

Column.Type has exactly one writer, scope.go:774, from projectionType. Every
arm of the (ResolvedType, error) surface — projectionType, refProjectionType,
resolveType, callProjectionType, unionProperty, unionNodeProperty,
PropertyUseWitness — returns a value it constructs, or nil with a non-nil
error, or panics. Measured over all 57 return sites in those seven functions:
25 return a composite literal with a nil error, 18 return nil with an error,
10 forward to another function, 4 return a variable. Zero return `nil, nil`.

Two things make that a proof rather than a spot check:

- The surface is CLOSED under forwarding. All 10 forwarding returns target a
  function already in the set, so there is no unaudited edge out of it.
- The 4 variable returns are individually accounted for. Three are assigned a
  composite literal on every path. The fourth is the carried-alias bypass
  (scope.go:956, `return rt, nil`), which returns a value from outside the
  function — and that is the inductive step, not a hole: carriedResolvedTypes
  has one writer (scope.go:145) fed from exportedResolvedTypes, which has two
  (scope.go:1054, 1060), both assigning `s.columns[i].Type` verbatim. A Part
  can PROPAGATE a nil; it cannot originate one, and Part 0 carries nothing.

So the ResolvedList{Element: nil} case #2087 pinned is the same answer one
level down, and its narrower prose reading ("all three ResolvedList
constructions assign a non-nil Element") is true and is a corollary.

## Neither branch of this bead applies as written, and that is the finding

The bead offers exactly two, and says one must be true. The live-panic branch
is out: nothing originates nil. But the dead-guard branch's PROOF is no longer
obtainable either. It asks for resolvedTypeEqual's nil guard to be deleted, with
the evidence being that reinstating it inverted "reddens nothing". #2087's own
battery row M4 mutates that guard to `return true` and reports it KILLED, by
TestCompareBranchColumnsSurvivesANilListElement. A merged test now depends on
the guard, so deleting it reddens the suite — and it depends on it for a real
reason: the guard reporting nil-versus-populated UNEQUAL is precisely how
describeColumnType's nil render gets reached as part of a refusal.

I did not delete the guard. I took the bead's own third option, which it lists
beside deletion: "make the impossibility structural."

## What landed

- `internal/resolver/nilorigination_test.go` — TestNilColumnTypeIsNotConstructible,
  five rows: the audited surface equals an enumerated set; no arm returns a nil
  type with a nil error; forwarding returns stay inside the surface; returns of
  a non-constructed value are enumerated with a reason each; the carry maps are
  written only from column types. It converts the prose reachability argument
  into something that FAILS when an arm changes.
- Comments at both guards now point at that test instead of each implying its
  own answer, which is this bead's closing requirement ("must agree ... and say
  so in one place"). resolvedTypeEqual's guard had no comment at all — the exact
  trap this bead describes, where the next reader reads a guard as evidence that
  nil is expected.

## Mutation battery (ADR 0005)

Base 0349b1cd. Guard committed BEFORE mutating, so a restore cannot delete it.
Per row: apply, read the diff back, `go test -c` compile screen, run, restore,
`git status --short` empty. Baseline asserted green unmutated first.

| # | mutation | want | verdict |
|---|---|---|---|
| M1 | callProjectionType's TypeUnknown arm returns `nil, nil` | KILL | KILLED |
| M2 | a new (ResolvedType, error) function lands unenumerated | KILL | KILLED |
| M3 | a forward routed through a local variable, hiding the callee | KILL | KILLED |
| M4 | unionProperty reshapes its result past the enumerated form | KILL | KILLED |
| M5 | carriedResolvedTypes seeded from a source other than s.columns | KILL | KILLED |
| M6 | resolveType takes named results (a naked return could yield nil,nil) | KILL | KILLED |
| M7 | CONTROL: an arm changes WHICH non-nil variant it returns | SURVIVE | SURVIVED |
| M8 | blind the guard: auditedFuncs reads no non-test source | KILL | KILLED |

M7 is what bounds the claim. The sweep is about nil origination and nothing
else; an arm swapping ResolvedUnknown for ResolvedScalar is invisible to it, by
design, and a battery of kills alone would not have shown that. M6 and M8 fail
at the parent test rather than a named subtest, because both assertions live in
the helper that runs before the subtests — recorded so the table is not read as
claiming subtest-level attribution it does not have.

## Limit of the guard, stated because a sweep's silence is not evidence

It is SYNTACTIC. A helper returning a nil-valued variable through one of the
four enumerated arms would satisfy every row. That is why part three is an
enumeration that fails on a new entry rather than a pattern that accepts one —
a new non-constructing return arrives as a failure with a name on it and has to
have its argument written by a person.

## Filed, not ridden

`gqlc-945h7` (P2) — the two comments I added cite a test by name, and nothing in
this repository checks that such a citation still resolves. Measured: 102
non-test comment lines cite 74 distinct test names; 20 have no declaration,
which is an upper bound containing line-wrap and illustrative artifacts. Two
confirmed dangling by hand, one of them in THIS package —
`resolve.go:1859` makes `TestAnEmptyHopRangeIsNotAWitness` the stated reason
for a `== 1`, and no such test exists. A citation-integrity sweep is a new
instrument surveilling for something other than what this bead asks, so it does
not ride this diff.

## Landed 2026-09-02

PR #2104 squash-merged as 734b8730; GH #722 auto-closed through the verified
closingIssuesReferences. Verified on origin/master rather than inferred from the
merge status: nilorigination_test.go present, both comment edits present in
resolve.go and sumdefaults_internal_test.go, and TestNilColumnTypeIsNotConstructible
PASSES at master head 442af1f2 -- which already carries a LATER resolver commit
(#2103), so the sweep is green against a tree that moved after mine.

The answer: a nil Column.Type is NOT constructible from user input. Established
over all 57 return sites of the seven functions returning (ResolvedType, error),
plus closure under forwarding and an induction on the carry maps. Neither branch
the bead offered applied as written -- the live panic is out (nothing originates
nil) and the dead-guard proof is no longer obtainable (#2087/gqlc-t802 merged a
test that KILLS the guard mutation, and the guard is load-bearing). Took the
third option: make the impossibility structural.

title: resolver: ErrUnionColumnMismatch's name arm prints the same column index twice
description:
## CORRECTION (2026-08-03) — the original diagnosis was wrong

This bead used to claim the name arm "prints a value that is never what it
says". That is **false**, and it was disproved by execution in the `gqlc-nkjt`
round-4 adversarial review. Do not act on the old wording.

Both `%d` column arguments are `i`. But `compareBranchColumns` compares the two
branches **index-wise** — `for i := range base`, `other[i]` against `base[i]` —
so `i` *is* branch 0's column index. The message states a true fact twice under
two labels. The defect is **redundancy, not falsehood**.

Confirmed by output:

    union_column_name_mismatch.cypher
      -> branch 1 column 0 named "name2"; branch 0 column 0 named "a.name"
    union_column_name_only_mismatch.cypher
      -> branch 1 column 0 named "y"; branch 0 column 0 named "x"

## What is actually left to do

### 1. Delete the second index

`internal/resolver/resolve.go:316`:

    "branch %d column %d named %q; branch 0 column %d named %q"

The third `%d` cannot differ from the second while the comparison is positional,
so printing it invites the reader to check two numbers against each other and
learn nothing. One index, named once:

    "branch %d column %d named %q; branch 0 named %q"

or some equivalent that does not restate `i`. If the comparison ever stops being
positional — a named-column join across branches, say — the second index becomes
a real fact and comes back with the code that makes it one.

### 2. The arm-direction question, now that the type arm has settled

The old wording said the name arm "leads with the failing branch, not branch 0"
and that this made two arms of one error read in opposite directions. That split
no longer exists: PR #717 reverted the type arm to lead with the failing branch,
so **all three arms of `ErrUnionColumnMismatch` now lead with the failing branch
and name branch 0 second**. There is nothing inconsistent to fix.

What is left is a single design decision, and this bead is the one place to make
it: **is branch-0-first the better convention?** The argument for it is that
branch 0 names the result columns (R5 §3.1), so it is the reference the other
branches are measured against and reads naturally first. The argument against is
that the reader is looking for the culprit, and the culprit is branch N.

Whichever wins, all three arms move together. Do not change one arm.

### 3. Neither name-arm fixture observes anything about it

`union_column_name_mismatch.cypher` and `union_column_name_only_mismatch.cypher`
both reach this arm, and on both the mismatch sits at column index **0** — so
the duplicated index prints `0` twice and is invisible, and no assertion looks at
the branch order at all. `invalidFixtureContains` has no entry for either. This
is the same pattern the rest of the epic keeps finding: the fixtures reach the
code and observe nothing about it.

A fixture whose mismatch sits at a **non-zero** column index is what makes a
duplicated index visibly wrong rather than coincidentally right — for example
two branches agreeing on column 0 and disagreeing on the name of column 1.

## Acceptance

- The name arm prints each column index once.
- All three arms of `ErrUnionColumnMismatch` state their branches in the same
  order, and that order is a decision recorded here rather than an accident.
- A pinned fixture has its name mismatch at a non-zero column index, so the
  index in the message is a fact about that fixture and not the constant 0.
- Mutation: swapping the name arm's branch order, or replacing either printed
  index with a literal `0`, reddens a test. Both mutations must be compile-valid
  and neither may be blessable by `-update` — invalid fixtures have no golden,
  so the pin belongs in `invalidFixtureContains` or an equivalent hand-written
  assertion.
notes:
2026-08-03: body REWRITTEN. The original diagnosis — that the second index 'prints a value that is never what it says' — was disproved by execution in the gqlc-nkjt round-4 review. The comparison is index-wise, so i IS branch 0's column index: the message is redundant, not false. The 'two arms read in opposite directions' half is also gone; PR #717 reverted the type arm to lead with the failing branch, so all three arms now agree. What remains: delete the duplicated index, decide the branch-order convention for all three arms in one place, and fixture a mismatch at a non-zero column index.
PRIORITY RAISED P3 -> P2 by agent-a 2026-08-30, under the king's ruling on gqlc-nhv64.

WHY. The RCA behind that ruling found the fleet had spent 88% of its completed
work since the founding on the machinery and 12% on gqlc. Part of the remedy is
that the router's max_priority is 2, so this bead sat where nobody could ever be
routed to it. It is gqlc work and the fleet is being pointed back at gqlc.

This is a deliberate, reasoned promotion and not a sweep: of 92 product beads on
the floor I promoted 42. Left down there on purpose were 37 that are prose,
comment, fence and witness defects rather than gqlc capability — the same
meta-work pathology the RCA found in the machinery, and promoting those would
have moved the disease into the product — plus 6 blocked on the missing ISO
arbiter (gqlc-lir), 4 misfiled machinery beads, and 3 deliberately deferred to a
later version.

If you believe this bead was sorted wrongly, say so and I will re-rule it; the
classification was mine and it was a judgement, not a measurement.
WORKED 2026-09-01, agent agent-e, branch fix/gqlc-eb5j-union-column-mismatch-index.

Item 1 (delete the second index) and item 3 (a fixture that observes it) done
together, test-first. Item 2 (arm direction) answered and recorded in code.

THE RED, before any change to resolve.go. New fixture
invalid/union_column_name_mismatch_nonzero_index.cypher — branches agree on
column 0 (both "x", both STRING NOT NULL, so the name arm is reached rather than
the type arm) and differ on column 1's name. Pinned the intended single-index
message in invalidFixtureContains and ran it:

  Error "union column mismatch: branch 1 column 1 named "z"; branch 0 column 1
  named "y"" does not contain "branch 1 column 1 named "z"; branch 0 named "y""

That failure is also the control the bead asked for: it confirms the fixture
reaches the name arm at a NON-ZERO index, and shows the duplicated index
printing 1 twice. Both existing name-arm fixtures sit at column 0, where the
restated index prints 0 and is indistinguishable from a coincidence.

THE FIX. resolve.go:341, third %d and its second `i` argument removed. Green.

ITEM 2 — ANSWERED NO, keep the failing branch first. Branch 0 defines the
result columns (R5 §3.1), which is the argument for leading with it, but the
reader arrives already knowing that and looking for the branch to go and edit.
PR #717 had already moved the type arm deliberately to this direction, so
reversing now would undo a considered decision to no benefit. Recorded in
compareBranchColumns' doc comment naming this bead, so it reads as settled
rather than unasked.

SPEC. docs/specs/resolver-stage-r5.md §4.3 Rule 2 quoted the old format string
and is corrected here, since my change is what made it false.

FILED, NOT RIDDEN IN: gqlc-eeq4y — the same section's Rule 3 quotes a type-arm
message the code has not emitted since PR #728. Pre-existing, different defect.

SWEEP MANIFEST. test/data/resolver/sweep.manifest.tsv regenerated. Delta audited
row by row rather than accepted: header 322->323 queries and 12880->12920 cells
(+40 = one fixture x 40 schemas, accept unchanged at 3856, refuse +40); three
union msg digests rewritten to the single-index spelling; two new
"unknown property: c.ein" messages from the new fixture against schemas without
Company.ein. No unrelated row moved.

NOTE for the PR body: the manifest already pins message text, so it — not my
new assertion — is what would catch a bare wording regression. The new
fixture's actual contribution is the non-zero index, which no existing fixture
could observe.
PR #2103 opened (head eae7195b), Closes #716 verified via closingIssuesReferences. just gates green on the final tree. Mutation battery of four rows all KILLED, plus a measured counterfactual: the row that prints the branch index in the column position SURVIVED against the earlier column-1 fixture and is KILLED against the shipped column-2 one, which is what justifies the third column. No review owed — no design bead blocks this, no protocol amendment, nobody asked.
close_reason: Merged as 442af1f2 (PR #2103). The name-mismatch arm now reads 'branch %d column %d named %q; branch 0 named %q' — one index, because the comparison is positional and the doubled index read as if branch 0's column could be elsewhere. New fixture union_column_name_mismatch_nonzero_index.cypher pins a mismatch at column 2 of branch 1, so column index and branch index disagree and a mutation printing b for i is visible. R5 spec 4.3 Rule 2 corrected to quote the emitted string. Item 2 (should branch 0 lead?) answered no, in the doc comment on compareBranchColumns.

title: spec: C1/C4/C5 still document the parameter-name-derived bare arg lhs3 removed
description:
The C1/C4/C5 specs still document the single-parameter signature as taking a
**parameter-name-derived** bare argument. That derivation is dead code, and the
name it derives is the capture vector `gqlc-lhs3` exists to close.

`docs/specs/codegen-stage-c1.md` §5.x `<param-list>` (lines 662-667) states the
rule in full: `paramFieldName(name)` → `MinAge` → lowercase → `minAge`. The
emitter does not do that. It emits `arg`, unconditionally, precisely so that no
author-chosen parameter name reaches the signature and captures a
generator-owned local.

So a reader implementing to spec reintroduces the vulnerability. This is not
cosmetic drift — it is a spec that documents the defect as the design.

## Sites

`docs/specs/codegen-stage-c1.md` — the authoritative section, per
`codegen-stage-c0.md:1112`, which routes "Method-signature naming rules (Params
vs bare arg…)" here:

- §3.1 line 243 — `func (q *Queries) PersonById(ctx context.Context, id int64)`;
  emitted is `arg int64`.
- §3.2 lines 273-275 — "single-parameter takes the bare typed arg". Shape right,
  name wrong.
- §5.x `<param-list>` lines 662-667 — the whole `<bareParam>` derivation rule.
  Dead.
- §5.x `<paramsMap>` line ~678 — "One parameter:
  `map[string]any{"<rawName>": <bareParam>}`". Emitted is `arg`. Note the map
  **key** is still the raw name and correctly so; only the value moved.
- §5.5 worked example lines 1203-1204 — `PersonName(ctx context.Context, id
  int64)` / `map[string]any{"id": id}`.
- §9 fixture table line 1152 — "single-param bare arg (`func (q *Queries)
  PersonName(ctx, id int64)`)".

`docs/specs/codegen-stage-c4.md` — lines 362, 403, 838. Line 838 is inside the
`WriteQuerier` **interface** member, so the drift is in a declared surface, not
only in prose: `RemovePerson(ctx context.Context, id int64) error`.

`docs/specs/codegen-stage-c5.md` — lines 438, 996: `PersonAction(ctx, id
int64)`, `GetAction(ctx, since int64)`.

## Separately, §4.6 is falsified

`codegen-stage-c1.md` §4.6 lines 513-529 — "Why `<methodName>QueryText` consts
do not participate in the sweep" — rests on the claim that "a duplicate at this
axis would already imply a duplicate method-name collision the exported sweep
catches first". `gqlc-igs4` is a worked counterexample: schema label
`FooQueryText` plus `// name: DecodeFoo` collides a generator-owned const with a
generator-owned func, no method name is duplicated, and the axis §4.6 defers to
never sees it. The corresponding code comments were corrected on `lhs3`'s
branch; the spec was not.

Fix §4.6 to state the hole, or to state the disambiguation once `gqlc-igs4`
lands. Do not restate `gqlc-igs4`'s argument here — cite it.

## Why this recurs

Nothing holds these specs against the emitter. Every `func (q *Queries) …`
signature in the specs is a claim about emitted bytes that the golden corpus
already contains, and no test compares them. Consider whether the worked
examples can be extracted and diffed against a golden, or a fixture named from
the spec section — and if that is not tractable, say so explicitly in the fix so
the next drift is expected rather than surprising.

Acceptance: no spec under `docs/specs/` shows a single-parameter query method
taking a parameter-name-derived argument; §4.6 states what is true about the
QueryText const namespace; and either a check exists that reddens when a spec
signature diverges from the emitted one, or the specs carry a note recording
that they are unfenced prose and why.

title: codegen/age: the Scalar type table has zero corpus reach
description:
AGE's `Scalar` type table has **zero** corpus reach. It is checked only by a
hand-written mirror of itself.

Reproduction (from `gqlc-9n6t`'s review): replace all six AGE `Scalar` arms in
`internal/codegen/age/types.go` with garbage — `MUT_bool`, `MUT_int64`, and so
on — and run

    go test -count=1 ./internal/codegen/conformance/ -update

**Zero goldens change.** `TestValid`, `TestDoubleRun`, `TestGoldenBuild` and
`TestBackendInvariantSurface` all stay green. The only test that fires is
`internal/codegen/age/types_test.go:TestTypeMapScalar`, which is a hand-written
copy of the table it is checking — so it asserts the table equals itself and
would move happily alongside any edit to it.

`ScalarBool`, `ScalarInt`, `ScalarFloat` and `ScalarString` are *served* by AGE,
so this is not a case of nothing being reachable. No valid fixture enrols an AGE
target on a query projecting a bare scalar **expression** column. Property
columns take a different path (`Property`, not `Scalar`) and are well covered,
which is why the gap is easy to miss.

This is another instance of the pattern this epic keeps turning up: a check that
is green because it is looking at nothing. It is pre-existing — `9n6t` neither
caused it nor worsened it — but `9n6t` added the claim that the type tables are
"total, and on a ground that can be checked", and on AGE the ground is not
checked end to end.

Fix: enrol at least one AGE-targeted valid fixture per served `Scalar` arm,
projecting a bare scalar expression column (e.g. `RETURN 1`, `RETURN 'x'`,
`RETURN 1.5`, `RETURN true`, or the same via a function call whose return type
resolves through `callProjectionType`). Then the golden diff is the check and
`TestTypeMapScalar` stops being the only thing standing between a wrong arm and
a green build.

Acceptance: mutating any served AGE `Scalar` arm reddens the conformance suite
through a golden diff, not only through `TestTypeMapScalar`; and the mutation
survives `-update` (regenerating must not make it green, because the emitted Go
must stop compiling or stop matching the invariant surface).
close_reason: Fixed and merged in PR #1381, squashed onto master as sha e08ceea5. Verified on master rather than on the branch: the fixture test/data/codegen/valid/scalar_expression_columns/ exists with manifest.json, queries.cypher, schema.gql and goldens under apache-age-pgx-v5, neo4j-go-v5 and neo4j-go-v6. Before this, no fixture anywhere projected a bare scalar expression column, so every served arm of the AGE Scalar table was pinned only by a hand-written copy of itself in types_test.go and a wrong arm reached a green build. The authoring lane measured the guard rather than assuming it: mutating ScalarBool to return int64 reddens TestValid on the golden diff AND survives -update, because the regenerated golden then fails TestBackendInvariantSurface/scalar_expression_columns. I closed this bead, not the lane -- it was killed after merging but before finishing its closes. Not verified by me: I did not re-run that mutation, and I confirmed artifact presence on master rather than re-deriving the table.

title: captured agtype corpus text is never checked against a live AGE 1.7.0
description:
The AGE decode tests assert against **captured** agtype text — literal strings
committed to the corpus as the representative of what a live server returns.
Nothing checks that capture against a live AGE 1.7.0.

So the decode path is tested against the author's belief about agtype's wire
form rather than against agtype. If a capture is wrong — a nested list rendered
one bracket-depth off, a float spelled without its `::float` annotation, a null
element spelled `null` where the server sends something else — the unit tests
are green, the live tests are green (they exercise a different, real path), and
the divergence surfaces only on a shape the live corpus happens not to cover.

This matters more after `gqlc-35yu.13` than before it. Scalars are easy to get
right by inspection; nested lists (`[][]float32`) and heterogeneous ANY lists are
not, and those are exactly the shapes `.13` added. The nested case is where a
capture is most likely to be wrong and least likely to be noticed.

The obvious fix — assert the captures against a live server — has a scheduling
problem: AGE live tests run only nightly on master (`live-smoke-age` is
`if: github.event_name != 'pull_request'`), so a wrong capture would not redden
a PR. That is acceptable for a drift detector, which is what this is: the
captures are correct today or they are not, and a nightly job that reddens
tells us within a day.

Fix: a live test behind the `codegen_live` tag that, for each captured agtype
literal in the corpus, issues the query that produced it against the pinned AGE
image and asserts the server's bytes equal the capture. Keep the captures — the
point is not to stop using them but to know when they stop being true. Where a
capture cannot be reproduced by a single query, either drop it or record in the
test why it is synthetic.

Acceptance: every captured agtype literal used by a decode test is either
reproduced from the live pinned image (`apache/age@sha256:4241e2d8bb86a6b2ea44e9ad06c73856e12b209de295124603a599dd7feb70eb`,
PostgreSQL 18.1 / AGE 1.7.0) or is explicitly marked synthetic with a reason; and
corrupting any one capture reddens the live suite.

title: codegen/age: list expression columns still refused though .13 built the decode path
description:
`gqlc-35yu.13` taught the AGE backend to serve list-valued *properties*. It did
not lift the refusal on list-valued *expression* columns: `resolver.ResolvedList`
is still listed in `unservedColumn` for `apache-age-pgx-v5`.

That refusal was correct when AGE had no list decode path at all. It now has
one — agtype carries arrays natively, which is precisely why `.13` was
tractable — so the refusal outlives its reason.

The gap is visible as a backend asymmetry, which is the property this project
most cares about: a query returning `collect(p.name)` or a list literal generates
on the neo4j targets and is refused on AGE, so the Go surface a caller writes
against *does* vary by backend for that column kind. `TestBackendInvariantSurface`
does not catch it because the AGE side never generates at all.

Not folded into `.13` because `.13`'s scope was properties, and the expression
path reaches `ResolvedList` through `callProjectionType` rather than through a
schema property — different provenance, different width reasoning. Worth its own
bead precisely so the width argument gets made rather than assumed: a property's
element type comes from the schema and is therefore known, whereas a
`collect()`'s element type is inferred, and the inference may admit element types
the decode path cannot represent. The refusal may narrow rather than disappear.

Acceptance: a list *expression* column either generates on AGE with the same Go
surface the neo4j targets emit, or is refused for a reason that names the
element type it cannot represent rather than the column kind. Either way
`ResolvedList` stops being an unconditional entry in AGE's `unservedColumn`, and
a fixture pins whichever verdict lands.
close_reason: Fixed, not stale. Confirmed on master before touching it that the agtype list decode path already existed (agtypeList[T] plus the per-slice wrappers writeListHelper emits, selected by Go type text through decodeFunc) while resolver.ResolvedList was still an unconditional refusal in age/errors.go — so the refusal had been outlived by its own decode path. Replaced it with unservedListElement, which reviewers the ELEMENT: scalars bool/int/float/string and lists of them are served, ScalarNull and ScalarMap refuse, an uncarried property width refuses by name, goInstant refuses because its zone has no sidecar to ride in, node/edge/edge-union refuse, and nesting recurses. Measured by a 14-row table in internal/codegen/age/list_expression_column_test.go pinning each refusal's exact text, plus four corpus fixtures (list_int, list_string, list_list_int, list_unknown) newly enrolled for apache-age-pgx-v5 with generated goldens. Honestly recorded side effect: opening the path re-exposes codegen.Prepare's list-element temporal fail-site, so TestListOfTemporalYieldsToTheTypeTable and a new subtest in conformance/assembled_input_test.go pin that error from both sides. Merged in PR #1381.

title: decoder/QueryText-const namespaces can collide; generate exits 0 on non-compiling Go
description:
A schema label ending in `QueryText` collides with the query-text constant of a
like-named method, and `gqlc generate` exits 0 while emitting Go that does not
compile.

Schema label `FooQueryText` plus `// name: DecodeFoo` emits both

    func decodeFooQueryText(...)
    const decodeFooQueryText = `...`

into one package, and `go build` then fails:

    decodeFooQueryText redeclared in this block

This is the **loud** half of the capture class `gqlc-lhs3` closed the silent half
of. It fails at build time rather than shipping a wrong runtime value, so it is
not urgent — but it falsifies two statements the codebase now asserts, and those
are what make it worth fixing rather than documenting:

- the `QueryTextConst` doc comment says the method name is "already unique
  across the package". It is not unique against the **decoder** namespace.
- `sweepIdentifiers`' comment says `<methodName>QueryText` consts "stay off the
  sweep … a QueryText collision is caught by the method-name axis first". It is
  not caught: the collision is between a generator-owned const and a
  generator-owned func, so neither the method-name axis nor the parameter-name
  axis sees it.

So the emitted package has two generator-owned namespaces — decoders derived
from schema labels, and query-text consts derived from method names — that can
collide with each other. Both are generator-owned, which is why the capture
guards (which police *author*-chosen identifiers against generator-owned ones)
are structurally blind to it.

Confirmed identical at `9b87846`, so `gqlc-lhs3` neither causes nor worsens it.
The two comments above were corrected on that branch to state what is true; this
bead is the collision itself.

Fix: the two namespaces need to be disjoint by construction, the same way
`gqlc-ak39` made the generator-owned scope a closed set. A suffix or prefix that
cannot appear in a derived decoder name, or a single collision check across all
generator-owned package-level names, either would do. Prefer the closure
approach — a guard asserting the generator-owned package-level names are
pairwise distinct is an equality assertion, not a disjointness one, and cannot
be blessed away.

Acceptance: `FooQueryText` + `// name: DecodeFoo` either generates a compiling
package or is refused at generate time with a message naming both colliding
constructs; a fixture holds it; and the guard goes red if the disambiguation is
removed.

  $ go build ./gen/              -> exit 1

title: codegen: a relationship type the schema does not declare is narrowed away without a diagnostic
description:
A query naming a relationship type the schema does not declare is accepted
silently. gqlc narrows the candidate set to the declared subset and leaves the
query text verbatim (ADR 0005), so the emitted code is well-typed over the
declared types while the *server* may return edges of the undeclared one.

Surfaced on `gqlc-35yu.14`, where this is exactly what makes the edge-union
the router's `default:` arm reachable — and there it is legitimate. It models
**schema drift**: the graph grows a relationship type ahead of the GQL schema,
and the sealed interface correctly has no member for it, so the row fails at
runtime with a clear error rather than decoding into the wrong arm.

The problem is that the same silence covers a **typo**. An author who writes
`ACTED_INN` gets no diagnostic at generate time — only a runtime failure on
rows that will never arrive, or worse, a query that quietly matches nothing.
Drift and typo are indistinguishable to gqlc today.

They are not indistinguishable in principle: drift means the query names a type
the schema lacks *and* the author expects rows of it; a typo means the same
shape with no such expectation. gqlc cannot read intent, but it can say what it
did — narrowing the candidate set is a decision the author should be told about.

Fix: emit a diagnostic (warning, not refusal — refusing would break the drift
case the `.14` fixture depends on) naming each relationship type in the query
that the schema does not declare, and stating that it was excluded from the
candidate set. Refusing is wrong here; silence is also wrong.

Acceptance: generating `edge_union_undeclared_relationship_type` still succeeds
and still reaches the `default:` arm live, but names the undeclared type on
stderr, and a test holds that message.
notes: 2026-08-23 (compiler lane, PR #1329 session): not attempted, out of that session's lane. Recording the shape so the next attempt does not re-derive it. The narrowing this bead complains about lives in internal/resolver/resolve.go (candidateTypes / NarrowPluralEndpoints), not in internal/codegen, so the diagnostic has to originate there. The second half is harder than it looks: the bead asks for a non-fatal warning on stderr, and no such channel exists. internal/cli/pipeline/pipeline.go's Diagnostics is a fatal-accumulation channel, every entry appended to it fails the run, so a warning would either have to be a new severity on that type or a separate sink threaded from the resolver out to the CLI. Design that before writing the detection, or the detection will end up wired to a channel that refuses the compile.
close_reason: Merged as master b30d41e1 via PR #1356. ADR 0032 decides WARN, not refuse: refusing would delete this repo's only live reach into an edge-union default arm, so ADR 0030's silent-wrong asymmetry does not transfer. Built the smallest non-fatal lane the previous decline said did not exist: ValidatedQuery.Warnings, pipeline.Result.Warnings, printed to stderr by generate before the diagnostics and not counted by the summary error. Detector fires only on a relationship type declared in NO edge declaration; an endpoint-narrowed but declared type stays silent, pinned by TestEndpointNarrowedButDeclaredTypeIsSilent. Corpus witness for the omitempty: twelve thousand seven hundred and ninety-eight of the sweep's twelve thousand eight hundred and eighty cells unchanged, and the eighty-two that moved are exactly the foreign-schema cross-product cells. Nine mutations screened for compilability and all killed. Open question filed as gqlc-he8v.

title: [bug] codegen/age: the capture guard parses only .cypher.go, so cross-file emitted names are unswept
description:
The AGE capture guard parses only `.cypher.go` — `emitQueryFiles` filters to that
suffix — so package-level declarations emitted into `db.go` and `models.go` are
never seen, even though the generated package is one Go package and a query
method's body can resolve them.

Demonstrated by the `gqlc-gjqo` reviewer at `8f80a46`: adding
`const gqlcDefaultGraph = "gqlc"` to `render_db.go` plus a reference to it from
the `.cypher.go` body emits a package that compiles (`just test-codegen-fence`:
0 issues) with **both** capture guards green at exit 0.

## Why this is not already covered

`capture_test.go:322` says capturing a cross-file name "is a hard failure of the
generated package rather than a silent one (gqlc-ni66)". That is true **today**
and **by accident**. The current cross-file package-level set is
`ErrNoRows`/`ErrMultipleResults` (typed `error`), `DBTX`/`Queries` (types), `New`
(func), and `maxGraphNameBytes` (untyped int, unreferenced from `.cypher.go`).
Every one is loud when shadowed by a `string` parameter because of how it
happens to be typed — not because anything prevents a future `string`-typed
cross-file declaration.

A `string`-typed one is exactly the silent case: it type-checks, and the caller's
runtime value silently becomes whatever the emitted body uses it for. That is the
same shape as the `<bare>QueryText` const, which is the worst instance of this
whole class and the reason it blocked `gqlc-35yu.10`.

**Not covered by [[gqlc-ni66]]**, despite the comment's pointer: ni66 is the
*loud* signature-binder class (`q`, `ctx`, receiver). It does not carry the silent
cross-file class. **Not covered by [[gqlc-3o3p]]** either, which is the
lift-the-sweep-to-neo4j axis.

## Why it was not fixed on gqlc-gjqo

gjqo is scoped to shape coverage *within* a backend's `.cypher.go` emission, and
it closed that. The reviewer notes a per-method free-identifier diff would detect
the cross-file class cheaply, but it would go red on findings belonging to other
beads, so folding it in would have coupled three separate fixes on one branch.

## Scope

Widen the guard's parse set beyond `.cypher.go` to the whole emitted package, so
the reachability check is over the package's real scope rather than one file's.
Expect it to go red on constructs owned by `gqlc-ni66`; sequence accordingly or
scope the new assertion to the silent (string-typed) subset.

Also: correct the `capture_test.go:322` comment, which currently asserts a
structural guarantee the code does not have. (A one-line wording fix is being
taken on the gjqo branch itself; this bead owns the actual detection.)

Acceptance: a `string`-typed package-level declaration emitted into `db.go` or
`models.go` and referenced from a `.cypher.go` method body is caught by the
capture guard, and the catch survives `go test ./internal/codegen/conformance/
-update`.
notes: MEASURED, 2026-08-23: the bead's own falsifier does not falsify. codegen.ParamArg means a query parameter name never becomes a Go identifier in the emitted signature, so adding a string-typed gqlcDefaultGraph const to render_db.go plus a plain reference from a .cypher.go body captures nothing and is correctly green. The parse-set hole is real; the witness proposed for it was not. The witness that works: the same const PLUS a body local named after the query parameter that reads it. Old guard on that emitter exits zero; the widened guard fails at all three arities. Fixed in PR #1356.
close_reason: Merged as master b30d41e1 via PR #1356. The capture sweep now parses the whole emitted package, and the reachability claim became differential against a baseline emitted under a generated parameter name, because the absolute claim is false of the package: ReadQuerier is resolved by callers and by nothing the emitter writes. Measured, not read. Witness: a string-typed gqlcDefaultGraph const in render_db.go plus a body local named after the query parameter that reads it. Old guard on that emitter exits zero; the widened guard fails at all three arities. The bead's OWN falsifier does not falsify, because codegen.ParamArg means a query parameter name never becomes a Go identifier; recorded in the notes and followed up as gqlc-9o4t.

title: [bug] bd-gh-sync push path keeps the id-quoting hazard the pull path just closed
description:
The *pull* path in `.githooks/bd-gh-sync` was hardened on `gqlc-63y`'s branch:
ids are batched by hand rather than through `xargs`, refused by name when they
carry characters that would re-parse (quotes, spaces, leading dashes), and the
summary reports what was actually pulled rather than what failed to fail.

**The push path was left exactly as it was.** It still does the equivalent of
`bd github push $_ids` under `xargs`, so:

- an id containing a quote or a space re-parses and aborts the batch;
- an id with a leading dash arrives as a flag rather than a value;
- `|| true` swallows the non-zero, so the batch silently pushes nothing and the
  run still reports success.

That is the same defect class the pull path just closed, on the arm that
*mutates GitHub* rather than the one that reads it.

Why it was not folded into `gqlc-63y`: push has no summary contract to assert
against — the pull fixes are all anchored on "the summary must say what
happened", and push says nothing at all today. Closing this properly means
first deciding what push's success/failure contract is, which is a design
question rather than a hardening one, and it does not belong riding on a branch
that was already on its fourth round.

Scope: give push the same id-refusal gate and hand-rolled batching as pull, and
give it a summary contract that distinguishes "pushed N" from "pushed nothing
because every batch aborted". Reuse the `bd_list_fails` / `bd_list_emits` stub
knobs that branch added — the harness can now express the breaking input.

Acceptance: a bead id containing a space, a quote, or a leading dash makes
`bd-gh-sync push` exit non-zero and name the offending bead, rather than exiting
0 having pushed nothing.
