title: [EPIC] codegen: multi-backend architecture + Apache AGE (pgx v5) target
description:
Why: internal/codegen emits only neo4j-go-driver v5/v6, and neo4j specifics live in the shared core (prepare.go decode strategies are named after neo4j.GetRecordValue/dbtype shapes; render templates inline neo4j API). Goal: refactor so each backend is its own sub-package implementing the Generator seam, then add Apache AGE (Postgres extension, github.com/apache/age) as a second backend family.

Locked design (grill session 2026-07-31):
- Seam: internal/codegen keeps Input/File/Generator/errors + phases Z/A/B (admission, naming) with the Go-type mapping parametrized per backend; internal/codegen/neo4j and internal/codegen/age each implement Generator end-to-end and own their render layer. No fine-grained render-plugin interface — AGE emission differs too radically for holes shaped by n=1 backend.
- AGE runtime: generated code imports github.com/jackc/pgx/v5 only (major-only import paths; consumer go.mod picks the minor, like neo4j today). DBTX interface satisfied by pool/conn/tx + WithTx(pgx.Tx). gqlc emits its own agtype decode helpers. The apache/age Go driver is disqualified for generated code: its parameter path is fmt.Sprintf interpolation into Cypher text (injection vector), it drags lib/pq + the ANTLR runtime into consumer builds, and it has been dormant since 2024 (verified from drivers/golang source 2026-07-31).
- Registry: codegen.Registry + Entry{Key, New}, constructed explicitly at the CLI composition root — no init() registration, no package-level state. Keyed by config wire strings. Config keeps its closed Driver enum and parse-time errors; a parity test asserts registry keys == config.DriverValues(). New wire key: apache-age-pgx-v5 (const DriverApacheAgePgxV5).
- Graph lifecycle: New(db DBTX, graph string) — graph name is a runtime arg (AGE analogue of neo4j database selection). EnsureGraph/DropGraph are methods on the generated Queries handle (join the reserved-identifier sweep; excluded from the Querier interfaces); package-level SessionInit matching pgxpool AfterConnect runs LOAD age; all emitted SQL fully qualifies ag_catalog.cypher / ag_catalog.agtype so search_path is never a session dependency. This makes parallel acceptance tests trivial: unique graph per test + EnsureGraph + Cleanup DropGraph, one shared container.
- Type gaps: agtype has NO native temporal types (verified against src/include/utils/agtype.h enum: NULL/STRING/NUMERIC/INTEGER/FLOAT/BOOL/VERTEX/EDGE/PATH/ARRAY/OBJECT). Spike bead validates real temporal + parameter behavior against a live container FIRST; agreed fallback is faithful per-type encodings (timestamp=epoch-micros integer, date=ISO string, duration=ISO-8601 string, zoned=offset-preserving string) with the Go surface identical across backends; generate-time error reserved for types with no faithful encoding.
- Tests: fixtures restructure to one dir + per-target golden subtrees with a manifest targets list (omitted = all registered); the suite iterates fixtures x registry, so registering a backend auto-enrolls it and a missing golden subtree is a red test. TestGoldenBuild stays the fully generic compile gate (compiles the whole nested module). Live tests: shared scenario battery against a test-local structural interface + per-backend adapters (generated method sets are signature-identical across backends); AGE arm uses unique-graph-per-scenario parallel isolation; joins the codegen_live nightly job; AGE image digest-pinned (gqlc-9u5 precedent). PR CI wall-time untouched.
- Process: every implementation bead follows TDD (failing golden/fixture/live test first), one sibling worktree + stacked branch per bead, PR per bead.

Child DAG: core-split -> registry -> fixture-migration -> live-refactor; spike independent (parallel); C0 needs registry+fixtures; scalar-reads needs spike+C0; live-arm+CI needs live-refactor+scalar-reads; entity-columns and write-path need scalar-reads+live-arm; temporals need write-path+live-arm. Dialect-gap posture is unblocked backlog.
acceptance_criteria: All child beads closed; gqlc generate with gen.go.driver apache-age-pgx-v5 produces a package that compiles (generic golden build gate) and passes the shared live scenario battery against a live AGE container.
notes:
=== SPIKE gqlc-35yu.5 OUTCOME (2026-07-31) — TWO LOCKED DECISIONS AMENDED ===
Owner-approved amendments. Full evidence (818 lines) in gqlc-35yu.5.
AGE image pinned for all downstream work:
  apache/age@sha256:4241e2d8bb86a6b2ea44e9ad06c73856e12b209de295124603a599dd7feb70eb
  (PostgreSQL 18.1, AGE 1.7.0)

1. SEARCH_PATH — the locked claim is FALSE, decision reversed.
   Locked text said: "all emitted SQL fully qualifies ag_catalog.cypher /
   ag_catalog.agtype so search_path is never a session dependency."
   Empirically: full qualification is NECESSARY BUT NOT SUFFICIENT. AGE's own
   Cypher->SQL transform emits BARE OPERATORS (=, >, +, @>) and does not emit
   the OPERATOR(ag_catalog.=) form, so Postgres resolves them through
   search_path. With ag_catalog off the path and every identifier qualified:
   RETURN 1, bare MATCH and ORDER BY succeed, but
     WHERE n.name = 'alice'      -> ERROR: cannot cast agtype string to boolean
     MATCH (n:P {name:'alice'})  -> ERROR: operator does not exist: agtype @> agtype
     RETURN 1+1                  -> same, for +
   gqlc CANNOT fix this by emitting better SQL: the operators come from AGE's
   transform, not from us.
   AMENDED DECISION (owner, 2026-07-31): ag_catalog MUST be on the session
   search_path, and SessionInit is the enforcement point. SessionInit runs
   LOAD 'age', then SET search_path = ag_catalog + the caller's, then a CANARY
   that exercises an operator (RETURN 1 = 1) and returns an error if it fails.
   Rationale for the canary: SessionInit is the pgxpool AfterConnect hook, so
   returning an error there keeps the connection OUT of the pool — the failure
   surfaces at connection establishment (at startup for a pinging/pre-warming
   consumer) rather than when the first WHERE clause runs. This matters because
   AGE's failure mode is PARTIAL: simple queries succeed while operator queries
   fail, so a misconfigured deployment otherwise looks healthy until first use.
   Costs one round trip per new pool connection; pool conns are long-lived.
   New(db, graph) is UNCHANGED — verification lives in SessionInit, so the
   constructor still does no I/O and still returns no error.

2. TEMPORAL ENCODING TABLE — 2 of 4 amended (spike mandate covered this).
   Failed encodings round-trip correctly but SORT WRONG, which breaks
   WHERE n.ts > $param. Ordering, not round-tripping, is the real gate.
     timestamp/instant | epoch-MICROS int64                    | CONFIRMED
     date              | ISO 'YYYY-MM-DD' string, zero-padded  | CONFIRMED
     duration          | total-MICROS int64                    | AMENDED
     zoned datetime    | TWO int64 props: <f> epoch-micros     | AMENDED
                       |   plus <f>Offset offset-seconds       |
     calendar duration | no faithful encoding (months/years    | generate-time
                       |   are not a fixed micro count)        |   error
   duration as ISO-8601 string sorted P1D, PT10H, PT1H, PT2H, PT90M — and
   WHERE v > 'PT2H' returned only PT90M (1.5h): one false positive, two false
   negatives. zoned as offset-preserving string returned an 07:00Z row for
   WHERE v > '...08:00+00:00'. A map {t,o} also sorts wrong (jsonb key order)
   and would force gqlc to rewrite user ORDER BY; the FLAT SIDECAR keeps the
   sort key as the property itself, so user ORDER BY passes through untouched.
   date stays a string by owner decision (2026-07-31) despite agtype string
   comparison using DB COLLATION rather than byte order — ISO dates are
   fixed-width digits and hyphens, and readability in the stored graph wins.
   No temporal casts exist in AGE (full pg_cast table captured in the spike);
   the only temporal function is timestamp(), returning epoch-MILLIS.

3. PARAMETER MECHANISM — selected: direct cypher('<graph>', $$...$$, $1) over
   the pgx extended protocol. age_prepare_cypher REJECTED: it latches query
   text into the plan via connection-global state at Parse time, which pgx
   statement caching schedules unpredictably. Server-log evidence: parse/bind/
   execute are separate phases and the logged statement text ends in the
   literal $1 at every phase, with the payload appearing only under
   DETAIL: Parameters. A Cypher-injection canary table survived intact.
   Note: pgx SimpleProtocol — the only interpolating mode — is the one mode
   AGE rejects outright, so the unsafe path fails closed.

=== AMENDMENT 3 (owner, 2026-08-01) — FIXTURE ENROLLMENT IS EXPLICIT, NOT AUTOMATIC ===

--- agent-a, 2026-08-29: LABELLED class:designer. The old protection is dead. ---

title: bd pull re-derives in_progress from started_at, silently reverting a deliberate 'open'
description:
`bd update <id> --status open` does not stick for any bead that was ever
claimed. The next `bd-gh-sync pull` re-derives `in_progress` from the bead's
non-nil `started_at`, and the next `chore(bd)` export PR then silently
reverts master.

## Evidence

`gqlc-4np` was deliberately set to `open` last session, pending an ADR call,
and committed to master that way. It came back as `in_progress`.

It is not coming from GitHub: `GH#503` is OPEN with zero assignees, and
GitHub has no in-progress state to map from. It is bd reconstructing the
status locally from `started_at = 2026-07-28T09:55:09Z`.

Proof it was the pull and not a human: `gqlc-4np.updated_at` is
`2026-07-31T00:05:31Z`, byte-identical to the epoch embedded in the ghost
bead id the SAME pull minted (`gqlc-1785456331014`). The hook reported
"Pulled 2 issues (1 created, 1 updated)" -- this is the updated one.

## Why it cannot be worked around

`bd update` exposes no flag to clear `started_at`. `--defer` and `--due` both
take an empty string to clear; `started_at` has no equivalent. So `open` is
not a reachable steady state for a previously-claimed bead.

Worked around for now by using `blocked`, which carries the same intent
("not being worked, waiting on a decision") and sits outside the
re-derivation path. Whether `blocked` also gets re-derived is untested --
the next pull will tell.

## Review implication

Diff every `chore(bd)` export record by record, parsing the +/- JSON lines
and printing `id | status`. This revert is one line out of 234 and is
invisible in a diffstat. Cf. memory `patch-check-does-not-detect-reverts`.

Memory: `bd-pull-rederives-in-progress-from-started-at`.

## Correction 2026-07-31: `blocked` is NOT a workaround

The original text above proposed `blocked` as a status that carries the same
intent and sits outside the re-derivation path. That was asserted without
testing and it is **false**. Measured, both arms, deterministic:

    bd update gqlc-4np --status blocked ; .githooks/bd-gh-sync pull  -> in_progress
    bd update gqlc-4np --status open    ; .githooks/bd-gh-sync pull  -> in_progress

The re-derivation overrides *any* non-closed status. For a bead that was ever
claimed, `in_progress` is the only reachable steady state short of closing it.

PR #612's body and commit message carry the same wrong claim; this bead is the
correction of record.

Caught only because `just init` re-activated the local hooks, so `post-merge`
started firing the pull again and the revert reappeared within one merge. It
had been latent while `core.hooksPath` was pointing at an empty directory.
notes:
=== SAME CLASS, DIFFERENT TRIGGER: a git-side revert of the JSONL rolls the DB
back silently. Observed 2026-08-01 while merging gqlc-35yu.7's ledger PR. ===

This bead is about `bd pull` re-deriving status. I hit the mirror image of it
through a plain git operation, with no bd sync command involved.

Sequence, all of it routine ledger hygiene:
  1. bd update gqlc-35yu.8 --status in_progress   -> DB: in_progress. Correct.
     (an auto-export wrote AND staged .beads/issues.jsonl)
  2. git checkout master  -> refused: local changes to .beads/issues.jsonl
  3. I inspected the staged diff, saw the ONLY delta was
     gqlc-35yu.8 open -> in_progress, i.e. state already in the DB, and
     discarded it with `git restore --staged --worktree .beads/issues.jsonl`
     on the reasoning that the Dolt DB is authoritative and the JSONL is a
     passive export, so the file could be regenerated.
  4. merged the PR, pulled master, re-ran `bd export -o .beads/issues.jsonl`
  5. The export wrote status "open". `bd show` confirmed the DB itself had
     reverted to OPEN -- while still carrying `Started: 2026-08-01`.

So the export is NOT passive in the direction the docs imply: reverting the
working-tree file propagated back into the DB. started_at survived and status
did not, which is the same torn state this bead already describes, reached
without `bd pull`.

WHY IT MATTERS MORE THAN IT LOOKS: the reasoning in step 3 is correct given a
genuinely passive export, and it is exactly what anyone will do when git blocks
a branch switch on this file -- which happens on EVERY bead, because closing a
bead and starting the next one both dirty it. The failure is silent: no
warning, and the next `bd export` cheerfully writes the reverted value into the
committed ledger, so the wrong state can reach master looking freshly exported.
I only caught it because I diffed the regenerated file against what I expected.

WORKAROUND until fixed: after any git operation that reverts, stashes or checks
out .beads/issues.jsonl, re-assert status with `bd update` and verify with
`bd show` before exporting. Do not trust an export taken straight after a
working-tree revert.

Worth deciding as part of the fix whether the JSONL should be import-on-change
at all. If it is meant to be an export, the DB should ignore it; if it is meant
to be bidirectional, `git restore` is an unguarded write path into the DB and
the guard (internal/tools/bdguard) does not cover this direction.
=== INVESTIGATED 2026-08-01 (branch fix/bd-gh-sync-state-fidelity): the stated
mechanism does NOT reproduce on bd 1.0.4, and the opposite one does ===

This bead says the pull re-derives in_progress from a non-nil started_at, and
the 2026-07-31 correction escalates that to "the re-derivation overrides ANY
non-closed status ... in_progress is the only reachable steady state". Both
claims fail against measurement.

DISCONFIRMING EVIDENCE 1 -- the live corpus. Four beads currently sit with
started_at set and a non-in_progress, non-closed status, some for weeks:
  gqlc-do1    open    started 2026-07-12
  gqlc-h9n.33 open    started 2026-07-28
  gqlc-h9n.1  blocked started 2026-07-28
  gqlc-23e    blocked started 2026-07-02
If any non-closed status were overridden, none of these could persist. The
correction claim that `blocked` is also re-derived is contradicted twice over
by gqlc-h9n.1 and gqlc-23e.

DISCONFIRMING EVIDENCE 2 -- isolated scratch DB (/tmp, `bd init`, no GitHub,
no shared state). Create bead, --claim (-> in_progress, started_at set),
`bd update --status open` -> open WITH started_at retained. Export, then
import that file back: status stays open. No re-derivation.

WHAT DOES REPRODUCE, deterministically, is the reverse direction -- and it is
gqlc-63y third repro, not this one:
  DB set to in_progress; issues.jsonl on disk says open; then
    bd list            -> in_progress survives (auto-sync does NOT import)
    bd hooks run post-merge -> status becomes OPEN, started_at retained
So the clobber is the JSONL replay inside `bd hooks run post-merge`, it goes
in_progress -> open, and it produces the torn open+started_at pair. The two
beads are NOT mutually contradictory observations of one bug; 63y direction is
real and this bead direction is not reproducible. Treat this as the stale one.

Corollary: open+started_at is a NORMAL bd-producible state (see evidence 2),
not the signature of a torn write, so it cannot be used as a detector.

MANAGER FORK (remove the re-derivation vs gate it, teaching the sync to record
what it last wrote): declined as posed, because it presumes a re-derivation
that does not exist here. It would also be unreachable from this script -- any
such logic lives inside the bd binary, and `.githooks/bd-gh-sync` cannot gate
it. Nothing is removed, so nothing is lost: the "started but never updated"
signal the fork worried about is still carried by started_at itself.

WHAT SHIPPED INSTEAD, which serves this bead intent without guessing at a
cause: a postcondition. After the scoped pull, bd list is re-read and any bead
that was HELD OUT of the pull but whose status moved anyway is reported by
name with the exact `bd update <id> --status <old>` needed to re-assert it.
That is agnostic about which component moved it, so it catches the JSONL
replay above even though this script never invokes it. Pinned by tests in
both arms (moved -> warns; unchanged -> silent).

NOT FIXED, and out of reach of this branch: `bd hooks run post-merge` still
replays the JSONL over newer DB state. Note it is currently UNREACHABLE in
this repo -- core.hooksPath is .githooks, and nothing in .githooks, the
justfile or .claude/settings.json chains to .beads/hooks/ or runs `bd hooks
run`, so the beads-managed hooks are inert. That is why the postcondition
warns rather than blocks. If those hooks are ever re-activated, the underlying
replay needs its own bead against bd itself.
MANAGER CORRECTION: this bead's stated mechanism does not reproduce. I verified the refutation myself.

The bead claims `bd pull` re-derives `in_progress` from a non-nil `started_at`, so `--status open` cannot stick for a previously-claimed bead. If that were true, no bead could sit in open-with-started_at for any length of time. Four do, and two have for over a month:

  gqlc-h9n.1    blocked  started=2026-07-28  updated=2026-07-28
  gqlc-h9n.33   open     started=2026-07-28  updated=2026-07-28
  gqlc-do1      open     started=2026-07-12  updated=2026-07-14
  gqlc-23e      blocked  started=2026-07-02  updated=2026-07-19

gqlc-do1 has been open with started_at set since 12 July and gqlc-23e blocked since 2 July, across many pulls. The implementer independently reproduced the negative in an isolated scratch DB: claim, then --status open, leaves it open with started_at retained, and re-importing that export re-derives nothing.

Note also that the bead's own Correction says `blocked` sits outside the re-derivation path and is a usable workaround; two of the four above are blocked, but two are plain `open`, so `open` is not special either.

WHAT ACTUALLY HAPPENS, and it is the opposite direction. `bd hooks run post-merge` replays the JSONL over newer DB state, reverting in_progress -> open while KEEPING started_at. That is deterministic and was reproduced. So the status damage is real; the arrow was drawn backwards, and the bead named started_at re-derivation for what is actually stale-export replay.

HOW THE ORIGINAL EVIDENCE MISLED. The bead's strongest-looking argument was that gqlc-4np.updated_at is byte-identical to the epoch embedded in the ghost bead id minted by the same pull (gqlc-1785456331014). That correctly proves the same pull touched both. It does not prove WHY the status moved — identical timestamps establish co-occurrence, not mechanism. The ghost-minting is gqlc-onji; the status move is replay. One pull, two effects, and the shared timestamp says nothing about which caused which.

I RESTATED THIS BAD DIAGNOSIS TO THE IMPLEMENTER as settled fact when I added jwuw to their scope, including the "no flag to clear started_at" framing that follows from it. They checked instead of believing me, and were right to. Recording that here rather than quietly dropping it: the bead was filed from a real symptom and a plausible story, and the story was wrong.

gqlc-63y and gqlc-jwuw were flagged as mutually contradictory. That is resolved: 63y's direction is the real one.

DISPOSITION: not fixed as filed, because there is nothing to fix at the stated site. The implementer added a POSTCONDITION instead — held beads must return unchanged from a pull, warning by name with the re-assert command. That is the right shape for a bead whose mechanism was misidentified: it pins the observable property the bead actually cared about without encoding the wrong cause. Whether that fully retires this bead is for the review round to say.
close_reason: Closed

title: gqlc-fex has two GH mirrors (#597/#598) plus a sync-created ghost bead — cleanup needs an owner decision
description:
Bead `gqlc-fex` acquired two GitHub mirrors, and the pull sync then manufactured
a second bead for one of them.

## Timeline (2026-07-30, all UTC)

- 00:49:40  GH #597 created — short body ending "Bead: gqlc-fex".
- 00:52:02  GH #598 created — same title, long body (TDD plan, acceptance
            criteria). `gqlc-fex.external_ref` points here, orphaning #597.
- 00:53:41  PR #599 merged carrying `Closes #597` → #597 closed at 00:53:42.
- 00:53:43  Bead `gqlc-1785373131289-1-b6686b0c` closed — a ghost bead the
            GH→bd pull created for #597, whose description is #597's body,
            which itself reads "Bead: gqlc-fex".
- 00:59:30  #598 closed separately.

## Current state

Both GH issues are closed and both beads are closed, so nothing is incorrectly
open — the residue is cosmetic but misleading:

- Two GH issues describe one bug, neither marked as a duplicate of the other.
- The ghost bead is now in `.beads/issues.jsonl` (landed by #609, deliberately,
  because the export must mirror the Dolt DB rather than be hand-edited).
- PR #599's `Closes #597` did not match `gqlc-fex`'s mirror (#598). The
  check-pr-closes gate did not catch it: `gqlc-fex` was not yet in the
  committed export, so the gate took its "unknown bead — PASS (don't block on
  stale export)" branch. That escape hatch is load-bearing for same-day beads
  and is worth re-examining.

## Likely cause

The `--prefer-github` amendment ordering recorded in memory
`bd-gh-sync-reverts-descriptions`: the description was amended and a second
issue was opened instead of editing the first. This is plausibly downstream of
`gqlc-63y` — the divergence guard that would have flagged the amendment never
ran.

## Decision needed

1. Delete the ghost bead from the Dolt DB, or keep it as an inert record?
   Deletion is destructive and propagates, so it needs an owner call.
2. Mark #597 or #598 as a duplicate on GitHub so the pair reads correctly.
3. Decide whether the gate's unknown-bead PASS should stay, given it is what
   let the wrong `Closes` number through.
close_reason: Ghost bead deleted and the drop declared (PR #611). #597 closed as DUPLICATE of #598; gqlc-fex intact on #598. Deletion is not permanently durable — the pull re-mints a ghost for any touched orphan issue; durable options filed as a P1 follow-up.

title: check-pr-closes gate does not re-evaluate on body edits — unre-triggerable, and bypassable after opening
description:
The `check-pr-closes` gate in `ci.yml` (tidy job) reads the PR body from the
workflow event payload:

    PR_BODY: ${{ github.event.pull_request.body }}

and `ci.yml` declares `on: pull_request:` with no `types:`, which defaults to
`[opened, synchronize, reopened]` — `edited` is not included.

Two consequences, found while fixing PR #600 on 2026-07-30.

## 1. A correct fix cannot re-trigger the gate

Adding the missing `Closes #N` to the body fires no event, so the check stays
red. A re-run does not help either: a re-run replays the original event
payload, so the gate re-reads the stale body. The only ways out are pushing a
commit or closing/reopening the PR. Neither is discoverable from the failure
message, which just says "Add 'Closes #598' to the PR body".

## 2. The gate is bypassable after the fact

A PR can carry `Closes #N` at open time, pass the gate, then have the line
edited out of the body. No `edited` event, no re-evaluation, and the PR merges
green with the GH issue left open — the exact failure the gate exists to
prevent.

## 3. The gate assumes any PR naming a bead is closing it

The bead id is taken from the branch name when the body has no `Bead:` line,
and the gate then demands a `Closes #N`. That is wrong for a PR that changes a
bead's status without resolving it. PR #609 reopened `gqlc-4np`; had the branch
been named after the bead, the gate would have demanded `Closes #503` and
closing that issue would have been precisely the wrong outcome. Working around
it by choosing a branch name that avoids the id is not a control.

## Fix direction

Add `types: [opened, synchronize, reopened, edited]`, or have the step fetch
the body from the API at run time rather than trusting the payload. The API
read also fixes consequence 2, since a re-run would then see current state.
Separately, give the gate a way to express "this PR touches the bead but does
not resolve it" so item 3 does not depend on branch naming.

## Acceptance

- Editing a PR body to add the missing `Closes #N` turns the check green with
  no push and no close/reopen.
- Removing `Closes #N` from a previously-passing PR body turns the check red.
- A status-change PR can name its bead without being forced to close it.
notes:
PR #867 https://github.com/areqag/gqlc/pull/867 — head e9119f75, branch fix/pr-closes-gate-reevaluates, worktree /home/antranig/Developer/gqlc/gqlc-w4al. AWAITING MERGE (orchestrator holds merge authority; do not merge from this session).

LIVE WITNESS of the acceptance property, run on PR #867 itself, head unchanged at e9119f75 throughout (no push, no reopen):
 1. baseline: all 8 required contexts green, mergeStateStatus CLEAN.
 2. 07:21:00Z removed the 'Closes #617' line -> run 32005420996 created 07:21:03Z, same SHA.
 3. its tidy (job 95313776365) FAILED: "ERROR: PR body is missing 'Closes #617'".
 4. with the line still absent, re-ran the PRE-EDIT run's tidy ('gh run rerun 32004817300 --job 95312044713') -> job 95313989391, run_attempt 2, FAILED, same message. Attempt 1 of that same job had PASSED on the frozen payload. This is the half 'edited' alone would not cover.
 5. mergeStateStatus BLOCKED; both tidy check runs on the SHA were failure.
 6. 07:22:56Z restored the body -> run 32005559232 created 07:22:57Z; tidy (job 95314195022) SUCCESS, '[check-pr-closes] gqlc-w4al -> Closes #617 (ok)'.
Acceptance property HOLDS: a body that loses its Closes line is not mergeable green, and a body edit alone both breaks and repairs the verdict.

CERTIFIED at e9119f75 (head), detached worktree: fmt-check, tidy-check, actionlint, test, lint all exit 0. Docker down locally so test-codegen-live* not run.

RESIDUE: gqlc-1ekq (consequence 3, gate assumes bead-naming == closing), gqlc-2rli (full-re-run cost / separate-workflow shape), gqlc-xdd0 (NEW: selective tidy re-run can leave lint/test/codegen-fence 'skipped' = pass at a SHA where they never ran; this change is what makes tidy re-passable at an unchanged SHA).

Consequence 3 (a status-change PR forced to Closes its bead) is NOT closed here — deferred to gqlc-1ekq / GH #862, named in both the PR body and the commit message. Independent review PASS, zero blockers, verdict at /tmp/factory/verdict-867.md.

title: schema/gql: which endpoint's rejection wins when both edge endpoints are defective is unpinned
description:
A mutation sweep over `internal/schema/gql/listener.go` (81 cases, 73 caught) left one
survivor that is a genuine coverage gap rather than a defensive tripwire.

## The survivor

`EnterEdgeTypePattern` reads its two endpoints in written source-then-destination
order, short-circuiting on the first failure (listener.go:353-365):

```go
if r := directed.EdgeTypePatternPointingRight(); r != nil {
        src, refErr = sourceRef(r.SourceNodeTypeReference())
        if refErr == nil {
                dst, refErr = destRef(r.DestinationNodeTypeReference())
        }
        filler = r.ArcTypePointingRight().EdgeTypeFiller()
}
```

Swapping the two so the destination is read first — keeping the short-circuit
intact, so this changes only *which* rejection is reported when both ends are
defective — leaves the entire suite green.

## Why nothing sees it

`sourceRef`/`destRef` return only what `fillerLabels` returns, which is one of two
sentinels: `ErrEndpointFillerHasProperties` and `ErrEndpointFillerImpliesLabels`.
Every existing fixture has a defect on exactly one end, or the same defect on both:

- `invalid/endpoint_filler_properties.gql` — destination only, HasProperties
- `corpus/18.3-edge-type/endpoint_key_label_set.gql` — source only, ImpliesLabels
- `TestEndpointFillerRejectsProperties`' "both sides carry properties" case — both
  ends, but the *same* sentinel, so the order cannot be observed

With one end defective the short-circuit reports that end whichever way round the
reads go. With both ends carrying the *same* sentinel the answer is that sentinel
either way. The order is only observable when the two ends carry *different*
sentinels, and no file does. The "both sides" case above is the near miss: it was
written for this construct and stops one sentinel short.

## The behaviour, confirmed by probe

The source's rejection wins, and it wins *by role, not by written position*:

| written                                              | reported          |
|------------------------------------------------------|-------------------|
| `(:Person => :Employee) -[:E]-> (:Post { x :: INT })` | ImpliesLabels (source) |
| `(:Person { x :: INT }) -[:E]-> (:Post => :Article)`  | HasProperties (source) |
| `(:Post { x :: INT }) <-[:E]- (:Person => :Employee)` | ImpliesLabels (source) |

The last row is the one worth pinning. In a left-pointing arc the grammar reports
the *rightmost written* endpoint as the source, so "source first" and "leftmost
first" disagree, and the code follows the role. That is the right answer — the
reported end is the same end regardless of which direction the author wrote the
arc in, so the diagnostic does not move when the edge is respelled — but nothing
says so and nothing would notice it changing.

This is the same class as the check ordering in `EnterEdgeTypePhrase` and
`EnterEdgeTypePattern`, where the mismatch sentinel deliberately fires before the
directed-only bail so the message names the author's actual mistake. That ordering
carries a comment arguing for it and tests that go red when it is swapped
(sweep cases 43 and 44, both caught). This one has neither.

## Proposed fix

Test-only; no product change. Extend the endpoint-filler coverage with the
mixed-sentinel pairing on both arc spellings, asserting the source's sentinel is
the one reported and the other is *not* — a bare `ErrorIs` on the winner would
still pass if both were somehow reported. Add the sentence about role-vs-position
to `sourceRef`/`destRef` or to the pattern collector.

## Provenance

Sweep script `/tmp/gqllist_sweep.py`, results `/tmp/gqllist_sweep.json`, case 56.
The other seven survivors were each instrumented with a logging probe and run
against the whole suite; all seven are defensive tripwires or equivalent mutants
and are correct as written:

- `SyntaxError`'s `tok.GetText() != ""` — 0 hits on an empty-text token, 4 on a
  non-Token offending symbol, so the `ok` half is load-bearing and the text half
  cannot fire
- `SyntaxError`'s `return` after the token branch — masked by `fail()` idempotence
- `walk`'s pre-walk `l.err != nil` bail — taken 6 times, but removal is invisible
  because `fail()` is first-wins; it guards against a panic on an unreliable tree
- `unsupportedSource`'s `src == nil` arm and its sentinel — 0 hits, error recovery only
- `unsupportedSource`'s trailing `return ErrUnsupportedSource` — 0 hits, unreachable
  by construction: `graphTypeSource` has exactly three alternatives (GQL.g4:347-350)
  and the guard tests for the third, so it is the documented forward-compat arm
- `nestedDepth` starting at `ctx` rather than its parent — 0 hits; no caller passes
  a `nestedGraphTypeSpecification` context, so it is an equivalent mutant

title: schema/gql: nothing reaches fillerLabels' trailing nil bail; ({ }) is the only spelling that does
description:
`fillerLabels`' trailing bail (internal/schema/gql/edgetype.go:125-127) was reached
by no test:

    if impliedLabels == nil {
        return nil, nil
    }

Neutralising it — `impliedLabels == nil && false` — leaves the whole suite green:

    go build ./...            ok
    go test ./internal/...    ok

It is not dead. Falling through calls `impliedLabels.LabelSetPhrase()` on a nil
interface, so any input taking this path would panic rather than fail a test.

THE ONE SPELLING THAT REACHES IT is `({ })`, an endpoint filler that is an empty
property block and nothing else. The path is narrow, which is why it was missed:

  - `f == nil` (`()`, no filler at all) returns from the guard at :96, not here.
    endpoint_no_filler.gql covers that.
  - `({ x :: INT })` is rejected at :112 as ErrEndpointFillerHasProperties before
    reaching this line. invalid/endpoint_filler_properties.gql covers that.
  - `(:Person { })` — the label-bearing sibling — leaves impliedLabels non-nil and
    returns at :128. corpus 18.3-edge-type/endpoint_empty_property_block.gql
    covers that, and it is the near miss: it was written for this construct and
    stops one label short of this line.

So only an EMPTY block with NO label lands here. Confirmed by probe:
`(:Person) -[:AUTHORED]-> ({ })` parses and rejects with ErrUnknownEndpoint,
which is endpoint_no_filler.gql's outcome reached through the other arm.

FOUND BY the 21-case mutation sweep of edgetype.go + nodetype.go (2026-07-28),
which caught 18. The two other survivors are inert by grammar and are recorded in
bd memory rather than filed:

  edgetype.go:106  `spec != nil` — nodeTypePropertyTypes has exactly one
                   mandatory child, propertyTypesSpecification (GQL.g4:1542-1544)
  nodetype.go:44   `spec == nil` — all three labelSetPhrase alternatives yield a
                   LabelName or a labelSetSpecification (GQL.g4:1679-1682)

THE FIX is a corpus entry, not an invalid/ fixture. The reading of a label-less
endpoint is open — endpoint_no_filler.gql records both, and gqlc-h9n.35 holds the
question — so if it is ever settled the "any node type" way, `()` and `({ })` flip
to resolves together and the entry moves with it. An invalid/ fixture would
survive that commit as an orphan.

SECOND FINDING, forced by the first. Adding the corpus entry turned
TestCorpusResolvingCarriers red, and the failure is a real one rather than
bookkeeping: `nodeTypeImpliedContent#2` was filed in declinedCarriers under
ErrUnnamedNodeType, and the register requires every carrier of a name to reject
with the group's sentinel. The new file carries it and rejects with
ErrUnknownEndpoint.

Both are true, and neither is a misfiling. The alternative is a filler that is a
property block and nothing else; declared as a node type it has no key label set
(ErrUnnamedNodeType), and used as an endpoint it references the type with the
empty key label set, which ADR 0018 makes undeclarable (ErrUnknownEndpoint). One
missing identity, reported from the two sides it can be seen from.

The register's own doctrine has an escape for a name carried by two families —
file it under the class — but that was written for ADR 0019's five value-type
families, which have ErrUnsupportedType. These two have no class, and inventing
one to satisfy a test register would be backwards.

So: a `declinedAlso` map keyed by name, one row, guarded four ways so it cannot
become a laundering channel. Each guard verified by breaking it:

  row deleted                     -> carrier unaccounted (the original failure)
  row for an unregistered name    -> "accounts for nothing"
  row repeating the group sentinel-> rejected
  row naming an unexercised error -> carrier unaccounted

It is a map rather than a field on declinedName so the fifty-odd existing
two-field positional literals stay untouched, and so a second row has to be
argued rather than appended.

title: resolver: ErrOutOfR0Scope has 18 emitters and 5 fixtures — path and unwind bindings rejected untested
description:
An audit of every ErrOutOfR0Scope emitter, prompted by gqlc-bef item 4. The
sentinel has eighteen emitters and five negative fixtures, and the five map 1:1
onto the five proven sites — so thirteen emitters are unproven, and the sentinel
reads as fully covered anyway.

Method: swap ErrOutOfR0Scope for a different sentinel at one site at a time and
run the suite. CAUGHT means some fixture reaches that site; SURVIVED means none
does.

    CAUGHT     scope.go:701   refProjectionType property on var-length edge
    CAUGHT     scope.go:933   PropertyUseWitness property on var-length edge
    CAUGHT     resolve.go:464 untyped edge
    CAUGHT     resolve.go:791 list-of-nodes projection
    CAUGHT     resolve.go:793 list-of-edges projection

    SURVIVED   scope.go:622   wildcard-expanded name resolves to nothing
    SURVIVED   scope.go:642   unknown projection variant
    SURVIVED   scope.go:680   refProjectionType out-of-scope ref
    SURVIVED   scope.go:930   PropertyUseWitness out-of-scope ref
    SURVIVED   scope.go:983   WitnessUse unknown ExprUse position
    SURVIVED   scope.go:986   WitnessUse unknown Use variant
    SURVIVED   resolve.go:24  empty branches
    SURVIVED   resolve.go:133 empty parts
    SURVIVED   resolve.go:200 unsupported binding kind
    SURVIVED   resolve.go:394 no branch scope tables
    SURVIVED   resolve.go:406 Use Branch index out of range
    SURVIVED   resolve.go:453 PropertyUse Part index out of range
    SURVIVED   resolve.go:917 unknown Effect variant

TestSentinelReachability (resolver_test.go:499) asserts every canonical sentinel
has at least one negative fixture. It passes here while 13 of 18 emitters are
untested, because it is per-sentinel, not per-emitter.

## The one that was a real gap, and why the obvious fixture does not pin it

resolve.go:200 is the default arm of the Binding type switch. Five binding kinds
exist (query.go: node, edge, call, path, unwind); the resolver handles three and
rejects path and unwind as out of R0 scope. Both are ordinary Cypher —
`MATCH p = ...` and `UNWIND ... AS x` — and the parser emits them, verified
directly. Neither had a fixture.

Writing the obvious ones does not help:

    MATCH p = (a:Person)-[:KNOWS]->(b:Person) RETURN p
    UNWIND [1, 2, 3] AS x RETURN x

Both pass, and both are useless. Delete the rejection arm and they *still* fail
with ErrOutOfR0Scope, because p / x are then unbound and the projection walk
raises the same sentinel from scope.go:680. Measured: the sentinel-swap mutation
is caught, but dropping the arm outright survives. The guard and its own
downstream fallthrough collide on one sentinel, so errors.Is cannot separate
them.

The fix is in the fixture. Exercise the rejection without naming the rejected
binding, so that removing the guard makes the query *succeed* rather than fail
identically:

    MATCH p = (a:Person)-[:KNOWS]->(b:Person) RETURN a
    MATCH (a:Person) UNWIND [1, 2, 3] AS x RETURN a

Both mutations are then caught by exactly these two fixtures.

This also explains scope.go:680's SURVIVED above: with :200 intact, nothing
reaches :680, and with :200 relaxed, :680 covers for it. They mask each other
through the sentinel, across two files. See bd memory
sweep-negative-fixture-must-not-name-rejected-binding.

## The other twelve

Ten are defensive tripwires on closed sums or resolver-internal invariants, and
should not be re-filed:

  scope.go:642, :983, :986 and resolve.go:917  default arms of closed type
        switches / a position enum. Unreachable without adding a variant.
  scope.go:622  the comment says it outright — a name in scopeOrder that
        resolves to nothing is a resolver-side bug.
  resolve.go:24, :133  empty branches / empty parts; the parser never emits an
        empty query.
  resolve.go:394, :406, :453  index and table-presence checks on structures the
        resolver itself builds.

Two remain genuinely open and are the same guard-chain shape as gqlc-bef item 3:

  scope.go:930  PropertyUseWitness's out-of-scope arm, unreachable because
        WitnessUse gates on Contains() first (:963). Relax the gate and the arm
        starts mattering, with no test on it.
  scope.go:680  reachable only once :200 is relaxed, as above. Pinning it on its
        own needs either a message assertion or a distinct sentinel — that is
        gqlc-ka1's subject and wants the ADR decision, so it is not done here.

## Fixed here

test/data/resolver/invalid/path_binding.cypher and unwind_binding.cypher, their
schema.mapping.json entries (social_r3.gql, already present) and their
invalidFixtures rows. No production change.

Verified 1:1 — both the sentinel-swap and the arm-dropped mutation at
resolve.go:200 are caught by these two fixtures and by nothing else.

Related: gqlc-bef items 3 and 4; gqlc-ka1.
close_reason: Closed

title: resolver: CloseEdges' Phase C deferred-close error is swallowable — no fixture reaches the second emitter
description:
CloseEdges closes edges in two passes: Phase A2 for edges whose endpoints are
already typed, and Phase C for the edges deferred because an endpoint was still
unlabelled, retried after Phase B inference. Both passes propagate closeEdge's
error. Only the first was tested.

    scope.go:259-261  Phase A2   `if err := closeEdge(...); err != nil { return err }`
    scope.go:275-277  Phase C    the same, for the deferred list

The Phase C propagation could be replaced with `_ = closeEdge(...)` and the
whole tree stayed green. That is the fail-open shape: a resolution failure on a
deferred edge is silently discarded, and the Part resolves as if the edge had
closed, leaving edgeTypes / edgeKeys / edgeCands with no entry for it.

## Why no existing fixture reaches it

Six negative fixtures cover the A2 site — ambiguous_edge_orientation,
unknown_edge, unknown_edge_undirected, unknown_edge_multi_type_all_miss,
create_unknown_edge, merge_unknown_edge — and every one of them spells both
endpoints, so the edge never defers. Reaching Phase C needs an edge that both
(a) has an unlabelled endpoint at A2 and (b) still fails closure after that
endpoint is inferred, which is a narrow target: inference derives the endpoint
type *from* the touching edges' candidate sets, so an edge that constrains the
inference generally closes against it by construction.

The way through is orientation rather than labels. closeEdge's `default:` arm
(resolve.go:547) rejects an undirected single-label edge with more than one
surviving candidate, and that check runs after the label intersection succeeds:

    MATCH (a:Person)-[:KNOWS]->(x) MATCH (x)-[r:AUTHORED]-(b:Post) RETURN r

x is unlabelled, so both edges defer. Phase B intersects: KNOWS from a Person
source gives {Person}, and undirected AUTHORED against a Post gives {Person} in
both orientations, so x commits unambiguously as Person. Phase C then closes
the KNOWS edge fine and hits the AUTHORED edge with src=Person, tgt=Post,
undirected, one label — Person-AUTHORED->Post and Post-AUTHORED->Person both
survive, so it is ErrAmbiguousEdgeOrientation, raised from the deferred site.

## Fixed here

test/data/resolver/invalid/ambiguous_edge_orientation_after_inference.cypher,
its schema.mapping.json entry (social_r3.gql, which already carries both
AUTHORED directions), and its invalidFixtures row in resolver_test.go. No
production change.

Verified 1:1:

    CAUGHT   Phase A2 closeEdge error swallowed   -> the six pre-existing fixtures
    CAUGHT   Phase C deferred error swallowed     -> this fixture, and only this one

Note the shape for the next sweep: a sentinel that already has a negative
fixture reads as covered, but coverage is per-sentinel, not per-emitter.
ErrAmbiguousEdgeOrientation had a fixture; the *second* site that raises it had
none. Same class-2 collision as gqlc-bef item 4.

Related: gqlc-bef item 6.
close_reason: Closed

title: resolver: two anonymous edges collide on the empty-string nullability key, unpinned
description:
Two anonymous edges in the same Part collide on the empty-string key in
DemoteNullability's tables. Two guards stop it, they mask each other exactly,
and nothing in the suite pinned either — so the pair could be removed with the
whole tree green, silently reporting OPTIONAL-matched bindings as non-nullable.

    scope.go:340  SeedLocalNullability's  `if !ok || v == ""`
    scope.go:403  addMember's             `if v == "" || g <= 0`

## The defect

query.go:311 and listener.go:521 record that an anonymous *node* is not a
binding, and NewNodeBinding rejects the empty variable. Only an EdgeBinding may
be anonymous (query.go:86). So the "" key is reachable, and reachable more than
once per Part — every anonymous edge writes to the same slot.

    OPTIONAL MATCH (a:Person)-[:AUTHORED]->(b:Post)
    MATCH (c:Person)-[:KNOWS]->(d:Person)
    RETURN a, b, c, d

Two anonymous edges: the first nullable in group 1, the second required in
group 0. With both guards dropped:

  - SeedLocalNullability writes nullableBinding[""] twice, and the required
    edge is last, so the slot ends false.
  - addMember enters ("", 1) — the required edge's group 0 is still rejected by
    the `g <= 0` half — so groupsOf[""] = [1] and members[1] = [a, "", b].
  - The pre-fixed-point closure at :446 then sees nullableBinding[""] present
    and false, reads it as a proven witness for group 1, and demotes every
    member: a and b come out non-nullable.

The two anonymous edges are unrelated — different clauses, different labels, no
shared endpoint — and the required one's existence says nothing about whether
the OPTIONAL match found a row. This is a plain query, not a scope-layer
construction.

## Why the sweep saw nothing

Each guard survives alone, because each blocks the channel on its own: without
the "" seed the closure finds nothing present, and without the "" membership
there is no group to demote. Class-5 mutually-masking, measured:

    SURVIVED   SeedLocalNullability anon guard alone
    SURVIVED   addMember anon guard alone
    CAUGHT     PAIR seed + addMember
    CAUGHT     ALL FOUR anon guards

## The other two anonymous guards are not defects

Recording these so the next sweep does not re-derive them:

  :481  the endpoint loop's `v == ""`. Unreachable — NewVarEndpoint rejects the
        empty variable (query.go:1158-1161), and an endpoint with no name is an
        InlineEndpoint, a different sum member. Only the zero value
        VarEndpoint{} could carry "", and no constructor produces one. Class-3
        defensive tripwire.

  :759  Export's localGroup `v == ""`. A dead write — localGroup is read at
        :836 only for names in exportedNames, and "" never reaches
        exportedNames because buildScopeOrder excludes it (:540). Class-4
        equivalent mutant.

## Fixed here

test/data/resolver/valid/no_demote_disjoint_anonymous_required_edge.cypher plus
its golden and schema.mapping.json entry. No production change — the guards are
correct, they were merely unpinned. The golden records a and b nullable, c and d
not; the closest existing fixture, demote_from_anonymous_required_edge, shares
the endpoint `a` between the two clauses, so its group is demoted legitimately
and the collision is invisible in it.

Verified 1:1 — the pair mutation is caught by this fixture and by nothing else.

Related: gqlc-bef item 2.

title: resolver: BindCall's whole edge shadow cascade is unpinned — three scope unit tests assert through predicates that do not read the lanes they seed
description:
Found by a 120-case mutation sweep of internal/resolver/scope.go (83/120 caught). One shape accounts for every fixable survivor: a unit test seeds one carry lane and asserts through a read-only predicate that reads *different* lanes, so the seeded lane and the asserted lanes never intersect and the assertion holds vacuously.

## BindCall's entire edge cascade — a test that pins one fifth of what it claims

TestScopeBindCallShadowCascade's own comment says it seeds "carried node + edge state so BindCall's shadow cascade drops both". It seeds exportedNodeTypes and exportedEdgeBindings, then asserts HasNode("c") is false and HasEdge("c") is false. HasEdge (scope.go:319-325) reads edgeTypes and edgeCands — neither of which the carry seeds. The edge half of the assertion is therefore true before BindCall runs, and all four of BindCall's edge deletes survived:

    scope.go:199  delete(s.edgeTypes, v)
    scope.go:200  delete(s.edgeKeys, v)
    scope.go:201  delete(s.edgeCands, v)
    scope.go:202  delete(s.edgeBindings, v)

Dropping all four *together* also survived, so nothing elsewhere grounds them either — the cascade is unpinned as a whole, not merely under-discriminated. Only delete(s.nodeTypes, v) was caught.

This is the flip side of gqlc-2y7: the Has* trio has no production callers, and reaching for it in a test is exactly how the cascade went unpinned. TestScopeBindNodeShadowCascade is the model — it asserts NotContains on all four maps directly, and caught all four of its own.

## BindEdge's closed-edge reset — same shape, two lanes

TestScopeBindEdgeShadowCascade seeds only exportedNodeTypes, so BindEdge's reset arm has nothing to erase. scope.go:185 (edgeKeys) and :186 (edgeCands) each survived alone. :184 (edgeTypes) is caught by the golden suite, and that single catch masks the other two: the three-way combined mutation is caught, so the pair is only visible one at a time.

## Export's alias guard has two halves and one of them is tested

scope.go:805 is `if ref.Property != "" || alias != ref.Variable { continue }`. TestScopeExportWildcardVsExplicit drives `WITH v, v.name AS x`, which trips the property half. Nothing in the suite writes `WITH v AS w` — a rename of a bare binding — so the alias half could be dropped with the tree green, exporting v's node type into the downstream carry under a binding name that no longer leaves the Part.

## Fixed here

internal/resolver/scope_test.go only; no production change. Verified 1:1 — each mutation caught by exactly the test written for it, nothing redundant:

    TestScopeBindEdgeShadowCascade    -> :185, :186
    TestScopeBindCallShadowCascade    -> :199, :200, :201, :202, and the four combined
    TestScopeExportWildcardVsExplicit -> :805's alias half

Sweep score 83/120 -> 91/120. The remaining survivors are triaged separately.
close_reason: Closed

title: schema/gql: six fail-open arms in listener.go — the phrase-form collectors, and the entire edge property-error lane
description:
Found by a 64-case mutation sweep of internal/schema/gql/listener.go (54/64 caught). Six survivors are real fail-open arms, and they fall into two groups with one shape in common: a guard that exists in duplicate, where only one copy was ever exercised.

## Group 1 — the phrase form is systematically less covered than the pattern form

listener.go has four element collectors. EnterNodeTypePattern / EnterNodeTypePhrase and EnterEdgeTypePattern / EnterEdgeTypePhrase each copy fillerContent's fields through their own hand-written assignments and forward nodeContent/edgeContent's error through their own `if err != nil { l.fail(err) }`. Nothing is shared, so a pattern-form fixture grounds nothing about the phrase form.

Four mutations survived on that asymmetry:

    listener.go:189  EnterNodeTypePhrase  drop l.fail on the filler error
    listener.go:192  EnterNodeTypePhrase  n.hasKeyLabelSet = false
    listener.go:254  EnterEdgeTypePhrase  drop l.fail on the filler error
    listener.go:257  EnterEdgeTypePhrase  e.hasKeyLabelSet = false

Their pattern-form counterparts at :154, :157 and :416/:449 were all caught. Measured cause: every key-label-set corpus file is pattern form (18.2's pattern_key_label_set_only.gql — the name says the author saw the gap), and every value-type decline in 18.9 is written as a pattern-form node, so all of that coverage lands on EnterNodeTypePattern's error arm.

Consequence of the hasKeyLabelSet drop is not a missing flag but a different type: resolve() reads it to tell a declared key label set from an absent one, so dropping it sends the type down GG22's inference path instead.

## Group 2 — nothing anywhere puts an unsupported property type on an EDGE

    listener.go:374  EnterEdgeTypePattern  drop l.fail on the filler error
    listener.go:465  edgeContent           return fc, nil instead of the error

edgeContent's error arm never returned a non-nil error across the entire suite, because no fixture declares a declining value type on an edge. That is the root cause of :254 as well: with no erroring edge anywhere, neither edge collector's error arm could be reached. An edge carrying an unsupported property type was silently dropped from the schema, taking the relationship with it and reporting nothing — the class-2 shape.

## Fixed here

Five corpus files, verified 1:1 (each mutation caught by exactly the file written for it, nothing redundant):

    18.2-node-type/phrase_key_label_set_only.gql          -> :192
    18.2-node-type/phrase_unsupported_property_type.gql   -> :189
    18.3-edge-type/phrase_key_label_set_only.gql          -> :257
    18.3-edge-type/pattern_unsupported_property_type.gql  -> :374
    18.3-edge-type/phrase_unsupported_property_type.gql   -> :254
    (the two edge unsupported files jointly ground :465)

Sweep score 54/64 -> 60/64.

## The four remaining survivors are inert, not gaps — do not re-file them

  :67   walk's refusal to descend a tree that already has a syntax error. fail() is idempotent, so the returned error is the same either way; the guard protects against a panic on an unreliable tree, and no input in the suite panics. A tripwire, and see below.
  :92   the `src == nil` half of the source guard. The doc comment says src is nil only under error recovery — and walk's :67 guard is what makes error recovery unreachable here, so the two are a chain rather than two independent facts.
  :113  unsupportedSource's nil guard. Same fact as :92: GraphTypeSource() is never nil at any call.
  :487  nestedDepth counting from ctx rather than ctx.GetParent(). ctx is always one of the four element-type contexts and never a nestedGraphTypeSpecification, so the mutant is equivalent.

Worth a separate look some time: :67, :92 and :113 form a three-link chain where the first guard is what makes the other two unreachable. If :67 were ever relaxed, both downstream nil guards would start mattering and neither has a test.
close_reason: Closed

title: schema/gql: three unpinned guards in resolve() — implied labels in idx.declared, source-endpoint failure, and rejectInheritance past the first implied set
description:
A 51-case mutation sweep of internal/schema/gql's resolution lane (resolve.go,
nodetype.go, edgetype.go) run 2026-07-28 at 1cd1d1f. 45/51 caught after
repairing all 6 BUILD-FAILs and re-running them — BUILD-FAIL is an unknown
result, not a pass.

Three survivors are real, pinnable gaps.

## 1. idx.declared stops covering implied labels (resolve.go:66-72)

The comment there makes an explicit claim:

    // Every label the type answers to, implied ones included: idx.declared
    // exists to tell "you named a type where an alias belongs" apart from
    // "no such type", and an author who writes an implied label has made
    // that same mistake.

Narrowing the loop from complete.Split() to key.Split() SURVIVES. So the
"implied ones included" half of that claim is untested: no schema names an
IMPLIED label where an edge endpoint alias belongs. Under the mutation such a
schema reports ErrUnknownEndpoint instead of ErrEndpointNotAlias — the exact
misdiagnosis the comment says the code exists to prevent.

Needs: a node type declared with `=>` implied labels, and an edge endpoint
naming one of those implied labels. Expect ErrEndpointNotAlias.

## 2. The source endpoint failure stops being propagated (resolve.go:94-97)

    source, err := e.source.resolve(idx)
    if err != nil { return schema.Schema{}, err }   // SURVIVES when disabled

The TARGET arm four lines down is caught, so the corpus has a bad-target
endpoint fixture and no bad-SOURCE one. With the source arm disabled the edge
is built with an empty Source key and resolution proceeds, so the schema is
silently accepted with a bogus edge.

Needs: a schema whose edge SOURCE endpoint names an undeclared node type while
the target is fine. Expect ErrUnknownEndpoint.

## 3. rejectInheritance stops checking every implied set (resolve.go:173-181)

Capping the outer `for _, set := range implied` at its first element SURVIVES.
Every existing ErrImpliedLabelIsKeyLabel fixture puts the colliding declaration
first. The comment at resolve.go:80-82 says the check is deferred past the loop
precisely because "a later declaration's key label can collide with an earlier
one's implied label" — that ordering is the thing not covered.

Needs: a schema with two or more `=>` declarations where a LATER one carries
the colliding implied label.

## Non-defects, recorded so the next sweep does not re-flag them

- "the alias guard stops skipping the empty alias" (resolve.go:60) and "the
  name guard stops skipping the empty name" (resolve.go:63) both SURVIVE.
  Writing idx.aliases[""] / idx.declared[""] is unobservable because
  rawEndpoint.resolve only consults either map inside its own `ref.alias != ""`
  branch. This is a MUTUALLY-MASKING GUARD PAIR — the 6th instance of category
  5 in resolver-mutation-survivor-triage — and neither `!= ""` is load-bearing
  on its own.

- "labelSets stops cloning before appending" (resolve.go:149) SURVIVES.
  Every construction path for a graph.LabelSet has cap == len — labelSet()
  uses make(graph.LabelSet, len(names)) and the single-label form is a
  one-element literal — so append always reallocates and slices.Clone can
  never be observed. Category 3, defensive tripwire: correct to keep, provably
  redundant today.
close_reason: Closed

title: resolver: demotion, Export and the effect validators are 60/92 under mutation — and nine guards are unpinnable by construction
description:
Two more mutation sweeps, same verify-by-failure discipline.

Lane C — DemoteNullability, Export, ValidateEffects (scope.go).
48 mutations, 31 caught.

Lane D — validateEffect and the eight per-variant effect validators
(resolve.go). 44 mutations, 29 caught.

Combined 60/92.

REAL GAPS (4) — fixed here, each verified 1:1:

1. demoteGroupsOf visits every group a name belongs to, but no fixture
   put a name in two groups at once. The code comment at scope.go:401
   says groups "may span carry + local"; nothing tested it. Truncating
   the loop to its first group left the suite green.

2. validateSetPropertyEffect's SINGLE-candidate edge property check.
   Only the multi-candidate (unionProperty) arm had a fixture.

3. validateRemovePropertyEffect, same arm, same gap. DELETE's
   equivalent arm was already covered — the asymmetry is what makes
   this the kind of hole reading alone does not find.

4. ValidateEffects short-circuits on the first failing effect. No
   fixture had TWO failing effects with distinguishable sentinels, so
   returning the LAST error instead of the first was invisible.

NINE GUARDS ARE UNPINNABLE AS THE SUITE IS BUILT TODAY:

Every per-variant effect validator ends in the same three-arm ladder:

    if _, ok := sc.edgeBindings[v]; ok  { ...ErrInvalidEffectTarget }
    if _, ok := sc.carriedResolvedTypes[v]; ok { ...ErrInvalidEffectTarget }
    return ...ErrInvalidEffectTarget

All three arms raise ErrInvalidEffectTarget, and TestInvalid asserts
with errors.Is. Deleting either of the first two arms therefore falls
through to the third and the suite stays green — for all seven
projection-alias arms and both SET/REMOVE-labels-on-edge arms.

There ARE fixtures named for these guards —
set_property_on_projection_alias, set_labels_on_projection_alias,
delete_projection_alias and five more. They exercise the arm. They
cannot pin it. Nine tests that look like coverage and are not.

This directly contradicts gqlc-ka1's stated premise that "the sentinel
is correct and TestInvalid asserts via errors.Is, so nothing is
fail-open". Nine things are fail-open, precisely because the assertion
stops at the sentinel. See the comment added to gqlc-ka1.

Closing them needs a decision that is NOT test-local:
  (a) assert message substrings for these fixtures, or
  (b) split ErrInvalidEffectTarget into distinct sentinels.
(b) changes exported errors and wants an ADR. Neither is taken here.

REMAINING SURVIVORS, TRIAGED (19):

Defensive / parser-protected (6): the CREATE and MERGE anonymous-skip
and unbound-variable arms (the parser's referential-integrity check
rejects an unbound name before the resolver runs — confirmed by
observing the parser error "unbound variable: a"), the bare-ref
pre-pass's EdgeBinding arm (its comment says the parser passes a
constant false; the mutation confirms it), and Export's renamed-alias
exclusion (same parser gate).

Mutually-masking pair (2): addMember's `g <= 0` and demoteGroup's
`g == 0`. Either one alone can be deleted with no effect, because the
other still filters group zero. Only deleting BOTH would regress. A
fifth instance of the taxonomy category.

Equivalent mutants (9): the anonymous-name skips whose maps are never
keyed on "", the `present` guards whose spurious entries are never
read back, addMember's dedup (demoteGroup is idempotent), and Export's
zero-group suppression (masked twice downstream).

Fixed-point round two (2): the two `changed = true` assignments that
drive a SECOND iteration of the demotion loop. No fixture needs one.
Same shape as gqlc-3rj, which records that inferUnlabelled's
multi-round loop is likewise uncovered — worth folding together.
close_reason: Closed

title: resolver: binding-admission and helper lanes are 52/73 under mutation — seven fail-open gaps
description:
Two mutation sweeps over the resolver, run under the verify-by-failure
discipline (break the guard, prove a test fails).

Lane A — binding admission (scope.go: Ingest, BindNode, BindEdge,
BindCall, CloseEdges, InferUnlabelled, SeedLocalNullability,
buildScopeOrder, materialiseReturns, virtualProjection,
projectionType). 48 mutations, 35 caught.

Lane B — resolve.go helpers (useSitesToScopes, callProjectionType,
unionProperty, qualifiedDemoter, argAssignable). 25 mutations, 17
caught.

Combined 52/73. Triage of the 21 survivors:

REAL GAPS (7) — a guard can be deleted and the suite stays green:

1. BindEdge stops resetting carried closed-edge state. closeEdge writes
   edgeTypes/edgeKeys for a single candidate and edgeCands for many,
   and never clears the opposite lane. A carried SINGLE-candidate
   binding re-bound to a MULTI-candidate one keeps the stale
   single-candidate answer.

2. unionProperty stops reporting a nullability-only mismatch. The guard
   is `hit.Type != first.Type || hit.Nullable != first.Nullable`; every
   fixture differed in type, so the nullability half was masked by the
   type half raising the same sentinel first — the sentinel-collision
   pattern again.

3. unionProperty stops widening on a nullable binding. No schema had a
   NOT NULL property shared across two edge labels, so
   `first.Nullable = first.Nullable || bindingNullable` never had to do
   anything.

4. qualifiedDemoter's lower-bound threshold moves off 1. The three
   var-length demoter fixtures used *1..3 on an already-non-nullable
   endpoint, *0..3 (below the threshold either way), and unbounded
   (short-circuits before the comparison). None straddled 1.

5. argAssignable stops admitting an unknown-typed argument. No fixture
   passed a parameter as a CALL argument.

6. argAssignable's FLOAT token stops admitting a float. Only
   int-at-FLOAT was pinned; the exact-match arm was free.

7. argAssignable's STRING token stops requiring a string.
   call_arg_type_mismatch passes a good STRING and a bad INTEGER, so
   the INTEGER arm raises first — sentinel collision.

DEFENSIVE, UNREACHABLE (6) — tripwired with a panic, never fired:
five binding-lane arms (TRIPWIRE-T/U/V/W/X) plus argAssignable's
`default: return false`. The last is unreachable by construction:
procsig.validToken rejects any token outside the four-value closed set
at registry-build time, so the switch is total.

EQUIVALENT MUTANTS (6) — the mutation cannot change behaviour:
InferUnlabelled's method-level empty-pending check (redundant with
resolve.go:570), its labelled-binding filter (redundant with the
carry-wins resolved filter), SeedLocalNullability's anonymous skip
(nullableBinding[""] is never read), the empty-scope wildcard fast
path, buildScopeOrder's local-loop `|| seen[v]` (the cypher parser
already dedups binding records — proved with TRIPWIRE-S), and
callProjectionType's TypeUnknown arm (identical to its default).

DEAD CODE (2) — evidence for gqlc-2y7:
virtualProjection's TypeList stamp is confirmed never read (mutating
it to stop projecting as a list SURVIVED), and callBindingSlot declares
four fields of which only resultType is ever read — nullable,
procedure and sourceField are write-only.

Fix: seven fixtures, each verified 1:1 (the mutation it targets fails
that fixture and only that fixture).
close_reason: Closed

title: resolver: the parameter-witness scope gate fails open (8/33 mutations survive)
description:
A 33-case mutation sweep over the parameter-witness lane -- unifyParameterUsesAcrossBranches, selectPartScope, WitnessUse, partScope.Contains, PropertyUseWitness, scope.Snapshot -- caught 25 and let 8 through. No BUILD-FAILs. This is the best-pinned lane swept so far (write-effects 13/26, UNION 13/26, inference 25/37), and only ONE real gap came out of it.

THE REAL GAP -- one fixture, two survivors:
  * WitnessUse's out-of-scope PropertyUse arm ('if !sc.Contains(ref.Variable) { return nil, nil }') and unifyParameterUsesAcrossBranches' witnessless fallback ('if !seen { unified = ResolvedUnknown{} }') were BOTH unpinned. They are two halves of one path: a Use whose Ref names something partScope cannot see yields zero witnesses, and a parameter with zero witnesses across all its uses must resolve to unknown.

    Nothing in the corpus reached it because partScope deliberately narrows to the three entity lanes (nodeTypes, edgeTypes, edgeCands) per §2.3 invariant #3 -- callTypes is NOT observable through it. So a property Ref on a CALL YIELD variable is in parser scope but out of partScope scope. New fixture param_witnessless_out_of_scope.cypher:

        CALL test.labels() YIELD label
        MATCH (p:Person) WHERE label.zip = $z
        RETURN p.name AS nm

    $z's only use is label.zip; it resolves to kind:unknown. Verified: this single fixture catches both mutations and nothing else does.

SIX SURVIVORS ARE NOT GAPS. Five confirmed by planted panics across go test ./... -- none fired:
  * TRIPWIRE-M: Use.Branch index out of range. Parser attributes a valid query-level branch index by construction.
  * TRIPWIRE-N: PropertyUse.Part index out of range. Same posture.
  * TRIPWIRE-P: ExprUse's resolveType error propagation. resolveType returns an error on exactly two inputs -- TypeList{TypeNode} and TypeList{TypeEdge} -- and no ExprUse in the corpus carries a list-of-entities enclosing type. Every other resolveType arm either succeeds or panics.
  * TRIPWIRE-Q: unknown ExprUse position. The parser emits only the four declared positions.
  * TRIPWIRE-R: PropertyUseWitness' '!singleCand && !multiCand' out-of-scope arm. STRUCTURALLY unreachable, not merely uncovered: WitnessUse gates every call behind Contains, and Contains tests exactly the three lanes PropertyUseWitness consults (nodeTypes, then edgeTypes/edgeCands). If Contains passed and nodeTypes missed, one of edgeTypes/edgeCands must hit. Note this is the mirror image of the real gap above -- the SAME Contains gate that makes this arm dead is the thing that had no fixture.

  The sixth is an equivalent mutant, argued from code rather than comment: selectPartScope hands a zero partScope to non-PropertyUse Uses. Swapping in branchScopes[0] survives because WitnessUse's ClauseSlotUse and ExprUse arms never dereference the receiver -- read the switch body, not the doc comment.

Fixed test-only. No production change.
close_reason: Closed

title: resolver: parameter-unification and inference-round guards fail open (12/37 mutations survive)
description:
A 37-case mutation sweep over the binding-inference and type-unification lane -- edgeCandidates, closeEdge, endpointLabels, inferUnlabelled, candidateTypes, touchingSide, unify, resolveNodeLabels, satisfyingNodeTypes -- caught 25 (after repairing 2 BUILD-FAILs) and let 12 through. This lane is markedly better pinned than the write-effect (13/26) and UNION (13/26) lanes swept earlier; five survivors are real gaps and are now pinned 1:1.

THE REAL GAPS, all fixed test-only:
  * unify's property-type check. Third instance tonight of a sentinel collision. parameter_type_conflict_two_properties.cypher is 'p.name = $x AND p.age = $x' -- STRING NOT NULL against a nullable INT, so it differs in type AND nullability. unify tests both side by side and both raise ErrParameterTypeConflict, so the adjacent nullability check caught the fixture and left the type check free for its whole life. The new fixture uses two NOT NULL properties.
  * inferUnlabelled's CALL YIELD scalar collision (R7 4.1.2.1 addendum). part_binding_type_conflict_call_vs_node.cypher pinned the LABELLED arm's Phase A1 check; the unlabelled path carries its own copy and had no fixture.
  * candidateTypes' undirected reverse orientation. Needed a pattern where ONLY the reverse orientation supplies a candidate: 'MATCH (a:Person)-[:EMPLOYS]-(b)' against social_r5, where Company-EMPLOYS->Person means b can only be Company via the reverse.
  * candidateTypes' non-touching-edge skip. Needed a second edge in the pattern that does not touch the unlabelled binding.
  * resolveNodeLabels' empty-satisfying-set arm -- every queried label declared somewhere, but no declared type carrying all of them.

SEVEN SURVIVORS ARE NOT GAPS. All verified by planted panics, not by reading:
  * unify's ResolvedNode, ResolvedEdge and ResolvedList arms, and its absorb-unknown-on-the-left arm (TRIPWIRE-G/H/I/J). None fired across go test ./... . unify is reachable only from unifyParameterUsesAcrossBranches, whose witnesses come from WitnessUse: ResolvedProperty, ResolvedScalar, or resolveType's output -- and resolveType PANICS on bare TypeNode/TypeEdge, so the node and edge arms are structurally unreachable. Defensive tripwires.
  * closeEdge's orientation-ambiguity check requires BOTH !e.Directed() and len(e.Labels()) == 1. Dropping the directedness half is an equivalent mutant: a directed single-label edge yields at most one candidate (one orientation x one label), so the multi-candidate arm the check guards cannot be entered. TRIPWIRE-K confirmed -- never fired.
  * satisfyingNodeTypes' sort affects only diagnostic ordering, and the suite asserts sentinels rather than messages. Unpinnable as the suite stands; see gqlc-ka1.

ONE SURVIVOR IS UNCOVERED PRODUCTION CODE, not a fail-open. TRIPWIRE-L (panic when inferUnlabelled starts a second round) never fired: no fixture in the corpus needs more than one inference round, so the outer 'for len(pending) > 0' loop is dead in practice. Truncating it to one round is therefore invisible. This is not provably unreachable -- it needs a binding that is ambiguous when evaluated but unambiguous once a later binding in the same round commits -- so it wants a purpose-built schema. Filed separately.
close_reason: Closed

title: resolver: UNION branch-column comparison and grouping-key fills fail open (13/26 mutations survive)
description:
A 26-case mutation sweep over fillGroupingKeys, compareBranchColumns, resolvedTypeEqual and computeDistinct (internal/resolver/resolve.go:254-381) caught 13 and let 13 through. Ten of the thirteen are real fail-opens and are now pinned by ten new fixtures, each catching exactly one mutation.

HEADLINE: a mutually-masking guard pair. test/data/resolver/invalid/union_column_name_mismatch.cypher is

    MATCH (a:Person) RETURN a.name UNION MATCH (a:Person) RETURN a.age AS name2

Branch 1 differs from branch 0 in BOTH name and type. compareBranchColumns checks name first and type second, both raising ErrUnionColumnMismatch, and the suite asserts only the sentinel. Deleting the name check outright left the fixture red for the other reason, so the name check has never been pinned despite carrying a fixture named after it.

The same masking runs through resolvedTypeEqual, reachable only from compareBranchColumns. Four arms were unpinned: ResolvedNode value equality, ResolvedEdgeUnion key identity, ResolvedEdgeUnion nullability, and ResolvedList element type. No fixture unioned two branches projecting different whole-entity or list types under a common column name.

Also unpinned and now fixed:
  * compareBranchColumns only ever compared branch 1 against branch 0; no fixture had three branches.
  * computeDistinct folds Part.Distinct across every branch x Part, but truncating either loop to its first element survived. No fixture carried DISTINCT in a non-first Part, or in a non-first branch under UNION ALL (plain UNION masks it via the UnionDistinct combinator fold).
  * fillGroupingKeys treats LiteralProjection and FuncProjection as grouping keys; neither appeared in a Part alongside an aggregate.

THREE SURVIVORS ARE NOT GAPS:
  * resolvedTypeEqual's nil guard. TRIPWIRE-E (panic on a nil operand) never fired across go test ./... — the function is never reached with nil. Defensive tripwire.
  * The 'break' short-circuiting the hasAggregate scan. hasAggregate is monotone, so the break is pure optimisation and the mutation is provably equivalent.
  * The 'if part.ReturnsAll { return }' early exit is behaviourally inert, but NOT for the reason the source claimed. The comment asserted 'A ReturnsAll-expanded Part's Returns is empty (parser guarantees mutual exclusion)'. That is FALSE: TRIPWIRE-D fired on seven standalone CALL ... YIELD fixtures, which set ReturnsAll AND a non-empty Returns. TRIPWIRE-F then showed cols and Returns are index-aligned in exactly those cases (the only length mismatches are the 0-Returns plain RETURN * expansions), so no latent indexing bug is being masked. The guard is inert because neither a RETURN * expansion nor a YIELD item list can carry an AggregateProjection. Comment corrected in place; that is the only production change.
close_reason: Closed

title: resolver: REMOVE LABELS and DELETE effect validators fail open (13/26 mutations survive)
description:
A 26-case mutation sweep over the write-effect validators in internal/resolver/resolve.go (validateEffect and its eight variant validators) caught 13 and let 13 through.

Bead gqlc-ag5 previously swept this lane and pinned nine fail-opens, but it mirrored only the SET family. The survivors are concentrated entirely in the halves ag5 did not mirror:

  * REMOVE LABELS is SET LABELS' twin and carries the same three guards (edge-binding rejection, projection-alias rejection, node-target requirement). SET had set_labels_on_edge.cypher behind it; REMOVE had nothing, so its edge rejection and the node-target gate the two share were both free.
  * Neither SET nor REMOVE pinned the projection-alias arm on labels at all.
  * DELETE is the third property validator. SET and REMOVE each pin the variable-length-edge guard and the property-existence check on both the single-type and multi-type edge shapes. DELETE pinned neither guard, on either shape.
  * Two loops that walk a list of things to validate stopped at their first element with the suite still green: validateDeleteEffect over e.Targets(), and validateMergeEffect over e.OnMatch().

Twelve of the thirteen are real fail-opens. The thirteenth -- validateCreateEffect's 'if v == "" { continue }' skip of anonymous variables -- is a defensive tripwire, not a gap: a panic planted on that branch never fired across go test ./..., matching the source comment that its reachability from parser input is zero.

Fix is test-only: eleven new fixtures under test/data/resolver, ten invalid plus one valid (DELETE of a bare multi-type edge binding). No production behaviour changes.
close_reason: Closed

title: resolver: five WITH-boundary carry lanes in scope.Export are unpinned
description:
A 26-case mutation sweep over scope.Export / scope.ValidateEffects (internal/resolver/scope.go:727-860) caught 17. Of the nine survivors, five are real test gaps: each mutation silently changes resolved output and no fixture notices.

1. scope.go:840 — the else-if fallback to s.carriedGroups. It only fires for a name exported WITHOUT a local re-declaration, which needs a second WITH. Every OPTIONAL fixture had at most one WITH, so an OPTIONAL group id that survives one boundary but not two was undetectable. Deleting the fallback leaves a provably non-null column nullable.

2. scope.go:750 — the EdgeBinding arm of the localGroup lookup. The NodeBinding arm was pinned; the edge arm was not (the recurring 'one half of a symmetric pair' motif). An edge's OPTIONAL-group id was dropped at the boundary with the suite green.

3. scope.go:818 — the exportedEdgeCands lane. Masked for a bare 'WITH r RETURN r' by the section 4.5.4 carried-alias bypass, which serves the whole type out of carriedResolvedTypes. Only a PROPERTY projection on the carried union reaches the edgeCands table, and no fixture did that.

4. scope.go:836-842 — the group-id precedence rule (local shadows carry). Needs a name carried under one group id AND locally re-declared under a different one; no fixture had that shape. Inverting the precedence strands a name in a stale group so a later proof of its real group does not demote it.

5. scope.go:854 — ValidateEffects' loop over s.effects. No fixture had two effects where the SECOND is the invalid one, so validating only s.effects[0] passed the suite.

The remaining four survivors are equivalent mutants, proven not argued:
- 'alias must match the variable' (scope.go:806): the cypher parser rejects a reference to a renamed-away binding first ('unbound variable: a'), so the leak is unobservable.
- 'non-Ref projection' (scope.go:797): masked by the following alias != ref.Variable guard, since a zero RefProjection has Variable "". Tripwire on a non-Ref projection with an empty alias never fired.
- 'localGroup keeps anonymous bindings' (scope.go:759): tripwire on an empty variable reaching the export binding loop never fired.
- 'propagate a zero local group id' (scope.go:837): s.carriedGroups has exactly two readers, DemoteNullability's addMember (guards g <= 0) and scope.go:840 (guards g > 0), so a zero entry is inert.

Fix is five fixtures, each proven load-bearing by re-running its mutation.
close_reason: Closed

title: schema/gql: the last-wins duplicate property name is not pinned anywhere, so it can flip to first-wins silently
description:
Splits the shippable half off gqlc-4np, and deliberately does NOT decide gqlc-4np's ADR.

gqlc-4np measures that `{ id :: INT NOT NULL, id :: STRING }` parses, resolves, and yields ONE property — the last one — with the first declaration's type and its NOT NULL discarded and no diagnostic. Whether that should be rejected (a new sentinel, consistent with ErrDuplicateNodeType / ErrDuplicateEdgeType) or defined as explicit last-wins precedence is a dialect choice that needs an ADR, and gqlc-lir declined to buy the PDF that would arbitrate it. That question stays open on gqlc-4np.

But gqlc-4np states a second thing that needs no decision at all:

    REGARDLESS OF WHICH IS CHOSEN, the current behaviour is unrepresented in
