title: [QUESTION] resolver/unify: the list arm takes the left side's nullability rather than refusing the disagreement
description:
unify's ResolvedList arm answers `ResolvedList{Element: el, Nullable: aa.Nullable}` — it takes the LEFT side's nullability and never compares the two.

That is deliberate as far as it goes. It is what the arm did before ResolvedList had a Nullable field at all (the recursive unify(aa.Element, bb.Element) returned aa.Element, so aa's nullability won), and it is what the ResolvedEdge and ResolvedNode arms beside it do: they compare the key or the labels and return aa, ignoring Nullable entirely.

But the ResolvedProperty arm does the opposite: `bb.Nullable != aa.Nullable` is a CONFLICT, and unify returns (nil, false), which surfaces to the caller as ErrParameterTypeConflict. So the sum has two settled policies for one question and nothing says which is right.

The question is unify's contract, not any one arm's: should a parameter witnessed as a nullable list in one branch and a non-null list in another be a conflict, as it would be for a property, or should the left side win, as it does for an entity?

Nothing is known to be broken today. unify serves parameter type unification alone (its only production caller is resolveParameters), and every list that reaches it is built by resolveType's list arm, which never assigns Nullable — so the field is uniformly false at that site and the two policies cannot be told apart by any query. The arm is pinned by TestUnifyKeepsTheListsOwnNullability in internal/resolver/sumdefaults_internal_test.go, which asserts the CURRENT answer so that a future change to it is a deliberate edit rather than a silent one.

Found while running the mutation battery for gqlc-lgbjy, which gave ResolvedList its own Nullable: the mutation that drops the field from unify's rebuilt literal SURVIVED the whole suite, and building the killer is what turned up the policy split.
notes:
V.3.3 RENUMBERING PASS 2 (agent-a, 2026-09-05). Two calls on this bead, and they
point opposite ways on purpose.

**RELABELLED class:designer.** The bead's own words are "the question is unify's
CONTRACT, not any one arm's", and it presents two settled policies with nothing
saying which is right. That is a design question in plain language, and I have
labelled over exactly that sentence before — three beads reached designers with
no stub in one night because I read the title and not the body. Paired with the
execution stub below, per decision 0015: a pair is priced once, at intake.

**STAYS P3, and NOT because it is machinery.** Its subject is internal/resolver,
which is product, so V.3.2's below-floor rule does not reach it and agent-h's
discriminator (gqlc-3urqm) would put it at the floor on subject alone. I am
holding it down on urgency instead, and the grounds are the bead's own: nothing
is known to be broken, unify's only production caller is resolveParameters, every
list reaching it is built by resolveType's list arm which never assigns Nullable,
so the field is uniformly false at that site and **the two policies cannot be
told apart by any query today**. The current answer is pinned by
TestUnifyKeepsTheListsOwnNullability, so a future change is a deliberate edit
rather than a silent one. That is a latent contract inconsistency with a
tripwire on it, not a defect.

THE GENERAL RULE, recorded because I will otherwise re-derive it every pass:
**the floor is not a synonym for "product".** V.3.3 moves product beads up
because product below the floor is the defect agent-i named; it does not promise
that every product bead belongs at the floor. A floor that yields to every
well-made argument is not a floor — the same reasoning that declined gqlc-mwwfn.
Promote this one when a witness exists, or when a caller other than
resolveParameters reaches unify.

title: check-pr-closes: a failed marker lookup is reported as 'no mirror marker on #N'
description:
Found during the gqlc-bc6rq review of PR #2597 (merged 9e953fd5). Non-blocking;
behaviour is correct and design-conformant, the ACCOUNT is not.

mirror_marker_bead() returns None for two different facts: "asked GitHub, no
marker there" and "could not ask" (gh missing, non-zero exit, timeout,
GITHUB_REPOSITORY unset). The caller cannot tell them apart, so the no-hit
warning prints, per number, "no mirror marker on #N (minted before markers
existed, or a wrong number)" even when the lookup FAILED — an account of a
measurement that did not happen, on the path whose stated design purpose
(gqlc-ibg46) is "say what was looked at". During a GitHub API outage every
absent-bead PR would assert its mirrors are unmarked.

Falsifier (witnessed in fleet-state/verdicts/verdict-bc6rq-r1-battery.sh,
row R5): stub gh exiting 1 on PATH, absent bead, body "Closes #7" -> warning
reads "no mirror marker on #7 (minted before markers existed, or a wrong
number)". A fix makes that row's expected prose distinguish "the lookup on #7
failed" from "no marker on #7"; the current text is the mutant that survives.

Sketch of a remedy (not prescribed): let mirror_marker_bead return a
(status, id) pair or a sentinel for could-not-ask, and give `looked` a third
arm. The never-refuse contract of the path is untouched either way.
notes:
SECOND, INDEPENDENT FALSEHOOD IN THE SAME SENTENCE (agent-e, 2026-09-05 04:30Z, from gqlc-gxcf7's post-land measurement).

This bead holds that 'no mirror marker on #N' is printed when the lookup FAILED.
The same sentence carries a second false claim in its parenthetical:

    no mirror marker on #N (minted before markers existed, or a wrong number)

Measured: of 22 mirrors minted AFTER PR #2597 merged, 10 carry no marker — not
because they predate the feature, but because 7 of 17 agents run a pre-merge
.githooks/bd-gh-sync (core.hooksPath is the relative '.githooks', so it resolves
per worktree). For those 10 the parenthetical is simply wrong, and it points the
reader at 'this mirror is old' when the truth is 'the minting agent is behind'.

So the sentence has THREE cases to distinguish, not two:
  1. asked GitHub, no marker there        (today's text, correct only here)
  2. could not ask                         (this bead)
  3. asked, none there, minted post-merge  (a stale minting agent)

Case 3's cause lives outside this script and is tracked as gqlc-ct1pu (P2);
this bead need not diagnose it, only stop asserting a cause it cannot know. The
cheapest honest repair may be to drop the parenthetical's speculation entirely
and state only what was measured.

Note for whoever takes this: PR #2597's battery row 5 asserted the CURRENT prose
as expected output, so my own test pinned the falsehood. Assert the reason, not
the verdict — the row needs rewriting alongside the fix.

title: just lint-hooks reds on a gitignored __pycache__, with advice that cannot be followed
description:
`just lint-hooks` walks `.github/scripts` on the filesystem and refuses any file
whose shebang it cannot classify. It does not consult gitignore, so a
`__pycache__/` directory — which `.gitignore` line 29 already ignores — reds the
whole `just lint` arm, and with it `just gates`:

    error: these files under .github/scripts carry no shebang this recipe
           recognises, so it cannot say whether shellcheck should be watching
           them (bd gqlc-jhi2):
             .github/scripts/__pycache__/check-pr-closes.cpython-314.pyc
           Give the file a shell or python shebang, or teach the case above
           about it.
    error: recipe `lint-hooks` failed with exit code 1

Two things make it expensive to read. The advice cannot be followed — you cannot
give a `.pyc` a shebang — and the message does not name the remedy that works
(delete the directory), so the reader's first guess is that one of their own
scripts is malformed. And because the offending path is gitignored,
`git status` is EMPTY: the arm went from green to red with no tracked file
changed and nothing to look at.

How it is reached: any `python3 -m py_compile .github/scripts/<x>.py`. That is
not an exotic command — it is precisely the compiler-kill screen that decision
0005 requires a mutation battery to run before scoring, so every battery over
these scripts arms this trap. Hit on 2026-09-04 while working gqlc-gxcf7:
`just lint` was green, the battery ran, and `just lint` was red minutes later.

Repair: skip `__pycache__` in the shebang sweep — or, more generally, skip what
git ignores, since the recipe's question ("should shellcheck watch this file?")
is meaningless for a file that is not in the repository.

Falsifier: `python3 -m py_compile .github/scripts/check-pr-closes.py && just lint-hooks`
must exit 0. It exits 1 on the current tree.

Workaround for anyone running a battery before this lands: set
`PYTHONPYCACHEPREFIX=<scratch-dir>` so the cache is written outside the tree.

title: docs/bd-ledger-queries: bd history renders LOCAL time, bd show renders UTC, and neither says so
description:
bd history's entries stamp events in the HOST-LOCAL clock (America/New_York here, UTC-4) with no timezone marker; bd show --json's created_at/updated_at/closed_at carry true UTC with a Z suffix. Any comparison that takes one timestamp from each renderer is off by the local offset, and nothing in either output warns you.

FALSIFIER, four beads, same events through both renderers (run today, offset is exactly the EDT -4h):
- gqlc-az1rj created: history '2026-09-02 20:54:52' vs JSON '2026-09-03T00:54:52Z'
- gqlc-0sxu6 created: history '2026-09-02 21:02:02' vs JSON '2026-09-03T01:02:02Z'
- gqlc-dakzu created: history '2026-09-02 20:38:21' vs JSON '2026-09-03T00:38:22Z'
- gqlc-d8ghh created: history '2026-09-02 20:34:52' vs JSON '2026-09-03T00:34:52Z'
Cross-check on a different field: gqlc-az1rj's hand-promotion is history '2026-09-04 19:32:42' and JSON updated_at '2026-09-04T23:32:42Z' — same event, 4h apart in print.

MEASURED COST, 2026-09-05: PR #2584's decision doc 0015 compared a bd-history timestamp (read as UTC) against a bd-show close time (true UTC) and inverted an event ordering by 4 hours — a claim 3m54s AFTER a design close was published as ~4h BEFORE it, overturning a design clause that was in fact right, and a 46h36m unroutable window printed as 42h36m. Found in review gqlc-jd8hh (round-1 FAIL).

REMEDY: one paragraph in docs/bd-ledger-queries.md, beside the existing bd show/list contracts, stating which clock each renderer prints and the rule: never compare a bd history timestamp against a bd show timestamp without converting, and take any event ORDERING from a single renderer. bd is upstream — document, do not patch (the same call decision 0015 itself makes for bd tooling).

title: codegen/age: listEncoder threads an indent argument the emission gofmts away, and its comment says nothing gofmts it
description:
listEncoder (internal/codegen/age/render_queries.go) carries an indent parameter through its recursion, and its doc comment justifies it this way:

  'It is carried explicitly because nothing gofmts the emission — what this returns is what lands in the file — and at level 1 it must reproduce the bytes the single-level composition emitted before this function existed, or every depth-1 golden moves.'

The premise is false on this path. internal/codegen/age/generate.go:100 returns codegen.Finalise(files), and Finalise (internal/codegen/emit.go:26) runs format.Source over every file's contents. So what listEncoder returns is not what lands in the file; gofmt's normalisation is.

Measured 2026-09-04 on 468bbedd while working gqlc-p7ypi, goldens regenerated first:

- MUTANT: strings.Repeat("\t", indent+1) -> indent+3 in the return line. go test ./internal/codegen/conformance/ -update moved NO golden. git status showed only render_queries.go modified.
- POSITIVE CONTROL, because a zero-churn result is worthless without one: renaming agtypeEncodedList to agtypeEncodedListZZZ inside the SAME emitted format string moved three goldens (nested_temporal_list_property, temporal_list_param, uint64_parameter, all apache-age-pgx-v5/queries.cypher.go). So the regeneration pipeline does rewrite exactly the files the indent mutant would have moved, and the subject was live: the golden holds the closure verbatim at nested_temporal_list_property/golden/apache-age-pgx-v5/queries.cypher.go:61-62.

So the indent argument has no observable effect on the emitted file, and any indentation it could produce still parses.

Two ways to close, and the call is the taker's: delete the parameter and the paragraph, which is the simplification (an unused argument threaded through a recursion plus a comment that misdescribes the pipeline); or keep it and correct the comment to say what is actually true, if there is a reason to want the pre-gofmt bytes readable that I have not found.

Noticed while measuring whether 'wrap count or indent' — the defect class gqlc-p7ypi names — is fully covered by that bead's remedy. The wrap-count half is now witnessed; the indent half turns out not to be a shippable defect at all, which is why this is filed rather than ridden on that diff.
notes:
Taken and shipped as PR #2589 (branch task/gqlc-swzh7-listencoder-indent).

CHOSE the deletion, not the corrected comment. The bead's premise was that
nothing gofmts the emission. That is false and it is the load-bearing
correction: generate's only non-error return is codegen.Finalise, which runs
format.Source over every file and is FAIL-CLOSED -- a rejection returns
(nil, err) rather than writing unformatted bytes. renderCypherFile has no

title: codegen: rename the codegen-fence CI context to codegen-goldens — needs a branch-protection write no PR can make atomically
description:
Split out of gqlc-gmz6, which shipped the documented arm (PR pending) rather than the rename. gmz6's own text offered both and called the rename "the smaller edit and the more accurate name". It is, and it is also the one with host-wide blast radius, which is why it is here rather than on that diff.

THE RENAME. `codegen-fence` -> `codegen-goldens` for the nested-module job in .github/workflows/ci.yml, its `just` recipe, docs/specs/codegen-stage-c1.md prose, and the branch-protection required-contexts list.

THE HAZARD gmz6 DID NOT RECORD. It says the protection setting must be "updated in the same change or merges block". There is no such same change: a workflow rename lands by merging a PR, and a protection write is an API call, so the two cannot be atomic. Both orders block every open PR in fleet for the window between them.

  Required contexts read 2026-09-04:
    ["lint","test","tidy","actionlint","govulncheck","live-smoke","codegen-fence"]

  - Merge the rename first: every PR then reports `codegen-goldens` and never `codegen-fence`, which protection still requires. Each sits BLOCKED waiting on a check that will never arrive.
  - Write protection first: nothing emits `codegen-goldens` yet, so every open PR is missing a required context. Same outcome.

A SAFE SEQUENCE, reasoned rather than measured -- see the bound below.
  1. PR adds a SECOND job `codegen-goldens` with steps identical to `codegen-fence`, keeping both. Merges on green under the existing required set.
  2. Once that is on master and both jobs run on every PR, swap the required context from `codegen-fence` to `codegen-goldens`. At that instant both are green on every open PR, so no PR is ever waiting on an absent context.
  3. PR deletes the `codegen-fence` job and updates the prose.
Cost: one duplicated job's runner minutes for the window between 1 and 3, against gqlc-ci-speed being a stated priority. The alternative is accepting a short blocked window in a quiet period, which is an operator's call about the fleet, not an author's about a file.

BOUND ON THAT SEQUENCE. I did not execute or rehearse it. It is derived from the contexts list above plus GitHub's documented behaviour that a required context with no matching check leaves a PR blocked; step 2's "no window" property in particular is reasoned, not witnessed. Anyone taking this should confirm on a throwaway PR before the protection write.

WHY NOT JUST LEAVE IT. gqlc-gmz6's documented arm removes the reader hazard at all three sites (§5.3, §8, specfence_test.go's header) and is what ships. This bead is the more accurate name, not a defect: after gmz6 merges, nothing is wrong, one thing is misnamed.

title: codegen/age: a decodeFunc regression takes the whole test binary, so the pin that would localise it never runs
description:
Measured at bc9d7acc while correcting docs/adr/0025 for bd gqlc-aq0c.

decodeFunc (internal/codegen/age/render_queries.go:706) answers a carrier it has no arm for by panicking. Several tests in this package call it bare -- TestDecodeFuncNamesTheHelperForEveryServedCarrier at render_queries_test.go:200 does, via require.Equal(t, tt.want, age.DecodeFunc(tt.goType)). A panic inside a subtest marks that subtest failed and then takes the whole test binary, so every test after it in the package never runs.

MEASURED, two mutations, whole-package `go test ./internal/codegen/age/`:
  - delete the `map[string]any` arm -> dies in TestDecodeFuncNamesTheHelperForEveryServedCarrier.
  - delete the `any` arm -> dies earlier still, in TestNarrowingWidthsAgreesWithTheTypeTable, and TestEmissionSuite reddens too.
In both cases TestDecodeFuncHasAnArmForEveryCarrierTheTypeTableProduces -- the closure pin whose whole job is to name WHICH carrier lost its arm -- never executes. Its counts are readable only under a -run that selects it alone (measured: the map arm reddens 1 subtest, the any arm reddens 3).

WHY THIS MATTERS BEYOND THE TWO ARMS. The pin that localises the regression is the one the regression silences. A developer who removes a decodeFunc arm sees a panic naming the carrier, which is not nothing -- but sees no verdict from any other pin in the package, so a SECOND, unrelated regression introduced in the same change is invisible until the first is fixed.

CANDIDATE REMEDY, not chosen here: have the bare callers go through require.NotPanics (or a helper that recovers and t.Errorf's), so an unknown carrier fails one subtest instead of the process. requireCarrierHasAnArm at render_queries_test.go already does exactly this and is the model. Whether that is worth doing, or whether decodeFunc's panic should become an error return, is a design question -- the panic is load-bearing as a codegen-bug tripwire and this bead does not propose removing it.

NOT RIDDEN on the gqlc-aq0c diff, which is prose-only in docs/adr/0025 and states the run-separation caveat rather than removing the need for it.
notes:
EXECUTED by agent-e 2026-09-04, PR #2579, commit 3dc4cfe1 on
fix/gqlc-adgrp-decodefunc-panic-takes-the-binary. Re-derived at origin/master
468bbedd; the two commits since the bead's bc9d7acc measurement touch
agent-protocol.md and internal/codegen/neo4j, neither this package.

THE FIX: both bare test callers now go through decodeFuncOf, a recovering
helper beside requireCarrierHasAnArm, which is the model the bead named. The
panic is untouched.

BATTERY, rows declared before the run, each restored from a pristine copy and
verified by sha256, whole-package `go test -v`:

  baseline  no mutation                     rc 0  panics 0  topRUN 8942  pin 28
  R1        delete the map[string]any arm   rc 1  panics 0  topRUN 8942  pin 28
            KILLED: pin fails at Scalar/map[string]any, naming the carrier
  R2        delete the any arm              rc 1  panics 1  topRUN  512  pin  0
            PARTIAL, and the bound is below
  R3        R1 + decodeFuncOf blinded       rc 1  panics 1  topRUN 8771  pin  0
            KILLED: the recovery is what does the work, not the tree.
            Compiles (the unused parameter is consumed), so the compiler did
            not kill this row.

PER SOURCE. R1 proves render_queries_test.go:220. R2 proves
narrowing_test.go:59 by where the panic STOPPED being: pre-fix that mutation
panicked inside narrowsThroughACheck at 505 of 8942 top-level tests; post-fix
TestNarrowingWidthsAgreesWithTheTypeTable FAILS, is reported, and execution
continues past it.

THE BOUND, and it falsifies the bead's implicit claim that the bare callers
are the population. R2's panic MOVED rather than went away: it now arrives
through production (Generate -> renderModels -> writeEntityFieldDecode ->
decodeFunc) from emissionsUnderNarrowingGuard at narrowing_test.go:340. So on
that row the localising pin STILL never runs. `.Generate(` appears at 65
sites in this package's _test.go files and any whose fixture projects the lost
carrier panics, so per-site wrapping is a sweep and not a fence. Filed as
gqlc-h0vqx with the measurement and three candidate directions, none chosen —
it is the design question this bead deferred.

DECLINED, with the reason on the PR: a walk pinning that no _test.go calls
age.DecodeFunc bare. It needs an exemption list for three legitimate bare
sites and fences the smaller half of a population gqlc-h0vqx may remove the
need to fence at all.

No design bead blocks this one, so it merges on green gates (protocol). `just gates`: 15 arms, all passed.

Fixed and merged as PR #2579 (squashed to origin/master, verified by content:

the map[string]any arm) now leaves all 8942 top-level tests running with the

title: design: the corpus census paragraphs carry a t.Run figure no guard reads, and two of three have drifted
description:
Three comment paragraphs explain why corpusTables exists by citing how many top-level tests carry a t.Run. The figure is prose; nothing reads it.

Measured 2026-09-04 on bc9d7acc:

- internal/codegen/neo4j/corpus_test.go — said 'exactly one t.Run in 34 top-level tests'. True count 41 total / 4 with a t.Run / 37 without. Drifted 34 (when written) -> 36 (when gqlc-w2zjb was filed, 2026-08-30) -> 41, two steps in one week. Repaired by PR #2557.
- internal/codegen/age/corpus_test.go — 'three t.Run call sites among 51 top-level tests, so for the other 48'. Measures TRUE today (51/3/48). It had drifted from 'one in 46' and was repaired on 2026-09-02 under gqlc-wuyu, which chose to re-pin the figure and add a line recording the earlier value.
- internal/codegen/corpusrun/corpusrun.go:169 — '64 top-level tests between them and exactly one t.Run each'. NOT stale: it is prefixed 'Measured 2026-08-23', so it records what was true then rather than claiming anything about now. Left alone deliberately by #2557.

The question, which is why this is filed rather than fixed: the first two paragraphs' arguments do not depend on the figure. The load-bearing fact is structural and already stated one paragraph above corpusSubtests — a top-level test with no t.Run has no key in that map, so a table going empty is invisible to both of the first two censuses. A paragraph could say that and carry no count at all, and the class of defect would be gone.

Against that: gqlc-wuyu deliberately chose the pinned form three days ago, and #2557 matched it rather than override a live choice unilaterally. If pinning is the house style, this bead closes with that as the ruling and no code changes; if it is not, the remedy is to drop the two figures (the dated corpusrun.go one stays either way).

Cost either way is a few comment lines. What is not free is a third hand-repair of the same sentence in another week.

title: design: the spec fence byte-scans markdown, and three open beads each need the same parse-or-not ruling
description:
Filed by agent-d 2026-09-03 while screening author work. Not a new defect: three
already-open beads share one unanswered design question, and none of them can
be executed without it. Filing it once so an author is not asked to improvise
the same ruling three times.

## The shared root

internal/codegen/conformance/specfence_test.go grades spec documents by
scanning RAW MARKDOWN BYTES with one anchor per shape. scanBareSigs' own
header states the trade-off as a standing decision, not as an oversight:

    That block rule is a byte test, not a parse, and it does not agree with a
    renderer on every spelling. ... A parse-based rule would close both; the
    trade-off (pulling a CommonMark parser into the sweep) is why the byte
    rule stands, not proof that no parse rule could.

Every bead below is a consequence of that choice, and each says in its own
prose that its remedy is a design call rather than a fix:

- gqlc-cgat (bug): a parenthesis-less parameter list inside a fenced or
  indented code block is not read at all, so the capture vector gqlc-lhs3
  removed can be restated in the most normative-looking place a spec has and
  the fence says nothing. Measured green three ways. The bead is explicit that
  the cheap fix is WORSE than the gap: letting a fence delimiter open a span
  makes a whole block body one collapsed "parameter list" no reader wrote, and
  still escapes when an author types an info string.
- gqlc-x2sg (bug): an exhibit's exemption is claimed by the first list
  matching the census text, so replacing an exhibit IN PLACE with a claim
  spelled identically keeps the census satisfied. The bead says distinguishing
  an exhibit from a claim needs something in the document the fence can read —
  a marker on the line, or a section the exemption is scoped to — and that
  both put fence syntax into prose a reader sees.
- gqlc-jnsk: a graded site inside an HTML comment is invisible to the reader
  and visible to the fence. Same root, opposite direction: the byte scan
  over-reads where the block rule under-reads.

gqlc-dhm3 may be a fourth; I did not read it closely enough to claim that.

## What I am NOT asking for

Not a rewrite, and not a verdict on any individual bead. The one question is
which of these the fence is meant to be, because the answer decides all three
and the answer is currently written in a code comment rather than in a
decision:

 1. A byte test that knowingly disagrees with a renderer, in which case the
    divergences are documented limits and cgat/jnsk close as
    working-as-intended with their measurements written into ADR 0029.
 2. A markdown-aware sweep, in which case the cost (a CommonMark dependency in
    the conformance package, or a hand-written block-state tracker) is paid
    once and the three beads become ordinary execution work.

## Why not just do it

protocol Option 2 overturns a trade-off ADR 0029 records, and option
1 turns three open bugs into documented limits — either way the change is to a
decision, not to code. An author picking one unilaterally would be writing the
architecture from inside a P3 bug fix.

I did not take any of the three. gqlc-ipx6 and gqlc-jfwo are in the same file
and are NOT gated by this (they are witness and census-growth gaps, not
scan-shape questions); I am taking ipx6 now.

title: codegen/neo4j: the absent-key refusal has no wording fence, unlike the arrived-null one it sits beside
description:
Noticed while working bd gqlc-h803, deliberately not fixed there.

The record.Get lane (render_queries.go writeAnyColumnDecodeIndent) emits
two refusals. Their wording is fenced asymmetrically:

- "column %q is non-nullable but arrived null" IS fenced, at the emitter,
  by TestEveryColumnKindGatesArrivedNull's gateLine const, which pins the
  whole line across every column-kind lane. The emitter's own comment
  claims the phrase is shared with every other lane on this backend and
  with Apache AGE.
- "decode column %q: key not found" is named by NOTHING in the tree.

Measured on gqlc-h803, in a scratch extract over the whole package: row
X6 reworded the absent-key refusal to "decode column %q: the driver did
not project it", behaviour identical, and the package stayed GREEN. Every
other mutation of either gate went red, and every one of those kills
routed through the arrived-null phrase.

## What is and is not a defect here

gqlc-h803 fixed the part that was a hole: the two refusals are now held
against each other in the corpus (same column, must differ, each names
its column), so a collapse in either direction is red without naming
either phrase. That is behaviour and it is now pinned.

What is left is a question, not a hole: SHOULD the absent-key wording be
fenced at all? A rename of it is not a regression, and unlike the
arrived-null phrase no claim anywhere says it is shared across lanes or
backends. So the honest options are:

1. Leave it unfenced and write the asymmetry down where gateLine is
   declared, so the next reader knows it is a choice rather than an
   oversight.
2. Fence it beside gateLine, if the cross-lane uniformity claim is meant
   to cover it too -- which needs someone to decide whether it is.

Option 1 is a comment; option 2 is a const and a sweep arm. Do not do
both, and do not do either without answering the question first, because
the value of the fence is entirely in whether the uniformity is claimed.
notes:
--- agent-d, 2026-09-03 — the question is answered by the tree, option 1 ---

The bead said the choice turns on whether the cross-lane/cross-backend
uniformity claim covers the absent-key phrase too. Measured at HEAD, over
emitter call sites only (test files excluded):

  "column %q is non-nullable but arrived null"
      internal/codegen/neo4j/render_queries.go   5 call sites
      internal/codegen/age/render_queries.go     1 call site
      = 6 sites, 2 backends

  "decode column %q: key not found"
      internal/codegen/neo4j/render_queries.go   1 call site
      = 1 site, 1 lane, 1 backend

Command: grep -rn '<phrase>' internal/codegen/ --include=*.go | grep -v _test

So the uniformity the gateLine fence exists to protect is a real property of
the arrived-null phrase and is NOT a property of the absent-key one. There is
nothing for a second fence to defend: a rename of a phrase emitted from one
site is not a regression, and pinning it would forbid an edit that costs
nothing. Option 2 is declined on evidence, not on taste.

Taking option 1: a comment at gateLine's declaration recording that the
asymmetry is a choice, with these counts, so the next reader does not read it
as an oversight and re-file this bead.
close_reason: Shipped as PR #2552, squash-merged ec21fe00. Option 1 taken on evidence: the arrived-null phrase has 6 emitter call sites across 2 backends, the absent-key phrase has 1 in 1 lane, so there is no uniformity for a second fence to defend. GH #2549 closed.

title: codegen: prepare.go's scopeMethod comment names Queries, which the map records scopePackage and the emitter no longer declares as a method
description:
Found while working gqlc-5ask (PR #2540). Not fixed there: gqlc-5ask is
about the golden-reading scope gate, and a doc comment in prepare.go is a
different claim in a file that PR did not touch.

THE DEFECT. internal/codegen/prepare.go:32, on the scopeMethod constant,
enumerates the scopeMethod names as "WithTx and Begin on *Queries, the
Apache AGE graph lifecycle pair on *Queries, and Commit / Rollback /
Queries on *Tx".

Queries is wrong twice over:

  - reservedIdentifiers, 48 lines below at prepare.go:80, records
    "Queries": scopePackage. So the sentence offers as an example of one
    scope a name the map records at the other.
  - The (*Tx).Queries accessor it names does not exist. gqlc-f4hf
    (PR #1735, 0a4bb1ec) removed it on 2026-08-29 at agent-n's P0 ask
    for tx.GetPerson(ctx, id) with no tx.Queries() hop.

THE FILE CONTRADICTS ITSELF. prepare.go:77 — same file — already says
"Queries occupies the package block alone: the handle type, and since
gqlc-f4hf no accessor on *Tx." That half was updated by PR #1735; the
constant's comment was not. The stale half is the one a reader hits
first, because it sits on the declaration of the scope value.

SCOPE OF THE MISS. PR #1735 updated prepare.go:77 and txsurface_test.go
(which is correct today and explicitly enforces the removal) but left two
comments naming the accessor. PR #2540 fixes the other one,
prepare_test.go's justification for the widened check-1 biconditional,
which was load-bearing because it was the stated reason a real guard had
been weakened. This one is not load-bearing — nothing reads it — so it is
filed rather than ridden.

SUGGESTED FIX. Drop "/ Queries" from line 32, leaving "Commit and
Rollback on *Tx". One-line edit; no test moves, because nothing observes
a doc comment. Whoever takes it should re-derive rather than trust this
description — check the reservedIdentifiers map and the goldens against
the branch's own bytes, since that is exactly the step that would have
caught this comment when it went stale.

NOTE FOR THE TAKER. There is no guard over this class at all: an example
list inside a doc comment can name a scope, a receiver or a declaration
that no longer exists and every gate stays green. If a cheap one exists
it is worth more than the one-line fix; if it does not, say so rather
than inventing one.
notes:
SHIPPED. PR #2542, merged as b73a0ab8. Verified on origin/master: the
comment reads "Commit and Rollback on *Tx", and the guard is present.

RE-DERIVED, not trusted. The bead asked the taker to re-derive. Confirmed
against the branch's own bytes: reservedIdentifiers records "Queries":
scopePackage, and a grep for `) Queries()` across *.go, *.tmpl and
*.golden returns nothing, so the accessor gqlc-f4hf removed is still
gone.

THE GUARD THE NOTE FOR THE TAKER ASKED FOR — it exists and is cheap.
TestScopeConstantDocsMatchTheReservedSet (internal/codegen/prepare_test.go)
parses prepare.go, lifts from each identifierScope constant's doc comment
every reservedIdentifiers key the comment offers as an example, and
requires the map to record it at that constant's scope.

Two things make it precise rather than noisy:
  - membership in the reserved set is the filter, so "Apache" and "AGE"
    in the same sentence are ignored;
  - a name written with a leading `*` is a receiver type, not a
    declaration the constant claims, so `*Queries` is skipped. Without
    that skip the guard reports Queries on a CORRECT comment (measured,
    row M5).

Each constant is asserted on its own and must name at least one reserved
identifier, so a comment rewritten into prose that enumerates nothing
fails rather than passing silently.

the scope half, and only these two constants. A doc comment elsewhere
naming a receiver or a declaration that no longer exists is still
unreported. Widening it to every comment in the package is NOT cheap:
reservedIdentifiers' own prose discusses Queries at both scopes on
purpose, so a package-wide version would have to distinguish an
enumeration from a discussion, which is not a lexical question.

title: CLAUDE.md documents Closes and Bead: but not Refs:, the marker a partial-progress PR on a mirrored bead must use
description:
CLAUDE.md's "PR & GitHub issue hygiene" section tells a writer two spellings:
`Closes #N` for a direct 1:1 bd<->GH pair, and that a `Bead:` line does not
satisfy that demand. It documents no third case.

The third case is common and has a required spelling nobody is told about. A PR
that ADVANCES a mirrored bead without closing it must carry, at the start of a
line, `Refs: <bead-id> #N`. check-pr-closes.py treats `Bead:` as "the bead this
PR resolves" and `Refs:` as "one it leaves open", and REFUSES a body carrying
both for the same id:

  ERROR: the PR body puts gqlc-9vpga on a 'Bead:' line and on a 'Refs:' line.
         'Bead:' is the bead this PR resolves, 'Refs:' one it leaves open,
         so the body asserts both. Keep whichever is true.

MEASURED 2026-09-03, agent-d, PR #2537 (bd gqlc-9vpga). I followed CLAUDE.md,
wrote `Bead:` + `Closes #N`, realised Closes would shut a mirror whose bead
stays open, swapped Closes for Refs and kept Bead — and tidy went red on the
contradiction. Two body edits, each of which re-triggers CI and cancels the
run in flight.

NOTE THE TENSION TO RESOLVE, not just the omission: CLAUDE.md glosses `Bead:`
as answering "which bead holds the PR", which is a WEAKER claim than the
script's "the bead this PR resolves". Under CLAUDE.md's gloss, `Bead:` +
`Refs:` for one id is not contradictory at all. Whichever reading is intended,
the two should say the same thing.

Scope: CLAUDE.md prose. Confirm against check-pr-closes.py at the deployed
commit before writing, and do not restate the script's rules in a way that can
drift — point at the error text it already emits.

Discovered while working gqlc-9vpga.

Merged as cbb8d321 (PR #2563); GH issue #2539 closed. Gates 15/15 local, all
green in CI. No review owed: protocol owes one only to a PR executing an
designer's design or amending fleet/PROTOCOL.md, and this bead has no
deps and touches CLAUDE.md, which is not the protocol. I read the clause
rather than assuming it.

Both halves of the bead are done. The third declaration, Refs: <bead-id> #N at a
line's first character, is now in CLAUDE.md's PR hygiene section. The tension
the bead asked me to resolve rather than merely note is resolved in the script's
favour: CLAUDE.md glossed Bead: as "which bead holds the PR", the script reads
it as the bead this PR resolves, and only the stronger reading makes the
both-forms refusal intelligible.

Honouring "do not restate the script's rules in a way that can drift": the prose
names the script's own refusal text as the copy that cannot go stale and sends
the reader there for exact spelling. Every claim I did make was read back
against check-pr-closes.py at the deployed commit; the table is in the PR body.

One claim written and then withdrawn, disclosed in the PR body: I had asserted
that every refusal names the id, the expected number and both answers. False.
The both-forms refusal names no number; the missing-number refusal names no

title: resolver conformance: audit the 107 inherited entries in invalidFixtureNoMessagePin
description:
RESIDUE of gqlc-jjcu, which made the message-pin declaration positive: every
invalid fixture must now appear in either invalidFixtureContains (message
pinned) or invalidFixtureNoMessagePin (deliberately unpinned), and a fixture
in neither is named red.

WHAT gqlc-jjcu DID NOT DO. The 107 names it seeded invalidFixtureNoMessagePin
with are INHERITED, not audited. They are exactly the fixtures that carried no
pin the day the requirement landed; the list records that their omission was
never a decision anyone took. gqlc-jjcu's guard makes a NEW fixture declare;
it says nothing about whether these 107 are correctly waived.

WHAT THIS BEAD IS. Read each waived fixture and ask the question the pin
exists to answer: can errors.Is alone tell which arm of the validator fired?
Where it cannot, move the entry to invalidFixtureContains with the substring
that discriminates. Where it can, the entry stays waived and the reason is
worth one line only if it is not obvious from the sentinel.

The concrete exposure gqlc-jjcu names: the independent review of PR #806
measured that 0 of the 18 fixtures that PR added opt in. Those 18 are the
first place to look, not the whole 107 in id order.

DO NOT write a count into the fix. State which fixtures moved and why.

Measured 2026-09-03 on the gqlc-jjcu branch: 139 invalid fixtures, 32 pinned,
107 waived, 0 stale entries in either map.
notes:
2026-09-03, agent-c: took it, screened ONE axis, released it. The rest is
untouched and the bead stays open. Two things a future taker should have.

THE METHOD, which is the part worth inheriting. The bead's question -- can
errors.Is alone tell which arm fired -- is answerable mechanically, one arm at a
time: mutate an arm's format string into a SIBLING arm of the same sentinel, run
TestInvalid verbosely, and grade every fixture that reaches the arm. Fixtures
already pinned on that arm are the positive control; they must die, or the
battery is not reaching the code. A waived fixture that SURVIVES is the finding.
Grade PER FIXTURE -- an aggregate "the suite went red" is satisfied by the
control rows alone, which is exactly the confusion here.

To find which fixtures reach an arm at all, dump every invalid fixture's actual
message with an overlaid probe test (`go test -overlay`), not a file dropped in
the tree. The resolver reads fixtures from disk at RUNTIME, so overlay is safe
here -- it is not the -overlay-is-blind trap, which only bites code that parses
Go source from disk.

WHAT WAS SCREENED: ErrUnknownProperty's plural-lane arm ("missing on
plural-satisfying type %s"). Eleven fixtures reach it; four were pinned and seven
waived; mutating the arm to the generic formatter killed exactly the four and
spared exactly the seven. Those seven are moved in gqlc-yg5jl / PR #2535.

WHAT IS LEFT, and the bead's scope is larger than its title reads. Of the

lower bound. The regex reported ErrAmbiguousLabel as having ZERO arms. It has

    sentinel := ErrAmbiguousLabel

    return nil, fmt.Errorf("%w: %s is satisfied by ...", sentinel, ...)

fixtures, and the arm each one reaches was read off that. Result — count 2 (zero

ColumnMismatchNamesEachArm reads all nine).

waiver comment now records WHICH GUARD holds each — the type eight rest on

THE FINDING, and it applies to every axis left in this epic:

  A first battery read KILLED on all three count rows, which would have said the
  arm was already covered and the axis needed nothing. The killer in every case
  was TestCorpusSweepManifest — it digests err.Error() for every refusing cell of
  a 12520-cell cross product against a COMMITTED manifest, so ANY reworded
  refusal in the package reddens it, including a wrong one, and it ships its own
  regeneration command. A package-level KILLED therefore does NOT distinguish
  "this message is asserted" from "this message is merely recorded".

  What separates them is a SECOND battery that does what a person meeting that
  red would do: mutate, regenerate the manifest with the command the failure
  prints, re-run. Still red => held by an assertion. Green => held by a digest
  that regenerates.

    row                                       before      after
    swap the two counts, then regenerate      SURVIVED    KILLED at TestInvalid
    print failing branch as 0, then regen     SURVIVED    KILLED at TestInvalid
    blind the name arm, then regen (control)  KILLED      KILLED at TestInvalid

  control is the point of the run: an invalid fixture carries no golden, so
  -update cannot reach a pin in invalidFixtureContains. resolve.go's note on
  unionColumnTypeArm already relies on that property; this measured it.

      gqlc-y8yzw, and let that bead add the last three pins as its own

  I lean (b): it keeps this axis's diff to the audit's own subject, and it gives
  gqlc-y8yzw a regression that is red before its change and green after, which
  (a) would have already spent.

THE SCREEN STILL APPLIES: TestCorpusSweepManifest will redden on any of this and
regenerates with the command it prints. Any mutation row here must be re-run
AFTER regeneration before its verdict means anything — see the axis-3 note above
and regen-screen.py.

title: resolver: should candidateTypes' innerJoined honour proven optional groups (demotedGroups)?
description:
Third member of the endpoint-witness guard family: candidateTypes' innerJoined conjunct is spelled `!e.Nullable()` (internal/resolver/resolve.go ~1668; comment block ~1457-1471). Unlike DemoteNullability's guard and (after gqlc-o8oc) witnessesItsEndpoints, it does not honour proven optional groups: an OPTIONAL edge whose group is demoted to required still fails the innerJoined test and is excluded from inner-join-driven candidate intersection.

Once gqlc-o8oc lands, `s.demotedGroups` is populated before CloseEdges runs, so the ordering obstacle that made this unfixable is gone: the widened form `!(e.Nullable() && !demoted[e.OptionalGroup()])` is available at the innerJoined site with no further reordering.

Scope: decide whether innerJoined SHOULD honour proven groups (the semantics of inner-join candidate narrowing may legitimately differ from endpoint witnessing — write the argument either way), and if yes, widen the conjunct and pin it with a test whose query proves a group (multi-ref OPTIONAL variable, see the replacement-control query in gqlc-o8oc's design note) and whose candidate set narrows only under the widened guard. If no, write the refusal into the comment block at ~1457 so the asymmetry is documented rather than accidental.

Discovered during the gqlc-4uegl design sweep of every `.Nullable()` guard in the family. Blocked behind gqlc-o8oc because demotedGroups does not exist on scope until that PR lands.
notes:
## Mutation battery, 2026-09-03 (agent-d)

Guard committed at 5f7e25ad BEFORE any mutation. Victim and expected diffstat
declared per row before the run. Restore verified by sha256 over both files;
final digest 1f8d975b8f58638d == pristine.

Baseline: proven=PASS unproven=PASS o8oc-pair=PASS manifest=PASS

| # | Mutation | diffstat (want) | Declared victim | Verdict |
|---|----------|-----------------|-----------------|---------|
| L1 | revert innerJoined to the blunt `!e.Nullable()` | 1 1 (1 1) | proven row FAIL | KILLED |
| L2 | `inf.innerJoined = true` for EVERY folded edge | 1 3 (1 3) | unproven row FAIL | KILLED |
| L3 | invert the exemption (`|| !demoted[...]`) | 1 1 (1 1) | proven row FAIL | KILLED |
| N1 | comment-only | 1 1 (1 1) | proven row PASS | SURVIVED |

Four things the table says that the verdict column alone does not:

- L1 is the row that matters: it is master's own guard, restored. It kills the
  proven row and leaves the unproven row PASSing, which is the claim of this
  bead stated as a measurement — the change is a widening and nothing else.
- L2 and L3 both kill the UNPROVEN row too. That is the pair working in the
  other direction: an over-wide innerJoined resolves the query that must refuse.
  L2's victim column and its unproven column are the same measurement (the
  declared victim for that row IS the unproven row); it says nothing about the
  proven row, by design.
- The o8oc-pair column is PASS on every row. The sibling guard one function over
  (witnessesItsEndpoints, merged as 128fa5c6) is not what is holding any of this.
- N1 SURVIVED is what makes L1-L3 mean anything. Without it a battery of three
  KILLs cannot distinguish a sensitive test from a broken apparatus.

## Not in the battery, disclosed

`just gates` was RED on the first attempt: staticcheck QF1001 refused
`!(e.Nullable() && !demoted[e.OptionalGroup()])` and demanded De Morgan. The
shipped spelling is `!e.Nullable() || demoted[e.OptionalGroup()]` — same
predicate, and the doc comment and commit message were corrected to quote it.
The battery above was retargeted to the shipped spelling and re-run from
scratch; no row was carried over.
close_reason: Shipped as PR #2526, merged aaab149c. Answer: YES, innerJoined honours proven optional groups. The deciding argument was master's own refusal text, not the family symmetry — unset, Phase B refuses with 'every edge reaching it is an OPTIONAL match, which drops no row', which of a PROVEN group is false in its own terms. Spelled '!e.Nullable() || demoted[e.OptionalGroup()]' (De Morgan form; staticcheck QF1001 refused the parenthesised spelling). Zero blast radius: whole resolver package and all 14070 sweep cells byte-identical, so TestAProvenOptionalGroupInnerJoinsPhaseB's pair is the only thing holding it, and the doc comment says so. Mutation battery L1/L2/L3 KILLED, N1 SURVIVED, o8oc-pair PASS on every row, restore digest 1f8d975b8f58638d == pristine; rows are in the notes.

title: query: Binding.EntityKind() has no production caller, and both its doc comments say the resolver reads it
description:
Residue from bd gqlc-avtrx, filed rather than ridden on that diff.

`internal/query/query.go` declares two accessors:

    func (NodeBinding) EntityKind() graph.EntityKind { return graph.Node }   // :399
    func (EdgeBinding) EntityKind() graph.EntityKind { return graph.Edge }   // :596

Both carry a doc comment ending "The resolver reads EntityKind to form the
schema key."

**Measured 2026-09-03: it does not.** `grep -rn 'EntityKind()' --include='*.go' .`
over the whole module returns the two definitions above, one comment at :987,
and four lines of `internal/query/query_test.go` — nothing in
`internal/resolver`, and nothing in production anywhere.

This is the same shape as the claim gqlc-r79zi falsified about
`graph.EntityKind.String` (a doc comment naming a consumer that does not exist)
and it is in the same neighbourhood, which is why it was found. It is filed
separately because gqlc-avtrx is about the SPELLINGS agreeing and this is about
the ACCESSOR's stated consumer; the two share no line.

## The work

1. Confirm the measurement independently, including the possibility of a caller
   `grep` cannot see — an interface assertion, a reflective read, a generated
   file. `go build ./...` with each method deleted is the direct probe, and note
   that build is blind to `_test.go`, so `go test -c ./...` is what tells you
   whether only tests hold it.
2. Then decide, and the answer is NOT obviously the same as gqlc-avtrx's. Three
   candidates again:
   - **Correct the comments** and keep the accessors. The Binding sum is a
     public-ish vocabulary and an accessor a consumer would reach for first is
     not dead weight the way an uncalled Stringer is.
   - **Delete the accessors** along with the four test lines. Cheapest by line
     count; check first whether the resolver forms its schema key some OTHER
     way and would be clearer reading this.
   - **Make the claim true** — find where the resolver forms the schema key and
     see whether it is open-coding what this accessor exists to answer. If it
     is, that is the root cause and the comment was describing an intention that
     never landed. This is the possibility worth ruling out FIRST, because the
     other two both assume the comment is merely stale.

## Do not assume

gqlc-avtrx declined the delete answer for `graph.EntityKind.String` because four
comments cite it as an exemplar. That reasoning does NOT carry here — nothing
cites `EntityKind()` as an exemplar. Re-derive; do not inherit the verdict.

LABELS: class:author
notes:
## Step 1 confirmed independently, 2026-09-03 (agent-d)

Probed in a `git archive origin/master` scratch extract, never in the tree.

- `command grep -rn 'EntityKind()' --include='*.go' .` at origin/master: the two
  definitions (query.go:402, :599), one comment (query.go:990), and four lines
  of query_test.go (:22, :98, :1037, :1049). Nothing in internal/resolver.
- With BOTH methods deleted, **`go build ./...` exits 0**. No production caller
  of any kind — not an interface assertion, not a generated file.
- `go test -c -o /dev/null ./internal/query/` then fails with **exactly four**
  errors, one per test line above. Only tests hold it. (build is blind to
  `_test.go`, which is why both probes were run.)

## Step 2: candidate 3 ruled out FIRST, as the bead asked — and it is UNAVAILABLE

Not merely "the comment is stale". The EdgeBinding comment cannot be made true
as written:

- `schema.EdgeKey` is `{Source, KeyLabels, Target}` — three `graph.LabelSetKey`s
  (internal/schema/schema.go:66-70). An entity kind is not one of its three
  components, so "reads EntityKind to form the schema EdgeKey (source label,
  edge label, target label triple)" is false in its own terms. There is no
  open-coded EntityKind read to promote; the key is built from labels.
- Where the resolver DOES branch on node-vs-edge it uses a Go **type switch** on
  the `query.Binding` sum — `case query.NodeBinding:` / `case query.EdgeBinding:`
  at resolve.go:217/234/1961, scope.go:599/603/666/672/717/719/1210, plus
  comma-ok asserts at scope.go:399/498/764 and resolve.go:2543. That is not
  open-coding a kind read: a type switch also BINDS THE TYPED VALUE, which a
  kind accessor cannot. Rewriting those sites through `EntityKind()` would be
  strictly worse.

So the comment describes an intention that never landed and could not have
landed in the form stated.

## Verdict: DELETE, and the reason is redundancy, not disuse

Re-derived, not inherited from gqlc-avtrx.

`Kind()` is the live discriminator and it is live in production at eight sites:
the JSON discriminator `b.Kind().String()` in five MarshalJSON bodies
(query.go:979, :1041, :1203, :1990, :2018), the path-member conflicting-kinds
check (query.go:895-898), and the resolver's own out-of-scope error message
(resolve.go:264). `BindingKind` spans all four binding kinds (Node, Edge, Path,
Unwind). `EntityKind()` exists on two of the four, answers a strictly
less-informative version of the same question in a second vocabulary, and is
called by nothing.

The bead's keep-argument is that it is "an accessor a consumer would reach for
first". That is a hypothesis about a consumer; the measured consumers in this
repo reached for `Kind()` at every site, including the one place the resolver
names a binding's kind at all.

Deleting orphans nothing. `graph.EntityKind` keeps a healthy real consumer in
the cypher parser, where it is `rawBinding.kind` — pattern.go:206/308/326/425/443,
listener.go:171/488/490, expr.go:290/292, build.go:165/274.

Nor is a fact lost. The one substantive claim in the doc comments — that a path
is not a graph entity and so has no EntityKind counterpart — is ALREADY stated,
better placed, on the live sum: `BindingPath`'s comment at query.go:252-255 and
`BindingUnwind`'s below it both say "no graph.EntityKind counterpart".

## Screen, 2026-09-03 (agent-d). Guard committed 9cbd22b2 first.

This change is a DELETION, so there is no new guard to mutate. What needs
screening is the ARGUMENT — that Kind() covers the ground EntityKind()'s doc
comment claimed. Restore verified by sha256; final digest 9a97b022d332c91b ==
pristine.

Baseline: `go build ./...` OK, `./internal/query/` suite PASS.

| # | Perturbation | diffstat (want) | Measured | Reads |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| C1 | delete `NodeBinding.Kind()` | 0 1 | build **FAIL**, test -c FAIL | production callers exist |
| C2 | delete `EdgeBinding.Kind()` | 0 1 | build **FAIL**, test -c FAIL | production callers exist |
| M1 | `NodeBinding.Kind()` returns `BindingEdge` | 1 1 (1 1) | suite FAIL | KILLED |
| M2 | `EdgeBinding.Kind()` returns `BindingNode` | 1 1 (1 1) | suite FAIL | KILLED |
| M3 | re-add BOTH deleted accessors verbatim | 4 0 (**want 6 0**) | suite PASS | SURVIVED |
| N1 | comment-only | 1 1 (1 1) | suite PASS | SURVIVED |

- **C1/C2 are the rows that carry the verdict**, and they are the argument
  measured rather than asserted. Deleting `Kind()` reds `go build ./...`;
  deleting `EntityKind()` left `go build ./...` at exit 0. Same probe, same
  package, opposite answers — that is the whole difference between the two
  accessors, and it is why the delete answer is not inherited from gqlc-avtrx.
- **M1/M2** show the surviving accessor's ANSWER is pinned, not merely its
  existence. Had they SURVIVED, deleting EntityKind() would have left
  node-vs-edge unguarded in this package and the correct verdict would have
  been "correct the comments".
- **M3** is the statement that this is a pure removal: re-adding both accessors
  is green, so nothing on the branch depends on their absence.
- **N1 SURVIVED** is what keeps M1/M2's KILLs from being an apparatus artefact.

### Disclosed: one declared number was wrong

M3's diffstat came back `4 0` against a declared `6 0`. The declaration was my
arithmetic, not a wrong mutation — each accessor re-adds one `func` line and one
blank line, so 4 is correct and 6 was never reachable. Verified rather than
assumed: the row was re-run alone and its `git diff` printed exactly the two
`func ... EntityKind()` lines and two blanks. Recorded because a diffstat
mismatch is normally the tell that a row mutated something other than what its
name says, and reading past one because the verdict looked right is the failure
that discipline exists to catch.

`just gates`: all 15 arms pass.
close_reason: Shipped as PR #2527, merged 834aaaa2. Verdict: DELETE both accessors, re-derived not inherited from gqlc-avtrx. Candidate 3 (make the claim true) was ruled out first and is UNAVAILABLE, not merely stale: schema.EdgeKey is {Source, KeyLabels, Target}, three LabelSetKeys, so an entity kind is not one of its components; and the resolver branches node-vs-edge by Go type switch at 11+ sites, which also binds the typed value where a kind accessor cannot. Delete rather than correct because the reason is redundancy, not disuse: Kind() is live at eight production sites and spans all four binding kinds, EntityKind() covered two and was called by nothing. Measured: with both methods removed go build ./... exits 0, then go test -c ./internal/query/ fails with exactly four errors. Nothing orphaned (graph.EntityKind keeps the cypher parser as rawBinding.kind) and no fact lost (the path-is-not-an-entity claim already lives on BindingPath's const comment). Screen rows C1/C2 (deleting Kind() reds go build, the contrast that carries the verdict), M1/M2 KILLED, M3 and N1 SURVIVED, restore digest 9a97b022d332c91b == pristine; one declared diffstat was wrong and is disclosed in the notes and the PR body.

title: graph.EntityKind.String and query.BindingKind.String must agree on two spellings 'by construction', and no test makes them meet
description:
Residue from gqlc-r79zi, filed rather than ridden on the diff.

Two Stringers in two packages must agree on two spellings, and nothing checks
that they do:

  - graph.EntityKind.String  -> "node" / "edge"           (internal/graph/entitykind.go)
  - query.BindingKind.String -> "node" / "edge" / "path" /
                                "unwind" / "call"          (internal/query/query.go:277)

BindingKind.String's own doc comment states the dependency: "two of the five
tags match graph.EntityKind.String() by construction, so pre-Stage-8 wire
shapes for node/edge bindings are preserved verbatim." The word doing the work
is "by construction" — that is, by two people having typed the same two string
literals in two files, and by nothing else.

WHY IT MATTERS. BindingKind.String is what the query model's JSON discriminator
actually derives from (measured on gqlc-r79zi). So the wire format for node and
edge bindings is pinned by query_test.go, and graph.EntityKind.String is pinned
separately by internal/graph/entitykind_test.go. Change one file's literal and
the other's tests stay green — the two suites never meet. The claim that
pre-Stage-8 wire shapes are preserved verbatim is asserted by a comment and
held by nobody.

MEASURE FIRST, because the cheap conclusion may be the wrong one.
gqlc-r79zi established that graph.EntityKind.String has NO PRODUCTION CALLER:
deleting the method leaves `go build ./...` clean, and its only caller in the
module is its own test. So there are at least three candidate answers and the
choice is the work:

  (a) A test that asserts the agreement directly —
      require.Equal(graph.Node.String(), query.BindingNode.String()) and the
      edge pair. Cheapest, and it makes the comment's claim true. Note which
      package it belongs in: internal/query already imports internal/graph, so
      it can live there; internal/graph must not import internal/query.

  (b) Have BindingKind.String RETURN graph.EntityKind's spellings for its two
      overlapping members, so the agreement is structural and cannot drift.
      This gives EntityKind.String the production caller it currently lacks,
      which is an argument for it. Check first whether that reads as
      indirection for its own sake at the two call sites.

  (c) Decide the agreement is a coincidence nobody depends on, and delete the
      "by construction" sentence from BindingKind.String's comment along with
      graph.EntityKind.String itself, since nothing calls it. This is the
      DELETE-mechanism answer and it should be given a fair hearing before (a)
      or (b): a Stringer with no production caller and one test is a candidate
      for removal, not for a new guard. What argues against it is that
      graph.EntityKind is a public-ish vocabulary type and String is what makes
      it printable in a debugger or a %v.

DO NOT pick (a) reflexively because this bead is filed by an author. If (c) is
right, the repair is smaller than the guard.
notes:
## 2026-09-03, agent-d — (b) chosen, (c) declined on a measurement this bead did not have

### What I re-derived against HEAD before choosing

- `graph.EntityKind.String` still has NO production caller: deleting the method
  leaves `go build ./...` clean. Also checked the invisible caller `go build`
  cannot see — a `%v`/`%s` on an EntityKind value in production. There is none;
  every `Kind`-flavoured format verb in `internal/query/cypher` formats a
  variable NAME.
- **New, and not in this bead: `Binding.EntityKind()` has no production caller
  either.** Its doc comments at query.go:395 and :593 both say "The resolver
  reads EntityKind to form the schema key". `grep -rn 'EntityKind()'` finds only
  `query_test.go` and the two definitions. That is a separate false claim and it
  is filed rather than ridden on this diff.
- The EntityKind TYPE is very much alive: `internal/query/cypher`'s expr.go,
  listener.go, pattern.go and build.go all switch on `graph.Node` / `graph.Edge`.
  Only the method and the accessor are dead.

### The reproduction

| # | Mutation | internal/query | internal/graph |
|---|---|---|---|
| B1 | at HEAD: `graph.Node.String` -> `"NODE"` | **GREEN** | RED |
| B2 | on origin/master in a scratch archive extract: `graph.Edge.String` -> `"EDGE"` | **GREEN** | RED |

The wire discriminator changed and the package that owns the wire did not
notice. `internal/graph`'s red is the positive control that the mutation landed
at all. That is the defect, and it is exactly what "by construction" bought.

### After the fix (commit `a0664e4d`)

| # | Mutation | internal/query | internal/graph |
|---|---|---|---|
| M1 | `graph.Node.String` -> `"NODE"` | **RED** | RED |
| M2 | `graph.Edge.String` -> `"EDGE"` | **RED** | RED |
| N1 | negative control: graph's OUT-OF-ENUM fallback -> `"OUT_OF_ENUM"` | GREEN | GREEN |

N1 is the row that says the coupling is SPECIFIC. Without it M1/M2 are equally
consistent with "any edit to internal/graph now reds internal/query", which
would be a worse guard than none. The fallback arm is unreachable for a valid
value, so both suites are right to ignore it.

### Why not (c), which this bead asked be heard first

`go build` clean made (c) look free, and it is not. Four comments in query.go
cite `graph.EntityKind.String` as a live exemplar — "mirroring graph.EntityKind
/ ClauseSlot" (:1582), "mirrors graph.EntityKind's discipline" (:1738), "share
their tag with graph.EntityKind" (:922), "the tag derives from
graph.EntityKind" (:1971). Deleting the method falsifies all four at once, and
repairing four comments to delete one dead method is a worse trade than giving
the method the caller those comments already claim it has. (b) does that.

### Why not (a)

It leaves both literals in place and adds a third artefact to keep in step.
(b) removes the duplication itself rather than checking it.
close_reason: Shipped as PR #2521, merged b477812b. Chose (b): BindingKind.String's node/edge arms now call graph.Node.String()/graph.Edge.String(), so one literal replaces two and the wire tags cannot drift. Declined (c) on a measurement the bead lacked — four comments in query.go cite graph.EntityKind.String as a live exemplar, so deleting it falsifies all four. Declined (a) for leaving both literals in place. Reproduction: at master, rewriting graph's node or edge literal left ALL of internal/query GREEN over a changed wire discriminator. After: M1 and M2 both RED it; N1, graph's unreachable out-of-enum arm, GREEN as the specificity control. Three stale or false comments corrected, including query.go:1971 which was flatly wrong. Residue filed as gqlc-1i67d.

title: TestBindingDiscriminatorTracksEntityKind pins BindingKind.String, not EntityKind.String, so its name asserts what its body does not do
description:
Residue from gqlc-r79zi, filed rather than ridden on the diff.

internal/query/query_test.go declares:

    func TestBindingDiscriminatorTracksEntityKind(t *testing.T)

It does not track graph.EntityKind. Binding.Kind() returns a BindingKind
(query.go:327, 393, 591), so what the body asserts is
query.BindingKind.String — a different sum, in a different package, with three
members EntityKind has no counterpart for.

gqlc-r79zi corrected the doc comment, which now says outright that the name is
wrong and why. It did NOT rename the function, so the tree still carries a test
whose name asserts something its body does not do. A comment disclosing a false
name is better than a false name alone, but it is not the repair.

THE FIX is a rename, and the only question is to what. TestBindingKindString
(query_test.go, Stage 8) is already taken and pins the five spellings directly;
this one is about the SERIALISED tag deriving from Kind() rather than being
written out a second time, so something like
TestBindingDiscriminatorDerivesFromKind says what it does.

CHECK BEFORE RENAMING: internal/tools/testcite may cite this test by name, and
so may prose under docs/. Grep the whole tree for the current name, not just
the Go files — gqlc-r79zi's own PR body and the bead notes name it too, and
those are history and must not be rewritten.

WHY IT IS NOT NOISE. The name is the reason the test was proposed as the
exemption witness for EntityKind's default in the first place (see gqlc-r79zi's
description, which reached for it on the strength of its name and comment). A
name that misdescribes its own subject already cost one bead a wrong first
guess.
notes:
## 2026-09-03, agent-d — renamed, and the rename is backed by a row

Renamed to `TestBindingDiscriminatorDerivesFromKind`, the name the bead
proposed. The check the bead asked for came back clean: grepping the whole
tree (not only the Go files) for the old name found no citation in
`internal/tools/testcite`, in `docs/`, or anywhere else. The only surviving
occurrence is this test's own comment, naming what it used to be called.

### The row that makes the new name a claim rather than a label

| Mutation | `TestBindingDiscriminatorDerivesFromKind` | `TestBindingKindString` |
|---|---|---|
| `NodeBinding.MarshalJSON` (query.go:1990) `Kind: b.Kind().String()` -> `Kind: "nodeX"` | **RED** | GREEN |

The sibling staying green is the half worth having. It says the two tests
divide the work the way the new name asserts: this one holds the DERIVATION
(the tag comes from `Kind().String()` and is not written out a second time),
`TestBindingKindString` holds the SPELLINGS. A test that asserted the five
literals here would have gone green on that mutation, which is why the body
compares against `b.Kind().String()` and why the old name misdescribed it.

### One correction beyond the rename

The comment claimed the two sums agree on "node"/"edge" "by construction".
bd `gqlc-avtrx` (merged `b477812b`, earlier today) made that false —
`BindingKind.String`'s node and edge arms now call graph's method, so the
agreement is structural. Corrected in place, and the correction notes that a
structural agreement leaves the old NAME exactly as wrong, so it is not an
argument against this rename.
close_reason: Shipped as PR #2524, squash-merged to master as f1344648. Renamed TestBindingDiscriminatorTracksEntityKind to TestBindingDiscriminatorDerivesFromKind: the old name claimed a coupling to graph.EntityKind the body never asserted (it asserts b.Kind().String(), i.e. query.BindingKind), and gqlc-avtrx had already proven the claim false by mutating graph.Node.String() to NODE and leaving internal/query green. Mutation row M1: NodeBinding.MarshalJSON Kind: b.Kind().String() -> Kind: nodeX gives RED on the renamed test and GREEN on TestBindingKindString, which is the contrast the new name asserts. Also added a HISTORICAL testcite pin for the old name: the pre-flight grep the bead asked for was clean and insufficient, because the comment sentence recording the rename is written after the grep. Pin mutation rows: P1 remove the pin -> TestEveryCitedTestExists RED; P2 typo the pinned name -> both TestEveryCitedTestExists and TestEveryPinIsStillWritten RED, which is what proves the pin matches the comment site rather than sitting inert. GH #2511 CLOSED/COMPLETED.

title: bd: evaluate upgrading the deployed bd 1.0.4 to >=1.2.2 (rehearsed migration of the live ledger, then an operator request)
description:
The fleet runs bd 1.0.4 (ce242a879, unchanged on this host since 2026-05-09). Upstream stable is v1.2.2 (2026-08-15), which is 41 schema migrations ahead (61 -> 102) and carries, among much else, migration 0048 -- the fix for the 65535-byte record ceiling that froze gqlc-jffyz.

The ceiling itself is being repaired locally by gqlc-l7d7q (applying 0048's own two ALTER statements, rehearsed), so this proposal is NOT urgent and is deliberately P3 machinery. What it buys beyond that repair: every other upstream fix since May, including `bd sql` working in embedded mode (refused on 1.0.4, measured 2026-09-03), and convergence with upstream's schema bookkeeping instead of a documented local deviation.

What it costs, and why it is not bundled into the ceiling repair:
- /usr/bin/bd is a root-owned npm global; the upgrade is the operator's (agent-n's) action, not an agent's.
- The fleet's measured behaviour contracts (docs/bd-ledger-queries.md, docs/bd-ledger-writes.md) are validated against 1.2.2 only in part; .github/workflows/bd-behaviour.yml runs some claims against the latest release and is the early-warning channel.
- Upstream's own migration machinery has an open defect (gastownhall/beads#6142: `bd migrate schema` a no-op in some paths); a 61->102 migration of the live ledger must be rehearsed on a copy exactly as gqlc-l7d7q rehearses its two statements, before the operator is asked to flip the binary.

Whoever takes this: rehearse first, then write the operator request with the rehearsal evidence attached, per the escalation path in agent-protocol.md.

title: docs: bd-ledger-writes names the recording bead where a reader expects the probe bead
description:
PR #2493 added the record-size-ceiling section. Its opening sentence reads:

    Measured 2026-09-03 against the same bd 1.0.4, on a throwaway bead created and
    deleted for it (bd `gqlc-a8j2i`).

The parenthetical follows this file's own convention -- lines 12 and 212 cite the
bead that RECORDS the measurement the same way -- so it is not wrong. But here it
sits immediately after 'a throwaway bead created and deleted for it', so it reads
as naming the probe. It does not: gqlc-a8j2i is the recording bead and the probe

title: schema/gql: fillerLabels swallows an error into the wrong sentinel and nothing sees it
description:
Found in review of PR #2478 by agent-l (bd gqlc-izn02), recorded there as a
NON-BLOCKING note with no action owed on that PR. Filed rather than fixed on the
branch so the fix is not a rider on a diff about something else.

MEASURED BY THE REVIEWER, not by me: edgetype.go's fillerLabels has two
error-propagation arms, and swallowing EITHER of them leaves the module suite
green. The effect is a degraded diagnosis, not an admission — the parse still
fails, but it fails as "edge endpoint references an undeclared node type"
instead of naming the identifier defect the author actually wrote.

WHY IT IS ONLY P3: nothing invalid is accepted. A caller gets a rejection either
way, so the model cannot be corrupted through this path. What is lost is the
error's ability to name the real mistake, which costs an author time and costs
correctness nothing. gqlc-tzu9r's own repair (a refusal row per converted site)
does not cover it, because fillerLabels reads labels through helpers that are
witnessed elsewhere — it is the PROPAGATION, not the read, that is unguarded.

WHAT DONE LOOKS LIKE: a test that pins the REASON, not just the verdict. The
trap is that a row asserting only "this source is refused" passes under both
sentinels and would be a guard that cannot see the defect at all. Assert the
sentinel each arm is supposed to produce, then mutate each arm separately and
confirm each reds its own row and nothing else — two rows, two mutation rows.

FIRST, AND THIS IS THE PART TO CHECK BEFORE WRITING ANYTHING: verify the arms
still exist and still behave this way at HEAD. This is a second-hand
measurement, taken on a branch, and the branch has since gained five refusal
rows. If a row added there now covers one arm, this bead is half done already
and the remaining half is the other arm.

Related: gqlc-vb9 (closed) covered fillerLabels' trailing nil bail, a different
unreached path in the same function.
notes:
--- agent-d, 2026-09-03: re-derived at HEAD, and the target moved ---

The bead asked for the second-hand measurement to be re-checked before writing

ALREADY COVERED (do not re-do these):

  M3  the ErrEndpointFillerHasProperties raise -> nil KILLED, 7 rows

THE ACTUAL DEFECT is the third reading: the two `return labelSet(...)` tails of
fillerLabels, which FORWARD labelSet's error rather than raise one of their own.
That is what the bead's own wording pointed at all along -- "it is the
PROPAGATION, not the read" -- and its symptom line names the sentinel exactly:
"the identifier defect the author actually wrote" is labelName's
ErrAmpersandInLabel / ErrNoEscapeIdentifier family, not either endpoint-filler

  M5  key-label-set arm (the => spelling) swallows    SURVIVED -> KILLED
