ASK: the owners of chore/bd-ledger-p2 and of the 2026-08-17 specfence work confirm these are dead, then drop them. Cheap, but it should be a decision rather than a deletion.

title: postmortem: a mutation battery run concurrently with another restores the other's mutant, and reports it as a clean sweep
description:
Blame-free postmortem (protocol / agent-protocol: every mistake is a
failure of process and guardrails). Happened to me, agent-b, on gqlc-xtre
2026-08-22. Filed so the next agent who writes a mutation battery — which
is most of us, it is our standard discipline — does not lose a result the
same way.

## What happened

The battery harness backs up the live fleetctl / fleetctl-agent at start, mutates them in
place, runs the suite, and restores from that backup. I launched one run in
the BACKGROUND, then continued working in the same worktree and launched a
second battery before the first had finished.

The second run's backup was taken while the first run held a mutant in the
tree. So it "restored" the first run's mutant. fleetctl was left with its dirty
guard struck, and the run printed a report in which nearly every mutation
read as KILLED — killed by a row that was really just the lingering damage.

## What it nearly cost

A 12/12 clean sweep in a PR body, on a run where two mutations were never
applied at all and the rest were scored against a corrupt baseline. The
report was WELL-FORMED. It looked exactly like a good result.

## What made it detectable

Two tells, both cheap, neither one part of the harness by design:

  - ANCHOR-MISS on two mutations. The anchors were fine; the text they
    anchored to had been mutated away.
  - ONE ROW APPEARED AS A KILLER UNDER EVERY SINGLE MUTANT. A mutation that
    kills a row it has nothing to do with is not a kill.

The tell I did NOT have and should have: the harness never checked that its
baseline was green before starting. A red baseline is the direct signature of
a contaminated tree, and it was sitting right there in the output.

## What allowed it

  - The harness's backup source is the WORKING TREE, which is shared mutable
    state. It has no lock and no way to know another run holds it.
  - `restore` reports nothing. It cannot, because it has no notion of what
    the file SHOULD be — only of what it happened to copy.
  - The final `cmp` restore-check passed. It compares against the same
    poisoned backup, so it certified the contamination as byte-identical.
    A self-consistent check over a corrupted reference is not a check.
  - I treated a background job as finished because I had stopped thinking
    about it, and edited the same files it was mutating.

## What we change

  1. DONE, in my harness: refuse to start when the baseline is not green.
     Cheapest possible guard, catches exactly this signature.
  2. A battery should mutate a COPY of the repo (or a detached worktree at
     the SHA under test), never the live tree. This is already the fleet's
     rule for reviewer scratches; it has not been applied to batteries.
  3. Restore should be verified against a reference the harness did not
     produce in the same run — e.g. `git diff` against the commit, not `cmp`
     against its own backup.
  4. Never run a tree-mutating job in the background and then work in that
     tree. If it mutates shared state, it runs in the foreground, alone.
  5. A killer row that has no causal relation to the mutation is a signal to
     STOP and check the harness, not a stronger result.

## Note for reviewers generally

The corrected, serial numbers for gqlc-xtre are on gqlc-gx2y and in PR #1172,
and they were re-run from a verified-green baseline. If you re-run that
battery, run it alone.
notes: P2 -> P3 by agent-a, 2026-08-24, under protocol/V.3.3 (bead gqlc-f5m5). Machinery, and it passes neither V.3.2 test: it does not BLOCK product work, and the fleet has demonstrably done its work without it. A postmortem whose lesson is already written in it, and whose trigger is an operator choice (two batteries concurrently in one worktree). Nothing recurs unattended. P3 is 'filed and searchable, routed to nobody' — not declined, and not a judgement on the finding, which stands as measured. Raise it back the moment it blocks a gqlc change, and say so here.

title: bd auto-export's git add fails from an agent worktree, so the in-tree issues.jsonl never refreshes there
description:
MEASURED 2026-08-22 ~04:40Z, first-party, by agent-a from agent worktree
/home/antranig/Developer/gqlc/gqlc-agent-agent-a.

## The symptom

Every `bd update` I ran from my agent worktree tonight ended with:

    ✓ Updated issue: gqlc-cn8e — review: PR #1165 ...
    Warning: auto-export: git add failed: exit status 128: fatal: this
    operation must be run in a work tree

The write to the DB SUCCEEDS — I read the note back with `bd show` and it was
there. Only the export staging fails. bd exits 0 and prints ✓ first, so the
warning reads like noise after a success.

## What I measured

    $ git rev-parse --is-inside-work-tree        -> true
    $ env | grep '^GIT'                          -> GIT_EDITOR=true only
    $ git config --get core.hooksPath            -> .githooks   (not drifted)

So it is NOT the GIT_DIR-export failure mode from tonight's other incident
(gqlc-o13d / the postmortem). My environment is clean and my cwd genuinely is
a work tree.

    $ bd info
      Database: /home/antranig/Developer/gqlc/gqlc/.beads/embeddeddolt
      Mode: direct

    $ ls -la .beads/issues.jsonl                        (agent worktree)
      2319202  Aug 21 20:05      <- worktree creation time, never rewritten
    $ ls -la ../gqlc/.beads/issues.jsonl                (shared checkout)
      2943525  Aug 22 00:24      <- newer, but also hours stale

The DB is shared and authoritative; the jsonl is the passive export
(CLAUDE.md). The agent worktree's copy has not been rewritten once since the
worktree was created, across a night of bead writes.

## Hypothesis, NOT measured — this is the part to verify first

A linked worktree's `.git` is a FILE pointing at
`<shared>/.git/worktrees/<name>`. "fatal: this operation must be run in a work
tree" is what git says when it is handed a git dir with no work tree attached.
So the likely cause is that bd resolves a git dir and invokes `git add` against
it without also setting the work tree — correct in the shared checkout, wrong
in every linked worktree.

I have NOT verified this. I measured one agent (mine). Do not carry "this
affects all 13 agents" into anything durable until someone has run a bd write
from a second agent worktree and checked for the same warning. The falsifier is
cheap: if another agent writes and sees no warning, the hypothesis is wrong and
the cause is local to mine.

## Why it is P3 and not higher

The ledger is not at risk. The Dolt DB is the source of truth, it is shared,
and it took every write correctly. This is the passive export only.

It is worth fixing anyway for two reasons:

1. It is fail-silent in the direction that matters. `bd` prints ✓ and exits 0.
   An agent who commits `.beads/issues.jsonl` from an agent worktree commits a
   stale export believing it current — and the existing bd memory
   `bd-jsonl-export-lags-db` says committing in that window silently drops the
   newest beads. This gives that memory a mechanism rather than a folk rule.
2. A warning that appears after every single write is a warning agents learn
   to read past, and the next real one will be read past too.

## Suggested shape

Reproduce from an agent worktree, then fix bd's export invocation to pass a work
tree (or run from one). The regression row should assert the export FILE
CHANGES after a write in a linked worktree — not merely that bd exits 0, which
it already does today while doing nothing. Per the postmortem's own lesson:
assert the guard FIRES, not that it would fire.

title: pre-push runs the full suite on a branch DELETE, so removing a branch needs gates it cannot affect
description:
Hit 2026-08-22 by agent-a while removing an abandoned branch.

    $ git push origin --delete fleet/concurrency-raise
    error: recipe `test-hooks` failed on line 907 with exit code 1
    error: failed to push some refs to 'github.com:areqag/gqlc.git'

A delete pushes the zero SHA and changes no content, so no gate can be
informative about it. Worse, the gates ran against MY WORKING TREE state,
which had nothing to do with the ref being removed — so a branch becomes
undeletable whenever the local tree is red for an unrelated reason. That is
the state an agent is most likely to be in when abandoning a branch.

The workaround I used, which should not be necessary:

    gh api -X DELETE repos/areqag/gqlc/git/refs/heads/<branch>

That is a defect in its own right: it routes around the hook entirely, so a
agent who learns it has learned how to skip pre-push. Better that the hook
never fires on a delete than that everyone learns the bypass.

## The fix

pre-push receives `<local-ref> <local-sha> <remote-ref> <remote-sha>` on
stdin. A delete is local-sha all-zeroes. Skip the gates for those refs, and
run them normally for the rest. Take care with a mixed push (one delete plus
one update in the same invocation) — the update still needs its gates, so
this is a per-ref decision, not an early return for the whole push.

Witness it with a row that deletes a ref while the tree is deliberately red
and asserts the delete succeeds — a row that only checks "delete works on a
green tree" would pass today for the wrong reason.

title: close hook: a parameter-expansion ) closes the $( ) span early and the fallback never fires
description:
Second spelling of the disclosed case-pattern early-close class (PR #1029 header,
"the paren scan does not know shell grammar"), found in round-7 review of bd
gqlc-90vt at 67dee35b, pre-existing on the parent.

    echo "$(echo ${x%)}; git commit -m x)"   ->  allowed; bash runs the commit

The `)` in `${x%)}` is non-syntactic to bash but counted by the paren scan, so
the span closes early; the leftover is double-quoted and shlex collapses it.
Unlike the quoted-`)` and backslash-`)` spellings — measured fail-CLOSED, their
leftover breaks shlex and the ValueError fallback regex catches the commit —
this leftover tokenizes cleanly, so no fallback fires. Measured on the module:
targets=[], need_fallback=False.

Fix shape: name the spelling in the header's accepted-limitations enumeration
and pin it beside `case pattern ) hides a later commit` (same pair pattern), or
teach the scan the ${ } context if ever worth it.

title: check-worktree-upstream cannot see a misconfigured branch that has no worktree
description:
`just check-worktree-upstream` inspects the branch of the worktree it is pointed
at (default `.`). A local branch that tracks `origin/master` but is **checked out
in no worktree** is therefore invisible to it, and invisible to any sweep written
over `git worktree list` — which is how both previous sweeps of this defect were
written.

Measured 2026-08-22 while working bd gqlc-q9z2, over all 90 worktrees and all 197
local branches in this checkout:

    worktrees tracking origin/master from a non-master branch : 2
    BRANCHES tracking origin/master (excluding master)        : 4

The two the worktree sweep could not see:

    chore/gqlc-23e-release-pipeline-impl   (PR #334, merged 2026-07-18)
    fix/govulncheck-live-tree              (PR #725, merged 2026-08-03)

Both had sat misconfigured for weeks — one for over a month — through every
previous sweep, because every previous sweep asked the wrong population. Both are
now repaired (gqlc-q9z2), so this bead is about the blind spot, not the branches.

**Why it still matters with gqlc-tfh1 landed.** The misconfiguration arrives the
moment someone checks such a branch out into a worktree. At that point the
`pre-push` guard does cover the push path — `guard-push-destination` refuses a
push whose resolved destination is master. What it does not cover is `git pull`,
which silently merges master into the branch, and which no hook sees. So the
latent branch is a `git pull` hazard specifically.

The population is finite and shrinking: branches created by the now-documented
`--no-track` recipe get no upstream at all, so new ones arise only when someone
types the old recipe from memory. Hence P3 — a gap in a gate's reach, not a live
hazard.

**Candidate fixes**, not yet chosen:

1. Add a second, repo-wide arm to the recipe: iterate `git for-each-ref refs/heads`
   with `%(upstream:short)` and refuse on any non-master branch tracking
   `origin/master`. One `for-each-ref` call, no per-worktree cost. Risk: it makes
   `just test` fail for an agent because of a branch they have nothing to do
   with, which is the kind of noise that gets a gate disabled.
2. Keep the recipe worktree-scoped and put the repo-wide sweep somewhere
   advisory — `just doctor`, or whatever reaps stale worktrees.
3. Decide the latent case is adequately covered by (1) the checkout-time catch on
   the next `just test` and (2) the push guard, and close this by writing that
   reasoning into the justfile comment so the next person does not re-derive it.

Option 3 is a legitimate outcome; it should be a decision on the record, not a
silence. Whoever takes this should pick with the noise cost in mind.

**Testing note.** Whatever arm is added must be pinned by a row that FAILS when
the arm is removed. The existing suite's shape is
`.githooks/tests/worktree-upstream-test.sh`; a latent-branch row needs a branch
created with an upstream but no worktree, which the suite's throwaway-repo
fixtures can already express. An exit-0 reading proves nothing on its own — the
positive control used in gqlc-q9z2 (re-point a branch at origin/master, assert
exit 1 and the message) is the cheap way to show the row discriminates.

Related: gqlc-tfh1 (the landed fix), gqlc-lwoe (other survivors in the same suite).

title: ci: lint/test/codegen-fence are SKIPPED when tidy fails, and that is only safe while tidy is a required context
description:
Noted 2026-08-21 while landing bd gqlc-4thl (PR #1044). Latent, not live — filed
so the condition is written down rather than rediscovered.

## The shape

Three jobs in `.github/workflows/ci.yml` gate on the same pair:

    lint:           needs: [actionlint, tidy]    (line 41)
    test:           needs: [actionlint, tidy]    (line 80)
    codegen-fence:  needs: [actionlint, tidy]    (line 154)

So a `tidy` failure does not merely add one red check — it SKIPS the three jobs
that do the real verification.

OBSERVED on run 32329564664 (PR #1044, before the fix): `tidy` FAILURE, and
`lint`, `test` and `codegen-fence` all SKIPPED. Nothing about the branch's Go
code was checked by that run at all.

## Why it is currently harmless, and what would change that

Today `tidy` is itself a required context, so its own red blocks the merge and
the skipped trio never gets a chance to be mistaken for approval. The gate holds
because of `tidy`'s required status, not because of the `needs:` structure.

The failure mode is one branch-protection edit away: if `tidy` is ever dropped
from the required set — renamed, split, folded into another job — then a `tidy`
failure yields three SKIPPED contexts and no FAILURE, and GitHub does not treat a
skipped context the way it treats a failed one. The protection would then be
resting on a job nobody has to look at.

That is a load-bearing dependency between a workflow file and a branch-protection
setting, with nothing in either one naming the other.

## Not asserted

I did not test how this repo's branch protection actually scores a SKIPPED
required context — that behaviour has varied by configuration and I only read the
workflow. FALSIFIER: check the required-contexts list against the job names, and
push a scratch branch whose `tidy` fails while `tidy` is non-required, and see
whether the PR reports mergeable.

## Options

1. State the coupling where it can be read: a comment at the first `needs:` line
   saying that these three are only safe to skip because `tidy` is required, and
   that dropping it from the required set re-opens this.
2. Drop `tidy` from `needs:` for `lint`/`test`/`codegen-fence` and let them run
   regardless. Costs CI minutes on a branch that is already failing; buys a real
   FAILURE rather than a SKIP, and removes the coupling entirely.
3. Leave it and rely on the required-contexts list. Fine, but then (1) is owed.

(1) is cheap and worth doing whichever of the others is chosen — the point is
that the constraint currently exists only in whoever remembers it.
notes:
RESOLVED, from the repo's own documentation, same day I filed this.

The "not asserted" section above asks whether branch protection scores a SKIPPED
required context as a pass. It does, and `.github/workflows/ci.yml` says so in its
own header comment (lines 15-21), where it is used as the argument for NOT adding
a job-level `if:` to skip expensive jobs on an `edited` event:

    every job in a triggered workflow emits a check run, a skipped one is
    conclusion `skipped`, branch protection reads `skipped` as a pass, and the
    newest check run for a context wins.

So no falsifier PR is needed for that half. The coupling is exactly as described:
when `tidy` fails, `lint` / `test` / `codegen-fence` emit `skipped` check runs
that branch protection reads as passes, and the ONLY thing standing between that
state and a merge is `tidy`'s own required-and-red status.

Sharpens the ask rather than changing it. The file already contains the reasoning
that makes this dangerous, applied to a different case (`edited`) — it just does
not connect that reasoning to its own `needs:` lines. Option 1 above (state the
coupling at the first `needs:`) is now clearly the cheap right answer, and it can
cite the paragraph already in the file.

Second-order note worth keeping: that same paragraph means "newest check run for a
context wins" is load-bearing for THIS branch's workflow too. A body edit re-runs
everything precisely so a green context cannot be left standing over a red one.
close_reason: already resolved by PR 1331 (merged 2026-08-23) which took option 2 of the bead's own text: dropped every needs edge on lint/test/codegen-fence and wrote a 30-line explanatory header at .github/workflows/ci.yml:1-30 documenting the SKIPPED-satisfies semantics. Discovered during Batch 5 triage.

title: docs: .githooks/pre-push says the full test suite takes <1s; it takes ~50s
description:
.githooks/pre-push line 2 has said, since it was written:

    # Pre-push hook: run the full test suite (<1s — the TCK is vendored, no
    # network) and lint only the lines that differ from origin/master.

The `<1s` is stale by two orders of magnitude. Measured 49s at PR #1056's head in a
real clone with real hooks (round-1 review of that PR, 2026-08-20), and the local
`just fmt-check && just lint && just test` pass on 2026-08-22 took minutes.

Pre-existing on master — verified with `git show origin/master:.githooks/pre-push`;
PR #1056 edits that file but not that line, so it was deliberately left out of scope
there rather than fixed in passing.

Why it is worth fixing rather than ignoring: the number is the developer's only
advance warning of what `git push` is about to cost. Someone reading `<1s` and then
waiting a minute has reason to think the hook has hung, and the natural next move is
--no-verify — which is a protocol violation here (Article IV.4) and also the
one path that skips guard-push-destination entirely.

Fix: replace the parenthetical with an honest order of magnitude, or drop the timing
claim rather than replace one number that will rot with another. Re-measure before
writing anything down.

title: bd-gh-sync: a comment names a .beads/redirect mechanism that exists nowhere
description:
A comment in `.githooks/bd-gh-sync` explains how a worktree without its own beads DB reaches the main clone's, and attributes it to a `.beads/redirect` file.

The round-2 reviewer looked for that file and found none anywhere on the machine. It then confirmed the CONCLUSION directly — `bd show` from a DB-less worktree does reach the main clone — so the comment's claim is right about the outcome and wrong (or at least unwitnessed) about the mechanism.

Same shape as gqlc-z8ay and the memory note on mechanisms named in passing: the sentence was arguing the outcome, so the outcome got checked and the mechanism leaned on to say it did not.

Fix: either find the real mechanism (bd's own discovery walk is the likely answer) and name it, or state the outcome without attributing it.
notes:
2026-08-28 — verification finding, before actioning:

The reviewer's premise ("found no .beads/redirect file anywhere on the machine") reproduces — 0 of 27 sibling worktrees under /home/antranig/Developer/gqlc/ carry one right now. But the CONCLUSION ("the comment's mechanism is fiction") is falsified by .beads/.gitignore itself, which names the file with a doc comment matching bd-gh-sync's claim exactly:

    # Worktree redirect file (contains relative path to main repo's .beads/)
    # Must not be committed as paths would be wrong in other clones
    redirect

So the mechanism IS documented as real. What is unverified is whether it is the mechanism actually operating today, since bd works from every linked worktree (each has its own .beads/ without a dolt DB or a redirect file). Two live possibilities:
  a) bd creates redirect on demand and no worktree here has tripped that path
  b) bd's discovery walk supersedes the redirect file and the .gitignore is stale doc

Either way this is not a comment-tweak bead; it needs one probe into bd's source to say which of (a)/(b) holds, or a live experiment (rm -rf a worktree's .beads, run bd show, watch what materializes).

title: bd-gh-sync tests: two guards whose deletion nothing detects, and a fixture missing the GIT_ env scrub its siblings carry
description:
Three residue items from the round-2 adversarial review of PR #1037. None blocked the merge; all are suite-integrity gaps.

1. Deleting EITHER `win_check` call in the timing fixture is undetected — the suite stays green. A guard nothing observes is a guard that can be removed by accident.

2. The concurrency fixture lacks the `unset "${!GIT_@}"` scrub its three sibling fixtures carry. The reviewer proved both halves: the leak has a real cost if it lands, AND it is unreachable on git 2.55, and the row fails closed anyway. So this is consistency, not a live hole — but the asymmetry with three siblings is the kind of thing that reads as deliberate when it is not.

3. `git worktree add` in the fixture lacks the `-c core.hooksPath` its neighbouring `git commit` has, and it DOES fire `post-checkout`. Given gqlc-7ijy (agent worktree creation is the identified writer of core.hooksPath drift) and the hooks-drift tripwire now installing a `post-checkout` arm, a fixture that fires real `post-checkout` unpinned is a future flake.

title: justfile house rule 3: two prose qualifiers narrower or looser than the measurements behind them
description:
Non-blocking residue from the round-7 review of PR #1031 (merged as 359e48f8). Both concern the SIGPIPE/pipefail house rule now on master in the justfile; the rule itself is sound, these are two prose seams.

1. The rule says the readable safe case is 'a single write() of AT MOST the pipe capacity', and gives as its reason that 'the write lands with the reader alive'. That reason is false above capacity — but so is the qualifier's necessity. Measured in review, holding write-count at 1 and match position at line 1 and varying only size across a fcntl-confirmed 65536-byte capacity: 65,536 / 131,072 / 1,048,576 all returned rc 0 in 60 of 60. At 16x the writer genuinely short-wrote (`wrote=131072 of 1048576`) and the pipeline still returned 0, because a partial write to a closed pipe returns a COUNT, not SIGPIPE. So the 'at most the pipe capacity' bound is stricter than anything measured, and the reason given for it does not hold in the region it excludes. The sentence is scoped below capacity so it is not false, but it advertises a limit that is not the real one.

2. The measurement table says the safe two-write case has the match on the last LINE; the sentence generalises it to the last WRITE. Those coincide only for the producer that was measured (one write per line). A producer batching several lines per write makes them come apart, and the rule is stated in terms of writes.

Fix is prose only, on master's justfile, and should carry the short-write measurement rather than just dropping the bound.

title: close hook: the close arm's reachability list omits the unterminated-heredoc case
description:
A `bd close` on a line following an UNTERMINATED heredoc is classified `no-close-seen`, hook=allow.

Measured (round-5 review of PR #1029, residue row R4):
- `cat <<EOF.txt > /dev/null` / `notes` / `bd close gqlc-x -r "Closed at <orphan>."` -> `no-close-seen`, allow.
- Terminated control -> DENY.

This is a DISCLOSURE gap, not a new mechanism: the header already discloses it for the `git commit` arm (the tokenizer consumes the rest of the input as heredoc body). What is missing is that the close arm's own 'reaches / does not reach' list does not name it, so a maintainer reading that list concludes the close arm is unaffected.

Fix is a line in the close arm's list plus a pinning row, so the omission cannot silently return.

title: justfile: {{mode}} is raw-interpolated into the tmp-reap shell case header
description:
The tmp-reap recipe uses quote(root) two lines away but interpolates {{mode}} unquoted into `case "{{mode}}" in` and into the error echo.

Two crafted payloads were tried in review and BOTH failed — the second raw interpolation in the error echo re-breaks the parse, so bash exits 2 without executing. That is accidental defence, not a guard.

Fix: mode={{quote(mode)}} into a variable, then case "$mode" in.
close_reason: Closed by PR #1334. tmp-reap binds its mode through quote(mode) into a shell variable used by both the case head and the message. Measured: 'just tmp-reap' with a value carrying a quote and a paren was a bash syntax error before and is reported as an unknown mode after. It also retired the one shellcheck exclusion the new lint-just gate needed.

title: resolver: commit()'s empty-intersection comment states a consequence its own named pin falsifies
description:
Round-2 review finding N7 on PR #1032 (bead gqlc-sxzj), found by the reviewer. Landed on master in b09b27ac.

`resolve.go`'s `commit()` comment AND PR #1032's commit body both say that substituting on a length-0 intersection 'would ACCEPT queries master refuses', and name `invalid/unlabelled_optional_hop_empty_intersection.cypher` as the pin.

Measured, it does not. Mutation MU-D (substitute on a length-0 intersection) across all 12880 corpus cells produces 0 DIFFERENT VERDICT and 2 DIFFERENT SENTINEL. The named fixture goes refuse ErrUnknownLabel -> refuse ErrUnknownEdge ('unknown edge: Company&Large-[HAS_DESK]->Desk'). Refuse either way.

The gate IS genuinely pinned — the fixture's `ErrorIs(ErrUnknownLabel)` is what dies — and the SAFETY property holds: this branch cannot accept on an empty intersection. Only the stated *consequence* is wrong.

There is a structural reason to expect it is always wrong: the very edge that emptied the intersection is still in the pattern, and it fails edge validation against whatever `attainable` substituted. So the second line of defence catches it before any accept.

Fix: correct the comment to claim what is true and pinned (the sentinel moves, the refusal stays) rather than a verdict change that cannot happen. Same genre as round 1's N3, which was fixed properly; this is its neighbour.

Note the commit-body half is unrecoverable — this repo squash-merges with squash_merge_commit_message=BLANK, so the branch commit body never reached master. Only the in-tree comment can be corrected.

Source: /tmp/lead/verdict-sxzj-r2.md, Non-blocking residue, N7.

title: codegen/conformance: requireCensus refuses on three arms but its comment and message say 'either/both directions'
description:
`internal/codegen/conformance/specfence_test.go` — `requireCensus` refuses on three distinct arms (duplicated, lost, undeclared), while the surrounding doc comment and the failure message it prints both frame the reconciliation as "either/both direction(s)".

A reader who hits the refusal and counts directions from the prose gets a different shape than the one the function implements. Two-directional framing over a three-armed check.

Cosmetic and pre-existing — the framing predates PR #1025, which is what surfaced it. Graded non-blocking residue by that PR's round-1 review; the arms themselves were confirmed load-bearing under deletion in the same review.

Fix is to the prose, not the arms. Do not substitute a count for the count — name what the check refuses on and let the reader derive, per this repo's settled shape for these.

Re-derive before acting: do not trust the arm names or the function name in this description without reading the current master.
close_reason:
Fixed and merged as PR #2538, squashed onto master as 38036067. GH mirror #1026
closed at merge.

THE GAP. requireCensus' doc comment opened by calling the function a
reconciliation "in both directions", then went on to describe two further
refusals — a name declared twice, and a census that declares nothing. A reader
who hits a refusal and takes the shape from the summary counts two where the
code has four.

RE-DERIVED, AS THE BEAD ASKED. It said "do not trust the arm names or the
function name in this description without reading the current master", and two
of its own claims did not survive that:

  - It says THREE arms. There are FOUR. The empty-census arm arrived with
    PR #1025 — which is the PR the bead says surfaced it — so the bead
    undercounted the thing it was filed about.
  - It says a FAILURE MESSAGE frames things as "either/both direction(s)". No
    message does. The nearest is the duplicate arm's "either copy", which is
    about the two copies and not about directions. The real message-side defect
    is a different one: the empty arm's failure said "the comparison below" over
    THREE comparisons.

The prose was byte-identical to the day it was filed (checked against
adfc50d3), so the bead was live and unfixed rather than stale.

WHAT SHIPPED.

  - The summary now names what the function refuses on instead of counting
    directions. Per the bead's own instruction it does not substitute a count
    for the count: a sentence that names the refusals cannot go stale against a
    fifth arm the way a bare number would.
  - "the comparison below" -> "every comparison below".
  - One new row in TestSpecFailuresAreWired, pinning a precedence the comment
    ALREADY ASSERTED and nothing observed.

THE PRECEDENCE IS THE PART THE BEAD DID NOT KNOW WAS THERE. The empty arm's
comment said it is "refused before either direction is consulted". require.Fail
ends the run, so precedence decides which failure a reader ever sees — and
nothing tested it. That is an unwitnessed promise sitting inside the very
comment the bead was filed against. Adding prose about the arms while leaving it
unwitnessed would have been the same defect in a new coat, so it is pinned, not
merely reworded.

STATED WITH ITS LIMIT rather than as a universal: the pin holds against the
UNDECLARED arm, which is the only arm an empty census can trip at the same time.
The duplicate and lost arms are quantified over the declared names, and an empty
census has none, so their order against this one is not observable at all. The
comment says so.

MEASUREMENT. Declared-victim battery (decision 0005), two phases. Every row
declared its verdict before the run, asserted its anchor matched exactly once,
asserted its named witness row actually RAN, aborted on a build failure, and
restored from a pristine copy under a sha256 check.

Each arm is disabled in turn and required to die BY ITS OWN WITNESS ROW — an arm
that dies only to some other arm's row would mean the headlines are
interchangeable, and then naming them in prose would mislead.

  row                                       pre        post       killed by
  A1  empty-census arm removed              KILLED     KILLED     its own row
  A2  duplicate arm disabled                KILLED     KILLED     its own row
  A3  lost arm disabled                     KILLED     KILLED     its own row
  A4  undeclared arm disabled                KILLED     KILLED     its own row
  O1  empty arm moved past every other arm  SURVIVED   KILLED     the new row, alone

A1-A4 are the positive controls: they die in both phases, so O1's SURVIVED
cannot be a battery that is not reaching the code. O1 moving SURVIVED -> KILLED
over an unchanged mutation is the whole claim.

TWO THINGS THAT LIED TO ME.

1. A2 and A3 first read KILLED — by the COMPILER. reconcile returns its three
   slices in one assignment, so deleting an arm orphans its variable and Go
   refuses to build. A build error wearing a mutation's clothes vouches for
   nothing and is indistinguishable from a real kill in the exit status alone.
   The runner aborts on `^# ` and `build failed`, which is what caught it.
   Rewritten as an unsatisfiable threshold, keeping the variable read.

2. O1'S FIRST FORM WAS A NO-OP, and this is the one worth carrying forward. It
   moved the empty arm below `reconcile` only. reconcile is a plain assignment
   that cannot fail, so the arm still ran first among the arms that CAN — and O1
   duly SURVIVED the post phase, reading exactly like a new row that pins
   nothing. I nearly concluded my own fix was decoration. The tell was that its
   NAMED WITNESS PASSED rather than failing on the wrong message: a battery that
   records only KILLED/SURVIVED cannot tell "the guard is missing" from "my
   mutation changed nothing". Corrected to move the arm past every other arm,
   and BOTH phases re-run over the corrected mutation so the pair is one
   experiment rather than two.

   The false sentence that mistake produced — "move the empty check below
   reconcile and the message becomes the undeclared one" — was written into the
   new row's comment before I measured it. It is now corrected there, stating
   that it takes moving past EVERY arm. Shipping that inside a PR about false
   sentences is the accident this bead exists to prevent.

VERIFIED BY BEHAVIOUR, not by presence: master extracted with `git archive` into
scratch and the post battery re-run against those bytes — all five rows KILLED,
each by its own named witness.

TIDY WAS NOT VACUOUS, checked by running the gate rather than reading the check
colour: `[check-pr-closes] gqlc-eu9y -> Closes #1026 (ok)`. The mirror link was
confirmed through closingIssuesReferences rather than by grepping the body.

NO DESIGN GATE: `bd dep list` reports none. No other open PR touches
internal/codegen/conformance/. `just gates`: 15 of 15.

Battery preserved to fleet-state/verdicts/gqlc-eu9y/mutate-eu9y.py.

ONE THING I CHECKED AND DID NOT FILE. fenceT's comment says "the part of
*testing.T the three helpers above use" while FOUR helpers take fenceT —
requireClean is the fourth and sits below the type declaration, so the sentence
is positionally true. requireClean uses only Helper() and require.Fail, the same
two the others need, so the narrowing rationale is complete and the omission
costs a reader nothing. Not filed: a bead on a true sentence is noise.

title: modscope: justfile_test's provenance sentence credits a commit the comparison did not exist on
description:

The comparison is introduced by commit `0246c4bb` ("modscope: compare this reader against just on the real justfile"), which lands AFTER the fix commit. So on the commit the sentence names, the instrument it credits was not in the tree — the measurement must have been taken by transplanting the comparison backwards onto that tree.

title: PR #1001's round-3 correction list omits a fifth round-2 correction, and 'derived with an instrument' overstates what the script checks
description:
Found by the adversarial review of PR #1001 round 3 (bead gqlc-6n9y), 2026-08-18.
Residue: nothing false is live in code, so it did not block the merge. Filed
because both halves live in the PR body, which is a durable carrier that outlives
the branch.

HALF 1 -- A MISSING ENTRY. PR #1001's body carries a list of what round 2
corrected. Commit 0b49b868 replaced this sentence, which stood at
4aad2777:internal/tools/modscope/justfile_test.go:495-498:

  "This is the only one of the three that fails open -- a caller lost this way
   is not reported and nothing else here notices"

with a correctly-scoped one. No entry in the list describes that correction. It
is a false NEGATIVE (a real correction gone unrecorded), not the false POSITIVE
that made round 3's B2 a blocker, which is why it is residue.

Worth noting what the omitted sentence WAS: an "only one of the three" plus a
"nothing else here notices". That is precisely the defect class round 3's own
headline blocker was about. The list of corrections omits the correction most
similar to the thing the list exists to demonstrate.

HALF 2 -- THE METHOD CLAIM. The body says the list was "re-derived in round 3
with an instrument". The script, /tmp/factory/r3-list-check.sh, verifies rows it
is HANDED; it does not enumerate the round's corrections and hand them to itself.
So it can confirm every row present is real and cannot report a row absent --
exactly the failure that produced half 1. "Re-derived with an instrument" claims
a completeness the instrument does not have.

HOW TO REPAIR. Do not add the missing entry and leave the method sentence
standing -- that repeats the error one entry later. Either describe what the
script actually checks, or build the enumerating instrument: walk the round's
commits, extract every prose hunk, and require each to appear in the list. The
second is the honest form and is reusable, since this PR is on its fourth round
of the same defect.

Related: gqlc-6n9y, and the reviewer-instrument family generally -- a check
scoped smaller than the claim it is cited for.

title: modscope: justfileDisagreements compares per name last-wins, so a shadowed duplicate recipe's body difference is never asked
description:
Found by the adversarial review of PR #1001 round 3 (bead gqlc-6n9y), 2026-08-18.
Filed as residue: it does not block that PR and was explicitly withheld from its
round-4 scope.

THE GAP. In internal/tools/modscope/justfile_test.go the two sides disagree about
what a duplicate recipe name means:

  justfileDisagreements  :856-859   builds its map per NAME, last write wins
  unsweptModscopeCallers :391-395   decides per ENTRY

So when a justfile declares the same recipe name twice, the body difference
between the shadowed declaration and the winning one changes the answer the
DECISION consults, and this differential test never asks about it. The one thing
that would surface it is the read-twice complaint, which this test does not
raise (:519-522).

WHY IT IS LOW PRIORITY BUT REAL. This repo's justfile does not currently contain
a duplicate recipe name, so nothing is mis-swept today. The defect is that the
gate's silence on the shape is not a decision anyone took -- it is a consequence
of one side keying by name. That is the same fail-silent-where-fail-closed-was-
claimed shape the whole modscope cluster keeps producing.

WHAT WOULD SETTLE IT. A probe that puts a duplicate recipe name in a copy of the
real justfile, where the two declarations differ in whether the body names the
modscope package, and asks whether either test reports. Do it out of tree
(scratch probes never touch a real package directory). Note `just` itself may
reject or warn on a duplicate name -- establish what `just --dump` does with it
FIRST, because if just refuses the file the whole question is moot and that is
the answer.

DO NOT WRITE A COUNT OR A UNIVERSAL INTO THE FIX. State what was probed.

Related: gqlc-98ii (the `mod` blind spot, same test, same silence-by-agreement
shape), gqlc-k2jq, gqlc-2woz, gqlc-6n9y.

title: codegen corpus: two fixture tests are the sole user of an import, so their paired removal reds at require.NoError not the guard
notes:
A measurement worth not re-deriving, from the independent review of PR #1002
round 3 (bd gqlc-wla6). Classified residue there. Filing so the sweep is on the
record rather than in a /tmp log.

THE SWEEP. For each name in corpusTests, drop the name AND drop its func Test
block from the fixture, run, restore. Both packages, at 15e8f9d2, every row
screened with go test -c and restored to a pristine md5.

  neo4j  20 of 21 rc=0.  TestListyNarrowsEachElement is not.
  age    28 of 29 rc=0.  TestEmittedMethodBindsAnInstantAsMicroseconds is not.

Each is the only fixture test whose body uses a given import -- "time" on the
neo4j side, "context" on the age side. Removing it orphans the import, so the
child module fails to build and the run reds at require.NoError with
[build failed], NOT at require.NotEmpty and not at ElementsMatch.

Pruning the orphaned import in the SAME edit restores rc=0. So this is the Go
compiler refusing an intermediate state a real commit would not ship, not the
harness catching anything.

WHY THE SHIPPED PROSE SURVIVES IT. The code comment's clause is past-tense
existential -- "a run with one name and its test removed together came back
green" -- which 20 of 21 and 28 of 29 satisfy, and its unit is "one commit's
edit", which a three-line commit meets. Deleting the earlier "two-line change"
count is what inoculates it. Nothing to fix in the comment.

WHAT IS ACTUALLY WORTH DOING, IF ANYTHING. This is a fake-RED shape: a row reds
for a reason unrelated to what the test asserts, and the message a reader sees
names require.NoError rather than the corpus. That is the class the repo already
screens mutations for. Anyone building a future mutation matrix over this corpus
must screen for [build failed] and must not score these two rows as kills.

RELATED. Bears on gqlc-lwtp (sweep the conformance AST-census tests for the same
aggregate-emptiness shape) and gqlc-8bl0, both of which will want to mutate this
corpus. Same family as the go-test-c-is-the-mutation-screen note.

--- RE-MEASURED 2026-09-04 by agent-d, at origin/master 0d6a7940. THE RECORD ABOVE IS PARTLY WRONG AND NOW WHOLLY STALE.

METHOD. For each import in each fixture (internal/codegen/{neo4j,age}/testdata/corpus_test.go.txt),
count the top-level funcs whose body mentions "<selector>.", separating Test funcs from helpers, and
also checking the file header (consts/vars). An import is AT RISK -- i.e. removing one test orphans
it and the child module stops building -- only if exactly ONE Test func uses it and nothing else does.
Run at 15e8f9d2 as a positive control before being run at master, which is what caught the error below.

FINDING 1 -- THE age ROW REPRODUCES EXACTLY. At 15e8f9d2, "context" had exactly one user,
TestEmittedMethodBindsAnInstantAsMicroseconds. The mechanism recorded above is correct for age.

FINDING 2 -- THE neo4j ROW'S STATED MECHANISM IS FALSE. At the same commit, "time" was used by TWO
tests: TestBinNullabilityAndShape AND TestListyNarrowsEachElement. So TestListyNarrowsEachElement was
NOT "the only fixture test whose body uses time", and removing it orphaned no import. No import in the
neo4j fixture was sole-used at 15e8f9d2 at all.
  I cannot say what DID red that row. The original harness lived in a /tmp log that is gone, so the
  observation (rc!=0 with [build failed]) is unverifiable now while its explanation is refuted. The
  hypothesis I would test first, having hit exactly this today on bd gqlc-ipx6: the sweep's "drop its
  func Test block" edit cut the wrong span. A brace-counting or regex block cut that takes too much or
  too little produces a build failure that looks like an orphaned import and is not one. Nobody should
  carry the neo4j row forward as an explained result.

FINDING 3 -- NEITHER HAZARD EXISTS TODAY. At master, ZERO imports are sole-used in either fixture:
  neo4j  8 imports, 41 corpusTests entries (was 7 and 21)
  age    6 imports, 51 corpusTests entries (was 6 and 29)
The corpora roughly doubled, and every import now has several users, so dropping any single named test
orphans nothing. "time" now has 4 neo4j users; "context" now has 5 age users.

WHAT THIS CHANGES. The bead's advice to future mutation-matrix builders -- screen for [build failed],
do not score a compiler kill as a kill -- STANDS, and is durable independently of this bead in the
memories mutation-verdict-must-not-be-exit-status and a-compiler-killed-mutation-can-score-as-survived.
What does NOT stand is the two named rows: they must not be carried into a future matrix as known
exceptions, because one was never explained and neither reproduces. A builder who exempts them today
would be exempting rows that pass.

A SNAPSHOT, NOT A GUARANTEE. "Zero at risk" is true of master and can be undone by any fixture edit
that adds an import with a single test user. It is cheap to re-run; the method is described above. I
did not build a mechanical guard for it: it bites only someone hand-building a mutation matrix, never
CI, and the general screen already covers the class.
close_reason: Re-measured at 0d6a7940 and closed as a corrected record, no code change. The age row reproduces; the neo4j row's stated mechanism is FALSE (time had two test users at 15e8f9d2, not one) and its red is unexplained. Neither hazard exists at master: zero imports are sole-used in either fixture, which roughly doubled in size. The class-level advice survives in two bd memories; the two named rows must not be carried into a future mutation matrix as known exceptions.

title: modscope: goDirs' doc names two inputs where the code uses three
description:
Inherited prose defect, live on master, verified byte-identical between merge
base 49213009 and origin/master. Surfaced by the PR #1001 round-2 review, which
found the PR BODY claiming this had been fixed when the branch contains no
goDirs change at all. The claim was removed from that body; the underlying
defect is real and is this bead.

`internal/tools/modscope/main.go`: the sentence describing what `goDirs` decides
from names two inputs. The answer is decided by three:

  - moduleRoot
  - the `nested` prune set
  - **skipName** (main.go:157 — excludes `.`/`_`-prefixed entries, `testdata`,
    and `vendor`), applied in the walk at main.go:178 and again at :328

So an entry can be excluded from goDirs' answer by a rule the doc does not
mention. Verify the exact sentence and the exact input list yourself before
editing — do not take "two" or "three" from this bead. The repo's signature
defect is a count in prose that the artifact falsifies, and a bead is not
exempt from that.

FIX SHAPE: prefer stating the property over listing inputs. A list of N inputs
rots the moment someone adds an N+1th filter, which is exactly how this sentence
became wrong. If a list is genuinely the clearest form, derive it from the code
at the moment of writing and say what it is a list OF.
close_reason:
Fixed in PR #2599, squash-merged as 3dcbf3ae; GH mirror #1013 CLOSED. Verified on
origin/master by content, not by commit count.

WHAT THE BEAD ASKED AND WHAT I MEASURED. The bead warned not to take "two" or
"three" from it, so I re-derived at HEAD. The old sentence named moduleRoot as the
bound and the nested module roots as the stop; skipName was named NOWHERE. It is
applied twice, and the second application is the one no reader would guess:

  - main.go:342, to DIRECTORY names, returning filepath.SkipDir, which prunes the
    whole subtree;
  - main.go:350, to FILE names, so a directory whose Go files are ALL skipName'd
    never enters `seen` — it is ABSENT from the answer rather than present and
    empty.

TestGoDirsSkipsFilesGoListWillNotMatchEither (main_test.go:141) already pins the
file-name half. The doc simply never mentioned it.

TWO THINGS THE BEAD DOES NOT NAME, both now in the prose:

  1. The absent-rather-than-empty consequence above.
  2. moduleRoot is EXEMPT from skipName. The `if path == moduleRoot { return nil }`
     early return at main.go:339 precedes the skipName check at :342, so a module
     rooted at a dot- or underscore-named directory still walks. NO TEST PINS THIS.
     It is readable from those three lines and nothing else, which is why it is now
     written down. This is a doc-only bead so no test is owed, but the absence is
     recorded here rather than left implied.

A DRAFT OF MY OWN THAT WAS WRONG, caught before commit. I first wrote that goDirs
returns the directories "`go list ./...` could reach". The very next paragraph of
the same comment contradicts that: this walk exists BECAUSE `go list` does not match
a directory whose Go files are all excluded by build constraints. A build-constrained
directory is returned here and is not matched there. The shipped text claims only the
narrower true thing — skipName is shared with the `go list` side, and that sharing is
the only sense in which the walk tracks `go list`. The lesson is that a comment can be
falsified by another paragraph of the same comment, not only by the code.

A DUPLICATION REMOVED. My first draft restated skipName's "one predicate / answers to
the same question" clause, which already stands verbatim on skipName's own doc at
main.go:152-156. goDirs now points at it instead of carrying a second copy that could
drift.

FIX SHAPE, as the bead asked: the property, not the list of inputs. The first sentence
now states the whole answer; the elaboration follows and records why the shape changed,
so the next person to add a filter has a reason not to reintroduce a list.

GATES: go test ./internal/tools/modscope/ ok; just lint 0 issues; all seven required
CI contexts pass. tidy ran check-pr-closes POSITIVELY rather than skipping vacuously —
its log line reads `[check-pr-closes] gqlc-2woz -> Closes #1013 (ok)`, checked because
a stale .beads export makes that gate skip while still showing green.

NO RESIDUE FILED. Nothing was noticed and left undone.

title: codegen/neo4j: the G4/G5 record.Get gates are pinned only by wording the emitter itself chooses
description:
Residue of PR #990 (bd gqlc-1uic, GH #975), named in both review rounds.

The corpus's record.Get arms (matrix rows G4 and G5) ARE killed when their gate is dropped -- round 2 spot-checked G4 first-party and confirmed it (emitter md5 14aafff2, RED = TestAnythingColumnsCarryTheirNull, 20 sibling PASS, build failed 0). So this is not an unpinned gate.

The weakness is WHAT kills them. Those arms word their own refusals, and the corpus asserts those words. So the assertion is held against a string the EMITTER chooses -- change the emitter's wording and the corpus row goes RED for a reason that is a rename, not a regression; keep the wording and a behavioural change underneath it can pass. The gate and its test agree because they are the same author, not because they are independent.

Contrast with what PR #990 did for the entity and list arms: those propagate the DRIVER's error (GetRecordValue's own wording, copied verbatim into testdata/driverstub_neo4j.go.txt from the real driver), so the assertion pins that the emission propagated something it did not author.

NOTE THE STANDING LIMIT either way: the corpus runs against the stub, so even the propagating arms pin "the emission propagated whatever GetRecordValue said", NOT the real driver's wording. Do not let a fix here overclaim in the other direction.

Low priority: this is a robustness-of-pin issue, not a hole. Worth doing when the record.Get arms are next touched.
notes:
## 2026-09-03, agent-d — merged as c74a619d (PR #2550)

The bead's diagnosis was right and incomplete. Measured in a scratch
extract over the whole neo4j package, before writing anything:

  X1 absent-key branch borrows the null gate's words   red, incidentally
  X2 null gate reworded, behaviour identical           red
  X3 null gate stops naming its column                 red
  X4 absent-key gate deleted outright                  red
  X5 null gate borrows the absent-key branch's words   red
  X6 absent-key refusal reworded, behaviour identical  GREEN

Two things the bead did not have:

X6 GREEN. The absent-key refusal was pinned by NOTHING anywhere in the
tree -- its only assertion was a bare `err == nil`, which any error
satisfies. The bead described both gates as pinned by the emitter's
wording; only the arrived-null one was.

X1's kill is INCIDENTAL. It reddens because the mutated text happens to
equal the phrase the NULLABLE half of TestEveryColumnKindGatesArrivedNull
forbids -- a substring collision, not the distinction being defended.
The first run of the battery was scoped to the corpus entrypoint alone
and scored X1 SURVIVED; widening to the package flipped it, and reading
the failure MESSAGE rather than the test name is what showed the kill
was not about the collapse at all.

## The fix

Both refusals are taken over the SAME column (absent key vs arrived null,
both on payload / badge) and held against each other: each must name its
column, and the two must not read alike. It names neither phrase, so it
survives a rename and dies on a collapse in either direction. The two
prose Contains asserts are dropped as redundant with gateLine, which is
the single right home for a wording pin.

## Proving it, emitter fence blinded so the corpus is the only voice

  C0 baseline                                          green
  Y1 collapse toward the null gate's words             red, my assertion
  Y2 collapse toward the absent-key words              red, my assertion
  Y3 same collapse + differ assert blinded             green
  Y4 null gate reworded, fence blinded                 green
  Y5 null gate reworded, fence live                    red at the fence

All AS DECLARED with the victim named before the run. Y3 attributes Y2's
kill to the assertion rather than to the blinding. Y4/Y5 are the pair
showing a rename is now answered in exactly ONE place instead of three.

## Left open deliberately

X6 stays green: a rename with no collapse is not a regression. Whether
the absent-key wording deserves a fence at all is a question about
whether the cross-lane uniformity claim covers it, filed as gqlc-s6lif
rather than answered here.
close_reason: Merged as c74a619d (PR #2550). The record.Get lane's two refusals are now held against each other over the same column rather than against emitter-authored words: each names its column, the two must differ. Six-row pre-fix battery and six-row post-fix isolation battery, all as declared. The measured surprise was X6 — the absent-key refusal was pinned by nothing at all, not by wording as the bead assumed. Follow-up gqlc-s6lif filed for the wording asymmetry. GH #999 closed.

title: codegen.ResolvedTypeName: a String() returning empty yields a refusal that names nothing
description:
Inherited hole, NOT created by PR #991 (GH #961) -- measured identical at cbb11a7e and at PR #991's head, by Linus round 1 on that PR.

codegen.ResolvedTypeName guards against a FAULT (panic while asking for the name), not against EMPTINESS. A type such as `struct{ resolver.ResolvedNode }` that declares `String() string { return "" }` does not panic, so the guard passes it through, and the refusal renders as:

    column "n" projects
    parameter $p is

-- a refusal that names nothing useful. This does not violate PR #991's rule ("a refusal that names an unmatched type must not fault while asking for the name"), which is why it was not a blocker there.

WHERE TO FIX: in codegen.ResolvedTypeName itself, not at either call site. That is precisely what #991's export ruling bought -- one implementation, so both internal/codegen and internal/codegen/age move together. Do not fix it in age.unservedColumn/unservedParam.

Related thin spot, same file family: fallThroughComment's assertion in internal/codegen/age is a substring match, which is weaker than the surrounding AST guards in sealedsum_test.go. Pre-existing and untouched by #991.
close_reason:
Fixed in PR #1756.

WHAT WAS WRONG. `codegen.ResolvedTypeName` guarded against a `String()` that
*faults*, not one that *answers with nothing*. A `String()` returning `""`
faults nowhere, so it was taken at its word and the refusal rendered the two
symptoms this bead quoted, each ending mid-sentence:

    out of C6 scope: query "Fetch" column 0 "n" resolved as
    1 query would be dropped: Fetch (column "n" projects )

Both were reproduced before anything was changed.

THE FIX is one place, and that is what PR #991's export bought: the render is
shared, so `internal/codegen` and `internal/codegen/age` move together. The
guard now keys on the name being empty rather than on a flag saying whether
`String()` returned — a call that faults never reaches its assignment, so `name`
is still `""` at the deferred check either way. One condition therefore covers
both ways of arriving without a name.

The `answered` flag was not left in place as belt-and-braces. I asked whether it
could still fire, and had the compiler answer rather than reasoning about it: a
probe removing the disjunct produced `declared and not used: answered`. Flag,
assignment and its comment paragraph are deleted, and the function's
postcondition is stated once, where it is enforced.

`recover()` is called for its effect and not its value, deliberately. Under
`GODEBUG=panicnil=1` a `panic(nil)` makes `recover()` return nil, so a
`recover() != nil` test would read a faulted call as an answered one and hand
the caller the empty name the helper exists to prevent. That is battery row D.

WITNESSES IN BOTH PACKAGES. The AGE unserved-query gate runs *ahead* of
`codegen.Prepare` (generate.go), so it renders the arriving type first, not
second — a repair witnessed only in `internal/codegen` would not speak for it.
The empty-`String()` fixture is a sibling of the existing faulting ones and is
deliberately NOT added to `faultingShapes()`: it does not fault, and putting it
in a table of that name would make the table lie.

MUTATION BATTERY, 6 rows. Expected verdict and victim declared BEFORE the run;
NO-OP, FAKE (`go test -c`) and TRIP screens on every row.

  A  fallback disabled outright                              KILLED (as declared)
  B  the bead's defect restored: fall back only on a fault    KILLED
  C  the same single revert, read on the AGE side             KILLED
  D  guard reads recover()'s value instead of the name        KILLED
  E  compound: defect restored, only pre-existing tests run   SURVIVED
  F  fallback answers a constant instead of %T                KILLED

B and C are ONE source revert read from two packages — that is the measurement
behind "both packages move together", rather than an assertion of it.

E is the row that cannot be inferred from the others and is SURVIVED by design:
with the defect restored and only the tests that already existed in the tree
run, nothing went red. That is the evidence that this defect was uncovered
before this branch, not merely under-covered.

PROSE CORRECTED, both true statements that had gone stale:
  - the `panicnil` test's doc named the `answered` flag, which no longer exists;
  - docs/specs/codegen-sentinel-taxonomy.md §2 said the render bounds "the
    panic". It now says the panic and, since this bead, the empty answer.

LIMIT STATED, NOT PAPERED OVER. Emptiness is the whole of the test. A `String()`
returning `" "` or `"???"` is still passed through, and the doc comment says so
rather than implying the bound is general. Neither bound covers every way an
implementation can decline to answer.

CI. The first two runs failed `live-smoke` on
`TestEveryBatteryIsNamedInScenarioTables` — my own guard from gqlc-8jfj (#1748),
catching `localDateTimeColumnScenarios` arriving from #1679 declared nowhere.
Not a defect in this branch: master had already repaired it in #1760, and this
branch was cut from a base predating both. Rebased onto origin/master; the guard
then passed locally uncached, and the rebase was verified to preserve the diff
byte-for-byte by comparing merge-base deltas (identical apart from blob hashes),
not by reading the commit list.

FOLLOW-UP FILED, not ridden onto this diff: gqlc-2ccn (P4) — the codegen/age
fall-through comment guard is a substring match on prose and cannot tell naming
from disclaiming.

title: convention: a comment citing a test by name rots on rename and nothing checks it
description:
internal/query/cypher/typing.go carries a comment citing a test BY NAME. Nothing compiles, links or checks that citation, so it rots silently the moment the test is renamed or moved. Pre-existing convention across the repo, not introduced by any one branch; surfaced as residue F4 of the PR #965 round 4 Linus PASS.

The question to rule on is what the convention should be, not just this one site:

  (a) leave by-name citations and accept the rot;
  (b) drop the name and describe the property the test pins, so the sentence
      survives a rename;
  (c) gate it — a check that every quoted Test<Name> in a comment resolves to a
      declared test function.

(c) is cheap for Go (an AST walk over comments plus the test declarations in the module) and would convert a whole class of rotting prose into a CI failure. It also has a false-positive shape worth measuring first: a comment naming a test that lives in another module or was deliberately deleted.

Relates to gqlc-6xln (keep growing-range counts and universals out of durable carriers) — same family, different carrier: that one is about numbers going stale, this one about names going dangling.

Survey the repo for how many sites this affects before choosing; a convention ruling on one site is not a convention.
close_reason:
Answered by option (c) and shipped: internal/tools/testcite, merged as 6ab00421 (PR #2131, bd gqlc-945h7). A comment in a non-test source naming a test must name one that is declared, or the site is pinned in an `illustrative` map with the reason it is not a citation.

VERIFIED ON MASTER TODAY, not inferred. The guard is present at origin/master:internal/tools/testcite/citations_test.go and green: 1059 Go files examined, 1746 declared test functions, 104 citations in non-test sources, 3 pinned as illustrative. The one site this bead names, internal/query/cypher/typing.go:598 citing TestTypeListIsTheOnlyVariantDeclaringAField, is among the 104 and resolves.

THE SURVEY THIS BEAD ASKED FOR, before choosing. 104 citations, of which 3 do not resolve and all 3 are illustrative rather than dangling — the genuinely dangling population was ZERO. gqlc-945h7's own description said 20 and named two it had confirmed by hand; both of those resolve. title: convention: a published mutation must be reproducible as a diff, and a growing-range universal must not enter a durable doc
description:
Two conventions the PR #963 round-3 reviewer derived from measurements it made first-hand. Both are about how a measurement is WRITTEN so a later reader can re-run it, not about any one PR.

1. A PUBLISHED MUTATION MUST BE DESCRIBED AS A DIFF, NOT AS PROSE.

Every mutation row in this repository publishes an "md5 after" column. That column is author-self-certified by construction: a later reader can only reproduce it by guessing the exact bytes the author wrote.

MEASURED, not argued. The reviewer re-ran two inherited rows. MR-2 (delete an early-out) reproduced to the exact digit, b97b97d7, because deleting a named block is unambiguous. MR-2ctl (replace the same site with a panic) produced the SAME behavioural result to the digit — 268 panics, 275 FAIL — but a DIFFERENT hash, 027faa18 vs 276fafeb, purely because the two authors wrote different panic text.

So the column value is its MOVEMENT (changed=YES vs NO-OP), which is what it is actually for, and NOT its digits. Publishing digits invites a later reader to read a mismatch as a contradiction when it is only a difference in wording. Either publish the mutation as a literal diff, or say explicitly that the hash pins movement rather than identity.

2. A GROWING-RANGE UNIVERSAL MUST NOT BE COPIED INTO A LONGER-LIVED CARRIER.

A claim of the form "every commit since SHA is comment-only" is true when written and self-rots on the next code commit in that range, without anyone touching the sentence. It was acceptable in the #963 PR body, where the reviewer graded it correctly left alone: dating it would defeat its purpose and the PR was at merge, so the range closed at merge.

It is NOT acceptable in a spec, an ADR, a code comment or a bead — carriers that outlive the range. In those, either date the endpoint or state the claim over a closed range.

WHY THIS IS WORTH A BEAD: this repository has a signature defect — a prose claim the branch own artifacts falsify — that has cost five PRs a round each this wave. Both conventions above are that defect caught at the point of writing rather than at review.

ACCEPTANCE: written into the contributor-facing conventions the review briefs already draw on, so it is guidance rather than tribal knowledge. No CI gate is proposed; this is a writing convention and a gate for it would grade prose.

title: .githooks: claude-pre-bash's _EMITTED once-only guard is unpinned because main() exposes no seam
description:

title: docs/adr/0025: the account of what the two Scalar pins redden under-counts, and one pin is unobservable in a whole-package run
description:
Non-blocking residue from PR #956 (bead gqlc-0otp), found by the round-1 Linus review. All four items are the same class: the merged text's account of its own pins is imprecise. None is a false universal; each under-claims rather than over-claims, which is the safe direction, so this was correctly graded non-blocking.

2. Under the delete-'map[string]any' mutation, a whole-package run never reaches the closure pin at all: decodeFunc panics and the test binary dies. 'Reddens both' is only observable when the two are run separately. Worth stating, because a future reader reproducing the claim the obvious way will not see what the sentence promises.

3. 'only mention of agtypeMap outside its own declaration' — each golden also carries its doc comment.

4. The PR body says agtypeString 'is reached only through carrier == "string"'. True of decodeFunc's routing, which is the scope the sentence is about, but emitted helper bodies call agtypeString directly at render_models.go:519, :547 and :621. The PR page is a durable carrier, so the imprecision persists; not worth a CI-cancelling body edit on a merged PR, but worth recording here.

Verified by content, not by the merge: origin/master's docs/adr/0025 carries all four corrections -- "Six goldens carry them", the three-subtest count, TestNarrowingWidthsAgreesWithTheTypeTable, and "only CALL outside". ITEM 1 confirmed and split. The bead said "three, not one". That is right for the any arm and wrong as a general claim: with the closure pin run alone, deleting `any` reddens THREE subtests (Property/any, Property/[]any, Scalar/any -- the table names that text on both halves and once more as a list element, and requireCarrierHasAnArm strips [] and recurses), while deleting `map[string]any` reddens exactly ONE (Scalar/map[string]any). ITEM 2 is broader than recorded, in two ways. The bead named only the map[string]any mutation; the hazard holds for both arms. And for the any arm the killer is a different test entirely -- under whole-package `go test ./internal/codegen/age/`, the map mutation dies in TestDecodeFuncNamesTheHelperForEveryServedCarrier (which precedes the closure pin in the same file) while the any mutation dies earlier still in TestNarrowingWidthsAgreesWithTheTypeTable, with TestEmissionSuite red as well. MEASUREMENT DISCIPLINE. Both mutations were applied to a clean tree at HEAD and restored with `git checkout --` between rows, with `git status --short` read empty after each; the tree was committed before any mutation, so the restore could not delete an uncommitted guard. Baseline green was asserted before the first mutation.

WHAT I DID NOT DO. types.go:204 left alone -- this bead explicitly noted and declined it. No code change: the branch is one file, prose only, 33 insertions and 8 deletions.

RESIDUE FILED, NOT RIDDEN: gqlc-adgrp (P3, open, unassigned, on bd ready). decodeFunc answers an unknown carrier by panicking, and a panic in a subtest takes the whole test binary -- so the pin whose entire job is to name WHICH carrier lost its arm is the one such a regression silences, and a second unrelated regression in the same change stays invisible until the first is fixed. A candidate remedy is recorded there (require.NotPanics at the bare call sites, as requireCarrierHasAnArm already does), but whether decodeFunc's panic should remain a panic is a design question that bead deliberately does not prejudge. It was not absorbed here because this bead is prose-only and the fix is a code change.

title: resolver: validated.go's ResolvedType doc points at gqlc-edze as an open question
description:
internal/resolver/validated.go:106 ends ResolvedType's doc comment with:

    Whether the codegen boundary should normalise them away instead of

title: bdguard: the reopen recency condition is a shape check, not an anti-forgery control
description:
`.beads/allowed-reopens.txt` grants an exemption when the head record's
`updated_at` is strictly later than base's (plus the sha-citation condition and
the reachability veto). Base is read with `git show <ref>:.beads/issues.jsonl`,
so a PR's tree cannot restate it — but HEAD's `updated_at` is just a field in a
file the PR author is editing.

So the recency condition separates the two shapes it was built for — a stale
export copied forward before a close (updated_at at or behind base's) from a
correction written after it (ahead) — and it does that mechanically. What it
does not do is resist a hand-written timestamp: an author who edits
`.beads/issues.jsonl` to bump one bead's `updated_at` past base's, and adds the
matching `<bead-id> <closing-sha>` line, is granted.

That is not obviously wrong. The declaration file is deliberately read at the
PR head so the exemption lands in the diff a reviewer already reads, exactly as
`.beads/allowed-drops.txt` does; the human declaration is the authority and the
machine conditions bound what can be declared. The cost of the forgery is that
it is two visible edits rather than none.

Worth deciding explicitly rather than leaving implicit:

- Whether the export's `updated_at` for a declared id should be cross-checked
  against the bd DB (`refs/dolt/data`) rather than trusted from the file.
- Or whether to state in `allowed-reopens.txt`'s header that the recency
  condition is a shape check, not an anti-forgery control, so nobody later
  reads it as the latter.

Discovered while landing bd gqlc-npyp (PR for GH #922).

title: spec fence: ADR 0029 and specfence_test.go each carry a claim their own measurements falsify
description:
Residue from the round-7 review of PR #804 (merged as e7735736). The reviewer
declined to block on these: the normative spec text is correct, the code is
correct, and round 6 had already graded the same class in the same file as a
nit. Blocking round 7 on comment prose would have manufactured an eighth round.
They are still wrong, and they are the kind of wrong that misleads the next
reader about WHY a design choice was made.

1. `docs/adr/0029-the-codegen-spec-fence.md:245`

   "Neither direction can be closed by a better fence rule, because the
   line-opening test is reached only by a run of three or more."

   The reason attaches to direction B, not direction A. Measured: the option-2
   fence fix DOES close direction A -- probing the real `scanBareSigs` shows
   the line-opening triple go from 0 sigs to 1, with 82 corpus documents and
   17 of 18 rows still green.

   The CONCLUSION survives, for a different reason: under that fix, a
   line-opening triple *inside* a fenced block becomes a fresh divergence,
   because cmark renders it literal. That is exactly what
   `internal/codegen/conformance/specfence_test.go:1460-1462` already says
   correctly. So the fix is to give ADR 0029 the reason the test file already
   has, not to change the conclusion.

2. `internal/codegen/conformance/specfence_test.go:1843`

   "A tab-indented run is never a fence to cmark-gfm."

   False. Inside a list item the ticks ARE consumed and it IS a fence -- which
   is the construct the immediately preceding sentence itself names. Behaviour
   is correct either way; the sentence is not.

   This is the house no-universals defect: a `never` that the surrounding prose
   falsifies two lines up.

3. Smaller, same file family:
   - `docs/specs/codegen-stage-c1.md:763` -- "on every spelling measured" is
     ambiguous between "every spelling we measured" and "every spelling there
     is".
   - `docs/specs/codegen-stage-c1.md:1446` -- "Two divergences are measured"
     reads closed, but it is a floor: a third is pinned at :1094.
   - `docs/specs/codegen-stage-c1.md:41` -- one 30-column line the rewrap
     commit missed.

ACCEPTANCE. Each sentence is true of the tree, and item 2 states the negative
(what a tab-indented run IS a fence for) rather than asserting a universal.
Item 1 should name direction B explicitly rather than saying "neither
direction". No new universal introduced by the fix.

title: bdguard: the git boundary (run, showAtRef, gitRefContaining) has no automated test
description:
internal/tools/bdguard/main_test.go states at the top that it targets check() directly, with no git shellout, and that the git boundary of run() is exercised only by an end-to-end incident replay recorded in a PR body. The stated reason is that earlier attempts to stage a real repo per test occasionally landed git calls in the outer worktree despite GIT_CEILING_DIRECTORIES.

gqlc-npyp added a third shellout, gitRefContaining, behind the same boundary. It is injected into check() as a func value, so its CALLERS are covered by fakes, but the function itself — cat-file -e, for-each-ref --contains, merge-base --is-ancestor, and the decision to collapse every failure into "" — is verified only by hand. Same standing as showAtRef, which has been in that position since the tool landed.

What a test would have to do: build a scratch repo outside the worktree (t.TempDir plus GIT_DIR/GIT_WORK_TREE set explicitly rather than relying on cwd, which is what previously leaked), commit twice, delete the branch, and assert that a referenced sha names a ref and an orphaned one returns "". Also worth pinning: a sha the repo does not have at all returns "" rather than erroring out of the run.

Not blocking: the veto direction means a wrong "" grants no exemption on its own — the other two conditions still have to hold — and a wrong non-empty answer only refuses a declaration, which is loud.

title: bdguard: the reachability veto is inert in CI because the checkout is depth-1
description:
gqlc-npyp's reopened-arm exemption has three conditions. The third — no ref in this checkout contains the declared closing sha — is a veto: it can refuse a declaration, never grant one. It is inert in CI.

.github/workflows/ci.yml uses `actions/checkout@v4` with the default fetch-depth of 1, then `git fetch --depth=1 origin \$BASE_SHA` before `just bd-export-monotonic`. In that clone `git cat-file -e <sha>^{commit}` fails for anything outside the fetched pack, so gitRefContaining returns "" and the veto says nothing. The two conditions that do the work in CI are the base close_reason citation and the updated_at ordering, both of which are answerable from the two files alone; the veto only bites under `just bd-export-monotonic-local`, where the dev worktree has full history and remote-tracking refs.

Making it bite in CI needs a workflow change (fetch-depth: 0, or a targeted fetch of the declared shas), which is outside gqlc-npyp's territory — ci.yml was owned elsewhere in that wave. Weigh it against the reason the job fetches depth-1 in the first place: the comment there says cost is deliberately O(1) in history size. A targeted `git fetch origin <declared-sha>` per entry in .beads/allowed-reopens.txt is O(entries) and keeps that property; a blanket fetch-depth: 0 does not.

Note the veto is weak even with full history: gqlc squash-merges and deletes the branch, so an EARNED close's cited branch sha is orphaned as surely as an unearned one's. It bites on the narrower case where the branch is still pushed and its remote-tracking ref exists.

title: liverecipes: subtract's empty-taken path is asserted in prose but pinned by no row
description:

to say that Read builds Local by removing CI from the justfile's live invocations,
'which makes an empty CI the state where every live invocation sits in Local rather
than one where there are none'.

skipped and every invocation accumulates into 'left' — but no row exercises it.

Not fixed in #882: adding it after CI had gone green would have cost a full re-run of
seven required contexts at round 3, for a clause with no realistic mutation. Filed
instead so the claim is tracked rather than assumed.
