title: spec: C5 prints GetAction with two different parameter types in one document
description:
`docs/specs/codegen-stage-c5.md` prints one method under two different
parameter types:

- `:418` — `GetAction(ctx context.Context, arg GetActionParams)`
- `:996` — `GetAction(ctx context.Context, arg int64)`

One method name, two arities, in one document. At most one of them is what the
emitter produces for that method.

Confirmed present at `77a8cc12`, so it is **pre-existing** and not introduced by
`gqlc-rz0l`.

## Why the fence does not catch it

`gqlc-rz0l`'s spec fence grades the argument **name** position and explicitly
disclaims the type position. The name is `arg` in both lines, which is correct,
so both pass. The divergence is entirely on the axis the fence says it does not
read — this is the fence being honest about its boundary rather than failing.

## Fix

Work out which arity `GetAction` actually has by reading the emitter and the
goldens rather than by picking the line that looks more recent, then correct the
other site. If both are intended — two different examples that happen to share a
method name — rename one, because a reader who greps the document for
`GetAction` currently gets two incompatible answers with nothing to choose
between them.

## Acceptance

The two sites agree, and agree with what the emitter emits.

Worth considering while in there: whether the type position can be graded at all
for these signatures. If it can, this is the fixture for it. If it cannot —
`gqlc-vu7z` records why multi-parameter signatures are hard to grade without a
hand-maintained exclusion list — then say so and close this on the correction
alone rather than leaving an implied promise of a fence that is not coming.

Filed by the coordinator from `linus-rz0l-r2`'s non-blocking findings (NB-6),
who flagged it as pre-existing and off-axis so it would not be lost.

title: spec: prose can redefine the argument name under an intact code span the fence grades
description:
The spec fence grades **identifiers** — the argument name a signature, a
`<param-list>` bullet or a binding map literal spells. It does not read the
prose around them, and prose can contradict the code span it sits under.

Reviewer's mutation, green against the fence at `163d1873`:

Leave `` `, arg <T>` `` intact in C1 §5.3 and rewrite the sentence beneath it to

> the argument name is `arg` where the query parameter is named `arg`;
> otherwise it is the parameter field-name mangle

The graded span still says `arg`, so every assertion passes — and the document
now specifies the capture vector `gqlc-rz0l` removed, in the section that is
this repository's statement of the rule.

## Why it is filed rather than fixed

Out of the fence's declared scope, and the fence says so rather than
over-claiming. Closing it means grading natural language against an emitter,
which is not a thing a Go test can do honestly. Every cheap approximation —
keyword blacklists, "no sentence near this span may contain 'derive'" — is a
guard that passes over the rewordings nobody predicted and fails over innocent
prose, which is worse than the honest gap.

Noted rather than closed so no reader mistakes the fence for a claim about the
whole document.

## If it is taken

The tractable half is narrowing what prose *can* say by giving the rule one
canonical statement and having every other mention point at it rather than
restate it. A document with one place to change is one a reviewer can watch.
That is an editorial change to `docs/specs/`, not a test.

Do not close this by adding a fence that greps prose for suspicious words. The
repo's recurring defect class is a guard green over nothing, and a
keyword-matcher over English is that shape by construction.

## Related

`gqlc-vu7z` — the fence grades only one-parameter signatures.
`gqlc-173n` — the bind sweep grades every map literal under `docs/` and cannot
see a deref.

Filed by the coordinator from `linus-rz0l-r2`'s non-blocking findings (NB-3).

title: resolver: an OPTIONAL edge in a proven group is a witness NarrowPluralEndpoints throws away
description:
`NarrowPluralEndpoints` skips every edge binding that is nullable, so an
OPTIONAL edge never constrains its endpoints. That is the conservative fix
`gqlc-0tft` shipped, and it is correct: an edge that may not exist on a
surviving row is not evidence about that row's node type.

But it is *more* conservative than the truth. `DemoteNullability` at
`internal/resolver/scope.go:616` walks the identical shape and guards it with

    (e.Nullable() && !demotedGroups[...]) || !qualifiedDemoter(e)

— the extra clause being the point. An OPTIONAL edge **inside a proven group**
genuinely is a witness: the group's demotion is exactly the finding that every
surviving row carries that edge. `NarrowPluralEndpoints` throws that away.

## Why it was not taken with the fix

Ruled by the coordinator during `gqlc-0tft`'s review round. The refinement is a
*further widening* of what narrows, and a widening shipped without coverage is
precisely how the original defect arrived — `NarrowPluralEndpoints` was green
with the bug and green with the fix, which is to say the branch had zero
coverage for the distinction it got wrong. Fixing an unwitnessed widening with a
second unwitnessed widening is not a fix.

So the plain guard shipped, and the precision is filed here to be taken with
its own fixtures.

## Fix

Adopt `DemoteNullability`'s guard verbatim rather than paraphrasing it — the two
sites are answering the same question about the same shape, and a guard that
drifts from its sibling is how the next one of these gets written.

The `demotedGroups` set has to reach `NarrowPluralEndpoints`; check whether the
call order already computes it before the narrow pass runs, and say so
explicitly if it does not, because reordering the two passes is a larger change
than this bead's headline.

## Acceptance

The load-bearing half is the fixtures, not the guard. Required, in both
directions:

- An OPTIONAL edge in a **proven** group narrows its endpoints — the column that
  is now correctly NOT NULL is null-typed without the refinement.
- An OPTIONAL edge in an **unproven** group still does not narrow — this is the
  `gqlc-0tft` case and must not regress.

Each fixture must redden when the corresponding half of the guard is deleted.
A fixture that passes with and without the refinement is not coverage for it,
and this bead exists because that is what happened last time.

Filed by the coordinator from `linus-0tft-r1`'s findings.
notes:

## 2026-09-03, agent-h — DESIGN (gqlc-4uegl): hoist Phase D above Phase C, thread demotedGroups through the shared guard

The designer's call, with every claim below re-verified against master
1e279300 (post-#2519) by me, not inherited from the table.

### The ruling in plain words

The two guards ask one question — "is this edge guaranteed to exist on every
surviving row?" — and today they answer it differently for no recorded reason
except that the wider answer was deferred to gqlc-o8oc. The demotion pass that
computes the proven-group set reads nothing Phases A2/B/C write, so the order
that keeps its answer out of the narrowing's reach protects nothing. Swap it:
run Phase D first, keep ONE guard, let both Phase B and Phase C see the proven
set. This is prototype 4bec0326's exact shape, and it is the right shape.

### What to change (reference: commit 4bec0326, spike/gqlc-o8oc-proven-group-prototype, reachable from the shared object store)

1. **resolve.go resolvePart: move `sc.SeedLocalNullability(); sc.DemoteNullability()`
   ABOVE `sc.CloseEdges(s)`.** Carry the spike's replacement comment (it
   records why the old order's stated reason stopped binding, cites the bead,
   and names the R4 correction).
2. **scope.go: add field `demotedGroups map[int]bool`** to scope;
   DemoteNullability assigns its group-closure map to it (`s.demotedGroups =
   demotedGroups` right after the map is made — the closure then fills the
   shared map in place). Nil until D runs; nil reads false per id = the
   pre-refinement answer.
3. **Widen the guard once, in witnessesItsEndpoints:**
   `if (e.Nullable() && !demoted[e.OptionalGroup()]) || !singleHopPattern(e)`
   — new param `demoted map[int]bool`, threaded from s.demotedGroups through
   endpointNarrowing, inferUnlabelled, commitUnlabelledRound, candidateTypes
   (spike shows every call site; internal tests pass nil).
4. **This DELIBERATELY widens Phase B too** (candidateTypes' attainable-set
   conjunct), not only the Phase C narrowing gqlc-o8oc's headline names. Taken,
   not suffered: the soundness argument (a proven group's edge exists on every
   surviving row) does not care which phase asks, and the alternatives both
   fork the guard — see Rejected below. Say this in the PR body.
5. **Sweep manifest:** regenerate (`go test ./internal/resolver/ -run
   '^TestCorpusSweepManifest$' -update`), and INSPECT the diff: exactly one
   cell, DETAIL only (refusal names `d` instead of `a`). More than one changed
   cell falsifies this design — stop and say so. I re-ran the full resolver
   package on the prototype: with the control replaced (below), the manifest
   is the ONLY red.

### The falsified control, and its replacement (measured)

TestACommitmentFromTheAttainableSetIsLEARNEDFrom/the_control_with_no_witnessing_hop
flips refuse→resolve under the new regime, soundly (its required MATCH proves
the OPTIONAL group). Replace the control query by PREPENDING `MATCH (c) `:

    MATCH (c) OPTIONAL MATCH (c)-[h:HAS_DESK]->(d:Desk) OPTIONAL MATCH (p:Person)-[q:WORKS_AT]->(c) MATCH (c)<-[w:WORKS_AT]-(x:Person) RETURN x.personOnly

Why it works: the parser honours optionalGroup only on FIRST introduction
(pattern.go mergeBinding — the merge arm never touches it), so `c` introduced
by the required bare MATCH is group 0 forever; h/d's group has no other
required witness; the group stays unproven and h stays a non-witness under
BOTH regimes. Measured by me: refuses ErrUnknownProperty at master 1e279300
AND on the prototype (I edited the control in scratch extracts of each and ran
the test: all three subtests green both sides).

A one-token control cannot exist under the new regime in this clause order:
any required MATCH that reaches `x` through `c` proves c's group when c is
OPTIONAL-introduced. The extra token is inert for narrowing (a bare pattern
contributes no edge). Update the test comment: the delta from the accept rows
is now two tokens, and the control additionally pins the unproven-group limit
of the widening in the Phase B attainable-set context.

### The pin test (merged in #2519, 1e279300 — the spike predates that merge)

Do NOT cherry-pick the spike's resolver_test.go hunk; it conflicts with the
merged pin test. Edit master's TestAnOptionalEdgeNeverWitnessesItsEndpoints:
row 1 ("the group is proven") flips to NoError + Equal([]Column{{Name:
"c.smallOnly", Type: ResolvedProperty{Type: graph.PropertyType("STRING")}}}),
per its own comment's instruction; row 2 stays byte-identical (gqlc-0tft,
permanent). Rename to TestAProvenOptionalGroupWitnessesItsEndpoints (the old
name asserts a falsehood once row 1 flips). KEEP THE SUBTEST STRUCTURE — the
spike flattened the pair into sequential Requires, which re-loses the
report-both-rows property the merged test's own comment says the subtests
exist for. That part of the spike is declined.

### The new stated invariant (replaces "Phase D reads Phase C's committed shapes")

"Phase D is parse-local: it reads each binding's own Nullable / OptionalGroup /
Hops / ReferencedIn* flags and the carry (nullableBinding seed,
carriedGroups), and no table Phases A2/B/C write. Phases B and C consume Phase
D's demotedGroups through witnessesItsEndpoints, so Phase D completes before
CloseEdges runs." Witnessed by the flipped row 1: regress the order and
demotedGroups is nil at the narrowing, so the proven row refuses and goes red
(that is measurement CF, re-confirmed by construction). A future demotion
regime that DOES need committed edge shapes must run as a separate later pass,
not silently move Phase D back.

### Prose corrections, same PR

- **R4 spec (docs/specs/resolver-stage-r4.md): the §2.1-tail paragraph**
  ("Phase D runs after Phase C because the demotion algorithm reads committed
  edge shapes … resolvedEdgeKey / resolvedEdgeCand / edgeBindings") **and
  §2.2's `demoteNullable(bindings, edgeBindings, edgeKeys, edgeCands)` helper
  description** are stale: the shipped DemoteNullability takes none of those
  tables (grepped clean for s.edge*/s.node*/s.orientation/s.resolvedCovers/
  s.callTypes/s.pluralByInference at 1e279300, scope.go 652-785). Correct both
  to the shipped shape, the new order, and the invariant above, using the
  spec's own dated-strikethrough convention (see its §7/§8 closures).
- **witnessesItsEndpoints doc comment**, final paragraph ("deliberately
  blunter … filed rather than taken here"): now false. Rewrite: the OPTIONAL
  arm matches DemoteNullability's, same demotedGroups exemption, same reason;
  the surviving deliberate difference is singleHopPattern (stricter here,
  §4.4.3's lower-bound test there — that contrast paragraph stays).
- CONTEXT.md: untouched, deliberately — it carries none of this vocabulary
  (grepped Phase C/D, demot, witness: no hits).

### Mutation rows the PR owes (decision 0005 shape; guard changes, so the trigger fires)

- Drop `!demoted[e.OptionalGroup()]` from witnessesItsEndpoints → victim: the
  proven row's Equal in the renamed pair test. KILLED expected.
- Move Seed/Demote back below CloseEdges (the order regression) → same victim.
  KILLED expected. This is the row that pins the invariant.
- `if true` (refuse every witness — agent-d's disclosed SURVIVED M2) → victims:
  proven row AND both attainable accept rows. KILLED expected now; say that
  this closes the pair's disclosed directional gap.
- Replacement control's own falsifier: revert the control to the old query →
  its subtest goes red (resolves instead of refusing). KILLED expected.
- Compiler screen: `go test -c -o /dev/null ./internal/resolver`.

### Rejected alternatives

- **Standalone group-closure pass both phases read:** demotedGroups is
  interleaved with the nullableBinding fixed point (edge-driven demotion adds
  groups via demoteGroupsOf as entries flip) — extracting it means a second
  copy of the fixed point, which WILL drift. Not separable; rejected.
- **Move only NarrowPluralEndpoints below Phase D, leave CloseEdges where it
  is:** Phase B (candidateTypes, inside CloseEdges) would then read a nil
  demotedGroups while Phase C reads a populated one — one guard, two meanings
  by timing, invisible at the call site. Also discards a measured prototype
  for an unmeasured variant. Rejected.
- **Decline the refinement, record the difference as deliberate:** there is
  no soundness argument for refusing a proven group's edge; the only recorded
  reason for the difference was gqlc-o8oc's own deferral. Rejected.

### Risks / what to check before done

- Hoist safety, verified two ways: DemoteNullability's body reads no
  A2/B/C-written table (grep above), and nothing between the hoisted position
  and the old one reads s.nullableBinding (readers at 1e279300: newScope carry
  seed, projection walk, export/carry — all outside that window).
- `just gates` green (GOTOOLCHAIN=go1.26.6 locally); expect the manifest
  regen and pin-test edit to be the only test-side diffs beyond the control.
- Residue filed by me, not this PR's work: the third family member —
  candidateTypes' innerJoined is spelled `!e.Nullable()` (resolve.go ~1668)
  and does not honour proven groups; under the NEW order demotedGroups is
  available to it, so that refinement loses its ordering obstacle. Separate
  bead, blocked behind this one.

title: spec: the fence's bind sweep grades every map literal under docs/, and cannot see a deref
description:
Two reach limits in `scanSpecBinds`, `internal/codegen/conformance/specfence_test.go`.
Both were measured in the `linus-rz0l-r1` round; neither is live today.

## `unwrapConversions` strips `*`, so a deref is invisible (his #17)

The sweep reduces a binding expression to the identifier it ultimately
reads, peeling carrier conversions: `float64(arg)` binds `arg`. It also
peels `*` and `&`, so

    map[string]any{"x": float64(*arg)}

reduces to `arg` and passes.

This is DECLARED rather than concealed — C1 §5.3 scopes the fence to the
argument NAME, and `*arg` does carry the right name. But it is worth
recording because of what sits next to it. The `gqlc-rz0l` branch corrected
C3 §5.7 out of scope, precisely because a mechanical rename there would have
produced `float64(*arg)`, which is both wrong (a nullable parameter binds
bare — `paramBindExpr` at `internal/codegen/neo4j/render_queries.go:428`
returns before `driverCarrier` is reached) and a nil panic at runtime. So the
one correction on that branch whose whole point was the deref is unfenced
against its own failure mode.

Fix, if taken: grade the binding SHAPE for nullable parameters as well as
the name — a documented `map[string]any` entry whose expression derefs is
drift against `paramBindExpr`'s nullable-first ordering, regardless of what
identifier it names.

## The sweep grades every `map[string]any{` under `docs/` (his #39)

`docRoots` is the whole of `docs/` plus `README.md` and `CONTEXT.md`, and
`mapAnchor` is the bare literal `map[string]any{`. Any such literal in any
markdown file is graded as a documented parameter binding. A future ADR or
design note showing

    opts := map[string]any{"debug": true}

fails `TestSpecParamsMapBindsGeneratorOwnedValue` and is told its
"documented parameter binding is not generator-owned."

This FAILS CLOSED, so it is a maintenance annoyance rather than a hole — the
danger is that whoever hits it responds by narrowing `docRoots`, and the
breadth of `docRoots` is load-bearing (the original drift reached C1, C3, C4
and C5, and an ADR prints the same signatures). Verified as a live mutation:
an unrelated literal planted in a doc reddens the sweep.

Fix, if taken: require the literal to sit in a binding context — adjacent to
a graded signature, or inside a section the spec marks normative — rather
than widening the identifier allowlist, which would weaken the sweep in the
direction that matters.

Filed by the coordinator from `linus-rz0l-r1`'s non-blocking findings #17
and #39.

title: spec: the spec fence grades only one-parameter signatures, so multi-parameter drift is unswept
description:
`internal/codegen/conformance/specfence_test.go` pins the documented method
argument name against `codegen.ParamArg`, closing the capture vector
`gqlc-lhs3` removed from the emitter. It grades a signature only when the
parameter list splits into exactly two:

    params := splitTopLevel(list)
    if len(params) != 2 {
        continue
    }

So a documented signature carrying the query author's parameter names as
separate bare arguments —

    PeopleOverAge(ctx context.Context, minAge int64, locale string)

— is skipped. The emitter renders two-or-more parameters as a single
`arg <MethodName>Params` struct, so that signature is drift, and it is the
naive sqlc-shaped form a reader would plausibly write. Verified as a live
mutation (#31 in the `linus-rz0l-r1` round): the suite stays green over it.

## Why it is filed rather than fixed

Closing it means telling an emitted query method apart from the other
documented functions that also open `(ctx context.Context`. There are at
least two classes in `docs/` today: the 4-parameter `driverOrTx.run` seam,
and the godog step handlers. Neither is an emitted query method and both
would false-positive.

The only cheap discriminator is a hand-maintained exclusion list. That is
the same defect class this epic has already filed four beads against — a
hand-maintained set that silently shrinks, turning the gate off with no
diff to the gate (`gqlc-df3d`'s `-run` allowlist is the closest sibling).
A fence that false-positives also gets neutered by whoever it annoys first,
which is strictly worse than an honest gap.

## Fix

Needs a real discriminator, not a list. Options worth weighing: anchor on
the receiver (`func (q *Queries)`) plus the `WriteQuerier`/`Querier`
interface blocks, which is where every emitted query method is declared and
where nothing else is; or grade only signatures inside sections the spec
already marks normative. Whichever is chosen, the property to keep is the
one the fence already has: it must redden when it stops matching, rather
than grading zero sites and passing.

Note the arity rule itself is simple once the discriminator exists — for an
emitted query method, ANY parameter list longer than `(ctx, arg T)` is
drift, because the emitter has no such form.

Filed by the coordinator from `linus-rz0l-r1`'s non-blocking finding #31.

title: ci: the lint-hooks reachability walk accepts prose as a CI entry point, and cannot see a .yaml workflow
description:
`.githooks/tests/lint-hooks-test.sh` proves that some recipe CI actually runs
reaches `lint-hooks` transitively, so shellcheck is not merely present in the
justfile but wired to a job. It derives the entry-point set by grepping
`just <recipe>` out of `.github/workflows/*.yml` after stripping comments.

Two ways the derived set is wrong. Neither is live today — I enumerated every
`just` occurrence across all four workflow files — and the real regression
path (deleting the `- run: just lint` step) is caught.

## Comment stripping is whole-line only

The strip is `grep -hvE '^[[:space:]]*#'`. It correctly removes the two prose
`just lint` mentions at `ci.yml:40-41`, which is the hazard it was built for.
It does not remove a trailing comment on an otherwise-live line, so

    - run: just tidy   # just lint

is accepted as an entry point that CI does not run. Nor does it distinguish a
YAML key from a command, so

    - name: just lint

is accepted too. Both verified as live mutations (M11c, M11d in the
`linus-ghsync-r2` round): the walk starts from a recipe CI never invokes and
the guard goes green.

The direction matters — a FALSE entry point makes the guard pass over a
severed edge. That is fail-open. Contrast the `.yaml` case below.

## The glob is `*.yml`

A workflow added as `.yaml` is invisible to the walk. This direction fails
SAFE: fewer entry points means the walk is more likely to report UNREACHED
and redden. Worth fixing at the same time because it is the same line, not
because it is dangerous.

## Fix

Match a command position rather than a substring — the entry points live in
`run:` scalars, so read those rather than grepping the file flat. Whatever
shape it takes, the property to keep is the one M12 already pins: deleting
the real `- run: just lint` step while leaving the prose at `ci.yml:40-41`
must still redden.

Widen the glob to `*.yml` and `*.yaml` in the same change.

## Why filed rather than fixed

Coordinator ruling on `fix/bd-gh-sync-listing-and-shellcheck`. The guard is
new on that branch and holds under every mutation of the thing it protects
(M9 severs the sole CI-to-shellcheck edge and it reddens, naming all twelve
entry points). These are latent reach limits in the derivation, not a defect
in the guard, and closing them properly means parsing YAML structure rather
than tightening a regex.

Filed by the coordinator from `linus-ghsync-r2`'s non-blocking finding NB-6.
close_reason: Stale after PR #1595 (f6dc4c7b) herdr trim. The guard under discussion (.githooks/tests/lint-hooks-test.sh) is deleted along with the whole tests/ tree; there is no reachability walk left to fix. Aggressive-sweep per user 2026-08-29.

title: ci: the bd-gh-sync remedy guard reads only stderr and matches two tokens, behind a failure message that claims semantics
description:
`.githooks/tests/bd-gh-sync-test.sh`'s guard over the push-path remedy text
exists to stop a specific false instruction coming back — advice telling the
reader to wait for the bd database to unlock, when the database is not the
reason the push refused to count. It has two blind spots, neither live today,
both narrower than the failure message it prints.

## It matches two tokens, not a meaning

The negative arm is `grep -qiE 're-run|the database is free'`. Its failure
message reads "the remedy sends the reader to wait on a database that is not
the reason" — a claim about meaning, checked by a two-token pattern.

    Wait for the bd database to unlock, then push again

is the identical false advice and contains neither token. Verified as a live
mutation (M5 in the `linus-ghsync-r2` round): the suite reports 124 passed,
0 failed over it.

No grep can pin a paraphrase, so this is not straightforwardly fixable and
may not be worth fixing. What IS fixable is the mismatch between what the
message asserts and what the pattern can support. The realistic regression —
a revert, or a verbatim re-add — is caught twice over (M4 and M8 both kill),
and reflowing the original wording at different word boundaries leaves
`re-run` intact (M6 kills).

## It reads only `$TMP/err`

Both arms grep `$TMP/err`. The same false advice emitted verbatim without
`>&2` lands on stdout and is invisible to the guard (M7: 124 passed, 0
failed). A pre-push hook shows stdout to the operator just as plainly as
stderr, so the reader is misled either way.

This is the uniform convention of the whole file — every assertion in it
greps `$TMP/err` — so changing it at this one site alone would be worse than
leaving it. If it is worth closing, close it file-wide or not at all. It also
needs a compound regression to trip: re-add the line AND drop the redirection.

## Why filed rather than fixed

Coordinator ruling on `fix/bd-gh-sync-listing-and-shellcheck`. The branch's
three guards all hold under 34 mutations; these are reach limits, not
defects, and both need a regression that does not resemble the one the guard
was built for. Promoting them would have meant either an unfixable ask (the
paraphrase) or a file-wide convention change smuggled into a bug-fix branch.

Filed by the coordinator from `linus-ghsync-r2`'s non-blocking findings NB-1
and NB-2.
close_reason: Stale after PR #1595 (f6dc4c7b) herdr trim. The guard under discussion (.githooks/tests/bd-gh-sync-test.sh) is deleted; the mutations M4/M5/M7/M8 witnessing it are witnessed by nothing now. Aggressive-sweep per user 2026-08-29.

title: codegen: the decoder reachability gate checks each label guard alone, so a conjunction of two can be dead
description:
`gqlc-05tl`'s `TestEmittedDecodersGuardOnlyOnStampableLabels` asserts that every
string literal an emitted `decode<T>` compares for equality is a label the
fixture's schema declares. That is a **per-literal** check, and its doc states
it as such honestly.

Found by `linus-05tl-r1b` as mutation M19b.

## The hole

Two guards can each name a declared label and still be jointly unsatisfiable:

    func decodePerson(raw []byte) (Person, error) {
        label, props, err := agtypeEntity(raw, "::vertex")
        ...
        if label != "Person" { return Person{}, ... }
        if label != "Post"   { return Person{}, ... }

`label` is one string. It cannot be both. Every row takes one of the two early
returns, so `decodePerson` is dead on arrival -- the exact condition the gate
exists to refuse -- and the gate is **green**, because "Person" and "Post" are
both declared.

The gate reasons about each literal against the alphabet. It does not reason
about the guards as a conjunction.

## Why P3

The emitter does not currently produce this shape, so it is latent rather than
live. The reviewer classified it non-blocking on those grounds and I agree.

What makes it worth filing anyway is that it is the SAME defect one level up: a
guard that cannot fail, in the gate built to find guards that cannot succeed. The
gate's power is bounded by the granularity of its reasoning, and nothing in the
tree records that bound where a future reader would look before trusting it.

## Fix

Either widen the gate to decide satisfiability over the conjunction of guards in
a decoder body rather than each literal alone, or -- if that is disproportionate
-- state the bound explicitly in the gate's 'What it does not decide' section,
which is where its other four exclusions already live.

**Prefer widening.** That section is already carrying one falsehood this epic had
to correct (`gqlc-05tl` round 2 fixed a claim there that was the opposite of what
the code did), and adding a fifth exclusion to a list that has proven hard to keep
true is the weaker move.

## Acceptance

Emit the two-guard shape and confirm the gate FAILS. Today it passes.
notes:
--- agent-k, 2026-09-02, PR #2368 ---

WHERE THE DEFECT LIVED. Not where the bead's example put it. The bead reads
"two distinct required literals means dead", which would have reddened a
correct emission: neo4j's entity_multi_label_named demands TWO labels of one
node, and a node carries a SET of labels, so that is satisfiable. The real
rule is about a SINGLE-VALUED operand — an identifier cannot equal two
strings — and that framing is what let the reader need neither the axis nor
the alphabet, and so read every emitted function body rather than the
classified decoders alone. entityDecoder is untouched; no field added, so the
four require.Equal decoder tables did not move.

MEASURED, through the reader itself and not a proxy: 73 straight-line
requirements over 22 distinct decode<T> bodies, all apache-age-pgx-v5, all on
operand `label`, every one carrying exactly one literal. neo4j contributes
zero. The sweep asserts NotZero on the corpus total, so a reader that
silently stopped reading is not a green run.

TWO SOUNDNESS CONDITIONS, AND THE BATTERY SAYS BOTH ARE LOAD-BEARING. I had
written the doc claiming the straight-line restriction "is the whole reason
the rule is sound". M4b (group the whole body by spelling) did NOT red the
multi-label row, because its `label` is bound by two range statements and so
fails the single-assignment condition; only M4c (M4b + drop the stable check)
red it. Each condition holds that shape alone. Corrected in a second commit
so a later reader does not relax one believing the other decorative.

WHAT LIED TO ME.
1. `grep` is a shell function in this harness and dies under `set -u`, so my
   first two batteries' tripwire and victim capture never ran and all eight
   KILLED verdicts were scored by a test that never executed. `command grep`,
   plus an M0 no-mutation control row, which is what caught it: M0 read
   KILLED.
2. recordedConjunction always read 0 on refusal rows, because require's Len
   panics via FailNow so the assignment never happened. Split read from
   verdict: straightLineLabelRequirements returns reqs, callers take len(reqs)
   FIRST, then call requireSatisfiableGuards.
3. M10 (report drops the operand) SURVIVED — a real finding in my own guard.
   The refusal report explains itself with "each literal alone may well be a
   LABEL the axis carries", so a row asserting contains "label" was satisfied
   by the report's prose whether or not req.operand was ever named. Renamed
   the operand to wireLabel in the two rows that read the report; M10 now
   KILLED by both. Second instance of count-the-claim-not-the-keyword.
4. M5 first mutation orphaned `stable` -> BUILD-FAILED, not a kill. Mutated to
   `(false && !stable[name])` instead to keep it used.
5. M7's row did not exist until the battery demanded it. Committed it BEFORE
   re-screening, per the uncommitted-guard hazard.

BATTERY: M0 control SURVIVED. M1 M2 M3 M4 M4b M4c M5 M6 M7 M8 M10 all KILLED,
each named against its own victim rows. Table in the PR body.

Shipped in PR #2368 (squash-merged to master 2026-09-03; verified by content,
not commit count: straightLineLabelRequirements is present in
origin/master:internal/codegen/conformance/decoder_reachability_test.go).

The gate now carries a second reader, straightLineLabelRequirements, that
decides the conjunction the per-literal grading could not. It needs neither the
axis nor the alphabet — an identifier cannot equal two strings whatever the
schema declares — so it reads every function body an emission writes, not the
classified decoders alone. entityDecoder is untouched and the four
require.Equal decoder tables did not move.

The bead's framing was wrong in a way worth recording: "two distinct required
literals means dead" would have reddened a CORRECT emission. neo4j asks for
label-set membership, one loop per label, and a node carries a set, so
entity_multi_label_named demanding two labels is satisfiable. The shipped rule
is about a single-valued operand instead.

MEASURED through the reader itself: 73 straight-line requirements over 22
distinct decode<T> bodies, all apache-age-pgx-v5, every one carrying exactly
one literal. neo4j contributes zero. The sweep asserts NotZero on the corpus
total, so a reader that silently stopped reading is not a green run.

Mutation battery, per-row with declared victims: M0 control SURVIVED (the
harness scores); M1 M2 M3 M4 M4b M4c M5 M6 M7 M8 M10 all KILLED. Two findings
came out of it rather than out of me. M4b measured that the straight-line
restriction is NOT the whole reason the rule is sound — the single-assignment
condition holds the neo4j shape too, and each holds it alone; the doc had

because my rows asserted the refusal report contains "label", which the
report's own explanatory prose supplies; renaming the operand to wireLabel made
the assertion answer the claim.

Residue already filed: gqlc-ebkbs (a decoder written as a method naming two
entities is graded by nothing).

title: ci: ensure-shellcheck hardcodes linux.$(uname -m), so a non-Linux host silently gets no linter
description:
The `ensure-shellcheck` recipe fetches a release archive whose name it builds as
`linux.$(uname -m)`. The architecture is derived; the OS is a literal.

On any non-Linux host the fetch names an archive that does not exist. Depending
on how the recipe handles that, the developer either gets a confusing download
error or -- the case that matters -- gets no shellcheck and a lint step that
passes over unlinted shell.

## Why it is P3 and not higher

CI runs Linux, so the enforcing path is unaffected. This is a local-development
defect: the person most likely to hit it is someone on macOS editing
`.githooks/`, who would then be shipping shell that only the CI run lints.

## Why it is worth filing anyway

`gqlc-jhi2` was filed on the premise that 'a disable directive in a tree with no
linter is a comment', and the fix wired shellcheck into CI through
`justfile`'s `lint: ensure-golangci lint-hooks` edge. That closed the CI half.
This is the same sentence about a developer's working copy.

The failure is also silent in the direction that matters. A developer who never
had shellcheck does not see a warning that they are unlinted; they see a green
`just lint`.

## Fix

Derive the OS the way the architecture is already derived, and -- more
importantly than supporting every platform -- **fail loudly on a platform the
recipe cannot serve** rather than proceeding without a linter. Refusing to lint
is an acceptable outcome; silently not linting is not.

Check `ensure-golangci` in the same pass. If it has the same shape, it has the
same defect, and the point is the rule rather than the one site.

## Acceptance

Run the recipe with `uname` stubbed to report a non-Linux OS and confirm it
exits non-zero with a message naming the platform, rather than exiting 0 with no
shellcheck present.
close_reason: shipped in PR 1612 merged 2026-08-29

title: .claude/settings.json pipes bd-gh-sync pull through tail, reporting tail's exit status
description:
`.claude/settings.json` invokes:

    bd-gh-sync pull 2>&1 | tail -1

A pipeline reports the **last** command's exit status, so this reports `tail`'s,
which is 0 essentially always. If `bd-gh-sync pull` exits non-zero, the hook does
not find out.

This is the exact class this repo has been bitten by three times now — most
recently `gqlc-nsq4`, where `(...) 2>&1 | tee "${log}" || rc=$?` in the `vuln`
recipe was correct only by virtue of a `set -o pipefail` fifty lines away, and
was converted to `out="$(cmd 2>&1)" || rc=$?` for that reason.

## Why it is P3

Harmless *today*, and harmless by design rather than by luck: `bd-gh-sync pull`
always exits 0 on purpose, because a pull that cannot reach GitHub must not break
the developer's `git pull`. So there is currently no status for `tail` to
swallow.

That is a property of the script, asserted nowhere, sitting behind a pipeline
that would silently discard the status the moment it changed. `gqlc-nvjz` is
open against that same pull path and one of its candidate fixes is a BLIND exit
— which is precisely a non-zero status this pipeline would eat.

So the ordering matters: if `gqlc-nvjz` lands a non-zero pull exit first, this
stops being latent.

## Shape of the fix

`out="$(bd-gh-sync pull 2>&1)"; rc=$?; printf '%s\n' "${out}" | tail -1; exit "${rc}"`
— or whatever the settings schema permits. Whichever form, the status that
reaches the caller must be the script's.

Also worth checking the other hook invocations in that file for the same shape
rather than fixing this one site.

## Acceptance

Make `bd-gh-sync pull` exit non-zero under a stub and confirm the hook sees it.
A fix with no such demonstration is a change nothing measures — and this repo's
own history is that pipeline-status bugs are found by executing them, not by
reading them.

Filed by the coordinator from `carmack-ghsync-p3b`'s out-of-scope list.
Pre-existing; not introduced by that branch.
close_reason: shipped in PR 1609 merged 2026-08-29

title: walkListElemBody's innerAcc is a fixed name, one nesting level below the bug ibg5 fixed
description:
`gqlc-ibg5` fixed `writeListColumnDecodeIndent`, which hardcoded the
accumulator variable name `acc`, so two non-nullable list columns in one row
emitted `acc := ...` twice and the generated file did not compile:

    ./corpus_queries.cypher.go:124:7: no new variables on left side of :=

The fix derives the name: `"acc" + strings.TrimPrefix(varName, "value")`.

`walkListElemBody`'s `innerAcc` is the same shape one level down and was left
alone.

## Why it is currently safe, and why that is thin

`innerAcc` sits inside a per-iteration loop body, so a deeper nesting opens a
new scope and *shadows* rather than redeclares. That is a real argument and it
is why this is P3 rather than P2.

It is thin because the property it rests on is lexical scoping of the emitted
code, not anything the emitter checks. Two **sibling** nested lists rendered
into the same block — as opposed to one inside the other — would collide the
same way `acc` did. Whether the emitter can currently produce that shape is the
question this bead has to answer, and "I could not construct one" is a
different finding from "the emitter cannot".

## Shape of the fix

If the sibling shape is reachable: derive `innerAcc` the same way `acc` is now
derived, and add a fixture with two sibling nested list columns in one row.

If it is not reachable: say so in a comment at the declaration, naming the
invariant that makes it unreachable and what would have to change for it to
become reachable. A fixed name that is safe by accident and a fixed name that
is safe by argument look identical in the source, which is why the argument has
to be written down.

Do not fix it by renaming and stopping. `gqlc-ibg5` was found by a fixture that
compiled the emitted output; this needs the same. A rename with no fixture that
would have caught the collision is a change nothing measures.

## Acceptance

A fixture with two sibling nested lists in one row, and a demonstration that
reverting the derivation makes it fail to compile — or a recorded argument that
the shape is unreachable, with the invariant named.

Filed by the coordinator from `carmack-dcap-ibg5`'s out-of-scope list.
notes:
CORRECTION (2026-08-04, coordinator). This bead's own 'why it is currently safe' section is WRONG, and the reviewer proved it. It is not latent. It is broken today.

linus-dcap-ibg5-r1 constructed the shape and got a real compile failure at nesting depth >= 3:

    ./corpus_queries.cypher.go:302:33: cannot use innerAcc (variable of type []int64) as int64 value in argument to append

The shadowing argument is the defect, not the mitigation. The inner 'innerAcc :=' shadows the outer one, so 'append(accVar, innerAcc)' resolves BOTH operands to the inner variable. The outer accumulator is not merely hidden -- it becomes unreferenceable at exactly the point the emitted code needs to append to it. So the scoping property the description leaned on is what breaks it.

Raised P3 -> P2 accordingly.

title: ci: test-codegen-live-neo4j omits -count=1, so a live green can be a cache hit
description:
`justfile:186`, the `test-codegen-live-neo4j` recipe, runs `go test` without
`-count=1`. The other live recipes pass it.

The comment justifying the omission argues from Go's test cache key, and that
argument is sound **as far as it goes**: the key covers the test binary and its
inputs, so an unchanged tree legitimately serves a cached result.

The gap is the one the comment itself concedes: **the cache key does not
include the container runtime.** A live suite's real input is a testcontainers
Postgres or neo4j instance — its image, its extension version, its state. None
of that is in the key. So a green here can be a result computed against a
container that no longer exists, or against a different image than the one
currently pinned.

This repo has already been bitten by exactly this: a live suite reported
`ok ... 0.2s`, which is not a duration in which a container starts. That is how
the missing `-count=1` was found elsewhere.

## Why it is filed rather than fixed

Pre-existing on master. The `gqlc-35yu.14` branch only rewrites the comment
that justifies it, and rewriting a justification is not the same as accepting
the thing justified — but changing recipe behaviour was out of that branch's
scope.

## Fix

Add `-count=1`, and delete the cache-key argument rather than amending it. The
argument is not wrong about Go; it is answering a question about the wrong
input set, and a comment that reasons correctly to a wrong conclusion is worse
than none.

Check the other live recipes at the same time — the point is the rule, not the
one site.

## Acceptance

Every live recipe passes `-count=1`. Verify by running one twice in a row and
confirming the second run is not instant. A live suite reporting a sub-second
`ok` has served a cache hit and measured nothing.

Filed by the coordinator from `linus-35yu14-r5`'s non-blocking findings.
Adjacent to `gqlc-df3d` (live recipes select tests by a hardcoded `-run`
allowlist) — same recipes, different defect. Check whether they should be taken
together.
notes:
ADJUDICATED on branch fix/live-recipe-structural-selection (PR #882, bd gqlc-df3d).
Decision: do NOT add -count=1 to test-codegen-live-neo4j. No `Closes #765` on the
PR — the coordinator should close this as adjudicated.

WHAT WAS MEASURED (go1.26.6, `go version` in the repo):

1. Env vars read during a run ARE part of the test cache key. A probe module
   whose test calls os.Getenv("PROBE_SKIP") was run 7 times:
     1 unset      -> cold (ran)
     2 unset      -> (cached)
     3 PROBE_SKIP=1 -> miss, ran
     4 PROBE_SKIP=1 -> (cached)
     5 PROBE_SKIP=2 -> miss, ran
     6 unset      -> (cached)  [distinct entry from 3 and 5]
     7 PROBE_SKIP=2 -> (cached)
   Three distinct values produced three distinct cache entries. So
   GQLC_SKIP_LIVE=1 cannot poison the entry a real (unset) run serves: the
   skipped run and the live run key differently.
   (An earlier probe measured go1.26.5 because the /tmp module's go.mod said
   `go 1.26`; re-pinned to 1.26.6 and re-run — same result.)

2. Both container images are digest-pinned as compiled-in constants, so an
   image bump changes the test binary and therefore the key:
     test/data/codegen/live_neo4j_test.go:40
     test/data/codegen/live_age_test.go:34

3. What remains outside the key is the container RUNTIME (daemon present,
   image locally pullable) — which the in-tree comment already conceded.

WHAT WAS ACTUALLY WRONG: not the recipe, the comment. It claimed "every input
... is inside the test binary", which is false in the direction that matters
(the env vars are inputs, and they are outside the binary but inside the key;
the runtime is outside both). The comment on this branch is corrected to name
the env-var/cache-key half explicitly rather than overclaiming.

WHY NOT -count=1 ANYWAY: the bead's evidence for a stale green is a live suite
reporting `ok ... 0.2s`. That shape is a cache hit, and a cache hit here is only
reachable when the binary, the args and every env var read are identical — i.e.
when nothing about the run changed except the clock. The cost of -count=1 is
paid on every PR that touches nothing in the live tree. Adding it would trade a
measured, keyed cache for wall time on the argument that the runtime is
unkeyed; the runtime being unkeyed is a reason to distrust a green whose
CONTAINER changed, which -count=1 does not detect either (it re-runs against
whatever runtime is there).

The AGE half keeps its -count=1: it is not being removed, and this is a
decision about not adding a third.
close_reason: adjudicated on branch fix/live-recipe-structural-selection PR 882; do not add -count=1. Triage close.

title: resolver/codegen: the enum-growth fence lives across a package boundary, and Cardinality has none
description:
`gqlc-h4ug` round 6 built a guard that catches a `resolver.Temporal` member
declared without a `String()` arm. It works — three mutations redden it — but it
lives in `internal/codegen/conformance` and reaches across a package boundary
through a **hardcoded relative path**:

    "../../resolver/validated.go"

Two problems, one of them latent:

## The fence is owned by the wrong package

`resolver` owns the enum. A guard on the enum's shape belongs beside it. As
built, reorganising the codegen tree — moving the conformance package, renaming
a directory — silently breaks the path, and what breaks is a *derivation*: the
suite stops finding the constant block it is supposed to compare against.

Round 6's implementer hard-`Require`s the block shape, so this should fail
loudly rather than pass vacuously. **Verify that before assuming it.** A parse
that yields an empty set and an assertion that compares an empty set to an
empty set is this project's most-found defect, and a missing file is exactly
how it arises.

## `codegen.Cardinality` has no such guard at all

The same fail-open shape — a named integer enum whose `String()` can be grown
out of step with its constant block — applies to `codegen.Cardinality`, which
`docs/specs/codegen-sentinel-taxonomy.md` §2 already carries a row for. Nothing
guards it.

## Shape of the fix

Move the derivation into `internal/resolver` as a test on its own package, so
the path is local and a file move breaks compilation rather than a string. Then
apply the same treatment to `codegen.Cardinality` in `internal/codegen`.

If a shared helper falls out of doing both, good — but do not build the
abstraction first. Two similar tests in two packages is the right amount of
duplication for two enums.

## Acceptance

For each enum, all three mutations red: a const with no `String` arm; a `String`
arm with no const; well-formed growth of both. And: deleting or moving the file
the derivation reads must fail loudly, naming what it could not find — verify by
mutation, do not assume the `Require` covers it.

Filed by the coordinator from `carmack-h4ug-r6`'s out-of-scope list.
Discovered-from `gqlc-h4ug`.

title: codegen/age: propertyWidths claims to derive from the property table and is a literal
description:
`internal/codegen/age/render_models_test.go:16-22` declares `propertyWidths` and
says of it:

    Taken from the property table rather than written out here, so a width
    the table gains is a row these sweeps gain.

It is not taken from anything. It is a hand-written 7-element literal with no
cross-check against `typeMap.Property`. `grep -rn propertyWidths internal/`
returns the declaration and two `range`s over it — nothing that compares the
set to the table it claims to mirror.

So a Go carrier width the property table gains is a row the two sweeps **do
not** gain, and the comment says the opposite.

## Severity

Lower than the epic's usual instance of this shape. The sweeps still assert
something over the seven widths they do hold, so this is not a gate that is
green on nothing — it is a gate whose coverage silently fails to grow. The
blast radius is one width of coverage per new width, not the whole assertion.

It is filed because the comment makes a **derivation claim** that is false, and
a reader who trusts it will add a width to the table and believe the sweeps
picked it up.

## Shape of the fix

Two options, and the second is better:

1. Delete the sentence. Honest, cheap, and leaves the coverage gap.
2. Make the claim true: derive the row set from the distinct Go carriers
   `typeMap.Property` admits. Not a `require.Len` — a length pin is the same
   family of defect this epic keeps finding, and `gqlc-35yu.11`'s own
   `require.Len(temporalKinds, int(TemporalDuration)+1)` is the cautionary
   case, where both sides of the assertion moved together so it could never
   fire.

Prefer 2. Compare the swept set against the derived set as a **set**, so a
width added to the table with no sweep row reddens by name.

## Acceptance

Add a width to `typeMap.Property` without touching the test, and watch the
sweep redden naming the new width. Revert.

Filed by the coordinator from `linus-35yu11-r6`'s non-blocking findings.
Discovered-from `gqlc-35yu.11`.
