TWO MAGNITUDES I DECLARED TOO SMALL, DISCLOSED NOT RESTATED. (a) M1: I wrote "the
package stays green" and the sibling
TestDecodeFuncHasAnArmForEveryCarrierTheTypeTableProduces went red, because it pins
the carrier count at 21 by design. Worth saying, because it fires on M1' too: master
DID have a tripwire that notices the table growing, and it was that count pin --
never these sweeps. The bead's diagnosis "a width the table gains is a row the sweeps
do not gain" is right; "nothing noticed" would have been wrong. (b) M2 reddens all
three sweeps, not the one I named; marking zone instead of timeZone changes which
helper is emitted, so the import check and the closure check see it too. Named victim
and its message exactly as declared in both rows.

M4's TWO SURVIVED ARE A REAL LIMIT, REPORTED. Neither
TestImportsTimeAgreesWithTheEmittedFile nor TestEmittedHelpersAreClosedOverWhatTheyCall
has a non-degeneracy assertion of its own beyond the shared NotEmpty. They share the
helper with TestZone, whose sawInstant does die on a shrink, so the helper is not
unguarded -- but those two alone would not have noticed. Not papered over with a
second count pin, which would only duplicate the sibling's and add a number that
moves with nothing.

WHAT THE FIX DELIBERATELY DOES NOT CLAIM. The derivation inherits typeTableGoTypes'
reach, which is narrower than the table's output: it reads Go types returned as
string LITERALS, so the list arm's composed `"[]" + elem` contributes nothing and
LIST<ANY>'s own literal is the only list carrier swept. That is why the two
hand-written list rows are gone rather than carried over, and it is stated in the
helper's doc comment rather than left for a reader to discover. Nothing is lost to
these three invariants by it: helpers.need peels a slice to its element before
marking anything, so what the []Date row asserted about the time import is what the
Date row asserts.

title: ci: just --fmt --check fails at HEAD and is gated in no job
description:
`just --fmt --check --unstable` exits 1 at HEAD. Measured on `7005805`, so this
predates the vuln-gate branch and is not something it introduced.

No CI job runs it. The justfile is therefore unformatted, has been for some
time, and nothing in the tree says so — which is the same shape as every other
finding in this epic: a property that is supposed to hold, does not, and no
gate is looking.

## The two halves

**Formatting.** Run the formatter and commit the result. Mechanical, and the
diff should be inspected once rather than trusted, because `--unstable` means
the formatter's output is not covenanted across `just` releases.

**Gating.** Adding the check to CI pins a formatter whose behaviour is
explicitly unstable, so a `just` upgrade on the runner can redden a branch that
changed nothing. That is a real cost and it is why this is filed rather than
folded into the vuln-gate branch.

The trade to weigh: an unstable-but-pinned check that occasionally needs a
reformat commit, versus a justfile that drifts with nothing noticing. The first
failure mode is noisy and visible; the second is silent. Recommend gating, with
the `just` version pinned in the workflow so an upgrade is a deliberate edit.

## Constraint

Do **not** rename, split, add or remove any job in `.github/workflows/` —
GitHub derives required check contexts from job ids, and branch protection
names them. A new check goes inside an existing job.

## Acceptance

`just --fmt --check --unstable` exits 0 at HEAD, and a deliberate
misformatting reddens CI.

Filed by the coordinator from `carmack-vulngate-r2`'s out-of-scope list.
Discovered-from `gqlc-rohp`.

title: codegen/age: three arms of the multi-label diagnostic are unpinned
description:
Found by the adversarial review of gqlc-35yu.15, all non-blocking, all the same
shape: a live branch or a sweep with no test behind it.

## 1. The offender count is unpinned

The diagnostic says "This schema declares %d of them". Hardcoding that %d to 1
while the message goes on to list two offenders leaves the whole suite green.
The *per-offender* label count is pinned — dropping labels or truncating a label
set reddens `multilabel_test.go:146` — but the top-level count is not.

One line in TestMultiLabelDiagnosticNamesEveryOffenderAndItsLabels closes it:
assert the printed count equals the number of offenders the test found, not a
literal.

## 2. The singular/plural query branch is unpinned

The assertion is `Contains(msg, strconv.Itoa(queries)+" quer")`, which matches
both "query" and "queries". So deleting the `if queries == 1 { queryNoun =
"query" }` branch entirely survives. Cosmetic in effect, but it is a live
branch with no test.

## 3. The fixture list in the sweep is a literal, not a glob

`requireLabelsDistinguishable` — the guard that stops a fixture's own type name
from satisfying an assertion about its labels — runs over a hardcoded slice of
fixture names. A third multi-label fixture dropped into
`internal/codegen/age/testdata/` is not swept until someone edits the slice.

This one is defensible as written: that testdata directory holds fixtures for
other tests too, so a bare glob would sweep files the guard does not apply to.
But it is the one place in this test file that is not self-extending, and the
epic's recurring defect is exactly a hand-maintained list that nobody remembers
to update. If a glob is wrong, the fix is a naming convention the glob can key
on (e.g. `multi_label_*.gql`) plus a check that the convention is exhaustive.

## Not in scope

The review also found that `keyLabels` and `entityKindNoun`'s edge arms are dead
and untested — both mutate to nonsense with a fully green `./...`. That is
deliberate: multi-label EDGES are unreachable across three syntaxes (verified at
the grammar: `no viable alternative at input ':WORKED_FOR&FOR'`, `mismatched
input ':' expecting ']->'`, `no viable alternative at input 'LABELS
WORKED_FOR&FOR'`), and ADR 0027 documents the retention. Nothing would flag the
arm rotting if the grammar ever opened, but that is a different bead if anyone
wants it.

## Acceptance

Each of the three mutations above turns a gate red, naming what it caught.

Filed by the coordinator from the gqlc-35yu.15 review's non-blocking findings.
notes: 2026-09-03 PR #2435 opened (head bf522caf, rebased twice: onto 8b0b23cd #2433, then 82784a6a #2434). Battery N1-N5 declared-then-run, N4 the declared-SURVIVED negative control (renamed fixture + skipped convention test => whole package green). just gates 14/14. Bead IS in .beads/issues.jsonl (grep -c 1), so check-pr-closes does NOT skip here — unlike gqlc-qo6ul/gqlc-vqx87. external_ref issues/753 matches gh closingIssuesReferences [753].
close_reason:
Fixed in PR #2435, squash-merged as f1b273c372e378aa048b14f45ab0f0458b6c567e
(2026-09-03T04:13:21Z). GH #753 closed at 04:13:22Z. Verified by CONTENT on
origin/master, not by commit count.

WHAT WAS UNPINNED, AND WHAT NOW HOLDS IT

multiLabelDiagnostic promised three things the suite did not read back.

1. The offender count. errors.go:155 prints "This schema declares %d of them"
   from len(refused) and nothing asserted the number. Now asserted against
   strconv.Itoa(len(offenders))+" of them". The two fixtures declare DIFFERENT
   counts (2 and 1), which is what makes the assertion discriminate rather than
   restate a literal that the source and the test both write.

2. The query noun. The singular/plural branch at errors.go:140-143 was unread.
   The assertion takes the whole token ("3 queries" / "1 query"), not the digit,
   so the branch itself is under guard.

3. Fixture selection. The sweeps looped over a LITERAL SLICE of two fixture
   names, so a new or renamed multi-label fixture silently left the sweep with
   the package still green. The loop now globs testdata/multi_label_*.gql, and
   TestEveryMultiLabelFixtureIsNamedByTheConvention makes the naming convention
   itself the guarded claim, in BOTH directions.

WHY NOT A BARE testdata/*.gql GLOB

That directory holds fixtures for other tests, and a schema with no multi-label
type fails the sweep's own preconditions. So the glob is only sound if the
convention is exhaustive — which is exactly what the new test states. The
reverse arm is not decoration: a fixture named multi_label_* that declares no
offender would put the sweeps on a schema that CANNOT refuse, asserting nothing
while passing. Both populations are asserted NotZero SEPARATELY; one NotZero
over the total would be satisfied by a run where every fixture landed in one arm.

MEASURED BEFORE CHANGING: the fixture family

"&" counts over every *.gql in internal/codegen/age/testdata/:

  multi_label_pair.gql             & = 2   offenders 2
  multi_label_with_collateral.gql  & = 1   offenders 1
  corpus_schema.gql                & = 0   offenders 0
  shared_label_schema.gql          & = 0   offenders 0

The convention is exhaustive TODAY, so the glob selects exactly the two the
literal slice named: this changes which fixtures are swept by nothing at all.
What it changes is that the next one sweeps itself.

An earlier probe of mine returned empty for two of these files, which is equally
consistent with "no multi-label types" and "the probe cannot read this file".
The counting form above carries its own positive control — the lines and
NODE TYPE columns were non-zero for every row — so & = 0 is a measurement
rather than a silence.

MUTATION BATTERY (5 rows)

Each row declared with its expected victim AND diffstat BEFORE running, run
separately, compiler-screened with `go test -c -o /dev/null` (not `go build`,
which is blind to _test.go). The guard was COMMITTED FIRST so the per-row
`git checkout --` could not delete it; the restore was verified with
`sha256sum -c` over all six files after every row.

  N1  errors.go:155 len(refused) -> 1          1+/1-        KILLED
  N2  delete `if queries == 1 { ... }`         0+/3-        KILLED
  N3  git mv multi_label_pair.gql
        -> pair_multi_label.gql                rename       KILLED
  N4  N3 + Skip on the convention test         rename +1    SURVIVED (declared)
  N5  git mv shared_label_schema.gql
        -> multi_label_shared.gql              rename       KILLED

Three rows are worth reading past the verdict column.

N1's SPLIT is the point. A mutant failing BOTH fixtures would be killed by an
assertion merely requiring a non-empty message. multi_label_pair (2 offenders)
FAILs and multi_label_with_collateral (1) PASSes, because the mutant happens to
be correct for the one-offender schema. The assertion is discriminating on the
count itself.

N3 exposed the defect by what it did NOT do. The convention test killed it, but
the SWEEPS THEMSELVES PASSED with one fixture instead of two — precisely the
failure this bead is about, reproduced.

N4 is the declared-SURVIVED negative control. With the convention test skipped,
the renamed fixture drops out of the sweep and the WHOLE PACKAGE IS GREEN. That
is the measurement of the defect rather than an argument about it.

GATES AND BASE DRIFT

just gates 14/14 locally. CI on the merged head: 7 pass, 2 skipping (live-smoke-age
and nightly-alert, both expected), exit 0.

Rebased TWICE while open, and each time re-ran rather than trusting CLEAN:
  - onto 8b0b23cd (#2433, internal/query only)
  - onto 82784a6a (#2434), which touches internal/codegen/temporal.go — a
    different package, but one that age imports, and the new checker parses
    every fixture through it. A clean rebase is evidence of nothing there.
Both re-runs of ./internal/codegen/age/... ./internal/codegen/ were green.

This PR SHIPS A READER whose domain is age/testdata/, so before merging I swept
all 3 open PRs for additions to that directory — none touches it. The sweep
printed the scanned count as its positive control, so the empty result is a
measurement and not a broken loop. Had one been adding a fixture, my new guard
would have redded master under them with no conflict ever reported.

TIDY WAS NOT VACUOUS HERE

Unlike gqlc-qo6ul and gqlc-vqx87 in the same session, gqlc-bo16 IS present in
.beads/issues.jsonl, so check-pr-closes did not take its skip path. Read from
the job log rather than the check colour:

  [check-pr-closes] gqlc-bo16 -> Closes #753 (ok)

Three independent sources agreed: the bead's external_ref (issues/753), GitHub's
own closingIssuesReferences ([753]), and CI's checker above.

DESIGN GATE

No design bead blocked this. `bd dep list gqlc-bo16` shows one edge only —
discovered-from gqlc-35yu.15, closed — and the body carries no designer's-call
prose. Merged on green gates under protocol

title: codegen/age: the corpus template is unpinned against the emission it drives
description:
The AGE corpus harness (internal/codegen/age/corpus_test.go) now proves, via a
`go test -json` pass-set comparison, that every test the corpus template
declares actually ran. That closes the 'harness green on an empty test body'
hole.

It does not close the adjacent one. Nothing requires the template to **exercise
each emitted `agtype*` helper**. A helper could gain an arm that no corpus test
reaches, and the harness would stay green — it only checks that the tests the
template declares all ran, not that the declared set covers the emission.

## Shape of the fix

The emission side is enumerable: the helpers are rendered from a known set, and
`TestEmittedHelpersAreClosedOverWhatTheyCall` (added on gqlc-35yu.11) already
walks the rendered output for `agtype*` identifiers. The missing claim is the
converse — every `agtype*` helper the emission **declares** is **called** by at
least one corpus test.

Set equality between the declared helper set and the exercised helper set, not a
count. Deriving the exercised set is the harder half: either instrument via the
coverage profile the sentinel fence already collects, or have the template's
assertions name the helper they exercise and check that naming against the
declared set.

## Acceptance

Add an `agtype*` helper arm that no corpus test reaches and watch a gate go red
naming it. Then delete it and watch green.

Suggested by the gqlc-35yu.11 round-5 implementer; filed by the coordinator.
notes:
## 2026-09-03, agent-d — PR #2548

Branch test/gqlc-5et5-age-corpus-helper-coverage, three commits
(bd42bb24, a923367d, 63e6b48b), each verified to build and pass
./internal/codegen/corpusrun/ ./internal/codegen/age/ alone from a
git archive extract. just gates: 15/15.

### The gap, restated

The harness's three censuses (corpusTests, corpusSubtests, corpusTables)
all ask what the DRIVER declares. A driver internally consistent with
itself and reaching half the emission satisfies all three, because a
helper the emission writes and the driver never calls is declared by
nobody. The added claim is the converse and is taken from the RUN:
every agtype* helper the assembled module compiles must be entered,
witnessed by the child's own coverage profile.

Baseline measured in a scratch extract: 38 agtype* helpers declared,
54 functions entered. Non-degenerate.

### Acceptance battery, six rows, all AS DECLARED

C0 none                                    green
M1 emission gains agtypeNeverReached       red, names it exactly once
M2 same + census blinded                   green, silent on the name
M3 profile-to-source basename broken       red
M4 Run stops collecting, precondition live red, "no coverage profile"
M5 same, precondition removed              red, "emitted agtype* helpers"

M5 falsified my own declaration, and that is the finding worth keeping.
I declared want_red=False for it, believing NotEmpty(report.Cover) was
the detector. It is not. Removing it still reddens the census, because
a missing profile makes every helper read as unreached. The precondition
changes the REASON, not the verdict: without it a broken instrument
reports "38 emitted helpers no test enters", which blames the corpus for
a gap in the measurement of it. The code comment now says exactly that
rather than implying the line catches something.

### A defect the unit tests found

Entered and Functions shipped exercised only end-to-end by the AGE
suite, which cannot tell a census that reads the profile from one that
reads the source. Writing the malformed-profile row surfaced a crash:
a position with no '.' made strings.IndexByte answer -1 and panicked
the slice with "slice bounds out of range [:-1]", so a profile line
emitted.go:3,5.2 1 1 crashed instead of erroring. Measured red before
green in a scratch extract with lineOf reverted. Each malformed shape
now pins the message it earns rather than a bare require.Error.

### Deliberately not shipped

An unexercisedAgtypeHelpers exemption map with a staleness test. It
would have been empty by design on day one, so it was mechanism with
no occupant. If a helper ever earns a waiver, the map is three lines.
close_reason: Merged as 72977077 (PR #2548). The corpus now holds a fourth census taken from the run rather than the fixture's syntax: every agtype* helper the assembled module compiles must be entered, witnessed by the child's own coverage profile. Baseline 38 declared / 54 entered. Six-row acceptance battery all as declared; M5 falsified my own declaration and the coverage precondition is documented as a reason guard, not a detector. GH #750 closed.

title: codegen/age: the DATE encoding owes a year-range check and the collation ordering test the spike flagged
description:
The settled encoding table on gqlc-35yu.11 stores DATE as the
zero-padded ISO 'YYYY-MM-DD' string, on the argument that its lexical
order is its chronological order. The argument holds across
[0001-01-01, 9999-12-31] and nowhere else, and the claim as originally
written in internal/codegen/age/types.go carried no such bound. The doc
now states it; the check that would enforce it does not exist, because
DATE is still refused for want of a backend-invariant carrier. This
bead is the debt whoever admits the width inherits.

Two ways out of the range, both mis-sorting rather than failing:

  - Year 10000 and beyond needs a fifth digit. '10000-01-01' sorts
    under '2024-01-01' because '1' < '2', so every date past year 9999
    files at the front.
  - A proleptic year before 1 CE needs a sign. '-0500-01-01' sorts
    under every unsigned date for the same reason, and worse, the whole
    BCE era then sorts ascending where chronology wants it descending.

WHAT TO DO when DATE is admitted: range-check in the emitted encoder
and fail the value naming the property, rather than storing a string
the database will silently order wrongly. The precedent is CALENDAR
DURATION — an encoding that cannot be made faithful is a refusal, not a
best effort.

SECOND, SEPARATE DEBT ON THE SAME WIDTH, from the spike notes on
gqlc-35yu.11: agtype string comparison uses DB COLLATION, not byte
order. DATE stayed a string by owner decision, on readability in the
stored graph, with the note "if a collation is ever found where ISO
dates misorder, that reopens this - worth one explicit test". That test
does not exist either. Both are owed by the same change, so they are
one bead.
notes:
agent-h, 2026-08-23: the DATE range-check this bead files is designed into gqlc-mv3r (AGE admits DATE on a zero-padded ISO string, decode range-checked to the four-digit calendar, ADR 0033). Do not fix separately — the author executing gqlc-mv3r closes this bead citing that PR.
2026-08-29, agent-b. PR #1679 (bead gqlc-mv3r) admits DATE on AGE and discharges both halves. NOT closed yet — unmerged at the time of writing; close when #1679 lands.

FIRST HALF (range check): done as the bead prescribed. The emitted encoder range-checks to [0001-01-01, 9999-12-31] and fails the value naming the property rather than storing a string the server would misorder. Both out-of-range shapes the bead names are refused, not best-efforted.

SECOND HALF (collation): witnessed, with a stated limit. The live battery seeds seven readings including both range ends (0001-01-01 and 9999-12-31) and asserts the server's own ORDER BY answers exact chronological order, plus two range predicates. That runs against the digest-pinned apache/age image under ITS DEFAULT COLLATION ONLY — it is the one explicit test the spike notes asked for, not a sweep across collations. If someone later deploys AGE under a collation where ISO dates misorder, this row does not see it; that would be a new bead, and the row is where it would be extended.

The probes are load-bearing rather than decorative: mutating agtypeDateLayout to 02-01-2006 leaves every per-reading round trip green, because the layout serves both encode and decode, and is killed only by the ordering assertion.
close_reason:
Discharged by #1679 (gqlc-mv3r), merged 2026-08-29 17:34:29Z. Verified on origin/master as executable code, not as the doc comment that describes it.

FIRST HALF (range check): internal/codegen/age/render_models.go:689 — "if d.Year < 1 || d.Year > 9999" fails the value naming the property rather than storing a string the server would misorder, which is the CALENDAR DURATION precedent this bead asked for. The decode side range-checks too, at :530. Both out-of-range shapes the bead names are refused, not best-efforted.

SECOND HALF (collation ordering): test/data/codegen/live_test.go seeds 7 readings including BOTH range ends — dateValue{Year: 1, Month: 1, Day: 1} at L1398 and dateValue{Year: 9999, Month: 12, Day: 31} at L1404 — and asserts the server's own ORDER BY at L1478. temporalReadingsInDateOrder = {4, 2, 6, 7, 1, 3, 5} opens on the year-1 reading and closes on the year-9999 one, so both ends are load-bearing IN THE ASSERTION and not merely present in the fixture.

STATED LIMIT: that runs against the digest-pinned apache/age image under its DEFAULT COLLATION ONLY. It is the one explicit test the spike notes asked for, not a sweep across collations. If AGE is ever deployed under a collation where ISO dates misorder, this row does not see it — that would be a new bead, and L1478 is where it would be extended.

The probe is load-bearing rather than decorative: mutating agtypeDateLayout to 02-01-2006 leaves every per-reading round trip green, because the layout serves both encode and decode, and it is killed ONLY by the ordering assertion.

GH mirror #738 closed by hand with the same evidence (issue comment 5463984364). Necessary because #1679's body carries "Closes #1447", its own mirror, and a child PR does not close a sibling's issue.

title: bd-gh-sync: six diagnostic lines are untested, and the gh stub cannot fail at all
description:
Adversarial review of `gqlc-w4q9` applied 34 mutations to `.githooks/bd-gh-sync`
and killed 28. All six survivors are in diagnostic-refinement code: each one is
deletable, or invertible, with no assertion going red. None changes a verdict
line's pass/fail or the exit status — they change only the wording of a detail
line — which is why this was returned non-blocking.

The sites:

- `:661` — `[ -n "$_blind" ] && [ "$_post_rc" -ne 0 ] && _blind="'bd list' exited …"`.
  The **pull** side has the equivalent line *and* an assertion for it ("the
  blind notice names the exit status it saw"). Push has the line and no
  assertion.
- `:662` — the `_gh_rc` twin, and **the worst of the six**: `_gh_rc != 0` is not
  exercised at all, because the test harness's `gh` stub always exits 0. The
  reviewer proved the path correct by hand with a throwaway fixture (exits 1,
  prints `'gh issue list' exited 4`, verdict last), but **the suite cannot see
  it**. A stub that can only succeed cannot test a failure path.
- `:486-488` — the `_list_rc` diagnostic on push. New on the `gqlc-w4q9` branch,
  untested.
- `:628` — `bid = one_line(b.get("id") or "")` in the close comment. New,
  untested.
- `:399` — pull's `*) _blind="the check itself did not run"`. Pre-existing on
  master, untested there too.
- `:625-627` — the `close_reason` first-line extraction and 300-char clamp.
  Pre-existing on master.

## Why this is worth closing

These lines exist to tell a human *why* a run went blind. A blind run that
reports the wrong reason is worse than one that reports none, because it sends
the reader to the wrong place. And the `_gh_rc` case is not merely untested —
it is untestable with the current stub, which is a gap in the harness rather
than in the script.

## Fix

Teach the `gh` and `bd` stubs to fail on demand — an env var naming the exit
status is enough — then assert each diagnostic names the status it saw. The
pull side's existing assertion is the model to copy.

## Acceptance

Each of the six lines must be individually deletable-with-a-red-test. Verify
each currently survives deletion first, so the new assertions are known to be
watching something.

Found during the adversarial review of `gqlc-w4q9`, returned non-blocking.
close_reason: Merged in PR #778 (77a8cc12)

title: codegen/neo4j: driverSliceCarriers' []byte arm is unreached by the corpus it sweeps
description:
`driverSliceCarriers` contains a `"[]byte"` entry. No golden in the committed
corpus contains a `[]byte` assertion — an independent AST sweep of every neo4j
golden yields `[]any`×37, `bool`×4, `dbtype.Date`×2, `dbtype.Relationship`×13,
`float64`×6, `int64`×17, `string`×17, `time.Time`×5, and nothing else.

So the census's `[]byte` arm is dead over the corpus it sweeps. `[]byte` is
exercised at runtime by `internal/codegen/neo4j/corpus_test.go` (`Listy.Blobs`),
which is real coverage of the *decode path* — but it is not coverage of the
*census arm*, and those are different claims. The arm could be deleted, or
mistyped, and no test would notice.

`[]byte` is a genuine member of the driver's `PropertyValue` set
(`neo4j-go-driver/v5@v5.28.4/neo4j/graph.go:25-38`), so the entry is correct.
The gap is that its correctness is unwitnessed.

## Fix

Add a golden fixture whose entity carries a `BYTES`-width property, so the
census's `[]byte` arm is reached by the corpus it sweeps.

## Acceptance

With the fixture in place, deleting `"[]byte"` from `driverSliceCarriers` must
redden the census, naming the fixture. Verify it does **not** redden today
first, so the test is known to be watching something.

Found during the adversarial review of `gqlc-35yu.13`, returned non-blocking.
close_reason: Merged: PR #752 (3kds/6rh3/vcvh) and PR #754 (.15).

title: codegen/neo4j: the driver-carrier census's scalar axis cannot go empty, so it guards nothing
description:
`gqlc-35yu.13` gave the neo4j driver-carrier census two axes so that "one going
empty behind the other fails rather than hiding". That claim holds in one
direction only.

The **slice** axis does the anti-vacuity work: deleting every list-bearing
golden drives its count to zero and the sweep goes red naming the vacuity. This
was verified by mutation.

The **scalar** axis cannot do the same job. Its `NotZero` counts every non-slice
assertion in every neo4j golden — 64 of them at the time of writing, including
`v.(string)` from nullable scalars that have nothing to do with the carrier rule.
Removing every list fixture leaves it comfortably non-zero. There is no plausible
corpus edit that empties it, so it can never fire, and it contributes no
evidence to the claim it is written to support.

This is the same shape the epic keeps closing: a count that is satisfiable by
the wrong population. `NotZero` was already the wrong assertion in
`TestStageSpecsReadAsHistory`, where it stood in for "twelve".

## Fix

Either give the scalar axis a population it actually gates — the assertions that
ride the carrier rule, not every scalar assertion in the tree — or state
plainly in the test that only the slice axis carries the anti-vacuity claim and
drop the scalar `NotZero`, which is currently decoration.

Prefer the first. A census with one live axis and one decorative axis reads as
though it has two.

## Acceptance

Whatever population the scalar axis ends up over, there must exist a corpus edit
that empties it and reddens the axis. Demonstrate that edit. If no such edit
exists, the axis is not a guard.

Found during the adversarial review of `gqlc-35yu.13`, returned non-blocking.
close_reason: Merged: PR #752 (3kds/6rh3/vcvh) and PR #754 (.15).

title: vuln: the blind-package ratchet's own-module filter terminates instead of recursing
description:
The blind-package ratchet added by `gqlc-rohp` (`justfile:307-315`) decides
whether a package's in-package test pulls third-party code into a region
govulncheck cannot see. It tests the *direct* imports of the in-package test
against a third-party predicate, having first filtered out own-module imports.

That filter is the hole. A package whose in-package test imports **only an
own-module test-only helper**, where that helper itself imports third-party
code, is filtered out before the third-party test ever runs. The package is not
counted as blind. But govulncheck still loses the same call edges, because the
loss is caused by the `p [p.test]` path collision in
`x/vuln@v1.6.0 internal/vulncheck/packages.go:144`, not by who the direct
importer is.

So the ratchet would report a residual smaller than the real one, and — worse
than being merely wrong — it would report it in the reassuring direction.

## Not currently live

Probed at the time of filing: `comm -13` of the non-test closure against
own-module `.TestImports` is **empty**, so no package in the tree has this
shape today. The finding understates the residual only prospectively. That is
why it was returned non-blocking rather than promoted, and why it is a bead
rather than a fix in `gqlc-rohp`'s branch.

But "empty today" is exactly the state that makes it invisible when it stops
being empty — nothing announces the first package to acquire this shape.

## Fix

Make the third-party test transitive rather than direct. The own-module filter
should not be a *termination*; it should be a *recursion*. An own-module import
of an in-package test is a reason to look at that package's own imports, not a
reason to stop looking.

Take the transitive closure of the in-package test's imports through own-module
edges, then apply the third-party predicate to the frontier. `go list` already
gives both `.Imports` and `.TestImports`, so this needs no new tooling.

## Acceptance

Plant a package whose in-package test imports only an own-module helper that
itself imports a third-party module, and whose non-test closure does not reach
that module. The ratchet must name that package as blind. Under the current
predicate it does not — verify that it does not, first, so the test is known to
be watching something.

Found during the adversarial review of `gqlc-rohp` and returned as non-blocking.
Related to `gqlc-m5rc`, which is the residual this ratchet measures.
close_reason: Closed

title: codegen/age: the qualification sweep's witness table is keyed on a file only the test skeleton emits
description:
`sweptWitnesses` in `internal/codegen/age/age_test.go` is the table that keeps
the schema-qualification sweep honest: for each emitted file it names the
qualified spellings that must be present, so a sweep which silently stopped
looking at anything would be caught by the witness count going to zero.

It is keyed on three files, one of which is `q.cypher.go`. **Only the test's own
skeleton `emitReadBatch()` emits a file by that name.** The 30-plus corpus
fixtures emit their query files under their own per-source names, so none of them
is matched by a witness key.

So the witness half proves the sweep fires on a hand-built skeleton. It does not
prove the sweep fires on the corpus. The guard's comment claims more than the
guard does.

## Why this is worth fixing rather than shrugging at

The positive-count assertion still runs over the corpus, so this is not a case of
nothing being checked at all. But the count and the witness table answer
different questions. The count says "the sweep looked at something". The witness
table says "the sweep looked at the *right* thing, and here is the specific
qualified spelling it had to find". Only the second survives a refactor that
changes which region is swept — and the sweep's region is exactly what
`gqlc-du0k` moved, by cutting the embedded query text and the author's parameter
keys out of it.

That is the shape this epic keeps turning up: a check that is green because of
what it is *not* looking at. Here the blind spot is per-file rather than total,
which makes it harder to see, not less real.

## Reproduction

Emit any corpus fixture and list the file names the AGE backend produces. None of
them is `q.cypher.go`. Then confirm the consequence directly: unqualify an
`ag_catalog` spelling in the emitted query file of a corpus fixture — the witness
table has no key that would name it, so only the generic count and the bare-
spelling scan can react, not the per-file witness assertion the table exists to
provide.

## Fix

Key the witness table on something the corpus actually emits. The natural axis is
the *kind* of emitted file rather than its literal name — the statement-composer
file, the models file, the db file — since the per-source query file names vary
by fixture while their required qualified spellings do not. Deriving the key from
the emission rather than from a hand-written literal also removes the chance of
this drifting again the next time a file is renamed.

Do not solve it by adding `q.cypher.go`'s per-fixture equivalents as more literal
keys. A hand-maintained list of 30 names is the same defect with more rows, and
it goes stale the first time a fixture is added.

Found during the adversarial review of `gqlc-du0k` and returned as non-blocking:
it is a pre-existing question about the test's corpus reach, not a defect that
bead introduced. Confirmed present on `master` after `gqlc-du0k` merged.

## Acceptance

Unqualifying an `ag_catalog`-owned spelling in the query file of a **corpus**
fixture reddens the witness assertion by name — the failure message must name the
missing qualified spelling and the file, not merely report a count that moved.
And the witness keys must be derived from what the emission produces rather than
hand-written, so that adding a fixture cannot leave it unguarded.
notes:
--- agent-d, 2026-09-03 — shipped as PR #2551 ---

WHERE THE DEFECT ACTUALLY LIVED. Not where this bead says. The bead's premise
was that the literal key `q.cypher.go` missed the corpus because the corpus
names a batch's query file for its source. Half right. The sweep's FRESH
population emits with `servedQuery`, whose SourceFile is "q.cypher", so every
fresh fixture's query file is ALSO q.cypher.go and the literal key matched it
fine. The per-source names (queries.cypher.go x53, people.cypher.go,
directory.cypher.go) exist only in the GOLDEN tree — and the witness table
never ran over the golden tree at all. The unguarded population was the one
the bead did not name.

WHAT LIED TO ME. My first battery declared the literal-key revert RED and got
GREEN, twice (rows R1/R2 DISAGREES). I checked the mutation was not a silent
no-op — bytes changed, literal key present, suffix matcher gone — and only
then went looking for why. `grep -n 'SourceFile:' age_test.go` answered it in
one line. The declaration was wrong, not the code. If I had trusted the RED
declaration and "fixed" the test until it went red, I would have built a guard
against a defect that was not there.

THE FIX. sweptWitnesses keyed on a KIND (name + matches predicate +
witnesses), run over BOTH populations: the fresh per-fixture emission and the
committed golden tree regrouped into per-fixture batches. Two refusals, not
one: an unmatched KIND (a key matching nothing anywhere) and an unmatched FILE
(a file carrying an AGE identifier that matches no kind).

CORPUS SURVEY, measured over the committed goldens. 63 fixtures. db.go 63,
graph.go 63, *.cypher.go 55, models.go 63, querier.go 63, temporal.go 9. Only
witness miss: ag_catalog.cypher( absent from db.go in exactly 9 fixtures —
precisely the 9 emitting no query file, each carrying ZERO ag_catalog
occurrences. Declared as onlyWithQueries. No unkeyed file (models.go,
querier.go, temporal.go) carries ag_catalog in any fixture.

BATTERY, 9 rows, all AS DECLARED, git-archive extract with sha256 restore
tripwire, verdict + expected victim declared before each run:
  C0 none                                                  green / green
  D1 corpus query file's ag_catalog casts unqualified         red / red
  D2 D1 + per-spelling witness assertion blinded              red / red
  D3 D1 + corpus loop's own sweep blinded (witness alone)     red / red
  R1 query-file key reverted to literal q.cypher.go           red / red
  R2 R1 + golden pass removed = THE PRE-FIX STATE           green / green
  R3 R1 + unmatched-FILE refusal blinded                    green / green
  K1 graph.go key renamed to nothing, unmatched-FILE blind    red / red
  N1 both unmatched refusals + witness blinded, no defect    green / green

R2 is the reproduction: with the golden half gone, the revert is green — what
shipped before this PR. R3/K1 separate the two refusals, so neither is

D3 is the acceptance row. With assertQualified blinded so the witness table is

— fixture, file, missing spelling. Not a count that moved.

NOT DONE HERE. assertQualified fires before requireSweptWitnesses in the
corpus loop and Require aborts, so on an unqualified emission the witness
assertion is not what the reader sees first — assertQualified names it, which
it already did before this bead. That is correct ordering (the cheaper, wider

the R-rows, not the D-rows.

title: errors: AllSentinels' defensive copy is unwitnessed in codegen, cypher and queryfile
description:
Three packages export an `AllSentinels()` that hands out a defensive copy of
their canonical sentinel slice, and all three carry a doc comment asserting a
safety property no test checks:

- `internal/codegen/errors.go:204` — `slices.Clone(allSentinels)`
- `internal/query/cypher/errors.go:140` — `slices.Clone(allSentinels)`
- `internal/queryfile/errors.go:69` — `make` + `copy`

Each is documented "the slice is copy-returned so a mutation cannot leak into
the canonical set."

**Reproduction (MUT-O, run against `internal/query/cypher`).** Replace the body
with `return allSentinels` — no clone, the caller now holds the package's own
backing array — and run `go test -count=1 ./...`. The full suite stays green.
The same mutation on the other two packages behaves identically: every caller
in the tree (the conformance harness's `sentinelByName` builder, the
queryfile and codegen reachability sweeps) only ranges over the result, so
nothing in the corpus ever writes through the returned slice, and the copy is
therefore load-bearing for no live caller.

That is the whole problem. The defence exists for a *future* caller, which is a
reasonable thing to build — but the doc comment states it as a property that
holds, and nothing holds it. An untested doc comment claiming a safety property
is worse than no comment: a reader who wants to sort the result in place, or a
maintainer weighing whether the clone is worth its allocation, will trust the
sentence rather than check it, and the day someone deletes the clone as dead
weight the sentence keeps asserting a guarantee the code no longer provides.
Absent the comment, that reader would at least look.

The three are a **house pattern**, not a deviation any one package introduced,
so the fix belongs across all three at once rather than in whichever package a
reviewer happens to be reading. One shared shape of test, three packages.

Discovered by the `gqlc-rrtl` adversarial reviewer, who ruled it non-blocking
for that branch precisely because the sibling packages match: nothing was
regressed, the hole is pre-existing and uniform.

**Not in scope:** changing what `AllSentinels` returns, or whether ordering is
guaranteed. The contract stands as documented; this bead only asks that the
documented part be witnessed.

## Acceptance

For each of `internal/codegen`, `internal/query/cypher` and
`internal/queryfile`, a test exists such that mutating that package's
`AllSentinels` to return the canonical slice directly — `return allSentinels`
in codegen and cypher, `return allSentinels` in place of the `make`/`copy` in
queryfile — turns `go test -count=1 ./<pkg>/` **red**, with a failure message
that names the leak rather than merely reporting a length or ordering
mismatch.

Each mutation must be compile-valid: a mutant that fails to build proves the
code is load-bearing, not that a test is watching it.

A single shared helper exercised from three package-local tests satisfies
this; three near-identical tests also satisfy it. What does not satisfy it is
a test in only one package, since the finding is that all three share the
unwitnessed claim.
close_reason:
Fixed. PR #2486 merged; verified by content on origin/master, where all three
files exist and each carries its own package's TestAllSentinelsReturnsACopy:
internal/codegen, internal/query/cypher and internal/queryfile.

THE GAP, MEASURED AT THIS BRANCH'S BASE rather than inherited from this bead's
account: with a compile-valid leak applied to all three packages at once, and
before any test existed, go test over the WHOLE repository produced no FAIL.
Every caller only ranges over the result, so the documented copy was
load-bearing for no live caller and its removal was invisible.

THE FAMILY WAS MEASURED, NOT ASSUMED. grep over the tree finds exactly three
AllSentinels; internal/schema/gql is not among them. Three packages sharing one
unwitnessed claim needed three tests, because a battery mutating one package
would certify one guard and vouch for three. A shared helper package was
declined: it would add a package to save twelve lines, and a test must name its
own package's function to witness it at all.

BATTERY: 3 rows KILLED, each reddening only its own package's test and nothing
else in the repository, plus a declared-SURVIVED negative control. Two errors of
mine are recorded in the PR body rather than tidied away.

First, THIS BEAD'S OWN STATED MUTATION DOES NOT COMPILE. `return allSentinels`
orphans the `slices` import in codegen and cypher, so go build failed and ten
packages reported [build failed] -- a fake RED that would have scored two of
three rows on the compiler's verdict rather than the suite's. Re-derived as
`_ = slices.Clone(allSentinels); return allSentinels`, which keeps the import
referenced and still leaks the slice.

Second, I THEN WALKED INTO THAT SAME TRAP while building the control against it:
append([]error(nil), allSentinels...) also removes the only slices user. That row
is discarded rather than reinterpreted, and re-derived as a control that binds
the same Clone call to a name first.

The battery was also run TWICE. gates reported errorlint findings on the
assertion's ==, so the guard changed to compare messages, and a battery
certifies only the bytes it ran against. errors.Is was declined as the remedy
because it asks whether one error wraps another and the question here is whether
the slot still holds the same value; that reasoning is in the test's doc comment
so a future reader does not "fix" it back.

title: resolver: valid/ fixtures mean 'valid at R3', and nothing in the harness says so
description:
`test/data/resolver/valid/` means "valid **at R3**", not "valid". Nothing in the
harness says so, and nothing stops a fixture in that directory from encoding a
query the codegen stage refuses one stage later.

So the directory name asserts something stronger than the tests behind it check.
A reader adding a fixture there reasonably believes they are declaring the query
well-formed end to end; they are declaring only that the resolver accepts it.

## Why it matters rather than being a naming quibble

The two stages disagree in both directions and the disagreement is invisible:

- A `valid/` fixture that codegen refuses is not a test failure anywhere. It sits
  in the corpus asserting a claim no test makes.
- Worse for coverage: a reviewer reasoning about what the corpus proves will
  count `valid/` fixtures as end-to-end evidence. They are not. This is the same
  shape as the defect class this epic keeps turning up — a check that reads as
  stronger than it is, so the gap is invisible from the green build.

Found while implementing the `gqlc-nkjt` / `gqlc-ejn0` / `gqlc-9lew` /
`gqlc-ipdx` bundle, where several new fixtures had to be reasoned about
stage-by-stage precisely because the directory name does not carry the stage.
Deliberately left alone there — out of scope for those beads. Confirmed present.

## Fix

Two shapes are plausible and the bead should pick one rather than doing both:

1. **Say it.** Rename or document the directory so the stage is in the name or in
   a `README` the harness points at, and state which stage each `valid/` subtree
   is valid at. Cheapest, and honest.
2. **Check it.** Run every resolver `valid/` fixture through codegen and require
   either that it succeeds, or that it carries an explicit marker recording that
   codegen refuses it and why. That converts an unstated assumption into an
   assertion, and the marker file becomes the place the stage disagreement is
   written down.

Option 2 is the stronger answer if it is tractable — it turns the directory name
into something enforced rather than something believed. If it is not tractable
(for instance because codegen needs a target backend the resolver corpus does not
name), say so explicitly in the fix so the next reader does not re-derive the
question.

Do not do a third thing: do not silently delete or relocate fixtures that codegen
refuses. Some of them exist to pin resolver behaviour on shapes codegen will
never see, and that is legitimate.

## Acceptance

Either (a) every `valid/` fixture is run through codegen and a fixture that
codegen refuses without a recorded marker reddens a test — verified by adding
such a fixture and watching it go red; or (b) the corpus carries prose stating
which stage `valid/` is valid at and why the stronger check was not taken, and a
test or lint pins that prose to the directory it describes so it cannot silently
drift away from the fixtures.
notes:
== agent-d, 2026-09-03: shipped option (b). PR #2536.

WHY NOT OPTION 2 (the per-fixture codegen gate the bead favoured "if tractable").
Measured against both shipped backends before choosing:

  fixtures under valid/                       196
    behind a codegen-INADMISSIBLE schema      158
    behind an admissible schema                38
      generate clean                           26
      refused at query level                   12
  schemas under valid/schemas/                 20
    codegen-admissible                          8
    codegen-inadmissible                       12
    backends disagreeing on any                 0

Admissibility probed with an EMPTY query batch, so no query can be blamed for
the verdict; the 8 admitted schemas prove the empty batch is not itself refused.

Not tractable as imagined: 158 of the 196 markers would record, once per
fixture, one fact about that fixture's SCHEMA. That restates a single refusal
158 times, in the place a reader goes looking for a fact about the QUERY. A
per-fixture file is the wrong shape for a per-schema disagreement.

The refusal is ONE sentinel reached two ways: a node type with a multi-label
set (Employee&Person), and an edge label shared across endpoint pairs, both
need an explicit Name before codegen can derive a Go identifier. Those shapes
are a large part of what the resolver corpus exists to exercise (plural
endpoints, narrowing, orientation ambiguity), so this is not a defect to
repair. No fixture was deleted or relocated (the bead's "do not do a third
thing").

WHAT SHIPPED. test/data/resolver/valid/README.md states the stage and carries
the partition in two HTML-comment-delimited lists.
TestResolverValidCorpusStageBoundary (internal/codegen/conformance) reads them,
admits every schema through both backends, and reddens NAMING the offender on
four events: a schema changed sides, a schema is declared in neither block, a
name is listed but absent from disk, the two backends disagree.

DISCLOSED BOUND, and the README says it too: the query-level half is NOT
pinned. Which fixtures behind an admissible schema codegen accepts moves
whenever codegen grows a construct, and pinning it would redden this corpus for
changes that are not about it. The 26/12 split above is therefore a measurement
in this record, not a guarded invariant. Nothing holds it true.

MUTATION BATTERY. git archive extract, restore by cp from a pristine copy with
a sha256 tripwire, -run anchored, expected victim declared per row.
  C0 control                                        PASS
  M1 move social.gql between blocks                 KILLED, named it and the direction
  M2 list a schema not on disk                      KILLED, zz_ghost_schema.gql
  M3 drop certificate.gql from its block            KILLED, certificate.gql
  M4 delete a whole marker block                    KILLED, "has no codegen-inadmissible block"
  M5 empty a marker block                           KILLED, "block is empty"
  M6 force a backend split                          KILLED, named all 12
  M7 remove social_r3_unionnn.gql from both blocks  KILLED, named it
  C4 restored                                       PASS
Blinding rows over the WHOLE package, each with its triggering condition
present: B1 (M1's condition, "moved" arm blinded) and B2 (M7's condition,
"undeclared" arm blinded) both GREEN. So each arm is the sole reporter of what
it claims.

TWO THINGS THE PROCESS CAUGHT, both in my own work:

1. just vuln reddened: I wrote the test as "package conformance" while every
   sibling file is "package conformance_test". An in-package test importing
   testify takes the WHOLE package out of govulncheck's call graph, so a
   vulnerability called through that import reports nothing and just vuln
   exits 0. It needs no unexported state; moved to the external package.

2. The first draft compared declared vs measured with require.Equal. M1 was
   KILLED — but the message printed both lists whole and named no schema,
   while the README claimed the test names the schema that moved. The arm was
   right and its report was not. Second commit (9c838b09) replaces it with a
   per-schema comparison. This is the same idiom I criticised in the sibling
   totality checks one bead ago (gqlc-jjcu) and then reproduced by hand.

APPARATUS FAULT worth knowing: the first battery run piped go test through
bare grep, which is a shell function here that dies under set -u. All six rows
printed an identical "ZSH_VERSION: unbound variable" and no verdict. The
uniformity was the tell. command grep fixed it.
close_reason: Shipped option (b) in PR #2536 (squash 937a56cc): test/data/resolver/valid/README.md states that the directory means valid at R3 only, and TestResolverValidCorpusStageBoundary pins its declared admissible/inadmissible partition against both backends, naming any schema that changes sides, is declared in neither block, is listed but absent from disk, or on which the backends disagree. Option 2 (a per-fixture codegen gate) was measured and declined: 158 of 196 fixtures sit behind a codegen-inadmissible schema, so those markers would restate one schema fact 158 times where a reader looks for a query fact. No fixture was deleted or relocated. The query-level half is deliberately unpinned and both the README and the bead notes say so. Eight mutation rows KILLED with the victim named per row, plus two blinding rows green over the whole package. GH #719 closed.

title: resolver: ErrUnionColumnMismatch names neither arm nor what it projected
description:
`ErrUnionColumnMismatch` fires when the two arms of a Cypher `UNION` project
columns that do not agree. Its message prints `edge` for **both** branches, so
the author is told the arms mismatch without being told which side is which, or
what either side actually projected.

Found by the `gqlc-35yu.14` implementer while probing whether `UNION ALL` could
reach a multi-candidate edge column on AGE (it cannot — the arms are refused
before a union is formed, which is what made the message visible).

Fix: name each arm and what it projected, in the order the author wrote them.
The refusal is already correct; only the diagnostic is uninformative.

Acceptance: a mismatched `UNION` refuses with a message that distinguishes the
two arms, and an invalid-corpus fixture holds it.
close_reason: Landed in PR #728

title: codegen/age: the schema-qualification guard substring-matches, so a user parameter named $agtypeArgs fails it
description:
`TestEveryAgeIdentifierIsSchemaQualified` scans emitted output for `agtype`
without a word boundary, so it matches inside longer tokens — including tokens
that came from the **user's own query text**, which the emitter copies verbatim
per ADR 0005.

Reproduced by naming a query parameter `$agtypeArgs`:

    "agtype" at offset 14760 is not schema-qualified

The offset lands in the embedded query string, not in generated code. So the
guard fails on input it has no business judging, and an author's parameter name
can make a green build red.

Found on the `gqlc-lhs3`/`gqlc-ni66` branch and left alone there because
`age_test.go` was being rewritten concurrently by `gqlc-gjqo`. That rewrite has
since landed, so this is now safe to take.

The guard itself is worth keeping — AGE requires `ag_catalog.agtype` rather than
bare `agtype`, and an unqualified spelling is a real defect. It just needs to
scan generated identifiers rather than raw bytes: match on a word boundary at
minimum, and preferably exclude the embedded query-text literal from the scan
region entirely, since nothing in it is the generator's to qualify.

Acceptance: a query parameter named `$agtypeArgs` generates cleanly, and a
genuinely unqualified `agtype` in emitted code still fails the guard.
close_reason: Closed

title: codegen: a multi-parameter query using $_ emits Go that does not parse
description:
A multi-parameter query using `$_` or `$__` emits Go that does not parse:

    format failure: queries.cypher.go: 25:50: expected selector or type assertion, found ','

on all three backends. Cause: `paramFieldName("_")` returns the empty string, so
the generated `*Params` struct gets a field with no name and the bind expression
comes out as `arg.,`.

Found by the `gqlc-lhs3`/`gqlc-ni66` implementer while sweeping parameter names
for the capture class. **Deliberately left out of that branch**: the defect is in
field-name derivation, not in scope capture, and it fails loudly at generate time
rather than at exit 0. The single-parameter `$_` case *is* closed there and
covered, because the single-parameter form no longer derives a Go identifier from
the parameter name at all.

Fix: `paramFieldName` must either produce a usable identifier for every parameter
name the parser admits, or refuse the query by name. Refusing is probably right —
`$_` has no natural Go field spelling and silently renaming it would surprise the
author — but either is defensible as long as the outcome is a diagnostic rather
than unparseable output.

Acceptance: a two-parameter query using `$_` either generates Go that compiles or
is refused with a message naming the parameter, and a fixture holds whichever was
chosen.
close_reason: Closed by PR #1329. Phase B of codegen.Prepare now refuses a parameter whose section 4.2 mangle produces no Go field name, when the query binds two or more parameters, with ErrOutOfC6Scope naming the query, the parameter position and the parameter itself. The refusal is arity-conditional on purpose: the zero- and one-parameter emission forms take a bare typed argument and derive no identifier, so a lone dollar-underscore is still admitted and still emits. ErrOutOfC6Scope rather than a permanent sentinel because a later stage that spells Params fields positionally would admit the construct. Fixture test/data/codegen/invalid/out_of_c6_scope_blank_parameter was seen red before the fix on all three targets, failing with the old behaviour, a nameless struct field reaching gofmt. TestBlankParameterReachesOnlyTheSingleParameterForm in internal/codegen/conformance now asserts the sentinel and that the message names the parameter, instead of the bare fact of an error, and its comment records the fix rather than the pin. This was found, not looked for: the new section four fence from gqlc-4r01 reported ErrFormatFailure executed by one corpus binary on its first run, falsifying a taxonomy row that had claimed unreachability for as long as it existed. Fixing the construct was preferred to promoting ErrFormatFailure into allSentinels, which would have blessed a gofmt parser message as a user-facing diagnostic.

title: resolver: R3 §4.6 does not name the mixed-symmetry shape, where the arrow narrows without disagreeing
description:
R3 §4.6 classifies each candidate of an undirected edge binding as reading
both ways (skipped) or one way (a witness). `gqlc-kph4` fixtured the two pure
shapes: every candidate symmetric (accept, arrow inert) and asymmetric
candidates that disagree (refuse, arrow is the remedy).

The **mixed** shape is unnamed: one candidate reads both ways, one reads a
single way, and no two candidates *disagree*. Demonstrated by the kph4 round-3
reviewer with a self-edge plus a rev-only candidate, and generalised without
the self-edge (`L&M&X -> L&M&Y` reading both ways, plus `M -> L&M&X` rev-only).

Accepting is correct — refusing would demand an arrow to resolve a
disagreement that does not exist. But the arrow is **not** inert here: the
undirected form closes to a 2-key edge union where the directed form closes to
1. So the author's choice of marker silently changes the result type, which is
the property §4.6's two named shapes each avoid in their own way.

Consequences are backstopped rather than silent: a whole-entity `RETURN r`
refuses with `ErrUnrepresentableEdgeUnion`, and a property projection emits the
honestly intersected type. So this is a spec-completeness and coverage gap, not
a live defect.

Adjacent to `gqlc-9lew`.

Fix: name the mixed shape in §4.6 with its own row (what is skipped, what
survives, why acceptance is right), and add a corpus fixture on each side of
the marker so the 2-key/1-key difference is pinned rather than incidental.

Acceptance: §4.6 names three shapes rather than two, and a valid-corpus fixture
pair holds the undirected 2-key union and its directed 1-key twin.
close_reason: Landed in PR #728

title: resolver: orientation-ambiguity refusal names an empty edge on an anonymous binding
description:
The orientation-ambiguity refusal names the edge binding, so on an anonymous
edge it names the empty string:

    MATCH (a:Employee)-[:REVIEWED]-(b:Person)
    -> edge "" matches Employee&Person-[REVIEWED]->Person left-to-right and ...

Found by the `gqlc-kph4` round-3 reviewer while probing shapes the implementer
had not built. Pre-existing — `f1fd981` used the same `edge %q, v` — and
unfixtured, so no golden pins the degenerate spelling.

The message is otherwise good: both witnesses are formatted, and the prescribed
remedy (add the arrow) is still actionable. The defect is purely that `edge ""`
reads as a bug in gqlc rather than as a description of the author's pattern.

Fix: when the binding name is empty, describe the edge by its position in the
pattern rather than by a quoted empty name — e.g. `the edge between a and b`,
or the type where one is written. Add an invalid-corpus fixture with an
anonymous edge so the spelling is pinned; there is currently none.

Acceptance: an anonymous undirected edge with disagreeing orientation refuses
with a message that names something the author wrote, and a corpus fixture
holds that message byte-for-byte.
close_reason: Landed in PR #728

title: [bug] bd-gh-sync: a newline in a bead id splits the plan record, bypassing the id gate
description:
`.githooks/bd-gh-sync`'s pull path refuses bead ids that would re-parse — quotes,
spaces, leading dashes — and the in-code rationale says so: *"Taking it whole
lets the gate below see it and refuse it."*

That is true for a space. It is **false for a newline**, because the plan file the
gate reads is line-delimited: an `ALLOW <id>` record carrying an embedded newline
splits into two records *before* `sed 's/^ALLOW //'` runs, so the charset gate
never sees the corruption at all.

The consequence is not a crash — it is the script silently contradicting itself
inside a single run. Demonstrated by the round-4 reviewer with two beads,
`b-held` (`in_progress`, must be held out of the pull) and `b-held\ntrash`
(eligible):

    bd-gh-sync: holding b-held (GH #1) out of the pull — status-in_progress-unrepresentable-on-gh
    bd github sync --pull-only --prefer-github --issues b-held
    bd-gh-sync: pulled 1 bead(s), held 1, left 0 unmirrored GH issue(s) alone.

It announces the hold, then pulls the held bead, then reports success. The
postcondition is blinded too: `b-held` lands in `allow.txt`, so the moved-bead
check skips it.

**Reachability is nil today.** All 270 live ids match `[A-Za-z0-9._-]+`, and ids
are machine-minted by `bd`. This is the same corruption-only threat model the
pull-hardening already chose to defend, so it is an *incomplete* fix rather than
a regression — the base was strictly worse, refusing nothing.

Not folded into `gqlc-63y` because that branch was already on its fourth review
round and the finding is non-blocking with nil reachability. Filed so the stated
invariant becomes literally true rather than true-for-most-inputs.

Fix: about two lines in the selection Python — emit a corrupt id as a
non-`ALLOW` record rather than letting it split the line, so the existing charset
gate sees and refuses it by name like every other hostile shape.

Acceptance: a bead id containing an embedded newline is refused by name, and no
`--issues` batch is issued that names a bead the same run declared held.
close_reason: Landed in PR #733

title: vuln: the scanned-module list is hardcoded in two places, so a third module is silently unscanned
description:
The set of Go modules to scan is written out literally in two places:
`.github/workflows/vuln.yml`'s change detection paths, and the `vuln` recipe in
the `justfile`. Both name `test/data/codegen` by hand.

A third module added later is therefore both unwatched (the workflow will not
trigger on its dependency changes) and unscanned (the recipe will not visit it)
— silently, with no diagnostic and no failing gate.

That is the same defect class `gqlc-rohp` exists to fix: a required security
gate that is green because it is looking at nothing. rohp closed the instance;
this closes the mechanism that produced it.

Confirmed by the adversarial reviewer at `0475cdb`: the repo currently has
exactly two `go.mod` files and exactly one build tag (`codegen_live`, 4 files),
so there is **no third blind spot today**. This is prophylactic, which is why it
was ruled out of scope for rohp rather than folded in.

Fix: derive the module list rather than declaring it — discover `go.mod` files
under the tree and iterate, in both the recipe and the workflow's path filter.
If the workflow's path filter cannot be made dynamic, then at minimum add a
check that fails when the discovered module set differs from the declared one,
so adding a module forces the lists to be updated rather than silently
bypassing them.

Acceptance: add a third throwaway module with a known-vulnerable dependency and
confirm `just vuln` reports it without anyone editing a path list.
notes: Second fail-open axis, from the gqlc-rohp round-3 review: vuln.yml runs the scan only when a go.mod/go.sum changes, so a PR that newly *imports* an already-required module skips the scan entirely. Sharper than it sounds — the nested module currently carries GO-2026-5841 (klauspost/compress) in exactly that 'required but not imported' state, so the very next import of it lands unscanned. Same class as the hardcoded module list this bead already tracks: the trigger, like the list, is a proxy for the real condition rather than the condition itself.
close_reason: Closed

title: bd-gh-sync: an empty bead description is an unconditional ALLOW, and nothing pins it
description:
`.githooks/bd-gh-sync` decides pull eligibility with a prefix test: GitHub's
body must start with the bead description. When the bead description is the
empty string, `"".startswith("")` — and indeed `anything.startswith("")` — is
universally true, so the bead is unconditionally ALLOWed and GitHub's body is
pulled over it whatever it contains.

Found in the round-3 adversarial review of `fix/bd-gh-sync-state-fidelity` at
`d25d947`.

Ruled out of scope for that branch for a specific reason worth preserving: the
behaviour is **identical under the old subset rule**, so it is not a regression
that branch introduced. It is the degenerate endpoint of a bd-side deletion —
if a description has been emptied on the bd side, there is nothing to protect,
and pulling GitHub's version is arguably the right answer.

What makes it worth a bead is not the behaviour but the absence of a pin. The
sibling case (trailing-block deletion, [[gqlc-6mx3]]) IS covered by a fixture;
this one is not. So nobody would notice if a future change made the empty-desc
path do something else, and this script has now failed review three times for
exactly the reason that its fixture set could not express the input in
question.

Minimum work: add a test asserting the current behaviour, so the decision
becomes deliberate rather than incidental. Then decide separately whether
unconditional ALLOW on an empty description is actually what we want, or
whether an empty description should HOLD on the grounds that it is more likely
to be an accident than an intent.
close_reason: stale: bd-gh-sync fixture suite deleted in PR 1595 (herdr trim).

title: bd-gh-sync: the moved-bead list truncates by id sort, so the interesting id can be the one dropped
description:
`.githooks/bd-gh-sync:267-268` truncates the moved-bead list with `head -n 3`
over an **id-sorted** list, appending `+N more`.

Found in the round-3 adversarial review of `fix/bd-gh-sync-state-fidelity` at
`d25d947`. The reviewer constructed a run with 5 moved beads where the
interesting one sorts last, and got `(m-a, m-b, m-c, +2 more)` — the id of the
bead that actually mattered appears only in output lines that `tail -1`
discards.

Ruled non-blocking and out of scope for that branch because the **count**
survives into the last line, and the count is the actionable trigger: an
operator who sees `+2 more` knows to go look. Nothing is silently lost, only
inconveniently placed.

Worth doing anyway because the ordering is arbitrary — id sort has no relation
to interestingness. Options: sort by recency of change, or drop the truncation
entirely (a moved-bead list is already an exceptional event, so its length is
naturally bounded), or keep the truncation but make the omitted ids reachable
without re-running.

Related: [[bd-gh-sync-tail-1-contract]] — several findings on this script share
the same underlying constraint, that the session-start consumer reads only
`tail -1`, so anything actionable has to be on the last line.

title: bd-gh-sync: no circuit breaker on the ALLOW count
description:
Nothing caps how many beads a single run can hand to --prefer-github. The 129-vs-4 near-miss was caught by eye, not by the script. The ALLOW count does surface in the summary line, but that line prints on total failure too (the fail-open-in-reporting finding, promoted to blocking on gqlc-63y).

Once the eligibility rule narrows to append-only (gqlc-63y), the blast radius drops sharply, which is why this is P3 rather than a blocker there.

PROVENANCE: non-blocking finding 6 in the bd-gh-sync adversarial review (2026-08-01).

FIX: refuse and report when ALLOW exceeds a threshold (or a fraction of the mirrored corpus) rather than proceeding.

title: resolver: two distinct swapped pairs in one candidate set are fixture-uncovered
description:
A candidate set can contain TWO distinct swapped pairs, reachable via a 2x2 endpoint cross-product with all four EdgeKeys declared. The orientation-ambiguity refusal resolves first-in-candidate-order, and that order is deterministic (satisfyingNodeTypes sorts at internal/resolver/resolve.go:1391), so the behaviour is well-defined — but no fixture covers it, so the determinism is unasserted.

PROVENANCE: raised as a non-blocking finding in the gqlc-kph4 adversarial review (2026-08-01). I ruled it out of scope there: kph4 already carries three blockers plus three promoted findings, and this one asserts a property that holds today rather than fixing a defect.

FIX: add an invalid fixture with four declared EdgeKeys over a 2x2 endpoint cross-product; assert the refusal message names a stable pair.
