title: schema/gql: labelSets' defensive clone is unpinned — dropping it aliases the caller's label slice and the suite stays green
description:
`labelSets` (internal/schema/gql/resolve.go:140-150) builds a declaration's complete
label set by appending the implied labels to the key ones:

    return keyKey, append(slices.Clone(key), implied...).Key(), true

Dropping the clone — `append(key, implied...)` — leaves the entire suite green:

    go build ./...            ok
    go test ./internal/...    ok

That is an unpinned aliasing guard, not an unnecessary one. `append` on a slice with
spare capacity writes into the caller's backing array, so without the clone
labelSets would scribble the implied labels over whatever follows the key labels in
the caller's storage. The caller is resolve()'s node and edge loops, and the slice
is the rawNode/rawEdge's keyLabels — live data that is read again later in the same
pass (resolve.go:57 nodeKeyLabels, :113 edgeKeyLabels).

WHY IT CANNOT BITE TODAY, AND WHY THAT IS NOT REASSURING. Every LabelSet that
reaches labelSets is produced by labelSet() at nodetype.go:36-53, which returns
either `graph.LabelSet{name.GetText()}` (len == cap == 1) or
`make(graph.LabelSet, len(names))` (len == cap). With no spare capacity, append
always reallocates and the clone is redundant. So the clone's correctness depends
on a capacity invariant that

  - is established in a different file from the code that relies on it,
  - is stated nowhere, in a comment or a test, and
  - would be silently undone by any future collector that accumulates labels with
    append rather than sizing a make() up front — which is the obvious way to write
    one, and is how impliedLabels is already threaded through rawNode/rawEdge.

FOUND BY the 29-case mutation sweep of resolve.go (2026-07-28). The file is
otherwise in good shape: 26 of 29 mutations were caught outright, including every
sentinel swap and both duplicate-type checks. This was the only survivor that
represents a real guard. The two others are provably dead writes, recorded in bd
memory and deliberately not filed:

  :61  `if n.alias != ""` gating idx.aliases[n.alias]
  :64  `if n.name != ""` gating idx.declared[n.name]

Both widen to write under the "" key, and neither map is ever read with an empty
key: the only two read sites, resolve.go:209 and :211, sit lexically inside
`if ref.alias != ""` in rawEndpoint.resolve. Equivalent mutants.

THE FIX is a unit test rather than a code change, because the code is already
correct — what is missing is the assertion that keeps it correct.
TestLabelSetsDoesNotWriteThroughItsInput hands labelSets a key slice with spare
capacity and asserts the byte beyond len is untouched. It has to assert on the
backing array rather than on the slice: appending past len leaves the caller's
slice header alone, so `key` reads as one element with or without the clone, and
only the sentinel behind it moves. Verified 1:1 — the test fails with the clone
dropped and passes with it restored, and no other test in the suite moves either
way.
close_reason: Closed

title: test(resolver): pin the group-zero contract stated by three guards in scope.go
description:
The 120-case mutation sweep of internal/resolver/scope.go found three guards
that each state the same contract — group id 0 means "not in an OPTIONAL
group", not "in the group numbered zero" — and no test anywhere pinned any of
them.

    scope.go:403  addMember's    `if v == "" || g <= 0`
    scope.go:427  demoteGroup's  `if g == 0 || demotedGroups[g]`
    scope.go:837  Export's       `if g > 0`

## Why the sweep could not tell them apart

Each survives alone, so on a first read all three look inert. They are not: the
first two mask each other exactly. addMember refuses to enter a group-0 name in
the membership table, and demoteGroup refuses to demote group 0 even if a name
got in. Drop either alone and the other still blocks the cascade. Only the
COMBINED mutation discriminates — with both dropped, a proven non-nullable
binding demotes "group 0", which sweeps up every other groupless name in the
Part.

This is the class-5 mutually-masking pair from the survivor triage, measured
rather than argued:

    SURVIVED   addMember g<=0 alone
    SURVIVED   demoteGroup g==0 alone
    CAUGHT     PAIR addMember + demoteGroup
    CAUGHT     Export g>0 alone

Export's `g > 0` is the third statement of the same contract and a chained
link: relaxed, it writes a zero id into the carry, where addMember rejects it on
arrival. It is only reachable as a defect if addMember is also relaxed, so it
needs its own direct assertion rather than a behavioural one.

## Parser reachability

cypher/listener.go:159-162 records the invariant nullable <=> optionalGroup >= 1,
and build.go:280-290 reaches the nullable constructors only when
optionalGroup > 0, so the violating shape is parser-unreachable today. The
test-only constructor query.NewNullableNodeBinding (query.go:332, no group
argument) can express it at the scope layer, which is where the three guards
live. Same posture as the shadow-cascade tests merged in #569: pin the
invariant where it is stated, and treat parser-reachability as a separate
question.

## Fixed here

internal/resolver/scope_test.go only; no production change.
TestScopeGroupZeroIsNotAnOptionalGroup drives one nullable groupless binding
and one required groupless binding through SeedLocalNullability +
DemoteNullability, asserts the nullable one is not demoted by the other's
witness, and asserts directly that neither name reaches exportedOptionalGroup.

Verified 1:1 — the pair mutation and Export's half are each caught by this test
and by nothing else.

Related: gqlc-bef item 1.
close_reason: Closed

title: resolver: scope.go sweep residue — 8 of 10 survivors triaged and closed, the last 2 blocked on gqlc-ka1's ADR
description:
The residue of the 120-case mutation sweep of internal/resolver/scope.go that gqlc-efe did not fix. Filed so the next sweep of this file does not re-derive the triage from scratch, and so the genuinely-open items are not lost among the equivalent mutants.

STATUS: eight of the ten items are now closed. The two that remain (3 and 4) are
both blocked on the same ADR — gqlc-ka1's choice between per-fixture message
assertions and split sentinels. Nothing further in this bead is actionable
without that decision.

## Argued inert — do not re-file

  :606  virtualProjection's Hops() TypeList/TypeEdge stamp. Already gqlc-2y7's dead code.
  :298  InferUnlabelled's r3EdgeAdmissible re-check. The code comment says the check already ran at BindEdge, so every edge reaching here has passed it.
  :677  refProjectionType's carried-alias `ref.Property == ""` half. The doc comment says a property lookup on a carried alias is parser-unreachable — the scope check rejects Ref{"c","p"} unless c is a binding name.
  :387  DemoteNullability's 5xg EdgeBinding arm. The comment says it outright: an edge is never bare, so the parser passes a constant false (cypher/pattern.go:314).
  :380, :406, :432  the three "is the name already in the table" present-guards. Dropping them writes false where the entry was absent, and false is also the zero value every reader gets from a missing key, so the mutants are equivalent.
  :583  materialiseReturns' empty-scopeOrder bail. Returns nil rather than an empty non-nil slice; len is 0 either way and nothing compares against nil.
  :481  the endpoint loop's `v == ""`. Unreachable: NewVarEndpoint rejects the empty variable (query.go:1158-1161), and an unnamed endpoint is an InlineEndpoint, a different sum member. Only the zero value VarEndpoint{} could carry "", and no constructor produces one. (Resolved by gqlc-dg3.)
  :759  Export's localGroup `v == ""`. A dead write: localGroup is read at :836 only for names in exportedNames, and buildScopeOrder excludes "" at :540. (Resolved by gqlc-dg3.)
  :486  DemoteNullability's `changed = true` after the node write. Provably redundant rather than untested: nothing reads nullableBinding to decide edge admissibility, so any state change that could enable a new edge also sets changed via demoteGroupsOf at :488. Equivalent mutant.
  :292, :303  InferUnlabelled's two pending gates. See item 7 below.
  :540  buildScopeOrder's `seen[v]` dedup. See item 8 below.
  :232  BindCall's slot nullable bit. Dead field, not a missing test — see item 5 below; it belongs to gqlc-2y7.
  :977-980  WitnessUse's ExprUse error propagation. Unreachable by construction — see item 10 below.

## Closed

1. ~~The group-zero triple~~ — RESOLVED by gqlc-nu2 (PR #572). The premise in the original filing was wrong: the three do not all survive together. addMember's `g <= 0` (:403) and demoteGroup's `g == 0` (:427) are a mutually-masking pair (each survives alone, the PAIR is caught), and Export's `g > 0` (:837) is a chained link, inert behind addMember's rejection of a zero id on arrival, so it needs a direct assertion. The answer to "can a binding be Nullable() with OptionalGroup() == 0" is: not from the parser (cypher/listener.go:159-162 records nullable <=> optionalGroup >= 1), but the test-only nullable constructors can express it at the scope layer, which is where the guards live.

2. ~~The anonymous-binding guards~~ — RESOLVED by gqlc-dg3 (PR #574), and one of them was a real defect. "Does anything read the "" key" has different answers per site, so they do not triage as a class. Only an EdgeBinding may be anonymous (query.go:86), so two anonymous edges in one Part both write nullableBinding[""] and the last wins — making SeedLocalNullability's :340 and addMember's :403 a load-bearing masking pair that, dropped together, reports OPTIONAL-matched bindings as non-nullable. The other two (:481, :759) moved to the inert list above. See bd memory sweep-shared-sentinel-key-collision.

5. ~~BindCall's slot nullable bit (:232)~~ — CLOSED, and the premise was wrong twice over. The filing said "no fixture yields a nullable CALL YIELD scalar"; valid/call_standalone_yield_star_string_nullable.cypher does exactly that and its golden pins `"nullable": true`. The real reason the bit is unpinned is that it is never read: hard-wiring it to false SURVIVES, and hard-wiring it to true ALSO SURVIVES. Projection nullability comes from a different lane — callProjectionType (resolve.go:719-722) reads `nullableBinding[ref.Variable]`, not `slot.nullable`. Proven by deletion rather than by grep: removing the field from callBindingSlot and its write at :232 leaves `go build ./...`, `go vet` and the full `go test ./internal/...` all green. This is dead code, not a test gap, and gqlc-2y7's 13:36 comment already owns the field family. Moved there; do not re-file here.

6. ~~CloseEdges' deferred-close error (:275-277)~~ — RESOLVED by gqlc-0ul (PR #576). Such an input does exist: an edge deferred for an unlabelled endpoint that still fails closure after inference, reached via orientation rather than labels. All six pre-existing negative fixtures spell both endpoints, so none ever defers.

7. ~~InferUnlabelled's two pending gates~~ — CLOSED as inert, measured. Widening `len(bb.Labels()) == 0` (:292) to admit every node SURVIVES, and so does dropping `len(pending) == 0` (:303) and its duplicate at resolve.go:570. The reason :292 does not matter is that inferUnlabelled filters the candidates again at resolve.go:582 (`if len(resolved) > 0`), and THAT filter is pinned — dropping it is CAUGHT by valid/carry_wins_over_unlabelled_rebind.cypher. The two empty-pending bails are pure short-circuits standing immediately ahead of `for len(pending) > 0` (resolve.go:592), which is already a no-op on an empty slice. Equivalent mutants.

8. ~~buildScopeOrder's `seen[v]` dedup (:540)~~ — CLOSED as an equivalent mutant; the premise is impossible, not merely untested. The filing asked for "a Part whose bindings name the same variable twice". No such Part can exist: cypher/pattern.go:398-425's mergeBinding keys on `part.byVar[variable]` and folds a re-reference into the existing binding record, so Part.Bindings is variable-unique by construction. Probed directly — `MATCH (a:Person), (a:Person)`, `MATCH (a:Person) MATCH (a)` and `(p)-[r:KNOWS]->(p)` each yield exactly one binding per variable. A fixture was written for this, measured as non-pinning, and deleted rather than shipped. Agrees with gqlc-2y7's independent TRIPWIRE-S result.

10. ~~WitnessUse's ExprUse error propagation (:977-980)~~ — CLOSED as a defensive tripwire, unreachable by construction. Swallowing the error SURVIVES. resolveType (resolve.go:762-810) returns a non-nil error from exactly two arms: list-of-nodes (:791) and list-of-edges (:793); every other arm returns a value or panics. So the propagation fires only if an ExprUse's EnclosingType is LIST<NODE> or LIST<EDGE> — and it cannot be, because of the thing that creates the ExprUse in the first place. An ExprUse exists only because a parameter sits inside the enclosing expression; a parameter types as TypeUnknown; and listLiteralType (cypher/typing.go:558-568) takes commonType over the elements, which collapses to TypeUnknown the moment two element types differ. So any list containing a parameter has element TypeUnknown. The only other producer of LIST<EDGE>, refType at cypher/expr.go:294, fires on a bare var-length Ref, which is a RefProjection and bypasses resolveType entirely (gqlc-2y7 §2). Probed 22 shapes — list literals, nested lists, concatenation, IN, CASE, coalesce, indexing, SET value, both node and edge — and not one produced a list-of-nodes/edges enclosing type. The two list arms ARE pinned, via the projection path, by invalid/list_of_nodes_projection.cypher and invalid/list_of_edges_projection.cypher.

## Genuinely open — both blocked on gqlc-ka1's ADR

3. PropertyUseWitness's out-of-scope arm (:929-931) is unreachable because WitnessUse gates on Contains() first (:963). Confirmed independently by the gqlc-9gz emitter audit. A guard chain of the listener.go :67 -> :92 -> :113 kind: relax the gate and the downstream arm starts mattering, with no test on it. See bd memory listener-sweep-survivors.

4. refProjectionType's out-of-scope arm (:680) — DIAGNOSED by gqlc-9gz (PR #578), still open to fix. The full ErrOutOfR0Scope audit found eighteen emitters against five fixtures, with the five mapping 1:1 onto the five proven sites. :680 is unreached because resolve.go:200 rejects path/unwind bindings first; relax :200 and :680 covers for it, raising the identical sentinel from another file. Pinning :680 on its own therefore needs either a per-fixture message assertion or a split sentinel — that is gqlc-ka1's ADR, so it was deliberately not done. The ten defensive emitters are enumerated in gqlc-9gz and should not be re-filed.

## Method note

Two of the three items closed first were mutually-masking pairs whose members each read as inert alone. The COMBINED mutation is what discriminates, and it should be run on any group of guards that state the same contract *before* concluding they are equivalent.

More generally: in six of the eight closed items the original filing's stated premise turned out to be wrong or incomplete — not the verdict, the *reason*. Item 5 was filed as "no fixture covers this" when a fixture does cover it and the field is simply unread. Item 8 asked for an input the parser cannot construct. Item 1 asserted the three guards survive together when the middle pair does not. Measure the premise, do not argue it; and when a mutation survives, find out *which* downstream site is covering for it before deciding what the survival means.

## Sentinel-coverage note (from gqlc-9gz)

Per-sentinel coverage is not per-emitter coverage. ErrOutOfR0Scope had five
fixtures and eighteen emitters, and TestSentinelReachability was green
throughout. Worse, a fixture can prove a sentinel reachable without proving
*which site* raises it: if removing the guard under test leaves the query
failing with the same sentinel from a downstream site, the mutation survives.
Write the fixture so that removing the guard makes it PASS. See bd memory
sweep-negative-fixture-must-not-name-rejected-binding.

## Two ways a survivor can be "covered for" (generalised from items 7 and 10)

Both closed-as-inert items this round were survivors whose contract was held up
somewhere else, and the two mechanisms are worth naming because they look
identical from the sweep output:

  - A LATER FILTER restates the guard. :292 admits too much, but resolve.go:582
    narrows it again before anything observes the difference. The later filter is
    the one worth pinning; the earlier one is an optimisation.
  - THE INPUT CANNOT BE BUILT. :977-980 needs an ExprUse over a list of nodes,
    and the parameter that creates the ExprUse is exactly what forces the list's
    element type to UNKNOWN. The guard is not untested, it is unreachable, and
    the proof lives in the producer (typing.go's commonType), not in the consumer.

The first deserves a test somewhere else in the chain. The second deserves a
comment in situ and nothing more.
close_reason: Closed

title: schema/gql: canonicalSpelling's comma-space collapse is dead code until gqlc-5md lands, and nothing pins it
description:
Found by a 31-case mutation sweep of internal/schema/gql/propertytype.go (24/31 caught). Both comma-collapsing lines in collapseParenthetical can be deleted with the full suite green:

    propertytype.go:289    inner = strings.ReplaceAll(inner, " ,", ",")
    propertytype.go:290    inner = strings.ReplaceAll(inner, ", ", ",")

## This is not a missing fixture

The obvious diagnosis — nothing feeds a comma-bearing spelling through — is wrong, and checking it first is what makes the rest of this bead worth writing. The suite already drives all four comma-bearing grammar arms end to end:

  - propertytype_test.go:239   FLOAT(10, 2)
  - propertytype_test.go:244   DECIMAL(10, 2)
  - propertytype_test.go:273   DECIMAL(10, 2) NOT NULL
  - corpus_area_d1_test.go:267 STRING(2, 5)
  - corpus_area_d1_test.go:291 BYTES(1, 10)

They exercise the lines and still cannot observe them.

## Why — provable for every input, not just the ones in the suite

canonicalSpelling's result is consumed at exactly two sites, both in normaliseType:

  :253   typeSpellings[full]
  :256   typeSpellings[truncateParenthetical(full)]

At :253, no key in typeSpellings contains a comma (every parenthesised row is a single-argument binary width: INT(8) ... UINT(256)). So a `full` holding a comma misses whether or not the collapse ran.

At :256, truncateParenthetical returns s[:i] for i = index of the first '('. The collapse only rewrites `inner`, which lies strictly after that first '(' — head is built from s[:open] and is untouched. So the truncated key is byte-identical either way. This holds even for nested parentheticals, where `inner` itself contains a '(': the first '(' of the result still sits at len(head).

Therefore the two lines cannot change normaliseType's output for any input at all. This is dead code, not untested code, and no end-to-end fixture can ever pin it.

## Do not delete it

The lines become load-bearing the moment a comma-bearing row exists, and gqlc-5md (length/precision/scale field on PropertyType) is precisely the bead that adds one — DECIMAL(10,2) would start hitting :253, and a DECIMAL(10, 2) spelling that had not been collapsed would miss the new row and silently fall back to bare DECIMAL. That is the failure gqlc-5md's implementer would have to debug, having never seen this note.

## Proposed fix — pin the equivalence, not the key

Assert directly on canonicalSpelling that comma spacing does not change the lookup key:

    canonicalSpelling("DECIMAL(10, 2)") == canonicalSpelling("DECIMAL(10,2)")
    canonicalSpelling("DECIMAL(10 , 2)") == canonicalSpelling("DECIMAL(10,2)")

Asserting the equivalence rather than the literal string keeps the test tolerant of a future re-spelling of the canonical form, and it stays green after gqlc-5md lands rather than going red like gqlc-h9n.21 deliberately does. Testing the unexported helper directly has precedent: typeSpellingsRowFor (propertytype_test.go:440) already calls canonicalSpelling and truncateParenthetical.

## Also

collapseParenthetical's doc comment (propertytype.go:273-276) offers `FLOAT(10, 2)` as a motivating example of two spellings sharing a lookup key. They do share one — but that shared key is not a row, so the sharing buys nothing today. The comment should say which half of its claim is currently inert, the same comments-are-claims-not-facts problem found at resolve.go:66 in gqlc-zm2.

## Sweep survivors deliberately NOT filed

The other five survivors are all provably unable to change output and want no fixture:

  :279 / :283  the unbalanced-paren early returns. The grammar's LEFT_PAREN ... RIGHT_PAREN arms are always balanced, so neither branch is reachable; the :279 mutant is additionally masked by the :283 guard.
  :292         `+ s[end+1:]`. notNull is the only grammar element that can follow ')' (GQL.g4:1755, :1761, :1832, :1846, :1889), and canonicalSpelling:269 strips it one line before the collapse runs, so the tail is always empty.
  :297         TrimRight on the truncated head. collapseParenthetical:287 already trimmed that space before truncateParenthetical ever sees the string.
  :296         i >= 0 vs i > 0. No value-type spelling begins with '('.
close_reason: Closed

title: resolver: inferUnlabelled's multi-round loop is uncovered production code
description:
TRIPWIRE-L, planted during the gqlc-oou inference sweep (2026-07-28), put a panic at the top of the SECOND iteration of inferUnlabelled's outer 'for len(pending) > 0' loop. It never fired across go test ./... . No fixture in the resolver corpus needs more than one inference round.

This is NOT a fail-open defect and NOT provably unreachable -- it is genuinely uncovered production code. The corresponding mutation ('inference stops iterating past the first round', which caps the loop at one pass) SURVIVED the sweep for exactly this reason.

WHAT A FIXTURE WOULD NEED: a binding that is ambiguous when it is first evaluated but becomes unambiguous once a LATER binding in the same round commits its type. That requires a purpose-built schema -- none of social.gql / social_r2 / social_r5 / social_r6 / social_r7 / social_edgeunion has the right shape, because in all of them each unlabelled binding either resolves on its first look or never resolves at all.

Sketch of the shape needed: two unlabelled bindings b1 and b2 joined by an edge, where b1's candidate set is narrowed only by b2's committed type, and b2 is itself only resolvable after some third labelled anchor. Ordering matters -- the fixture must present b1 BEFORE b2 in whatever order inferUnlabelled walks pending, or the multi-round path is skipped again.

Until such a schema exists, the loop's termination behaviour, the carry-wins skip on already-carried bindings, and any interaction between rounds are all unexercised. Low priority: the single-round path is well pinned (25/37 caught in that sweep), and no known query shape reaches the second round.

Filed from gqlc-oou / PR #553.
close_reason: Closed

title: resolver: two pieces of dead code in scope.go — the Has* trio has no production callers, and virtualProjection's TypeList/TypeEdge stamp is never read
description:
Fell out of the gqlc-76y mutation sweep. Both are unreachable-by-construction, so
mutation testing can never cover them and no fixture would help. They need a
delete-or-keep decision instead.

## 1. scope.HasNode / HasEdge / HasCall have zero production callers

    grep -rn "\.HasNode(\|\.HasEdge(\|\.HasCall(" internal/ --include=*.go | grep -v _test.go
    -> nothing

They are only called from scope_test.go, as assertions about scope contents. The
HasEdge assertions there are all negative (require.False), which is why deleting an
arm of HasEdge leaves the suite green.

Options: delete them and have scope_test.go read the maps directly, or keep them as
deliberate test affordances and accept that they are uncovered by construction. If
kept, a comment saying so would stop the next sweep re-flagging them.

## 2. virtualProjection's variable-length arm is inert

scope.go:603-608 stamps query.TypeList{} on a wildcard-expanded RefProjection when
the edge binding is variable-length, and query.TypeEdge{} otherwise. That stamp is
never read:

- projectionType routes query.RefProjection to refProjectionType(pp.Ref(), sch),
  discarding pp.Type(). refProjectionType re-derives varLength from
  s.edgeBindings[...].Hops() itself (scope.go:682) and builds the ResolvedList there.
- Nothing downstream of the resolver reads it either. The only readers of
  query.TypeList are internal/query/cypher/typing.go and expr.go, both in the parser,
  which runs before the resolver; and resolve.go's resolveType, which RefProjection
  never reaches.

Proven rather than argued: collapsing the branch to always stamp TypeEdge survives
the full `go test ./...` on the gqlc-76y branch, where
valid/returns_all_var_length_edge.cypher's golden pins r as a list of edges. If the
stamp were observable that golden would have moved.

Options: delete the branch and always stamp TypeEdge (or TypeUnknown, since no value
is meaningful), or keep it as documentation of intent with a comment saying the
resolved type comes from refProjectionType.

Deliberately not doing either autonomously — these are production deletions and the
code may be scaffolding for a later stage.
close_reason: Closed

comments.author: areqag
comments.text:
Extended by a 33-mutation sweep of scope.go's projection lane (buildScopeOrder, materialiseReturns, virtualProjection, projectionType, refProjectionType, ResolveProjections), run 2026-07-28 at 9e743a3. 25/33 caught, no BUILD-FAILs.

THE STAMP FINDING IS WIDER THAN THIS BEAD RECORDS. gqlc-2y7 says virtualProjection's TypeList/TypeEdge stamp is never read. The sweep confirms that and adds the third:

    virtualProjection stamps a wildcard node as unknown        SURVIVED
    virtualProjection stops distinguishing a var-length edge   SURVIVED

The first replaces query.TypeNode{} with query.TypeUnknown{} in the node arm; nothing observes it. So ALL THREE of virtualProjection's Projection type stamps are inert, not just the edge pair — projectionType routes a RefProjection to refProjectionType, which re-derives the type from the binding tables and never consults the stamp it was handed. Whatever this bead does about the edge stamps should do the same for the node one, or the asymmetry becomes the next survivor.

NO NEW FAIL-OPENS IN THE PROJECTION LANE. The other six survivors were each probed or tripwired and are not test gaps, which is worth recording so the lane is not re-swept from scratch:

- buildScopeOrder's `v == "" || seen[v]` guard -- EQUIVALENT MUTANT, and this overturned my first reading. I expected removing it to let a re-referenced name into scopeOrder twice and emit a duplicate RETURN * column. It does not: the cypher parser's mergeBinding folds a re-reference into one binding record, so seen[v] never fires for a name in the tables, and an anonymous binding (v == "") is filtered by the three lookups below it anyway. Proven with a tripwire that panics when the guard fires AND the name would have passed a lookup: never fired across the whole suite.
- materialiseReturns' empty-scopeOrder short-circuit -- tripwire never fired; returnsAll with an empty scope is unreached.
- virtualProjection's out-of-scope error -- tripwire never fired. Documented in situ as a resolver-side-bug tripwire.
- projectionType's unknown-variant default -- defensive tripwire over a closed variant set.
- refProjectionType's final ErrOutOfR0Scope return -- tripwire never fired.
- the carried-alias bypass's `ref.Property == ""` condition -- documented unreachable in situ: the parser scope check rejects Ref{"c", "p"} unless c is a binding name in scope.

Sweep artefacts: /tmp/mkproj.py, /tmp/proj_cases.json, /tmp/proj_sweep.py.

comments.author: areqag
comments.text:
Mutation-sweep evidence (from gqlc-l7v):

1. virtualProjection's TypeList stamp is now CONFIRMED unread, not
   suspected. The mutation 'a wildcard var-length edge stops projecting
   as a list' — deleting the TypeList wrapper entirely — SURVIVED the
   full suite. Nothing downstream consumes it.

2. New instance in the same family: callBindingSlot (resolve.go:104)
   declares resultType, nullable, procedure and sourceField. Only
   resultType is ever read (scope.go:612, resolve.go:724). The other
   three are write-only.

3. Third instance: buildScopeOrder's local-loop '|| seen[v]' dedup is
   unreachable. TRIPWIRE-S (panic on a duplicate name arriving in the
   local loop) never fired across the whole suite — the cypher parser
   already dedups binding records before the resolver sees them.

comments.author: areqag
comments.text:
callBindingSlot's write-only fields, now proven by deletion rather than by grep
(follow-up to the 13:36 comment's finding 2, arriving from gqlc-bef item 5).

Deleting a field together with its write at scope.go:230-235 and rebuilding is a
sharper instrument than grepping for readers, because it also catches reads
through struct literals, embedding and reflection. Measured one field at a time
and all three together:

    nullable only      UNREAD    go build ./... = 0, go vet = 0, go test ./internal/... = 0
    sourceField only   UNREAD    go build ./... = 0, go vet = 0, go test ./internal/... = 0
    procedure only     build ./... = 0, TEST BUILD FAILS
    all three          build ./... = 0, TEST BUILD FAILS

So the 13:36 claim holds, with one correction worth writing down: `procedure`
has no reader either. It appears exactly once outside the write, at
scope_test.go:140, as a field NAME in the struct literal
`map[string]callBindingSlot{"c": {procedure: "test.proc"}}` — a value the test
constructs and never reads back. That is a construction reference, not a read,
but it does mean deleting `procedure` is a two-file change while deleting
`nullable` or `sourceField` is a one-file change.

The full reader set for the struct is two sites, both on resultType:

    grep -rn "\.procedure\|\.sourceField\|\.resultType" internal/resolver/
    resolve.go:724   switch slot.resultType.(type) {
    scope.go:612     return query.NewRefProjection(query.Ref{Variable: name}, slot.resultType), nil

WHY THE nullable FIELD IS THE INTERESTING ONE. gqlc-bef filed it as a test gap —
"no fixture yields a nullable CALL YIELD scalar, so the bit could be hard-wired
false". Both halves of that were wrong. A fixture does exist
(valid/call_standalone_yield_star_string_nullable.cypher, whose golden pins
"nullable": true), and the bit survives being hard-wired in EITHER direction:

    nullable: false   SURVIVED
    nullable: true    SURVIVED

A mutation surviving in both directions is the signature of a dead write, and it
is worth treating as a distinct sweep verdict — a live field can survive being
pinned to its common value, but it cannot survive being pinned to the wrong one.
Projection nullability reaches the golden by a different lane entirely:
callProjectionType (resolve.go:719-722) reads nullableBinding[ref.Variable].

The doc comment at resolve.go:104-106 is what made this look load-bearing — it
says the slot carries "bridged Stage-6 type, nullability, and the two identity
strings codegen may consult on the query.Query side (spec §4.1)". Codegen never
sees them: exportedCallTypes is resolver-internal, and scope.go:866 says so
outright ("carry-only lanes and callTypes are NOT observable through..."). If
the delete-or-keep decision lands on keep, that comment is the thing to fix,
because it is the reason two separate sweeps have now flagged these fields.

Still not deleting anything autonomously — same posture as the rest of this bead.

title: schema/gql: nothing pins that a syntax error names the offending token
description:
listener.SyntaxError has two branches, and the interesting one is unasserted. Deleting it -- so every syntax error falls through to the bare \"syntax error at %d:%d: %s\" form and never names the offending token -- passes the whole suite.

Measured at 61a6cd1 as part of a 19-mutation sweep of listener.go; 17 were caught and this was one of the two that were not.

listener.go states the reason for the branch: \"Naming the offending token alongside line:column makes the location concrete for a schema author scanning their source.\" Two places could have pinned it and neither does:

  invalidFixtures maps syntax_error.gql to nil, which TestInvalid documents as \"any non-nil error from the syntax error listener satisfies it\" -- so the message is not read at all.
  TestPropertyBareDurationRejectedAtParse asserts strings.HasPrefix(err.Error(), \"syntax error at \"), which is the half both branches share.

This is the same class as ErrEndpointNotAlias, a branch that exists purely to sharpen a diagnostic and decides no outcome -- and that one IS pinned (removing it is caught). The inconsistency is the finding: one diagnostic-only branch is evidence, the other is decoration.

FIX: assert on syntax_error.gql that the message names the token, not merely that it starts with \"syntax error at \". A `near %q` substring is the load-bearing half; asserting the exact token keeps it honest about which token ANTLR reports.
close_reason: Closed

title: Token-to-section attribution in obligationSections is unpinned
description:
obligationSections in internal/schema/gql/corpus_carriers_test.go attributes each grammar token to the section of the FIRST rule that references it. That choice is undefended: rewriting it to take the LAST reference instead moves 9 tokens to a different section (TYPE from 12.6 to 18.2, COMMA from 18.9 to 18.5, plus LEFT_BRACE, RIGHT_BRACE, TO, AS, NOT, IMPLIES, PERIOD) and every gate stays green.

Found during gqlc-ii8's mutation sweep: this was mutation C8, the one survivor of ten.

Why it does not bite today: attribution only matters for a token that one corpus area carries and another does not. All 9 movers are reached from both areas, so no area-ownership verdict changes. The rule is a choice no test currently defends, not a live defect.

What to do: either pin the first-reference rule with a test that fails when attribution moves, or establish that attribution is genuinely arbitrary for the property the carriers file measures and say so in the doc comment instead of implying a rule.
close_reason: Landed as PR #488 (squash 2026-07-28). Resolved by removing the choice rather than pinning it: a token is now attributed to every section naming it, and each section's areas are checked separately. Measurement behind it — 12 tokens had a smaller owner set than the grammar warrants, so first-reference was lossy, not merely arbitrary. Both carrier gates now route through unmetGroups. Strengthening is free: 34 parse-side and 30 resolving-side section groups, 0 gaps. Sweep: 10 mutations, 8 caught; the 2 survivors are the same measured fact (the corpus contains no case distinguishing old rule from new), which is why the witnesses are synthetic.

title: schema/gql: ANY VALUE and ANY PROPERTY VALUE need only a decision, not a model change
description:
Split out of `gqlc-h9n.6`. Unlike its sibling `gqlc-h9n.33`, nothing structural
blocks this one, which is the whole reason it is filed separately.

`ANY VALUE` (`openDynamicUnionType`, valueType alt 7) and `ANY? PROPERTY VALUE`
(`dynamicPropertyValueType`, alt 8) are atomic: they take no parameter, so a
single `graph.TypeAny` constant would hold them in the flat enum today. They are
declined with `ErrDynamicUnionType`, which they share with the closed unions —
and that sharing is deliberate (ADR 0019 keeps the sentinel taxonomy ISO's
rather than gqlc's), but it does hide that the two halves need different work.

What is actually missing is a decision about the generated Go, and the ground is
already broken: ADR 0010's mapping table emits `any` for `scalar null` and
`map[string]any` for `scalar map`, so "a generated repository may hand back an
untyped value" is not a new position for gqlc to take.

The open question is narrower than it looks. `ANY VALUE` includes paths and
element references — things `gqlc-h9n.6` decided are not property values at all —
whereas `ANY PROPERTY VALUE` is by construction the union of the storable ones.
Whether both map to `any`, or only the second one is accepted, is the decision.
close_reason: Closed

title: schema/gql: seventeen optionality classes the corpus exercises on one branch only
description:
gqlc-h9n.13 partitioned the grammar's 137 optionality points into 49 classes, keyed by (ISO clause, optional element), and gated on them: every class owes a corpus file taking its branch and one eliding it. 32 classes were already discharged by the corpus. The other 17 are registered in `owedOptionality` in internal/schema/gql/corpus_branch_test.go, each naming the exact spelling no file has ever parsed.

This bead is those 17 files. The register is a pin to repin: `TestOptionalityCoverage` fails once a class the corpus now parses both ways is still listed, so each file lands with its entry deleted, and the list reaching empty is the bead closing.

The spellings, by clause:

- 17.1 `../../gt` — a COPY OF source climbing more than one level
- 17.6 a dotted object path qualifying a COPY OF source name
- 18.2 a node pattern or phrase carrying no filler; a node type filler that is a key label set and nothing else
- 18.3 an edge type phrase that names the type and stops; an edge type filler that is a key label set and nothing else; an endpoint reference spelling `()`
- 18.5 the empty property block `{}`
- 18.6 propertyType's `::`-elided spelling, `{ id INT NOT NULL }`
- 18.8 `TABLE { ... }` without BINDING
- 18.9 a record type with more than one field; the empty `RECORD {}`; the RECORD-elided record type; `GRAPH` without PROPERTY; `ANY` without VALUE; a closed dynamic union with more than one member
- 18.10 fieldType's `::`-elided spelling

Several are in territory the resolver declines with ErrUnsupportedType (18.8, 18.10, and most of the 18.9 rows), so those files record a decline rather than a resolve and need a sentinel plus an Annex D feature classification. The classification is the expensive half and is per-construct research against ISO 39075 — it cannot be inferred from the grammar, and a fabricated Annex D code is rejected by isValidFeature but a real code cited on the wrong construct is not.

Files are split across corpus areas A, B, C, D1 and D2, so this can be taken clause by clause rather than in one PR.
close_reason: Closed

title: schema/gql: declared bit width on PropertyType — an ADR 0002/0017 reversal, blocked on a named consumer
description:
Third sibling to gqlc-5md (magnitude qualifiers) and gqlc-8pe (duration
qualifier). Same reversal shape — ADR 0002 keeps a fixed enum of widths, this
bead argues carrying the declared one — applied to the residue ADR 0017 decided
to accept and lose.

## What is lost

`INT(p)` / `UINT(p)` / `INTEGER(p)` under `binaryExactNumericType` take an
arbitrary bit width. `PropertyType` enumerates eight of them (8, 16, 32, 64,
128, 256 and the two machine words). gqlc-h9n.16 folds the ones with an exact
constant; every other p falls through `normaliseType`'s truncating fallback to
the unqualified type. `INT(7)`, `INT(10)` and bare `INT` are byte-identical in
the model.

ADR 0017 decides that this is accepted rather than rejected, and states the
fidelity limit. This bead is the fidelity limit's fix.

## Why sibling, not part of gqlc-5md

gqlc-8pe's three tests, applied here:

1. **Different missing thing.** gqlc-5md and gqlc-8pe are both "the model has no
   field for this kind of information". Here the model *does* have a width axis
   — it quantises it. The fix is not a new field of a new kind; it is replacing
   an enumerated axis with an integer, or accepting that the axis is enumerated
   and rejecting off-lattice widths. That is a different edit and a different
   argument.

2. **Different consumer trigger.** gqlc-5md unblocks on a length-validating
   setter or a `math/big` DECIMAL carrier; gqlc-8pe on a write-time selector
   over `dbtype.Duration`'s fields. This one unblocks on something that can act
   on a width Go has no type for — a range-checking setter, or a driver that
   round-trips a declared width. Go has `int8`, so `INT(8)` already emits
   something; `INT(7)` has no Go carrier at all, which is why the consumer
   question is sharper here than for either sibling.

3. **Different unify decision.** gqlc-5md warns that a length field makes
   `CHAR(4)` and `CHAR(8)` stop unifying at `unionProperty`
   (internal/resolver/resolve.go:744) and `unify` (:844). The analogous question
   here is not the same question: integer widths are ordered and nested, so
   "unify to the wider" is an available answer that has no counterpart for
   lengths or for disjoint duration fields. Deciding it inside gqlc-5md would
   smuggle a numeric-widening rule in under a string-length one.

## Prerequisite is already satisfied

gqlc-h9n.21 landed (PR #461), so the collision assertions exist. The three
corpus rows below already carry this bead and are asserted by
`TestSemanticCaseCollisions`; when a width field lands they go red, which is the
red-green signal that the blind spot closed.

## What's discarded, per corpus

- `corpus/18.9-value-type/scalar_signed_integer.gql`: `i_prec :: INT(10)` and
  `v_intprec :: INTEGER(10)` — 10 is not on the enum's lattice.
- `corpus/18.9-value-type/scalar_unsigned_integer.gql`: `u_prec :: UINT(10)`.
- `corpus/18.9-value-type/scalar_float.gql`: `f_prec :: FLOAT(10) NOT NULL` and
  `f_prec_scale :: FLOAT(10, 2)` — but see below.

## FLOAT(p) is carried here only provisionally

`FLOAT(p)` is not folded at all (ADR 0002), so its loss is total rather than
jagged. It is listed here because the missing slot looks the same from the
model's side, but which sibling owns it depends on gqlc-h9n.28: if `p` counts
mantissa bits this bead owns it, and if it counts decimal digits gqlc-5md does.
gqlc-h9n.28 is permanently blocked (no ISO arbiter, gqlc-lir), so the row stays
here and this paragraph is why.

## Acceptance criterion

Name the consumer first. Same bar as gqlc-5md and gqlc-8pe: a field nothing
reads is a model change with no observable effect and a live regression risk at
`unionProperty`.

title: schema/gql: duration-qualifier field on PropertyType — an ADR 0002 reversal, blocked on a named consumer
description:
Sibling to gqlc-5md. Same reversal shape (ADR 0002 says qualifiers are dropped; this bead argues preserving them), applied to a different qualifier kind: field-selector rather than magnitude.

gqlc-h9n.4 (PR #439) collapses DURATION(YEAR TO MONTH) and DURATION(DAY TO SECOND) onto a single TypeDuration. The ADR is amended in place to say so, and states the fidelity limit explicitly: after normalisation, the two spellings are indistinguishable at every downstream stage, exactly as CHAR(4) and CHAR(8) are today. The ADR points at gqlc-5md as the model for the fix — "the same way as", not "part of" — hence this sibling bead rather than a widening.

## Why sibling, not part of gqlc-5md

The taxonomic argument (different information, so a different field) is weak on its own: widening gqlc-5md's title from "length/precision/scale" to "length/precision/scale/qualifier" is a two-word edit. The reasons that actually make this a sibling are operational, and each one is a decision that cannot be taken jointly.

1. **Different consumer trigger.** gqlc-5md unblocks on a length-validating setter or a `math/big` DECIMAL carrier. This bead unblocks on a write-time field-selector over `dbtype.Duration.Months` vs `.Days`/`.Seconds`/`.Nanos`. Both are blocked on a named consumer, but not the same one — either can arrive without the other.

2. **Different `unionProperty`/`unify` decision.** gqlc-5md warns that adding a length field silently changes `unionProperty`: `CHAR(4)` and `CHAR(8)` start failing to unify, a large behaviour change that has to be decided explicitly. The analogous question here — should `DURATION(YEAR TO MONTH)` and `DURATION(DAY TO SECOND)` unify? — is a separate answer over two disjoint-field qualifier states with no numeric range. One PR cannot resolve both without smuggling one decision inside the other.

3. **Different collision prereq.** gqlc-5md is blocked by gqlc-h9n.21, which asserts the model collision for the five length/precision spellings against a bare carrier. The DURATION pair cannot be expressed that way — bare `DURATION` is a parser error, pinned by `TestPropertyBareDurationRejectedAtParse` — so it forces the `siblings []string` generalisation of h9n.21's design. That requirement is invisible if buried inside gqlc-5md.

## Prerequisite

Blocked by gqlc-h9n.21. The two DURATION corpus rows are declared as a semantic case there (row 10 of the collision table), and the equality assertion has to exist before this bead can be shown to have closed anything: when the qualifier field lands, the assertion goes red and the semantic case is deleted. Without the prereq there is no red-green signal that the blind spot closed.

## What's discarded, per corpus

- corpus/18.9-value-type/scalar_duration_year_month.gql: DURATION(YEAR TO MONTH) — the qualifier selects Months.
- corpus/18.9-value-type/scalar_duration_day_second.gql: DURATION(DAY TO SECOND) — the qualifier selects Days/Seconds/Nanos.

Both entries carry this bead as their `bead` field, with matching semanticCases rows, so the corpus and the model agree on which spellings are lossy.

## This is a reversal of a recorded decision

docs/adr/0002-bit-width-preserving-value-type-model.md as of PR #439 says: "the two ISO qualifiers correspond to populating disjoint subsets of those fields at write time. There is no distinct YearMonthDuration type to project onto." That is the design justification for the collapse. This bead argues that the write-time constraint (which fields of the carrier a value may populate) is worth preserving on the schema side.

## Blocked on a named consumer

Same discipline as gqlc-5md: implement when a downstream consumer (schema validator, write-time check, driver-level constraint) is named and wants the qualifier. Without one, growing the model to carry it is speculative surface.

title: BLOCKED (no ISO arbiter, gqlc-lir): retire or confirm ErrEndpointFillerHasProperties against ISO 18.3
description:
> **BLOCKED — permanently, as of 2026-07-27. Do not resolve this by inference.**
>
> This question is answerable only from ISO/IEC 39075's General Rules, which are
> in the paid PDF. `gqlc-lir` decided against the CHF 227 purchase, so there is
> no arbiter and there will not be one. The free BNF positively proves the
> ambiguity is not resolvable syntactically.
>
> A web-search paraphrase, a vendor conformance table, or an analogy to SQL is
> **not** a citation. If gqlc must pick a behaviour to ship, record it as a gqlc
> decision under gqlc's own name — never as "ISO says" — and leave this bead
> open, because the standards question stays unanswered either way.

Opened 2026-07-26 alongside PR #422, which introduces
`ErrEndpointFillerHasProperties`. That sentinel is correct today but may be
provisional, and this bead holds the evidence needed to decide.

## What #422 settled and what it did not

Before #422, an inline endpoint filler carrying properties —
`(:Person)-[:AUTHORED]->(:Post { extra :: STRING })` — parsed, resolved with
`err=nil`, and produced a model byte-identical to the label-only spelling. The
property declarations had no consumer and were discarded. That is the epic's
signature defect: accepted input, nil error, wrong model.

#422 rejects the spelling instead. What it did NOT settle is what the spelling
*means*, and the implementer was explicit that the grammar does not adjudicate:

- **Declaration reading.** `propertyType` is `propertyName typed?
  propertyValueType` — that is declaration syntax, not constraint syntax. On
  this reading the filler declares properties on the endpoint node type, and
  supporting it needs merge-and-conflict semantics against the standalone
  declaration of that node type.
- **Reference reading.** Alt 2 of `sourceNodeTypeReference` /
  `destinationNodeTypeReference` (GQL.g4:1620/1625) strips both the
  `nodeSynonym TYPE? nodeTypeName` prefix and the `localNodeTypeAlias?` from
  the full `nodeTypePattern`. CONTEXT.md:50 already codifies the endpoint as
  "resolved to the referenced node type's label set". On this reading the
  properties are a constraint over something declared elsewhere.

The load-bearing observation, and the reason #422 could land without waiting:
**accept-and-discard is not correct under either reading**, so the sentinel is
right now regardless of how this resolves.

## What this bead must produce

The ISO/IEC 39075:2024 subclause 18.3 semantic sentence for alt 2 of
`<source node type reference>` / `<destination node type reference>`. A
citation, not an inference — `gqlc-cfj` is open because this repo has a habit of
asserting what the standard says without sourcing it, and the two readings above
are exactly the kind of gap that gets filled by plausible-sounding reasoning.

Then one of:

1. **Declaration.** Implement merge semantics against the standalone
   declaration, and decide what a *conflicting* redeclaration does (same
   property name, different value type). Lift the sentinel. Note this drags in
   whatever gqlc decides about one-graph-type-per-file scoping.
2. **Constraint.** Implement satisfaction-checking: the referenced node type
   must already declare a compatible property signature, else a *different*
   error — a constraint violation, not an unsupported-construct rejection.

   which is the same shape of question one level up. Sequence after it.
3. **Standard does not specify.** Keep the sentinel permanently, record it in
   the gqlc-0ri deviation register, and rewrite the error's doc comment from
   "not yet supported" to a stated deviation. Silence in the standard is itself
   the finding and must be written down, not left as an open bead forever.

  lifting the sentinel later is not a redesign. If implementing (1) or (2) turns
  out to require restructuring how endpoints resolve, that invalidates a premise
  of #422's review and should come back to team-lead rather than being absorbed
  quietly.
- `(:Post {})` with empty braces is deliberately ACCEPTED and pinned by
  `TestEndpointFillerEmptyBraceAllowed`. Any widening must keep that pin green —
  it exists because an ANTLR accessor is non-nil for the empty-braces form, so a
  nil-check guard would over-reject. Do not regress it into an existence test.
- Symmetry is a stated invariant: source and destination behave identically,
  including under left-pointing-arc canonicalisation. Whatever replaces the
  sentinel keeps that property or explains why not.

comments.text:
2026-07-26, team-lead. Same verdict as gqlc-h9n.28: BLOCKED ON ISO PURCHASE, not on research.

ISO's free normative BNF (https://standards.iso.org/iso-iec/39075/ed-1/en/, verified by fetch) confirms the two-alternative structure this bead is about, verbatim at line 1250:

    <source node type reference> ::=
        <left paren> <source node type alias> <right paren>
      | <left paren> [ <node type filler> ] <right paren>

    <destination node type reference> ::=
        <left paren> <destination node type alias> <right paren>
      | <left paren> [ <node type filler> ] <right paren>

So the second alternative really does admit a full <node type filler> — the bead's premise is sourced, not assumed. But whether that filler DECLARES a node type or REFERENCES one is a semantic question the BNF cannot answer, and both readings stay viable. Subclause 18.3's General Rules are the arbiter and they are in the paid PDF only.

Difference from h9n.28, and why this one is lower stakes: PR #422 already fixed the immediate defect (endpoint fillers carrying properties were being accepted and discarded — accepted input, nil error, wrong model). What remains is only whether ErrEndpointFillerHasProperties should be RETIRED, i.e. whether we are currently rejecting something the standard permits. Rejecting a valid construct is a visible, loud failure that a user can report; it is not the silent-wrong-model class. So this does not on its own justify the CHF 227.

Recommendation: hold at current state. If the standard is purchased for h9n.28, resolve this in the same sitting — the marginal cost is one subclause read.

title: BLOCKED (no ISO arbiter, gqlc-lir): does FLOAT(p) precision count bits or decimal digits
description:
> **BLOCKED — permanently, as of 2026-07-27. Do not resolve this by inference.**
>
> This question is answerable only from ISO/IEC 39075's General Rules, which are
> in the paid PDF. `gqlc-lir` decided against the CHF 227 purchase, so there is
> no arbiter and there will not be one. The free BNF positively proves the
> ambiguity is not resolvable syntactically.
>
> A web-search paraphrase, a vendor conformance table, or an analogy to SQL is
> **not** a citation. If gqlc must pick a behaviour to ship, record it as a gqlc
> decision under gqlc's own name — never as "ISO says" — and leave this bead
> open, because the standards question stays unanswered either way.

Found 2026-07-26 by team-lead while reviewing the uncommitted gqlc-h9n.16 diff,
before it reached adversarial review. The implementer had extended the bit-width
fold from `binaryExactNumericType` to `approximateNumericType`, folding
`FLOAT(16)` -> `TypeFloat16`. That half was rejected; this bead records the
question it exposed.

## The question

Does the `precision` in `FLOAT(p)` count **bits of mantissa** or **decimal
digits**?

The grammar does not say, and its structure points the wrong way for a
bit-width reading:

```
GQL.g4:1801   INT              (LEFT_PAREN precision RIGHT_PAREN)?               precision only
GQL.g4:1814   UINT             (LEFT_PAREN precision RIGHT_PAREN)?               precision only
GQL.g4:1827   INTEGER          (LEFT_PAREN precision RIGHT_PAREN)?               precision only
GQL.g4:1832   DECIMAL | DEC    (LEFT_PAREN precision (COMMA scale)? RIGHT_PAREN notNull?)?
GQL.g4:1849   FLOAT            (LEFT_PAREN precision (COMMA scale)? RIGHT_PAREN)?
```

`FLOAT`'s parenthetical is identical in shape to `DECIMAL`'s — it carries the
optional `scale`. The criterion that justifies the INT fold (a binary type takes
precision alone; a decimal type pairs precision with scale, which is what
separates `binaryExactNumericType` from `decimalExactNumericType`) therefore
sorts `FLOAT(p)` with the decimal types, not the binary ones.

Against that: `FLOAT16|FLOAT32|FLOAT64|FLOAT128|FLOAT256` are siblings of
`FLOAT (...)` under `approximateNumericType` (GQL.g4:1844-1849), the same
sibling relationship that makes the INT reading work. So the grammar supplies
one argument each way and adjudicates neither.

## Why it matters more than INT(7)

`gqlc-h9n.25` asks what to do about widths with no exact model counterpart.
This is worse, because the plausible-looking fix is **strictly narrowing**:

- Today `FLOAT(16)` -> `TypeFloat` (64-bit). Whatever the author meant, the
  resolved type is a safe superset.
- Folded, `FLOAT(16)` -> `TypeFloat16`. Half precision holds ~3.3 decimal
  digits. If `p` is digits, a schema asking for 16 digits silently resolves to a
  type that holds three.

Strictly-widening is the property demanded of any resolution-rule change on this
epic. A digits reading makes the fold violate it, and the failure is silent —
accepted input, nil error, wrong model, which is this epic's signature defect.
We would be introducing one while fixing another.

## What this bead must produce

An **ISO/IEC 39075 citation**, not an inference. `gqlc-cfj` is open precisely
because this repo has a habit of asserting what the standard says without
sourcing it, and SQL tradition (where `FLOAT(p)` is binary mantissa precision
and has no scale) is not evidence about GQL — note that this grammar gives FLOAT
a scale slot, which SQL's does not, so GQL's FLOAT is demonstrably not SQL's.

Deliverable is one of:

1. Citation says bits -> fold `FLOAT(16..256)` the way INT is folded, in a
   follow-up PR, with the same equivalence test shape.
2. Citation says digits -> record in the `gqlc-0ri` deviation register that
   `FLOAT(p)` is lossy-but-safe, and comment the fallback in
   `internal/schema/gql/propertytype.go` naming it.
3. Standard does not specify -> same as (2), plus say so out loud, because
   silence is itself the finding.

Until then the status quo stands and is pinned: `FLOAT(16)` is a row in
`TestPropertyBinaryWidthNonFolds`, so the decision is asserted by a test rather
than implied by absence.

Scope note: `DECIMAL(p,s)` is not in scope (gqlc-5md owns the length/digit
qualifier question). `INT(7)` and friends are gqlc-h9n.25. This bead is only
about what `FLOAT(p)`'s precision denotes.
